Several schools nowpermit the use of mobile phones inside the classroom for instructional purposes. Permitting pupils to bring their own devices may improve the learning experience, since many of them already rely on phones on a daily basis. When students feel more comfortable with the tools they use, they are more likely to engage with class tasks. Moreover, the familiarity with technology can reduce anxiety about new platforms, making the transition to digital activities smoother for both teachers and learners.  

First, having a phone available can give students extra time to complete assignments. Some classes assign substantial homework, and a short break to finish a task on a phone can prevent a backlog. In addition, learners who face personal difficulties—such as stress that hinders concentration—or who work after school and feel exhausted may find it easier to finish their work when they can quickly check information or receive a reminder on their device. For instance, a student who returns home late after a shift can use the phone to look up a formula before starting the problem, which saves valuable time and reduces frustration.  

Second, phones make it possible to verify grades and assignments during class. Pupils who miss a lesson because of absence or a tight schedule often lack the chance to review what was given at home. Forgetting about a task is common; when a teacher allows a brief moment to look at the material, students can note missing work and ask the instructor for clarification, which can raise their overall performance. For example, a learner who returns home after a late shift may realize that a lab report is due the next day, and using the phone to check the teacher’s notes can prevent a rushed submission.  

Critics argue that mobile phones may distract learners, leading to texting or gaming instead of paying attention. While this concern is understandable, it overlooks the fact that teachers can integrate the devices into interactive lessons. For example, a trivia game played on a phone can turn review material into an enjoyable activity, encouraging memorisation and participation. When the technology is used purposefully, it becomes a learning aid rather than a source of diversion. Moreover, studies have shown that short, structured phone‑based activities can increase focus, because students know they have a limited time to interact with the device.  

Finally, the new generation is accustomed to digital tools, and leveraging them can enhance knowledge acquisition. By allowing cellphones in class, schools enable students to finish homework, check results, and study more effectively, which ultimately supports better academic outcomes. In addition, teachers can assign digital quizzes or collaborative projects that use the phone’s capabilities, giving learners immediate feedback and fostering teamwork.  

Teachers also benefit from quicker assessment of student progress, as they can view completed assignments instantly on their own devices, allowing timely interventions and personalized support.  

Overall, integrating mobile phones into classroom activities can modernize teaching practices, cater to varied learning styles, and better prepare students for a world where digital skills are indispensable. Such a shift aligns with the expectations of modern workplaces and can boost confidence in both academic and real‑life contexts.  

As technology continues to evolve, the ability to use mobile phones responsibly in school will become an essential skill, preparing learners for higher education and the workforce where digital fluency is a prerequisite. When schools adopt clear guidelines and supportive policies, students learn to balance device use with academic responsibilities, leading to improved concentration and deeper engagement in lessons.  

Overall, the thoughtful integration of cellphones can transform classroom dynamics, making learning more interactive, accessible, and relevant for today’s students.

Iagree with Ralph Waldo’s view that we can accomplish more than what seems possible and that we ought to follow our own aspirations. He emphasizes personal mastery, persistence, and the importance of choosing our own path. In my opinion, this counsel is valuable because believing in ourselves and resisting the pressure to be guided by others leads to growth and achievement.

First, education provides a solid base for future success. Finishing school, even at a basic level, opens doors to better employment and gives us the credentials many employers seek. When a person masters the fundamentals of schooling, they gain confidence that can motivate further study or entry into a chosen field, thereby creating opportunities for advancement.

Second, pursuing personal dreams is essential. Whether the goal is to become a singer, an athlete, or even a president, the journey starts with a clear vision and a willingness to work toward it. By ignoring the doubts of others and staying focused on what we truly want, we can reach milestones that once seemed unattainable. For instance, a person who keeps training despite criticism may eventually reach a professional level in sport or secure a leadership role in government.

Third, self‑belief and resilience are crucial. Critics may claim we are not capable, but maintaining confidence and refusing to quit can overturn those negative messages. When obstacles appear, remembering why we began and keeping steady effort helps us bounce back. This inner drive also enables us to disregard discouraging opinions and remain committed to our chosen path.

Finally, surrounding ourselves with supportive people enhances the likelihood of success. Family members, mentors, or friends who encourage us can supply resources, advice, and emotional backing that make the pursuit of our goals smoother. Their positive influence can turn challenges into stepping stones, fostering continuous growth.

In summary, I concur with Ralph Waldo that mastering a subject, following personal dreams, believing in ourselves, and avoiding the influence of others’ decisions are vital for a fulfilling life. Education, hard work, self‑confidence, and supportive relationships together create the conditions for achieving meaningful goals and advancing beyond what one might initially imagine.

I believe that achievement is built upon setbacks, though this holds true only for some people. True progress toward a better life inevitably involves obstacles that can feel overwhelming, sometimes prompting one to abandon the very actions needed for success. The crucial role of failure in achieving success lies in its function as a teacher; without encountering a setback, there is no opportunity to learn what went wrong. When we recognize our mistakes, we gain the insight needed to correct them in the future.

Sometimes individuals surrender too quickly to the challenges they face, losing enthusiasm for their goals, while others persist despite difficulty. I agree with this contrast; those who view failure differently can transform it into a stepping‑stone toward achievement. My aunt once told me to trust my capabilities rather than my potential for failure, and she never gave up on her own aspirations.

I come from a small town where my family speaks Spanish at home, and learning English seemed daunting. Yet I convinced myself that anything is possible, that each person is born with a purpose beyond mere parental desire. At one point I struggled with stress, anxiety, and depression, fell behind in school, and felt so discouraged that I considered giving up entirely. Failure followed failure, and I reminded myself that I would be okay, that I could pursue what I love, succeed, and make my parents proud. By adopting a positive mindset and correcting my mistakes, I gradually lifted my depression, though stress and anxiety lingered. Still, those early hardships no longer define me.

Failures can generate feelings of hopelessness, diminish motivation, and cause of​​r them leads to premature quitting, especially for those who lack resilience. Conversely, a strong belief in one’s ability to succeed fuels sustained hope, enthusiasm, and confidence, enabling perseverance despite obstacles. Challenges are inevitable; they act as additional trials that must be climbed to reach the summit, where the view of the ocean awaits. Beyond failures lie larger barriers, and sometimes others deliberately place traps along the path. Some individuals wish to see you fail, while others celebrate your eventual triumph. Many people stumble because they misunderstand the true meaning of failure.

In summary, I support the view that success is the result of moving from one failure to the next, even when hope or enthusiasm wanes. More than half of people, I estimate, devote substantial effort to shaping their future and, when possible, achieve it. Failures are not merely setbacks; they are essential components of the journey toward lasting success.

I agree with thestatement because being true to oneself is difficult in a world where everyone seems eager to judge and dictate how we should live. In my own experience, my family constantly tells me what to do, criticizes my choices, and tries to pick my friends, clothing, and even the shoes I wear. This makes it hard to express who I really am, since they rarely give me the chance to show my true self. A similar situation occurs with people outside my family. If a boy has a tattoo, they label him as bad; a girl who is heavier is called ugly, a thin girl is also judged, and a girl who wears a short skirt is deemed crazy. Such constant criticism leaves us feeling that we can never be accepted as we truly are.

One reason this is so hard is the emotional toll it takes. When we are constantly judged, we may feel sad, embarrassed, or exhausted from pretending to be someone else. We might start to think negatively about ourselves, repeating statements such as “I never do anything good” or “I am not a good person.” These thoughts can lower our confidence and make it harder to pursue our own interests.

Another reason is the lack of support for authentic self‑expression. Society often rewards conformity, encouraging us to follow trends, adopt certain behaviors, and hide parts of our personality that do not fit the norm. Without a safe space to be ourselves, we may avoid taking risks or making decisions that reflect our true wishes. As a result, we may feel trapped in a role that does not match our inner desires.

Despite these obstacles, it is important to develop inner strength and self‑acceptance. Loving ourselves is the foundation for genuine happiness; if we do not value ourselves, it is unlikely that others will value us either. Knowing what decisions we truly want to make, feeling comfortable with those choices, and showing the world who we are can lead to a more satisfying life. When we feel good about ourselves, we are more likely to act positively and radiate confidence.

Ralph Waldo Emerson captured this idea when he said that we should trust our own judgment and live authentically. I relate to his words because I feel proud of my personality, happy with who I am, and indifferent to what others think. My life is my own, and I make the choices that matter to me. Even if I am sometimes seen as overly outspoken or “crazy,” I am comfortable with that label because it reflects my true self.

In the past, I used to obey the expectations of others, but now I focus on being authentic. I have learned to accept myself, to celebrate my uniqueness, and to enjoy a life filled with laughter. This personal growth feels like a great achievement, and I am satisfied with the decisions I have made. I have demonstrated who I am, and I live a happy, vibrant life that is truly my own, and I feel very happy.

It's a good thing that kids should keep track of what they need to do in order to pass the grade and graduate.

Students ought to be given the chance to experience real‑world work because they are eager to acquire knowledge that will shape their future. When they see a profession up close, they can picture themselves in that role, which makes the choice of a career clearer. Schools therefore have a responsibility to provide such opportunities, as they directly influence students’ professional paths. Many young people already have aspirations about what they want to do, and they often ask why a particular activity will lead to a good job or a university degree. The primary benefit of allowing this experience is that it equips children with concrete insight, enabling them to discuss their learning with parents and make informed decisions about their education and future plans.  

For some students, deciding on a life direction is difficult; exposure to actual work environments can reduce uncertainty and help them choose a path that feels meaningful. Moreover, when students engage in jobs or internships, they can earn money, which lessens the financial burden on families and allows them to save for higher education. This practical approach also teaches responsibility and the value of hard work.  

Schools that incorporate real‑world projects, apprenticeships, or part‑time jobs reinforce classroom learning with tangible skills. Students involved in sports, for example, must balance training with homework and assignments, learning time‑management that benefits both their athletic and academic pursuits. By keeping track of their studies and meeting graduation requirements, they develop habits that serve them beyond school.  

In sum, providing students with opportunities to learn from professions supports their career preparation, personal growth, and family finances. It gives them the confidence to pursue their dreams, makes the transition from school to work smoother, and encourages a sense of purpose that lasts a lifetime.

It is a good ideato introduce a homework club at school. Every school ought to run such a club at least three times a week. The club can be scheduled after school or during a free period, making it easy for students to fit it into their timetable. A homework club is a place where teachers assist students with assignments or clarify difficult topics. By attending, pupils can deepen their understanding of the subject, become more active with classmates, and gain confidence in their work. The club is a valuable resource for learners.

There are many activities possible in a homework club. Students may finish a project together, prepare for a test or quiz, or complete homework early. When a pupil has a question about a project, the club provides immediate assistance. The more students who attend, the more they can help each other, creating a supportive community where anyone can ask for help. Working alone on a difficult project is challenging; having a club nearby makes the task easier.

Another advantage is the opportunity to study for exams. Teachers can guide students in making flashcards, reviewing study guides, or playing educational games such as Kahoot, which turns revision into a fun competition. Many learners find it hard to concentrate on studying at home, especially when they are alone. In the club, teachers keep them focused and prevent distractions, ensuring effective preparation. I recommend that every student attend the club at least three times a week to receive help with test preparation or any other academic need. With this support, students are more likely to succeed on their quizzes and exams. Regular attendance also helps students develop better study habits that they can use throughout their academic career.

The club also helps students complete homework ahead of time. Teachers explain assignments in greater detail, offering extra insight beyond regular classroom lessons. This additional explanation means students learn more about the topic. Teachers of mathematics, science, history and English all contribute, providing richer content. By doing homework during club sessions, students avoid the stress of completing it at home and benefit from the teachers’ thorough guidance. When homework is finished early, students have more free time to review notes or pursue extracurricular activities.

Overall, a homework club is highly beneficial. It allows students to learn more about their subjects, boosts their self‑confidence, and encourages collaboration with peers. The club creates a community of motivated students and dedicated teachers who volunteer their time. With the involvement of both students and teachers, the goal of establishing regular homework clubs in schools can be achieved, making learning more effective and enjoyable.

First, failing helps us gain useful experience. If we repeat a task after a mistake, we already know what went wrong and can avoid repeating it. For example, a student who fails a school exam and then retakes it understands the errors and therefore answers more accurately the second time, increasing the chance of success.  

Second, failure discourages giving up. When we encounter an obstacle, we can devise a new plan or approach. A personal illustration is my experience at age thirteen, when I needed to pass a difficult entrance test for the high school I wanted. I initially thought the test was too hard and refused to try again, but my sister urged me not to quit. I attempted the test repeatedly, and eventually passed on the second attempt.  

Third, patience is another benefit of failure. After a setback we often have to wait for the right opportunity to restart, and this waiting period teaches us to manage time and handle problems calmly. Although the process may be slow, persistent effort eventually leads to the desired outcome.  

Overall, failure acts as a key to success. Without experiencing a setback we cannot reach our goals. It is not something to feel ashamed of; rather, it is a gift that supplies experience, perseverance and patience. By staying positive, working hard and waiting for the proper moment, we can achieve our dreams.

To be yourself in a worldthat constantly pushes you to become something else is, in my opinion, the highest achievement one can make. First, being true to yourself creates independence. When you rely on your own abilities, you are able to handle your responsibilities without waiting for someone else to intervene. Since relationships are transient and few people stay with you forever, self‑reliance ensures that you can continue moving forward even when others leave. This autonomy lets you set your own objectives and work toward them without depending on external support, which is far more satisfying than constantly seeking help.

Second, authenticity builds confidence. Repeating affirmations such as “I can do this” strengthens your belief in your own capabilities. That inner conviction motivates you to improve in various areas of life, whether it is academic performance, professional development, or personal challenges. As confidence grows, you are more likely to arrive punctually, achieve good grades, or excel at work, because you trust in your own effort.

Third, the confidence you develop enables you to support others. When a friend is feeling depressed or going through a difficult period, your own experience of overcoming obstacles gives you the empathy and strength to encourage them not to give up. Your encouragement can become a vital source of hope, just as you needed it during your own challenging times.

I have personally endured a prolonged rough patch that lasted several months. During that period I learned that hardship does not have to halt progress; instead, it can forge resilience. As a confident and independent person, I continue to push forward and refuse to allow setbacks to determine my path.

In summary, staying authentic in a world that tries to reshape you leads to independence, self‑belief, and the ability to uplift those around you. Maintaining a positive mindset, even when circumstances are tough, reinforces your determination and helps you stay focused on your goals. When you combine self‑belief with persistent effort, you create a cycle of achievement that benefits both yourself and the community. Confidence and motivation are the essential ingredients for success, and they also empower you to help others succeed.

As Ralph Waldo Emerson famously said, “To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment.” His statement remains valid: embracing who you are, even when society pressures you otherwise, is the key to personal growth and to contributing positively to the lives of others.

Many people believe that teenagers should decide on a career before they start high school, but I disagree. When students begin high school they often take a part‑time job to earn money, yet committing to a single profession at such a young age can interfere with their studies, limit their enjoyment of other activities, and ultimately restrict their future opportunities.

First, devoting time to a specific job creates a distraction from school work. In high school the curriculum becomes increasingly demanding, with more homework, frequent tests, and higher expectations. A student who works after school, for example at a salon, will have less time to review lessons, complete assignments, and prepare for exams. Consequently, grades may decline, confidence can drop, and motivation to continue learning may wane, which can also lead to disciplinary problems.

Second, adolescents are still developing and need a broad education to discover their interests and abilities. High school should be a period for exploring various subjects and gaining knowledge rather than committing to one occupation. Moreover, a solid academic background is essential for admission to a good college, which provides the resources and credibility needed for a desired profession.

Third, engaging in activities that bring joy is important for mental health and overall well‑being. Hobbies such as playing a sport, joining a music group, or participating in clubs give students energy and relief from academic stress. When a part‑time job occupies most of their free time, these enriching pursuits become difficult to maintain, leading to higher stress levels and a sense of emptiness. For instance, a student who loves football may find it hard to balance practice, studies, and work, which can negatively affect both their performance in school and their happiness.

In addition, early work commitments can reduce the time needed for personal development and social interaction, both of which are crucial for building confidence and communication skills. Without sufficient time for these experiences, students may feel isolated and less prepared for the collaborative environment of higher education or the workplace.

In conclusion, students should prioritize their education during high school rather than lock themselves into a specific career too early. Maintaining a strong academic record, participating in enjoyable extracurricular activities, and allowing time for personal growth will better prepare them for university and their future jobs. By focusing on learning and exploration now, they can earn the necessary qualifications, secure a good college placement, and eventually achieve the financial stability and quality of life they desire.

Many argue that a first impression cannot be altered once it is formed. This view holds that the initial picture people form of us is shaped by what we do, say, and how we look, and those cues are difficult to erase. I share this opinion because the first moments we present ourselves heavily influence how others judge us.  

First, the behavior we display when we first meet someone carries great weight. Actions speak louder than words, and they are the most reliable indicator of character. If we act politely and show respect, the person is likely to view us positively. Conversely, being rude or dismissive can create a lasting negative impression, even if we later try to explain ourselves. Therefore, it is essential to conduct ourselves thoughtfully from the very start.  

Second, the way we speak matters just as much. Using harsh or offensive language can lead others to believe we lack manners, while a calm, clear tone demonstrates confidence and respect. Even if we stumble over words or pause frequently, a sincere effort to communicate well helps build trust. Small mistakes are often forgiven, especially when we show a willingness to improve.  

Third, appearance plays a decisive role. The way we dress, groom, and present ourselves forms an immediate visual cue. A neat, appropriate look suggests self‑respect and makes a favorable first impact. On the other hand, a disheveled or inappropriate appearance may cause others to assume we are careless or untrustworthy, which can hinder the development of a relationship.  

Although the initial impression is strong, it is not immutable. People can reassess us if we consistently demonstrate good conduct, speak courteously, and maintain a respectable appearance. A bad day or a momentary lapse does not necessarily seal our fate; others may give us a second chance if they see genuine effort. However, the effort required to change that first picture is significant, because the initial judgment is formed quickly and often remains vivid in memory.  

In summary, while some claim that first impressions are impossible to alter, I believe they are challenging but not impossible. The key factors—our actions, the words we choose, and our outward appearance—determine how others initially perceive us. By being mindful of these elements, we can improve the chances of making a positive impact and, when necessary, earn a fresh start.

Emerson's claimthat each person should stay true to themselves resonates with me. I feel that society often pushes us toward a particular shape, trying to mold our thoughts and actions. Yet, when we accept who we really are, we gain the freedom to pursue any path we wish.

For example, I enjoy wandering through untouched forests, where towering trees and hidden streams reveal the constant change of life. The sight of fresh fruit hanging from branches or clusters of wildflowers adds a simple joy that feels personal. Even a walk among blossoming trees offers a fresh perspective that no routine could provide.

Sometimes I climb a gentle hill rather than a steep mountain. The hill offers a clear, open view of the land without the harsh wind and cold that higher peaks bring. From its summit I can see a wide expanse of grassland dotted with trees, a scene that reminds me of how the world once appeared. This simple landscape shows that being authentic does not require grand gestures; it only needs a space where I can be myself.

These experiences support Emerson's idea that individuality is valuable. The world may try to dictate what we should think or feel, but my own observations in nature confirm that staying true to oneself leads to richer, more meaningful moments. When I reflect on these moments, I realize that the freedom to choose my own path comes from trusting my inner voice rather than obeying external expectations.

This conviction makes everyday decisions feel more authentic and purposeful. By staying true to myself, I can explore new places, meet diverse people, and grow in ways that a uniform life could never allow. It truly enriches my life. It makes every day feel truly meaningful. Therefore, embracing my true self not only brings personal satisfaction but also deepens my connection with the world around me.

Therefore, I stand with Emerson: embracing who we are allows us to live fully and appreciate the world on our own terms.

Attending school inperson rather than studying from home brings clear advantages. While online lessons provide flexibility, they lack many of the benefits that a traditional classroom offers. In a regular school students can interact with peers, join clubs, and receive direct assistance from teachers, all of which contribute to a richer learning experience.  

One of the main strengths of attending classes on campus is the chance to meet new people. A school environment brings together learners from diverse backgrounds, making it easier to form friendships and develop social skills. Those who avoid face‑to‑face contact often feel isolated, as illustrated by the case of a student who chose home schooling; after a short period she realized she had no friends and felt lonely. Speaking with her mother helped her see that staying at home limited her social opportunities.  

Another important benefit is the availability of extracurricular activities. Public schools typically organize clubs ranging from sports teams to artistic groups, allowing students to explore interests such as football, music, or science. Participation in a football team, for example, can lead to scholarships and exposure to future career paths. These activities also teach teamwork, discipline, and time‑management, skills that are valuable beyond the classroom.  

Some critics argue that distance learning saves time by eliminating commuting and allows students to work or care for younger siblings. While these points have merit, they do not outweigh the educational support that teachers provide on site. In a classroom, instructors can answer questions immediately, give personalized feedback on grades, and spend extra time after school helping students who struggle. This direct guidance enhances comprehension and academic progress.  

Finally, being present at school offers a break from the home environment. Lunch periods, after‑school programs, and casual conversations with classmates create a sense of community and keep students engaged. Therefore, despite the conveniences of online education, attending regular classes remains the more advantageous choice for most learners.

Did you realize that an active lifestyle paves the way to reaching our ambitions? When we move regularly, we not only make progress toward our objectives but also improve our physical well‑being. To chase our dreams we must stay determined and think long‑term. The experiences we gather through various activities shape our understanding from childhood onward. In my view, being active enables us to achieve more, to acquire knowledge and experiences, and to develop confidence and self‑esteem.  

First, staying active expands what we can do. For instance, a person who persists is more likely to succeed, whether in sport or in daily tasks. Moreover, an active life lets us explore the world around us, discover new places and engage with our surroundings, which are essential moments of personal growth. Thus, an active way of living prepares us for future challenges.  

Second, regular participation in different activities enriches our mind and skills. Activities stimulate brain growth, enhance abilities, and keep us healthy and stronger. Trying new things cultivates curiosity, turning habits into pathways for maturity and intelligence. When we consistently pursue our goals, they become stronger and our achievements more solid.  

Third, an active routine builds confidence and a positive self‑image. As we take on challenges, our character matures into a stronger, more self‑assured personality. This boost raises our rate of success and keeps us resilient. To keep moving forward we must step out, give our best, and embrace every opportunity.  

In summary, an active life is vital because it enables us to accomplish more, learn continuously, and feel confident. Whether in sports or at work, winning and progress reinforce a positive self‑view, and teamwork with others provides valuable support.

Working together in ateam or tackling a task solo – which approach is more advantageous? In my view, collaborating in a group offers greater benefits for several reasons.  
First, teammates can provide immediate assistance when you encounter difficulties, so you are never forced to solve everything on your own. If a concept is unclear, a fellow member can explain it in a different way, offer examples, or point you toward useful resources. This support reduces frustration and keeps you moving forward. This support also builds confidence, because you see that challenges can be overcome with assistance rather than isolation.  
Second, assigning specific responsibilities to each member speeds up the overall process; no single person has to shoulder the entire workload, which reduces stress and keeps the project moving faster. When tasks are clearly defined, everyone knows what is expected, and the group can coordinate its effort efficiently. For instance, in a recent history project we split the work so that I handled the citation list, a teammate collected all written material, another searched for relevant images, and the last member added short video clips that illustrated our points. Because each person focused on a narrow area, we completed the assignment within the class period and received an A. When each person knows their role, the group can avoid duplicated effort and focus on completing the task efficiently.  
Third, working with others expands your understanding of the subject; peers can share new information, offer fresh perspectives, and help clarify concepts that were previously unclear. When you discuss a topic with classmates, they may bring in examples or data you had not considered, which deepens comprehension and encourages critical thinking. Moreover, the collaborative environment prepares you for future situations where teamwork is essential, such as group presentations or workplace projects. In addition, group discussions often spark curiosity, leading students to explore topics more deeply on their own.  
For example, during a recent math assignment my partner sat with me, walked through the problem step by step, and suggested several alternative methods; without her guidance I would still be confused. In a history class, our group divided the work: I collected citations, another teammate gathered sources, a third located images, and the fourth added video clips that illustrated our points, allowing us to finish the project quickly and earn an A.  
These points show that group work provides help, distributes effort, and enriches learning, making it a more effective way to accomplish tasks than working alone. These abilities are essential in future academic work and in professional environments, where success often depends on the capacity to cooperate effectively. Therefore, group collaboration is the preferred method for most academic tasks. Overall, the advantages of teamwork make it the best choice for learning and completing assignments. Students who work together often achieve higher grades and develop skills that will serve them well beyond school. This makes group work a reliable strategy. It benefits everyone and improves collaboration.

Technology lets us finish many tasks while limiting face‑to‑face interaction, and it often reduces the amount of work and communication required. Even though it can make tasks easier, the absence of direct conversation can make work feel impersonal and may reduce the sense of teamwork that many people value. This raises the question of why anyone should still work when machines can do the job. Employees may become angry because they see their hours shrink and their roles being taken over by computers. Moreover, as automation replaces even low‑skill positions, the labour market suffers from fewer openings for people, which can lead to higher unemployment and greater job insecurity.

First, the reduced contact with colleagues can feel disrespectful to workers. Imagine a coworker who is more skilled than you; you would like to improve, but the competitor is a machine that knows everything about the task. In such a situation many people realize they cannot compete with a computer, which makes the lack of human respect evident and can lower morale.

Second, the decline in personal interaction caused by reliance on technology can harm well‑being. Although digital tools can be useful, people often feel uneasy when their jobs are automated and when they have less chance to talk with others. This isolation can contribute to stress and a feeling of disconnection, which are harmful to mental health and overall life satisfaction. They should value the benefits technology brings, yet many fail to recognize or appreciate this help, which may lead to feelings of isolation and dissatisfaction.

In short, Indeed, I maintain that technology has a harmful influence because it displaces workers, shrinks employment prospects, and erodes social contact. People may deny that technology actually assists them, but it indeed reduces the amount of work they need to do. Consequently, the negative consequences of technology outweigh its advantages, and society must consider how to balance efficiency with human connection. Therefore, while technology offers many benefits, it is important to keep human interaction alive to protect both productivity and well‑being. Balancing technology with human contact is essential for a healthy future. We should strive for that balance.

Businesses and schools ought to adopta four‑day work schedule because it would reduce energy consumption. If the workday were extended to ten hours for four days, the total weekly hours would stay the same. Pupils would then have two additional hours each day to complete assignments and study. Those who struggle academically could receive extra tutoring during this time, while teachers would not need to stay late after classes. With more classroom time, learning could improve. An additional day off would let students rest and spend time with family. Young people who work part‑time could use that day to earn money. Students with heavy homework loads could use the extra day to finish their tasks, and they could also engage in sports or other activities during the free time. This extra day could also give teachers a chance to plan lessons more effectively, reducing stress and improving the quality of instruction. Families might benefit from having a longer weekend together, which can strengthen relationships and support student well‑being. The lower operating costs could be redirected to educational resources or extracurricular programs. Overall, the four‑day model presents a practical way to balance academic needs with energy efficiency. From an environmental viewpoint, fewer operating days mean lower water and electricity use, helping to preserve natural resources. The reduced demand for power would cut utility bills for large school buildings, which is especially important given rising energy costs. Therefore, implementing a four‑day week would save both energy and money, ensuring schools have the resources they need for the future.

Is there a curfew set for your teenager? Should one be imposed? Keeping young people safe, especially after dark, is a pressing concern today. A city council is currently debating whether to introduce a curfew for minors. If such a rule were adopted, would every teen found on the streets after the designated hour be breaking the law? And would the measure actually prevent trouble, or would it unfairly restrict young lives?

The council’s discussion rests on three main points. First, officials want to protect teenagers from physical harm that could occur when they are out late. Second, they hope to shield youths from dangerous situations and criminal activity that may be more common at night. Third, they aim to reduce risky behaviour such as under‑age drinking or other misconduct that is unsuitable for minors.

If the curfew is enacted, does it mean that any adolescent on the street after the cut‑off time is automatically violating a law? Not necessarily. The legality would depend on the reason for being out. A teen who is working, attending an emergency, or accompanied by a responsible adult would not be breaking the rule. Conversely, a young person who is simply hanging out with friends, attending a party, or looking to drink would be in breach of the curfew.

Do curfews keep teenagers out of trouble, or do they unfairly limit their freedom? Many adolescents argue that the restriction curtails their ability to socialise and enjoy nighttime activities, which they view as an essential part of growing up. On the other hand, supporters claim that the law helps keep youths safe, because unforeseen incidents can happen even when one feels secure. Some teens also admit that staying out late without parental knowledge often leads to dangerous choices, and that considering the possible consequences is wise.

In the council’s debate, opinions are split. Some members believe a curfew is a necessary safeguard for young people, while others think it infringes on personal liberty and may not effectively prevent misconduct. Practical enforcement also matters: police resources must be allocated wisely, and the rule should be applied consistently to avoid targeting certain neighbourhoods or groups.

When the purpose is legitimate — such as work, an emergency, or being with a guardian — the curfew may be reasonable. When the intent is recreation or risky behaviour, the curfew could serve as a useful deterrent, but it must be applied fairly to avoid unnecessary interference in the lives of responsible teenagers. Ultimately, a well‑designed curfew can contribute to public safety while respecting the freedoms of law‑abiding youth.

In today's society each personfaces a series of choices that shape his or her future. Some people argue that it is wiser to ask for advice before deciding, but I believe that deciding on one's own is more beneficial because it strengthens self‑confidence and promotes responsibility, which together lead to a more satisfying life.  

First, when a person makes a decision without external help, the result belongs solely to him, and this sense of ownership boosts his belief in his own abilities. For instance, a young adult who chooses to move out of his parents’ home must organize his finances, pay rent and manage daily chores. This independence forces him to rely on his own skills, which raises his confidence and makes him a responsible individual. In addition, a teenager who decides to start a part‑time job while still in school learns to manage time, handle money and meet deadlines, experiences that further develop his self‑esteem. Likewise, university students who select their own courses decide which subjects best match their interests and future plans, thereby gaining confidence that they can succeed in their chosen direction.  

Second, independent choices tend to bring greater happiness. When a student decides not to attend university but to train as a professional soccer player, the effort he puts in feels personally meaningful. If he succeeds, the achievement feels earned and brings lasting joy, whereas following a parental suggestion might lead to dissatisfaction. My own experience of selecting classes that matched my ambitions in the sophomore year showed that the courses I chose helped me prepare for further study and made me proud of my decision.  

Some people claim that guidance prevents mistakes and protects individuals from poor decisions. While advice can be useful, relying on it exclusively may cause resentment or a lack of personal ownership. For example, a child who follows his parents’ wish to become a doctor might later discover that the profession does not match his passions, resulting in a stressful and unfulfilling career. In such cases the decision, though well‑intended, fails to satisfy the individual over the long term.  

Consequently, making one's own decisions offers clear advantages. It cultivates confidence, teaches responsibility, and enhances overall well‑being. By taking charge of choices, people learn to evaluate options, accept consequences, and pursue goals that truly reflect their values. Therefore, individuals should strive to decide for themselves rather than constantly seeking external guidance. Doing so not only builds a stronger sense of self but also paves the way to a happier, more purposeful life.

Avid is a program that manystudents find enjoyable because it blends personal growth, academic support, and a caring community. The first reason it stands out is that it helps participants become more responsible and motivated individuals while also guiding them toward higher education. Weekly binder checks require students to keep their materials organized, which builds discipline, and the program also includes goal‑setting worksheets that encourage students to think about short‑term and long‑term aspirations. These practices prepare them for the demands of college life and teach them how to manage time effectively.

Another key feature is the tutorial system. In these sessions, students present their work to classmates and teachers, explain difficulties, and receive feedback. This not only deepens their understanding of the subject but also sharpens public‑speaking skills and active‑listening abilities. Hearing peers’ explanations often reveals new ways of thinking, and the collaborative atmosphere encourages everyone to improve and feel confident in front of a group. The regular practice of speaking in front of others also builds self‑esteem that benefits students in other areas of their lives.

Field trips are another highlight that most regular schools cannot provide. Avid students travel to colleges, walk through campuses, meet current students, and sometimes visit cultural sites or community events, giving them a realistic view of post‑secondary options and broadening their horizons. These outings are both educational and fun, offering a break from the usual classroom routine and allowing students to experience new environments, which can spark interest in fields they had not considered before.

The sense of belonging that develops in Avid is often described as a second family. Members come from diverse backgrounds, yet they treat each other with respect and encouragement. When a student feels discouraged, peers step in to offer help, reinforcing the group’s motto “dream, believe, achieve.” This mutual support creates a safe space where individuals can be themselves without pretence, and it is especially valuable for those who lack strong encouragement at home. The community atmosphere also teaches empathy and cooperation, skills that are essential in college and beyond.

Responsibility is reinforced through the regular binder checks and through the effort required to prepare for tutorials. Students also keep reflection sheets that record what they have learned and what they still need to work on, helping them set personal goals and track progress. Such habits are valuable for future academic and professional challenges, and they give students a clear sense of achievement as they see their improvement over time.

Motivation also comes from the activities organized within the program. Fundraisers, for example, raise money for trips to places like an amusement park, teaching teamwork, budgeting, and planning. The excitement of earning a reward keeps students engaged and eager to maintain their effort, and the sense of achievement from these events adds to their confidence. In addition, the program often invites guest speakers who share their own success stories, further inspiring students to pursue their own dreams.

For teenagers who may be uncertain about college, Avid provides concrete information and role models. Visiting campuses, talking with representatives, and seeing student life in action make the prospect of higher education feel more attainable. This exposure helps students avoid negative influences from peers who might distract them from their goals and supports them in building a strong college application, including essays and recommendation letters.

Overall, Avid is enjoyable because it blends personal development, academic support, fun experiences, and a caring community. Students meet new friends, discover opportunities they would not otherwise have, and feel proud of their achievements. The program encourages risk‑taking, self‑confidence, and a sense of belonging that can be especially valuable for anyone with a dream.

A positive attitude is helpful, yetit does not by itself secure a successful life. The factor that truly drives achievement is a hard‑working, diligent mindset that compels you to act, persist, and step outside your comfort zone.  

First, a positive mindset alone cannot guarantee that you will meet concrete targets such as finishing high school with an advanced diploma, obtaining a desirable job after university, or even buying a car next year. Optimism may lift your spirits, but without sustained effort you will lack the necessary resources, qualifications, and experience to turn those aspirations into reality.  

Consider the goal of purchasing a vehicle within a year. Even if you feel certain you will have the car, you still need to secure insurance, arrange monthly payments, and possibly save for a down payment. Those financial obligations require regular employment and disciplined budgeting; a hopeful attitude alone will not generate the income or the paperwork needed to make the purchase happen.  

Likewise, graduating from high school demands twelve years of consistent study, attention to coursework, and perseverance through illness or family problems. Simply wishing for a diploma will not replace the daily attendance, assignments, and effort required to meet the academic standards that lead to certification.  

University life presents an even greater test. Students often juggle part‑time jobs, long nights of study, countless essays, and group projects while managing limited finances. Many face the risk of dropping out because they cannot afford tuition or need to work excessive hours, which leaves little time for learning. Overcoming these obstacles requires relentless work ethic rather than mere optimism.  

After completing studies, you must still secure employment and convince recruiters that you are the best candidate among many applicants. This involves polishing your résumé, preparing for interviews, and demonstrating concrete achievements that reflect the effort you have invested throughout your education and training.  

In summary, a positive attitude alone will not carry you to success. Real progress comes from setting clear goals, working hard, and persisting through difficulties such as long study periods, financial strain, and competitive job markets. Those who lack access to schooling or face constant economic pressure must rely on diligent effort to improve their circumstances, proving that optimism without action remains ineffective and often leads to stagnation.  

Many individuals around the world cannot even enroll in high school or university because of poverty, distance, or conflict. For them, success means finding any source of income, learning a trade, or saving enough to support a family. Their advancement depends entirely on persistent effort, practical skill development, and the willingness to seize every opportunity, rather than on a hopeful outlook that does not translate into concrete steps.

Self-esteem comes from achievement. My reason for saying this is because you shouldn't be getting praised for a low assignment that they did; then they are not going to grow. My other reason was that teachers are here to help students improve and if the student know they didn't the best they could've and get praised for it; then they're going to think that they don't have to do that much and will have a low self-esteem.

To elaborate more on my first reason for why I say self-esteem comes from achievement is because if you do excellent on a paper and are positively sure you did amazing then you should be getting praised. That shows how much a student can have a high self-esteem for themselves. Even though, the paper probably wasn't easy that person didn't get lazy. They wanted to do better which means that they want to grow and improve not just stay where they are.

I am going to explain my second reason for why self-esteem comes from achievement. This is all about the students and how they improve. Therefore, if a student knows they could've done better on an assignment and get praised for the lazy work that did then they are going out think that they don't need to do that much work anymore. Although, as the teacher; they shouldn't be praising students on lazy work. They should pull them aside and say " hey this was good but it wasn't you best work; I know you can do better".

My counterclaim is teachers shouldn't let students get away with lazy work. I say this because sometimes some students might think that the teachers don't pay attention to them or they don't care about their work. Even though, if the student approaches the teacher with a problem then the teacher will remember you and know to check up on you when it comes to your work.

In conclusion, true self-esteem does not come from praise on an effortless assignment. If you praise students on a low assignment then that's the level they are going to stay at because they got praised to be lazy. Which means that the teacher leaves the student not wanting to improve and expand on their writing skills.

Sincerely,

Generic_Name

Self‑esteem grows outof real achievement. I argue this because rewarding a student for a minimal effort does not encourage improvement; instead, it leaves the learner feeling satisfied with sub‑par work. Moreover, teachers are meant to guide pupils toward better performance, and praising lazy effort can reinforce a false sense of competence, ultimately lowering self‑esteem.

First, when a student produces work that truly reflects effort and skill, recognition is justified. Knowing that the result matches genuine ability boosts confidence and shows the learner that personal growth is valued. Even if the task was challenging, the student’s determination to improve—not to stay static—creates a solid foundation for high self‑esteem.

Second, self‑esteem is reinforced when students see clear evidence of their progress. If a pupil receives praise for work that falls short of their potential, they may assume that effort alone is enough and lose the drive to strive further. Teachers should therefore avoid celebrating superficial results. Rather than offering empty compliments, they can pull the student aside and say, for example, “Your essay shows good ideas, but it isn’t your best effort; I’m confident you can do even better.” Such feedback acknowledges the work while pointing out the need for deeper effort.

A possible counterargument is that teachers might seem indifferent if they do not immediately praise every piece of work. However, when students raise concerns or ask for help, teachers who respond attentively demonstrate that they do notice and care about each learner’s progress. This engagement counters any perception of neglect.

In summary, authentic self‑esteem does not stem from accolades given for easy or low‑quality assignments. When students are praised for work that truly reflects their effort and ability, they develop confidence that fuels further growth. Conversely, praising inadequate effort keeps learners at a low level, discouraging them from improving their writing and overall skills.

Online learning promises the comfort of studying from home, yet it often falls short of delivering a quality education. Many students are drawn by the promise of flexible schedules and no commute, but the hidden drawbacks quickly become evident. While it appears to save both money and time, the reality is that students frequently lose concentration, miss out on direct communication with instructors, and encounter technical obstacles that hinder effective learning.

One of the biggest drawbacks is the ease with which learners become distracted in their own environment. For instance, I was preparing for a history mid‑term when my friend sent me a text message. I replied, and before I knew it we were chatting until well past midnight. This episode illustrates how quickly a simple notification can pull a student away from their studies, especially when a personal device is always within reach. Many other learners report similar interruptions from social media, video calls, or household chores, which constantly pull their attention away from the lesson. These distractions often cause students to spend extra time reviewing material later, reducing overall efficiency.

Another limitation is the absence of face‑to‑face interaction. In a sophomore economics class, a classmate named Generic_Name fell ill and had to attend lessons online. He was previously an excellent student who always answered questions and asked them himself. After recovering, he told me that the online format made it difficult to get immediate help from the teacher and to discuss topics with peers, because the only communication was through a screen and occasional chat messages. Online chat rooms cannot replace the spontaneous questions that arise during a live classroom discussion. Consequently, his grades slipped from an expected A to a B‑, and he had to finish the course about a month later than his classmates.

Technical problems add further difficulty. Generic_Name frequently experienced laptop failures and unstable internet connections. When his computer stopped working, he had to wait for his father to repair it, causing the lesson to be paused and the class to fall behind schedule. Such interruptions are not uncommon; each month either the device or the network would malfunction, forcing him to catch up on missed material. He also had to deal with frequent software updates and occasional power outages that interrupted his sessions.

In summary, while online education may seem attractive for its convenience and cost savings, the frequent distractions, limited personal contact with teachers, and unreliable technology make it a less effective option. The examples shown demonstrate that these issues can seriously undermine learning outcomes, so the advantages of studying from home are outweighed by the disadvantages. Consequently, students who value consistent interaction and reliable equipment are better served by traditional classroom settings. Therefore, while the flexibility of online learning is appealing, the hidden costs often outweigh the benefits. Students should weigh these hidden costs before deciding to pursue online education, as quality matters more than convenience. In the end, quality matters more than convenience. Overall, the drawbacks of online learning make it a questionable choice for most learners.

Life brings both pleasant moments and challenges, yet when people talk about achieving success they often feel joy even after hardships. First, a positive mindset expands the way we think. It encourages creative problem‑solving and helps us focus on possibilities rather than obstacles. When we approach problems with optimism, we are more likely to generate new ideas and to persist despite setbacks. This mental flexibility enables us to adapt to changing circumstances and to recover more quickly. Consequently, people who maintain a hopeful outlook often find that challenges become stepping stones rather than dead ends. In this sense, enduring tough times is valuable because it teaches us how life really works.  

Secondly, I remember a classmate in seventh grade who was about to sit a crucial exam with thirty‑five questions. He was extremely anxious, worrying that his parents would be furious if he failed and that he would not pass. He confessed that he felt he would certainly lose, saying that he might as well give up. I told him to stay calm, do his best, and keep a positive attitude, reminding him that confidence could change the outcome. After a short break I returned to the classroom and saw him celebrating; he told me he had passed. The success was clearly linked to the confidence that a hopeful attitude gave him, showing how optimism can turn fear into achievement.  

Thirdly, a constructive attitude can transform any environment, whether you are on a plane, traveling abroad, or simply at home. When I tell myself that a good mindset makes the day better, I notice that even in moments of sadness or feeling stuck, positivity helps me stay motivated. By reminding myself that I can succeed, I am less likely to surrender, and this drive pushes me toward achievement. Moreover, a hopeful outlook enables me to view setbacks as temporary and to keep moving forward, which often leads to new opportunities. Thus, cultivating optimism is a powerful tool that works in every situation and supports long‑term success.  

In summary, a positive attitude improves thinking, fuels resilience, and creates the confidence needed for success. It works regardless of the setting and helps people turn obstacles into opportunities. Therefore, cultivating optimism is essential for anyone who wishes to achieve their goals and lead a fulfilling life. By practicing optimism daily, we build the mental strength that guides us toward lasting achievement.

Seeking several opinions canlead to better decisions because it offers diverse viewpoints, more choices, and alternative ways to solve a problem. Relying on just one suggestion may result in poor outcomes.

When people consider several viewpoints, they are less likely to miss important details and can avoid costly errors.

For instance, imagine a girl named Generic_Name went to a shopping centre looking for a specific shop. The first person she asked pointed to the second floor, but the store was not there. She then asked another person, who said it was on the first floor next to the ice‑cream shop. By following that advice she found the shop, bought an ice‑cream and felt relieved. Had she accepted only the first answer, she would have wasted time wandering the upper level and might still be searching, which could have made her late for her next appointment. She later told her friends about the mix‑up, and they laughed about how a simple question saved the day. People often find that hearing different perspectives helps them see angles they had not considered before.

A second illustration involves a new student arriving in New York for her first day of high school. She did not know where the school was and her parents told her to follow other students. She noticed a girl with blue eyes and asked for directions. After entering the building she still felt lost, so she asked many people in the crowded hallway. Everyone pointed to the same destination, which guided her safely to the correct classroom. If she had taken only one piece of advice, she might have entered the wrong room and missed her first class. The hallway was busy with other students, and the girl she first asked happened to be heading to the same class, which made the directions clearer.

A third situation shows how multiple opinions can prevent a disaster. During a sleepover, the girls were cooking when the oven suddenly caught fire and the alarm sounded. One friend urged her to call emergency services, while another suggested pouring water, claiming it would be fine. She chose to call 911, and the fire brigade arrived quickly, extinguishing the flames and protecting the house. The fire alarm’s loud ringing forced everyone to act fast, and the quick call to 911 meant the fire was out before it could damage the kitchen. Accepting the water suggestion could have let the fire spread and caused serious damage. This quick action not only saved the house but also gave the girls confidence that they could handle emergencies together.

In summary, obtaining various opinions helps people make wiser choices, provides more options, and enables effective problem solving. Avoiding a single viewpoint can lead to mistakes or even serious trouble, as shown by the examples.

Overall, listening to many voices creates a safety net that protects against poor decisions and unforeseen problems. It is a simple habit that can make a big difference.

They say the you should never judge a book by its cover and, especially regarding people, its true. In this case, the cover is not necessary meaning the appearance, but the first impression of another person. Like the cover of a book, first impressions are not always as appealing as what is really there. its not until after you start "reading" or get to know someone, when you really find out that what you see is not always what you get. There are several factors that can affect the first impression that one receives from another. Differing personality, situations and representation of a person, make impressions often the worst means of judging people.

A person's personality has a big effect on the first impressions that they emit. Everybody is different but when it comes down to it first impressions are really based off of whether you are shy or not. I met my best friend after moving during my junior year, at my new high school. Before i knew her, she never said a word to me or anyone else in the classes that she was kind of odd, but then realized that I was the same way, i didn't talk to many people either because of my personality. I knew that I was shy person and after I get to know someone, I put down my front and show my true colors. I thought that maybe she would be same way. After starting to talk to her a little more each day, our friendship grew and I learned that she wasn't odd at all, but just like me an outgoing person hidden by their shyness. Some people like me and my friend, are shy and put up a reserved and quiet front when facing new people. Based on my first impressions of my friend, I thought something that was far from the truth. One who has a shy personality might in reality be outgoing, but uncomfortable showing it at first, making the first impression of that person a mistaken one.

Your first impression of someone is not suitable because you do not know the situation they may be in. When seeing or meeting someone new, you have no idea the kind of day,

difficulties or kind of disappointment that person may be experiencing. They may have have recently lost someone, or could be someone new and yet still have to deal with the routines and stresses going through out their day. All of these situations can create a barrier between themselves and others, and setting of a good impression is probably not at the top of their list of important things to do.

On my first day of senior year, I walked hurriedly to my first class, even thought I had plenty of time to get there. When I walked into my class, the only thing on my mind was to find a seat right away, no matter if it was by another person or not. when the time come to eat lunch, I sat by myself and ate it quickly so I could proceed to my next class. I was so worried about being late for a class, finding a seat and just doing things right, that i didn't have time to try to leave any good first impression, on any of my peers. It wasnt even on my mind to do so. My peers received the impression that i was nervous and not a sociable person, when really I was acting the way I was because of the situation that I was in.

Someone;s personality, current situation, or the way they happen to present themselves all influences the way someone thinks about another when seeing or meeting them for the first time. Since what they think is based off of these judgments, their first impressions is usually wrong. If all friendships were based on first impressions, there would be a lot less of them in the world. First impressions are more often worst means of judging a person because its not until you get to really know a person, you are better equipped to understand what kind person they truly are, and really know the individual based on real values, rather than their first impression or "book cover".

Someone;s personality, current situation, or the way they happen to present themselves all influences the way someone thinks about another. when seeing or meeting them for the first time. Since what they think is based off of these judgments, their first impressions is usually wrong. If all friendships were based on first impressions, there would be a lot less of them in the world. First impressions are more often worst means of judging a person because its not until you get to really know a person. you are better equipped to understand what kind person they truly are, and really know the individual based on real values, rather than their first impression or "book cover".

People often say thatyou should not judge a book by its cover, and the same idea applies when we size up other people. The first impression a person gives is based on how they appear at that moment, not on who they truly are. Just as a book’s cover may look simple while the story inside is captivating, a person’s outward look can hide a different character.  

Several factors shape that initial impression. A person’s natural temperament, the situation they are in, and the way they present themselves all influence how others perceive them at first glance. Body language, tone of voice, eye contact, and even the clothes they wear can send signals that are easily misunderstood.  

In my own life, I met my closest friend after we both transferred to a new high school during junior year. At first she hardly spoke to anyone and seemed odd, which led me to think she was unfriendly. Because I was also shy, I kept to myself, and we gradually started talking. Over time I discovered that she was not strange at all; she was simply an outgoing person who kept a low profile until she trusted someone.  

First impressions can be misleading because we do not know what personal challenges someone might be facing. A student who has just experienced a loss, or who is new to a community, may be preoccupied with their own worries and therefore appear distant or uninterested. Other situations, such as fatigue, stress from work or studies, cultural differences, or simply having a bad day, can also create barriers that prevent a positive impression from forming.  

On the first day of my senior year, I hurried to my first class even though I had plenty of time. My only concern was finding a seat quickly, so I sat alone and ate lunch by myself to get to the next lesson. My haste and solitary behavior gave classmates the impression that I was nervous and unsociable, even though I was simply focused on keeping up with the schedule and avoiding being late.  

Consequently, first impressions are usually unreliable. If relationships were built solely on those initial judgments, there would be far fewer friendships. It is only after spending time with someone that we can see their true qualities, values, and character, which are far more accurate guides than a fleeting first impression or a superficial “cover.”  

To avoid being misled by a shallow first impression, it helps to pause before forming a judgment. Taking a moment to observe body language, listening for tone, and considering the context can reveal clues that the initial snapshot missed. Simple gestures such as a friendly greeting or a brief conversation can give a person the chance to relax and show their real self. When we make an effort to learn more about someone, we move beyond the surface and discover the qualities that truly matter, such as kindness, reliability, and shared interests. In this way, the gap between the first impression and the real person narrows, leading to more authentic connections.  

Therefore, taking the time to look beyond the initial picture allows us to form richer, more accurate understandings of the people around us.

Most pupils look forward to a long summer holiday because it gives them a chance to relax without worrying about school. While some learners prefer to shorten summer break and extend periods in winter, spring or autumn, I support keeping a lengthy summer vacation and only brief pauses in the other seasons.

The first reason I find most convincing is that a long summer break allows students to plan extended activities without the pressure of schoolwork. Many young people wish to travel abroad or visit relatives in other countries, and a whole summer provides enough time to organize trips, save money and enjoy experiences without constantly thinking about assignments. If the vacation were only a few weeks, they would have to balance travel with studying, which often leads to stress and a feeling of incompleteness. Moreover, families separated by distance can use the extended period to spend quality time together, something that may be impossible if they must return to school early. Students can also use the extra time to work part‑time jobs, learn new skills, or engage in community service, which enriches their personal development. Since these benefits are clear, I believe a long summer vacation is preferable.

A second, equally important argument concerns the efficiency of learning when school periods are short and followed by a break. Athletes train throughout their season without long interruptions, and musicians practice regularly rather than cramming for a week and then stopping. Likewise, students benefit from a steady rhythm; returning to class after a short break is often difficult, whereas adjusting to school after a longer summer break is smoother because the body has had time to adapt. Therefore, the long summer vacation supports better academic and extracurricular progress.

Some may argue that short, intensive study periods can work for certain students who prefer to review material quickly before a break. It is true that a few learners can achieve good grades by concentrating intensely for a short time. However, this approach carries the risk of rapid forgetting; after the break, the information is often lost because the brain needs time to consolidate what has been learned. When students cram in a short period, they often experience burnout and reduced motivation, further harming long‑term retention. Consequently, the overall effectiveness of a brief vacation is questionable, while a longer summer break offers more opportunities for meaningful activities, personal growth and preparation for the next school year.

In summary, summer break is the most valuable period of the academic year. It enables students to plan long‑term projects, travel, and family reunions, and it allows continuous practice in sports, music or other pursuits. Although a short, focused study interval may benefit a minority of learners, the advantages of an extended summer vacation outweigh the drawbacks. A longer vacation also allows teachers to refresh their methods and prepare new curricula, benefiting the whole class. Therefore, I firmly agree that a long summer holiday with shorter breaks in winter and spring is the better arrangement. Therefore, the evidence clearly supports keeping a long summer break.

For instance, we can decide to be cheerful, energetic, or optimistic, and then act in ways that reinforce those dispositions. When we consciously choose traits such as kindness or patience, we create habits that reinforce positive interactions and improve our overall well‑being. While our traits are influenced by our own choices and behaviors, they also respond to external pressures. In most situations we are capable of regulating our feelings, yet there are moments when emotions become overwhelming and we lose control. Traits such as anger, deep sadness, or depression often arise without our consent and can lead to impulsive or harmful actions if we are not careful. Consequently, character traits can be either beneficial or detrimental, depending on whether we can keep them under control. Some people maintain that we should pick our own traits, arguing that they can sense their emotions and act in the way that best suits them. Others contend that certain traits are beyond our influence and appear automatically, especially when we are confronted with stressful or upsetting situations. In such cases, simple techniques like taking a pause, practicing deep breathing, or reframing the situation can prevent emotions from dominating our behavior. By using these modest practices, individuals can reduce the risk of regret and maintain healthier relationships with those around them. Therefore, being able to manage our own character traits is fundamentally different from having them shaped by forces we cannot control. When we take responsibility for our emotional responses, we gain a sense of personal agency that influences many areas of life. This approach helps us stay balanced and resilient, and fosters lasting personal growth overall.

The debate about whether cell phones shouldbe allowed for learning inside the classroom is still ongoing. While some people claim that phones can be useful tools, I believe that letting students keep their phones during lessons is a poor idea. The devices become a constant source of distraction, they cause pupils to lose focus on the teacher, and they lead to less classwork and homework being completed. Many educators have tried to integrate phones into lessons, but the results are often disappointing because students cannot resist the temptation to check messages anywhere.  

First, when a phone is in hand, students often switch to music, social media platforms such as Snapchat, Instagram or Facebook, or they start texting friends instead of paying attention to the lesson. I remember a group project where one teammate kept his phone on and played audio while the teacher asked the class to present the results. The other members followed the instructions, but the student who was listening to music could not explain the details and ultimately received a failing grade for the assignment. Even a brief glance at the screen can break concentration, and the teacher often has to repeat the same instructions, which wastes valuable class time.  

Second, the mere presence of a phone makes it easy to ignore what the teacher says. I have even found myself watching a TV show instead of listening, and I am certain that, without any pressure from parents, very few pupils would stay attentive. When students do not hear the teacher’s instructions, they are more likely to misunderstand the material and consequently fail the course. Moreover, teachers frequently have to repeat explanations, which disrupts the flow of the lesson and reduces overall learning.  

Third, relying on a phone reduces the amount of work students actually do. If they know they can check their device at any moment, they become lazy and skip homework or class assignments. In a chemistry lab during my junior year, I accidentally dropped a chemical onto my phone, which stopped working. My parents were upset and blamed my careless use of the device for my poor grades in that subject. Furthermore, students may postpone studying because they prefer scrolling through social feeds, which leads to incomplete assignments and lower test scores.  

Consequently, cell phones in the classroom do not help learning; they promote distraction, lower attention, and diminish academic effort. Education depends on concentration and responsibility, qualities that are weakened when phones are allowed. When students focus on the teacher rather than on their screens, they develop the discipline needed for future success, and they are more likely to achieve better grades and retain knowledge.

However, if the student starts to fail classes or most of your grades keep dropping, the student's guidance counselor should talk to the student and see why.
