Lastly, if the child's attendance at meetings is bad and inconsistent, he should not be allowed to participate in extracurricular activities. The child should only miss up to five meetings per month without any consequences. By making the child leave the club and notifying his parents of the reason, the child should be kicked out. Without further reasons, the child could be suspended from attending meetings for a certain amount of time. In conclusion, the school should have very little say in the decision of a student being a part of an extracurricular activity. More or less, the families have the most say in the deciding factor, unless the student's grades are dropping or he starts to fail some of his classes. Their attendance at meetings is bad, or if they simply do not go to any meetings.

Should schoolsdictate how many extracurricular activities a student may join? I believe schools may place reasonable limits, but the ultimate decision should rest with the student’s family. The family’s judgment is paramount, except when academic performance or attendance problems arise, in which case the school should intervene.  

First, there should be a reasonable framework that tells students how many activities they may enroll in, yet the final choice belongs to the student and his or her parents. If the family feels that the child’s workload is too heavy and that homework or preparation for upcoming tests will suffer, they ought to discuss the situation with the youngster, listening to his or her perspective before making a decision.  

When a family decides that a child should step back from an activity, they must inform the student’s guidance counselor and the leader of the program. This communication ensures that everyone is aware of the change and can adjust responsibilities accordingly.  

However, if a student’s grades begin to decline or his overall academic record worsens, the guidance counselor should reach out to the student to discover the underlying cause. If the counselor determines that excessive involvement in extracurriculars is the reason, a conversation should be held to identify which activities can be set aside temporarily until the student’s grades improve. This approach reinforces the idea that participation in activities is contingent on maintaining acceptable academic standards.  

Finally, consistent poor attendance at meetings should also affect a student’s eligibility. A reasonable policy might allow up to five unexcused absences each month without penalty. If the student exceeds this limit or shows a pattern of irregular attendance, the club should be required to remove the student, and the parents should be notified of the decision. In cases of repeated violations, a temporary suspension from meetings could be imposed.  

In summary, schools should retain only a modest role in managing extracurricular participation. The primary decision‑making authority belongs to the family, except when a student’s academic performance drops or attendance becomes erratic. In such instances, the school’s guidance counselor should engage the student, suggest reductions in activity load, and enforce attendance rules, thereby supporting both the student’s education and involvement in extracurriculars.

Year-round schools havemore breaks throughout the year. You may have more breaks during the year, but you will have less vacation time over the summer. This shows that year-round schools have more stress, less vacation time, and less money earned over the summer. The first issue about year-round schools is more stress. The main thing students stress about is what clothes they should wear each day. This makes students buy more clothes even when they already have many, because some want to look better than everyone else by not wearing the same clothes every day. Students are not the only ones who stress; teachers also stress about what lessons to teach and they assign a lot of work to grade. The second issue about year-round schools is less vacation time. Students will have only a 3‑to‑4‑week summer vacation, which is not enough for them to travel abroad for a long time. Parents are also affected, because some responsible parents cannot leave their kids to travel abroad alone. The third issue about year-round schools is less money earned. Students cannot work over the summer because they have little time; one month is not enough to earn as much as they could in three months. Not only do students make less money, but the government also earns less, which affects spending on electricity, water, and other expenses. Some may say you will have more breaks throughout the year. However, you will not have as much vacation time over the summer. Others may argue that short breaks prevent forgetting what you learned, but learning every day without long breaks creates a lot of stress.

Implementinga year‑round calendar means students enjoy several short holidays throughout the year, but the summer break becomes much shorter. Consequently, the overall amount of free time is reduced, and many argue that this schedule creates extra pressure, limits leisure, and reduces earnings.  

One major drawback is the heightened stress it brings. Pupils often worry about what outfit to wear each day, feeling compelled to purchase new clothing even when they already own plenty. This desire to stand out can lead to unnecessary spending. Teachers, too, feel the pressure; they must constantly plan new lessons and assign more work to keep up with the faster pace.  

The second concern is the diminished summer vacation. Instead of a long, uninterrupted break, students receive only a few weeks off. This short span is insufficient for traveling abroad or engaging in extended activities, and parents who wish to accompany their children abroad find it difficult to do so without leaving the children behind.  

A third problem involves finances. Because the summer is brief, students have limited opportunity to work part‑time jobs. While they may earn a small amount during a month, they cannot accumulate the earnings they would have made over a three‑month period. In addition, schools must cover higher utility costs—electricity, water, and other expenses—throughout the year, which further reduces the financial benefit.  

Some supporters claim that frequent short breaks help students retain knowledge better than a long summer hiatus. However, the constant workload and lack of extended rest can increase anxiety rather than improve learning. Moreover, the reduced summer vacation means families lose the chance for a substantial holiday, and the overall financial gains are questionable.  

In summary, while a year‑round school calendar offers more frequent holidays, it also brings greater stress for both students and teachers, cuts down on meaningful vacation time, and limits the ability to earn money during the summer. These drawbacks suggest that the traditional summer break remains valuable.

Ralph Waldo Emerson observed that “To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment.” I agree with this statement because when others attempt to reshape you, staying true to yourself becomes a demanding effort. The constant pressure to conform makes it hard to stay authentic, because society often rewards conformity over individuality. 

In eighth grade a person I considered a friend told me I wasn’t cool enough and urged me to alter my behavior. At first I blamed myself, but I soon realized that genuine friends do not force you to change. Accepting who you are is one of the toughest challenges we face, often due to shyness, low confidence, and fear of judgment. These feelings of inadequacy can linger for years, affecting many aspects of life. 

I have struggled with self‑esteem for a long time; I felt unworthy of love or achievement, so I kept my thoughts hidden. At one point I even contemplated ending my life, but the fear of acting stopped me. I then pretended everything was fine, fooling myself into believing I was happy, though the illusion quickly faded. 

Now, as a junior in high school, I have met a partner who makes me feel genuinely joyful whenever we are together. Her presence reminds me how fortunate I am to have found someone who accepts me as I am. 

Emerson’s words still resonate: in a society where many hope for your failure, choosing to remain authentic is the most significant achievement an individual can claim.

People have the power to shape their own character through the choices they make. Each individual bears the responsibility of deciding whether to act in a positive or negative way. For instance, when someone hears that a friend is struggling and decides to offer help, that decision demonstrates the ability to form a personal character. Critics might argue that a person’s nature is predetermined and cannot be altered, but this view overlooks the fact that we can decide who we want to become by outlining the steps needed to reach that goal. When we understand the path to our objectives, we also know what is best for ourselves and what we ultimately wish to achieve.

Many people look to others for confirmation that their decisions are correct, yet relying on external opinions can erode confidence in one’s own judgment. A student who aims for a bright future, for example, must study diligently and avoid distractions; this self‑directed effort shows that confidence in one’s choices is essential. While seeking advice can be useful, constantly depending on it may cause doubt and hesitation, which is why thoughtful planning followed by decisive action is more reliable.

We possess the freedom to select the kind of person we wish to become and the life that suits us best. Knowing our own interests allows us to choose activities that align with our passions. If we discover a career that excites us, we are naturally motivated to work hard to attain it. Some may claim that others can see flaws in our plans and therefore our choices may not be optimal, but the appropriate response is to reflect carefully before acting.

The ability to decide our future extends to the professions we pursue. A person might aspire to be an artist, actor, singer, or doctor, a dream that often originates in childhood. Realising such ambitions requires focus, perseverance, and consistent effort. Opponents may point out that obstacles—financial hardship, lack of opportunity, or personal setbacks—can make these goals seem unattainable. However, when a desire is genuine, the individual will devote time and energy to overcome those challenges and prove both to themselves and to others that the dream is achievable.

In summary, a person’s character is constructed through the deliberate choices they make, the goals they set, and the steps they take to reach them. By understanding the necessary path, trusting our own judgment, and planning before we act, we can shape a character that feels authentic and satisfying. The freedom to choose our direction, combined with the determination to follow through, confirms that we are indeed capable of creating the person we want to become.

Students would benefit from attending school lessons from home rather than commuting to a classroom. First, they could learn at a speed that suits them, rather than being forced to keep up with a fixed class pace. Second, they would no longer have to rise early and feel exhausted before the day even begins; fatigue often leads to disengagement and incomplete work. Third, studying at home eliminates the need to attend every day, so when a pupil is ill and unable to come for several weeks, they can continue their studies without falling behind. Online lessons also remove the disruption caused by weather conditions such as snow days, which often force schools to close.

Another advantage is that students can finish assignments whenever they wish, without the pressure of a class ending mid‑task. This flexibility means they are less likely to submit incomplete work. Moreover, being at home reduces the amount of physical movement required, which can help students concentrate better because there are fewer distractions and less opportunity to converse with peers.

Students who are frequently absent from school can remain at home while completing coursework, which improves attendance records and academic performance. They are also more likely to achieve higher grades because they can submit work promptly and have ample time to understand material. If a concept is unclear, they can quickly search for explanations online or ask a family member for assistance, rather than waiting for a teacher’s help.

Taking short breaks during study sessions is easier at home, preventing fatigue and maintaining motivation. In addition, regular use of a computer for lessons enhances digital literacy, a skill that will be valuable in the future. Finally, parents can verify that their children have completed assignments, which may reduce the tension that arises when students hide their school work. Overall, online schooling saves time for both learners and teachers, makes education more accessible, and could increase student satisfaction.

Working together in a group tends to be more advantageous for students than tackling tasks alone. Although my friend Generic_Name is highly capable of handling school assignments by himself, he still required assistance to grasp certain concepts. Likewise, I am able to complete a project independently, yet I also benefit from hearing another person’s viewpoint. These experiences show that collaboration brings benefits.

For instance, Generic_Name, who consistently ranked at the top of his class, once attempted a project on his own. He submitted it on the due date, only to receive a failing grade because the teacher discovered he had misinterpreted the question. After a private conversation, she explained the misunderstanding and offered a chance to recover the points. Two weeks later a new assignment was given, and she instructed him to work with a partner. Reluctantly, he teamed up with a classmate. When the project was finally submitted, he was anxious because he rarely collaborated, but the teacher announced a perfect score. She explained that multiple perspectives made the solution clearer and helped him understand the material better.

A similar lesson emerged during my high‑school years when we were given a two‑part assignment. I completed the first part individually, and the teacher later asked us to pair up. I chose Generic_Name. After comparing our separate papers, the teacher noted that they presented very different angles on the same topic. She then asked us to combine our work into a single paper. Once we finished, we rotated the documents so each student read all three versions. The class unanimously selected the paper that had been created together, because it incorporated multiple viewpoints rather than a single‑sided argument. The teacher highlighted that the collaborative paper was the most balanced and logical.

Some may argue that working alone allows for greater independence, but both Generic_Name and I have learned that real‑world problems often require discussion and shared input. When we listen to another person’s perspective, ideas become clearer and decisions become easier to reach. This teamwork skill and the habit of considering others’ opinions have helped us make choices collaboratively rather than in isolation.

Working in a group also teaches students how to listen actively, share responsibilities, and resolve conflicts, skills that are valuable in any career or personal project. When students practice these collaborative habits early, they become more confident and adaptable in later life.

I encourage you to discuss with your teacher the value of more group projects, and to talk with your parents about applying these collaborative skills outside school. By embracing group work, you will notice that decision‑making becomes smoother and your overall experience improves.

Manypeople believe that children ought to study from home, while others argue that attending school in person offers greater advantages. In my view, going to school provides a richer learning experience than learning online. First, a classroom setting ensures that a qualified teacher is present to deliver lessons, explain concepts, and encourage students. Without a teacher’s guidance, learners often become distracted by phones, television, or other devices, and they may neglect their assignments. Moreover, the presence of staff members creates a structured environment where students can receive immediate assistance and feedback. Second, face‑to‑face interaction helps students build personal connections with both teachers and peers, which supports motivation and social development. Online courses lack this direct contact, making it difficult for learners to engage meaningfully. Consequently, the school environment promotes better academic outcomes and prepares students for future professional life. Third, the existence of teachers and support staff at schools safeguards employment within the community. If all education were conducted remotely, many positions related to schooling would disappear, affecting local economies. Additionally, schools expose students to a wide range of subjects that may not be accessible through a single online platform, thereby broadening their knowledge. Some critics claim that remote learning offers flexibility and wider access to education. While flexibility can be advantageous, it cannot replace the benefits of in‑person instruction, such as real‑time clarification, hands‑on activities, and the social atmosphere that schools provide. Therefore, students should attend classes on campus, because this setting ensures quality teaching, supervision, and a comprehensive education that prepares them for both academic and real‑world challenges. Students also benefit from interacting with classmates, which fosters teamwork, diverse perspectives, and a sense of belonging that is hard to replicate online. Remote learning can also widen the digital divide, as not all families have reliable internet or devices, limiting equal participation. Overall, the benefits of attending school in person outweigh the convenience of remote learning.

Technology brings both benefits and drawbacks, and its influence on everyday life is a matter of ongoing debate. While it can simplify tasks and even save lives, the way we depend on devices is increasingly cutting us off from real‑world interaction, which has negative consequences for mental and physical well‑being.  

Reduced face‑to‑face contact often leads to feelings of loneliness and depression. When people spend most of their time online, they miss the emotional support that comes from direct conversation, and this isolation can increase the risk of mental health problems.  

Social media platforms amplify the problem, as many young users experience bullying that can trigger deep emotional distress. At the same time, excessive video‑game playing draws people into a virtual world where they may lose track of time and withdraw from family and friends, further deepening isolation.  

Online content can also manipulate viewers, especially impressionable children who readily accept what they see. Misleading videos may spread false beliefs or even brainwash users, and adults are not immune to similar influence. Conspiracy theories circulate widely, suggesting that powerful groups use technology to control public opinion.  

Technology also harms physical health. Prolonged screen time strains the eyes, and sedentary habits reduce physical activity, leading to fitness problems. Moreover, people sometimes imitate dangerous stunts shown online, resulting in injuries that require medical care.  

On the other hand, technology provides clear advantages. It enables rapid communication in emergencies, supports medical diagnostics, and makes many tasks more efficient, which can improve quality of life. Nevertheless, these positives do not erase the growing problems of isolation, mental strain, and physical decline.  

In conclusion, while technology offers useful tools, its tendency to limit genuine human contact is causing serious mental and physical health issues. Unless we set clear boundaries and use devices responsibly, the negative effects will continue to expand.

Which subject should I choose to teach in an elementary school classroom? Should I focus on mathematics because children enjoy numbers, or should I choose science because they love hands‑on experiments? I would select science, since we rely on scientific ideas every day—turning on a lamp, throwing a ball, watching clouds form, or cooking a meal. In addition, students find science enjoyable because it offers many experiments that make learning lively and interactive.  

First, teaching science is fun. The subject provides a wide range of experiments that let learners see concepts in action. For example, to explore kinetic and potential energy, a teacher can have pupils toss a ball and observe how its speed changes. Other simple activities, such as mixing baking soda with vinegar to watch a fizzing reaction or using magnets to lift paper clips, keep students actively involved. When everyone participates in the same activity, discussion and sharing of observations become natural. An egg‑drop challenge, for instance, lets children test different designs to protect an egg and reflect on what worked or what could be improved. These hands‑on experiences show that science is engaging for both children and adults.  

Second, science is the easiest subject to teach. Unlike mathematics or language arts, it does not require constant memorisation of facts. Students only need to learn the specific terminology, after which they can investigate ideas through direct observation. Experiments are simple; all that is needed is careful watching and recording of results. When a learner pays attention to what happens during an experiment, the underlying principles become clear without endless repetition. Drawing pictures also supports understanding, because visual representation often explains a concept more clearly than words alone. Therefore, teachers can convey ideas with minimal lecture and maximum participation, making science a low‑stress subject for both instructors and pupils.  

Third, science is the most relevant to everyday life. Almost every daily activity connects to scientific principles. Light, for example, involves concepts of radiation and optics, while an air‑conditioner works by moving air through currents. A compass relies on magnetic fields, and understanding how a circuit functions helps people troubleshoot household electronics. Cooking, cleaning, weather forecasts, and even the operation of smartphones all depend on scientific knowledge. When students see how science explains the world around them, they become more confident and curious about the objects they use each day.  

In conclusion, I would design a science lesson for elementary school children because it is enjoyable, simple to deliver, and closely tied to daily experiences. The fun of experiments, the low demand for rote learning, and the clear connection to real‑world phenomena make science the ideal subject to introduce at this level. Therefore, preparing a science lesson for young learners promises a rewarding and stimulating classroom experience.

A common discussion today is whether technology improves or harms people's lives, and I maintain that it does more good than bad. First, the digital availability of books means readers no longer need to travel to a store; they can download titles instantly and read them on any device. Readers can also download books for offline reading, share passages with friends, and adjust font sizes for comfortable viewing. This convenience is especially useful during long journeys, when a smartphone or tablet can provide entertainment without the need for a physical book. The same device can also play games, stream music, or listen to podcasts, keeping travelers entertained in many ways. Parents, who often have limited free time, can read while their children nap in the back seat, taking advantage of the portability of e‑books. While reading, parents can also check messages or plan the day, making the most of limited moments. Digital texts also keep the reader’s place, allow bookmarks, and instantly define unfamiliar words or translate passages, making reading smoother. The built‑in search function lets users locate specific topics quickly, enhancing study and reference. People living far from family or friends find it difficult to stay in touch through letters or phone calls, but a tablet or laptop with a camera enables video calls at any moment, removing long waiting periods. Video calls can connect many people at once and be scheduled from any location, so meetings no longer require physical presence. Although some argue that technology has negative effects, the ability to communicate instantly outweighs the drawbacks of slower traditional methods. The rapid development of technology suggests that future innovations will further replace paper and pencils, offering even greater efficiency. While new gadgets such as tablets, laptops, smartphones, or headphones may be pricey, their advantages in productivity and connectivity make the investment worthwhile. Although devices have an upfront cost, they save money over time by reducing the need for printed materials and travel. Children now use tablets to practice basic literacy and numeracy, and schools frequently provide devices to support learning and give students tasks to complete. Students appreciate the freedom to research information for assignments, watch instructional videos, and receive explanations that clarify complex topics. Communication is no longer limited to spoken words; messaging apps, emails, and video calls enable interaction without saying a single word. Video calls can connect many people at once and be scheduled from any location, so meetings no longer require physical presence. Even though some may miss the feel of paper and pencil, digital solutions offer a safer, more efficient means of communication and information access. These benefits make technology an essential part of modern life.

Human beings are inherently social creatures; we constantly depend on other people for support and companionship. Not everyone arrives in the world fully formed, yet cultivating one's own identity is valuable. At the same time, we are capable of evolving when the circumstances call for it. However, allowing another person to dictate our transformation would be disastrous, because such a person might be misguided or driven by negative emotions. In my view, Emerson's claim that individuality is inherently beneficial is misguided, and I can illustrate why.

First, the presence of caring individuals is essential for a smoother life journey. My mother, father, sister, and several close friends function as an extended family offering encouragement and assistance whenever I need it. Their support makes challenges more manageable and enables me to adapt as I grow. If I were to cut all ties and live in complete isolation, I would likely experience profound loneliness and a lack of motivation. Trust and mutual reliance among people are not trivial; they form the foundation for overcoming obstacles.

I recall a period when I was between twelve and fourteen years old. At the start of each school year I struggled with my grades and felt a persistent unease about attending classes. I barely tried to improve my performance or develop social skills, and after returning home I often felt depressed and worthless. Eventually I realized that I needed help from others. Over time, the encouragement and guidance from my peers and teachers allowed me to change my habits, raise my academic results, and become more confident in social interactions. This transformation happened gradually, without me even noticing the shift at first, which shows that personal growth is frequently sparked by the people around us.

Second, living without companions can be extremely dull and unfulfilling. When we are alone, there is no one to share activities, converse, or provide emotional support. Friendships open doors to enjoyable experiences such as playing games, traveling, and simply spending time together, which enriches life and teaches valuable lessons. Moreover, individuals who consistently adopt a negative outlook may drag others down, eventually ending up isolated because their pessimism alienates those around them. This demonstrates that the quality of the people we associate with matters greatly.

Some may argue that modern society is indifferent and that no one is willing to help. This perception is inaccurate; the impact of others can be both positive and negative, depending on how we engage with them. In other words, the presence of others does not diminish our individuality; rather, it provides a framework within which we can develop while still preserving our core self.

In summary, while being true to oneself is important, complete solitude is detrimental. The people we surround ourselves with enable us to lift each other up, prevent feelings of worthlessness, and make life more enjoyable. Therefore, we should cherish our connections, allow mutual growth, and avoid letting others force us to abandon our authentic identity. We are the main characters of our own stories, and having a supportive cast makes the narrative richer and more rewarding. Such support not only eases daily challenges but also fosters personal confidence, allowing us to pursue our goals with greater assurance. When we feel understood and valued, we are more likely to take risks learn from mistakes and grow in ways that solitary living cannot provide. Thus, building meaningful relationships is essential for a balanced and fulfilling life for all today.

Imagine having the possibility to attend your lessons without leaving the house. While some people argue that learning from a distance does not benefit students, I believe it actually offers real advantages, especially for learners with special needs and for those who feel out of place in a regular classroom setting. Students can arrange their study schedule around family duties, part‑time jobs, or personal health needs, which makes education more adaptable to real‑life circumstances.  

Those who oppose distance learning usually raise two main concerns. First, they worry that students may miss out on face‑to‑face interaction, which could hinder the development of social skills later in life. Second, they fear that learners might become overly dependent on screens and digital tools, losing the ability to engage in traditional classroom activities. Moreover, schools can schedule regular video chats, group assignments, and extracurricular activities online, so the lack of face‑to‑face contact is not an unavoidable drawback.  

To illustrate the benefit for students with disabilities, consider a friend I knew while living in Honduras. She was born with a condition that prevented her from walking, so each morning her mother had to push her wheelchair the thirty‑minute distance to school. The long trek, the effort of getting to the restroom, and the lack of sleep made it very difficult for her to stay focused in class. If she had been able to attend lessons online, she could have saved that travel time, rested better, and concentrated more, which would likely improve her academic performance and reduce the stress she experienced. In addition, online lessons can be equipped with captions, screen readers, and other assistive tools that make learning accessible for a wider range of students, not only those with mobility impairments.  

Another illustration comes from my cousin, who used to dread going to school. At the beginning of the first quarter his grades were low, and he constantly complained about feeling exhausted because he had to wake up early. He believed he was not suited for education. After speaking with his counselor, he tried an online schedule. The flexibility allowed him to study at his own pace, and his marks improved quickly. He also reported sleeping longer hours because he no longer had to rush in the morning, which contributed to his better concentration during class sessions. He told me the experience was rewarding, giving him a fresh perspective on learning and boosting his confidence.  

These examples demonstrate that distance learning can support students with physical challenges and those who feel disconnected from conventional schooling. By providing flexibility and a different learning environment, it helps them overcome obstacles, improve their academic results, and feel valued as learners. Consequently, offering the option to study from home is a meaningful step toward a more inclusive and equitable education system. Policymakers and school administrators should therefore consider making distance learning a permanent option, as it can help level the playing field for all learners, regardless of their circumstances.

Many parents want their children to experience the realities of adult life, such as budgeting, saving, and handling the responsibilities that come with earning money. Humanity has survivedfor millennia because we learned to cooperate and to share responsibilities. The saying “two heads are better than one” captures the idea that a group can achieve more than an individual working alone. Over time we have built complex structures and found ways to cross oceans quickly, feats that would be impossible for a single person. That is why teamwork is essential.

When a person joins a team, it is because they bring a particular skill that adds value. For instance, a web developer with a degree in coding and graphic design might work for a firm that builds sites for government agencies. In that role the individual functions as a single gear in a larger machine, fitting precisely into the system without disrupting its steady rhythm.

In any collaborative setting the workload is divided appropriately. A construction crew, for example, lets the cement worker portion the material so that it is not wasted, and each worker receives a manageable amount to avoid overload. Similarly, in a kitchen one person chops vegetables while another prepares the batter and a third adds the final garnish, ensuring that each task is completed efficiently.

These examples show that teamwork creates clear communication and a shared understanding of each person’s role. Like a well‑oiled machine, a group functions smoothly when everyone knows what they are supposed to do and trusts that the others are doing their part, just as in a kitchen where one peels, another mixes, and the last refines the dish.

Consequently, teamwork offers countless advantages for everyone involved. It enables people to combine their strengths, distribute effort fairly, and achieve goals that would be out of reach alone. The lesson is clear: we can accomplish far more together than we ever could by ourselves.

Self‑reliance is essential for achieving success because it involves taking personal initiative and making independent decisions. I firmly believe that individuals ought to decide for themselves, since this preserves their freedom to choose what they truly desire. When people are free to select their own options, external authorities are less likely to impose choices that do not suit them. For instance, imagine someone wishes to purchase stylish shoes, but officials deem those shoes unsuitable and force a different pair on them. In such a case I would be unhappy if someone else dictated my selection, because they cannot know my preferences. If people allow others to decide for them, they will rarely feel satisfied, as the decisions will reflect the preferences of the authorities rather than their own. Moreover, the capacity for independent thought is crucial. A person who cannot think critically will encounter difficulties when confronted with decisions, because officials may step in and choose for them, resulting in outcomes they dislike. For example, in a cafeteria filled with many food options, a lack of personal freedom might lead staff to select meals for patrons, preventing them from eating what they actually prefer. This illustrates how dependence on others can restrict personal satisfaction. Additionally, the ability to think for oneself helps avoid life‑long problems. When individuals are asked a question and cannot respond thoughtfully, experts may intervene and decide on their behalf, often selecting options that are unappealing. Hence, cultivating independent thinking equips people to navigate situations without unwanted impositions. In summary, the freedom to make one’s own decisions is valuable because everyone prefers to determine their own path rather than be directed by others. By maintaining self‑reliance, individuals can choose what aligns with their wishes, think critically, and avoid the negative consequences of external control. Therefore, preserving personal autonomy is a key factor in leading a fulfilling life.

The statement is "the first impression is almost impossible to change" which is a different feeling for everybody, but for me, I disagree. In fact, the first impression is really important and sometimes true, but I think the first impression does not define a person, an object or a situation. Having a first impression is a human reflex, like having an opinion or a judgment. We are doing it unconsciously.

The first impression is most of the time not real, you need to search deeper to make an opinion and when you really have an opinion, then, the first impression is not important anymore. For example, when you meet someone, your first impression might be that you think she is supercilious and even a little bit mean. Therefore when you really get to know her deeper then you will find that she just had a bad day and that she is nice and sociable. Sometimes it's the contrary, a person seems really nice but in reality she is not, so your first impression was wrong. It is not good to stay on a first impression because most of the time it's wrong.

Moreover, the physic, behaviors or attitude can change an impression. If the person do not smile and seems to be rude but in reality is the nicest person, then it will be awkward for you because you thought she was bad. Sometimes a person can have a bad reputation because of the first impression he shows and it is not his fault, some persons just don't smile every time. Sometimes you can be disappointed because you didn't get to know the person because of your first impression.

The first impressions is not only for people but also for a situation or an object. For example if you are in a library and you want to buy a book, the first thing you are going to do is looking at the cover of the book. If it's pretty you will more easily choose this one instead of a book with a black cover and only the title, because it is your first impression. But your first impression is wrong because you didn't take time to read the resume and you will find soon that the pretty book is actually boring instead of the black book which is really interesting. An object can look nice but have a bad quality. The first impression is the color and the shape of the object, like the physic and the attitude of a person.

In conclusion I would say that the first impression is sometimes right but most of the time it's not. In my opinion, you must not keep in mind your first impression of a person, it's most of the time wrong. You have to get to know the person to build your own opinion. It is normal to have a first impression, like judging, but you must not take the habit to stick with your first impression.

People often say that a first impression never fades, but I think that is not true. While an initial judgment can be strong, it is not a permanent label for a person, thing, or situation. The moment we meet someone or see an object, our brain automatically makes a quick assessment, much like an instinctive opinion. This happens without us even noticing.  

In many cases the first view is misleading. For example, when we first meet a person we might think they are aloof or even rude. After spending time together we discover that they were simply having a bad day and are actually friendly and outgoing. Conversely, someone who appears warm at first glance may turn out to be selfish once we get to know them better. Because these experiences show that initial impressions are frequently wrong, it is unwise to rely on them as the final verdict.  

Physical appearance, behavior, or attitude can also reshape our view. A person who does not smile may seem unfriendly, yet they could be the most helpful individual you meet. Likewise, a reputation that stems from a single awkward encounter can be unfair, especially when the person habitually keeps a neutral expression. In such cases, staying fixed on the opening impression can lead to disappointment and missed opportunities to understand the true nature of the subject.  

The same principle applies to objects or environments. When choosing a book in a library, the cover often dictates our first choice. A colorful cover may attract us, while a plain one might be overlooked. However, the cover does not guarantee the content’s quality; the book with the simple design could be far more engaging, while the attractive one may be dull. Thus, the visual first impression can be deceptive.  

Even in everyday choices, such as selecting a coworker or a vendor, the initial impression can steer our decision, but a brief conversation or additional observation often reveals a more accurate picture. Therefore, giving each encounter a chance to develop is essential.  

In summary, a first impression can sometimes be correct, but most of the time it is not reliable. It is natural to form quick judgments, yet we should avoid letting those initial thoughts dominate our perception. To form a more accurate opinion, we need to gather more information and look beyond the surface. By doing so, we can make better decisions about people, objects, or situations.

Should pupils havefewer summer holidays and more time off in winter? Is there any reason to alter the current schedule? Would learners actually welcome such a shift? And would it improve their academic performance? In my view, most students would oppose this rearrangement. During winter the weather is often freezing, making it difficult for children to spend time outdoors, walk, or play. The cold can lead to illnesses, and a prolonged stay outside might cause a sickness that forces them to miss classes, putting them behind in coursework. Moreover, the summer break provides an opportunity to be outside and explore various places. In winter, staying out for long periods could result in sickness and reduced attendance, which would negatively affect learning. Conversely, some may argue that a longer winter break could be appealing because summer heat can be oppressive; high temperatures may cause dehydration and make outdoor activities uncomfortable. Yet summer offers many pleasant experiences: trips to the beach, visits to amusement parks, camping trips, and travel adventures. Students would appreciate additional vacation days, pleasant weather for outdoor recreation, trips to the pool, exploring nature, and a chance to reduce screen time. Personally, I would not support the proposal, as I enjoy warm weather and outdoor activities, and I would dislike having less summer vacation and more winter time. I also dislike the idea of missing school because of snow days. Currently, the existing schedule works well because everyone can choose the period they prefer most for leisure. I am confident that the majority of learners prefer to keep the present arrangement, as they want more, not fewer, days off. In summary, the vacation schedule should remain unchanged, since students will likely favor the current balance. If anyone wishes to modify it, they should first consult the students to gauge their feelings; if opposition is strong, a different solution should be sought.

Allowing students to bring mobile phones into class for learning purposes may seem convenient, but schools ought to prohibit their use during lessons. The primary reason is that phones become a constant source of distraction. A sudden ringtone or vibration can break the concentration of an entire class, and students often divert their attention to messages, games, or social media instead of the lesson. Moreover, phones create opportunities for cheating. During exams, pupils can snap photos of answers and transmit them to peers, or store information for later reference, which undermines the purpose of assessment. The ease of storing data also discourages genuine study; why invest time in reviewing material when the answers are just a tap away?

Another concern is that mobile devices foster laziness and superficial learning. When learners rely on their phones to look up facts, they may stop thinking critically or engaging deeply with the content. Consequently, they may achieve short‑term success on tests while retaining little knowledge in the long run. This pattern also leads to postpaced, as students postpone in favor of device, in favor scrolling through their devices.

Some argue that phones can be useful after a test, offering a brief respite, or that they provide entertainment that helps relax. While these points have not outweigh risk. In addition, the presence of classroom order. The noise generated by content, and students may be tempted to share content, further the cumulative a decline in reduction quality of education.

Therefore, schools should maintain a ban on cell phones inside classrooms. By doing so, educators can preserve a focused atmosphere, minimize cheating, and encourage students to develop genuine understanding and disciplined study habits.

Do curfewskeep teenagers from getting into trouble? The city council is currently weighing whether to set a curfew of ten o’clock on weekdays or midnight on weekends. Anyone who stays out after the designated time would be violating the law. Even if we do not agree with the rule, we are expected to follow it. I believe the council should adopt a curfew for minors because it safeguards their well‑being.

Young people are still growing, and the world today presents many dangers. Parents naturally worry about what might happen when their children are out without adult supervision. I am not saying that something terrible will inevitably occur, but the fact is that anything can happen, especially when no adult is watching. Numerous reports show that minors become victims of violence, assault, or even fatal incidents for reasons that are often unclear. A curfew can act as a simple preventive measure, limiting the hours they spend in risky environments.

Take the tragic case of Generic_Name from New York. He was an excellent student, well‑behaved at school, and lived with his family. His mother said he rarely went out with friends and was usually at home with his sister. Unfortunately, he was stabbed a few blocks from his house after dark, near a small grocery store. This heartbreaking incident shows how a curfew might have kept him from being out at that hour, potentially preventing the tragedy.

Some people argue that teenagers deserve freedom and that a curfew infringes on their independence. They claim that trusted youths should be allowed to go out whenever they wish, and that parents should rely on their own judgment rather than an imposed rule. However, freedom does not have to mean unrestricted nighttime wandering. Daytime outings are generally safer because more people are around, making it easier to obtain help if needed. At night, the streets are quieter, fewer witnesses are present, and the risk of assault or accident rises sharply.

Teaching teenagers the reasons behind a curfew can also promote responsibility. When young people understand that the restriction is intended to protect them, they are more likely to respect it and make better choices. Even if some adolescents initially resist, the knowledge that their parents care deeply about their safety can encourage compliance. Personal experience shows that when a parent expresses concern, the teenager often realizes the importance of staying safe.

In addition, curfews can ease the burden on law‑enforcement agencies. When police know the expected hours when minors should be home, they can focus their patrols on other areas, which may reduce the number of unnecessary encounters and improve overall community safety. This practical benefit supports the idea that a curfew is a useful tool for keeping teenagers out of trouble.

When families have a clear curfew, parents can feel more at ease, knowing that their children are home during the hours when streets are darkest. This reduces nighttime arguments and gives families more quality time together. Moreover, many neighborhoods that have implemented curfews report a noticeable drop in juvenile-related incidents, showing that the policy works in practice.

In conclusion, the council should consider the real dangers that teenagers face and adopt a curfew as a protective measure. A curfew does not eliminate all freedom; it sets reasonable boundaries that allow teens to enjoy daytime activities while reducing exposure to nighttime risks. By doing so, the community reinforces the priority of minor safety and helps prevent trouble before it occurs.

Everywherewe go, people are thinking about future plans or goals. Some manage to reach them, while others lack the time or motivation. Everyone has a method to succeed in what they enjoy, yet many prefer to remain inactive or avoid taking steps toward their objectives. Others choose to act continuously in order to achieve what they want. Thomas Jefferson once said, “Determine never to be idle… it is wonderful how much may be done if we are always doing.” I fully agree with his view that activity leads to greater accomplishment.  

First, taking action speeds up the attainment of future objectives. When a task is assigned, waiting idly or hoping for a miracle will not finish it. For instance, a student who wishes to graduate with a scholarship must study diligently; likewise, a job seeker needs a strong résumé and hard work to secure a permanent position. Such effort makes each subsequent assignment easier to handle.  

Second, being active keeps one engaged and improves performance. After receiving a poor grade, a student cannot claim indifference; instead, they must study harder and aim for better results on upcoming exams. Personally, when I receive a low mark, I review the material in advance for the next unit rather than avoiding the retake. Preparing notes and planning ahead prevents idle day‑dreaming about the future.  

Planning itself is a powerful tool for achieving goals. By setting clear targets and organizing steps, individuals are more likely to move forward rather than remain stagnant.  

Critics argue that staying idle reduces stress, especially because some high‑school students resort to stimulants to stay awake while cramming for exams. They claim that the pressure to succeed leads to pill use, which can cause health problems. While this concern is understandable, constant activity actually builds responsibility and prepares one for the future job market, where experience and competence are often required.  

In addition, being proactive helps develop skills, broaden knowledge, and increase confidence. It enables a person to discover new interests, improve academic results, and become a more useful employee. Teachers and colleagues tend to admire and respect those who consistently take initiative, sometimes even regarding them as role models. Consequently, a student who plans ahead and works diligently is more likely to gain admission to their desired college and fulfill personal aspirations.  

In short, continual action and forward‑looking planning are essential for reaching future goals. They accelerate progress, foster personal growth, and enhance employability, leading to a successful and respected life.

One time in high school I met a teacher who appeared mean and who rarely interacted with students or explained material again. I asked my counselor if I could change classes, but she said no. After taking the class for a while, I realized the teacher was actually very good and kind, because whenever I asked for help he made every effort to clarify the topic and help me do well on quizzes and tests. First impressions are often said to be hard to change, and some claim you can judge a person's character from that initial impression. However, first impressions can change if the person has had a bad day, and you must understand the character before judging. People everywhere experience good and bad days, which is normal; a bad day can lead to a poor attitude toward others. For example, problems at home, work, or school can affect behavior, making someone seem rude or friendly depending on the situation. Seeing someone who looks like a bad person does not mean they are mean; they may simply be having a bad day or dealing with recent difficulties. To judge someone you need to know their character first. In life you should not judge people merely by their actions or appearance. The saying “Don’t judge a book by its cover” means that looking at a person’s exterior does not reveal their inner nature. Some people appear friendly but may act poorly, while others may look harsh yet be helpful when needed. First impressions can change because a bad day may pass, and after getting to know a person’s true character you may view them differently. It is important to understand a person’s character before judging them, since the individual you dismiss now might be the one you need most later.

Once, during my high‑school years, I encountered a teacher whose demeanor seemed harsh and who rarely took the time to explain concepts again. Feeling frustrated, I asked my counselor whether I could switch to another class, but she replied that it was not possible. After attending his lessons for a while, however, I discovered that he was actually a caring educator who always tried his best to help me understand the material and perform well on quizzes and tests. It is often said that first impressions are difficult to alter. Some people claim that a person’s character can be judged instantly from the very first encounter. I believe that initial judgments can be revised because a bad day or a personal problem may cause someone to act negatively. Everyone experiences ups and downs, and a rough moment does not define a person’s true nature. For instance, a student who appears rude might simply be dealing with difficulties at home, at work, or at school, and this situation can temporarily affect his behavior. When we first meet someone and get the impression that they are unpleasant, that does not automatically mean they are a mean person. They could just be having a bad day or dealing with an unexpected issue. To make a fair assessment we need to know the individual’s character, not rely solely on appearance or a single incident. In everyday life we should avoid walking around with preconceived notions about people based only on what they have done or how they look. The well‑known proverb “Don’t judge a book by its cover” captures this idea. Just as a book’s exterior does not reveal its story, a person’s outward look does not guarantee how they will behave inside. Some individuals who seem friendly may turn out to be unkind, while others who appear aloof may prove to be supportive when we need help. Therefore, first impressions are not permanent; they can shift when we learn more about a person’s true character. It is essential to give ourselves the chance to understand someone before forming a final opinion, because the person we dismiss today might become the one we rely on tomorrow. By taking the time to talk with someone and observe their actions over time, we can form a more accurate picture of who they really are. Even if a person seemed unfriendly at first, a simple conversation can reveal kindness and willingness to help. This approach helps us avoid misunderstandings and builds stronger relationships in life.

Would you liketo add two extra hours to a school day that already lasts ten hours while you work four days a week? In my view, the answer is no. First, many students need to spend time with their families. Some live far away and want to visit relatives before they move away, while others want to be with grandparents who may need assistance. Spending time with cousins or other relatives is also important, especially when visits have been infrequent.  

Second, students often have responsibilities outside school. After classes they may have sports practice, which prevents them from staying longer at school. Others must go home to look after younger siblings because their parents are working, or they have to start a job immediately after school and cannot risk being late. In such cases, extending the school day would make it impossible to complete homework at home or would leave them exhausted after a long shift.  

Third, free time is valuable. Young people want to enjoy leisure activities, meet friends, go shopping, or simply relax before adulthood reduces the amount of spare time they have. If school were prolonged, there would be less opportunity for these experiences, and students might become disengaged from their studies.  

Finally, additional hours could lead to fatigue and a loss of motivation. When I finish school I have to care for my little sister, and after a long day I feel tired and would rather sleep. Staying in school for two more hours would push my return home late, interfere with any work schedule, and likely cause me to fall asleep instead of studying.  

For these reasons, I believe the school timetable should remain as it is; adding two hours would compromise family bonds, practical responsibilities, personal enjoyment, and overall well‑being.

Many claim that remote schooling is auseful option for students. Learners who study from home often show higher attendance, encounter fewer disturbances, and can better manage health or disability‑related challenges. Critics, however, say that without a physical campus pupils become idle and irresponsible. I maintain that distance education brings clear benefits to both learners and schools.  

A key advantage is more consistent attendance. Online lessons let students log in from anywhere, reducing the chance of skipping class. Moreover, the early‑morning routine that forces many pupils to rise before sunrise and sit in a classroom for eight hours can cause fatigue; learning at home removes that demanding schedule.  

Students with chronic illnesses or physical impairments also benefit. Those who cannot travel to school because of health issues can still receive instruction via the internet, guaranteeing their right to education. This flexibility, I believe, is the strongest argument for remote learning.  

Remote study also lessens school‑related problems such as bullying, peer pressure, or disruptive behavior. In a traditional setting, many youngsters face harassment or drama, which distracts them from learning. By studying at home, a child avoids seeing classmates and therefore experiences less conflict, creating a calmer environment and reducing disciplinary issues for schools.  

Some opponents fear that remote learning makes students lazy or irresponsible. While self‑discipline is required, the responsibility rests with the learner, not the format. When students take ownership of their work, remote education can actually promote independence and accountability.  

In summary, distance learning offers clear benefits, including better attendance, support for students with special needs, a safer and quieter study atmosphere, and the development of personal responsibility. These advantages outweigh the concerns about a loss of discipline.

Have you ever visiteda destination you’d never explored before? What did you do to stay busy? If I could choose any spot in the world, I would pick Jamaica. The island offers countless activities, a wide range of cuisine, and many different kinds of wildlife.  

When I arrive, I plan to explore the sights, take a dip in the sea, and hike up a mountain or walk toward a scenic viewpoint. Swimming at a beach lets me feel the cool water, while climbing a hill gives me fresh air and a sense of freedom. From the summit I would love to admire the landscape and perhaps spot marine life while I’m in the water. I also enjoy simply lying on the sand, soaking up the sunshine and relaxing.  

Food is another reason I’m drawn to Jamaica. I can eat at local restaurants, pick fresh fruit from trees, or fish from a creek. Dishes such as rice and beans are common on restaurant menus, while coconut and banana grow on tropical trees. In the water I might catch crayfish or other fish, which I would fry for a tasty meal. With so many culinary options, I could easily change my eating habits while I’m there.  

Finally, the island is rich in animal life. I expect to see chickens and other birds that run or fly, stray dogs that wander the streets, and a variety of fish, including those with claws or fins. Poisonous and non‑poisonous frogs may be found near streams, and goats often graze on vegetation. Snakes, some with fangs and others harmless, also inhabit the area.  

The combination of diverse activities, abundant food, and plentiful wildlife makes Jamaica feel unique and full of natural beauty, which is why I would love to visit it if I could travel anywhere.

Many schools now provide distance‑learning as an alternative that lets pupils join lessons from home using online platforms or video calls. I firmly believe that giving students the chance to attend classes remotely would be advantageous. For instance, I once faced personal difficulties that made attending school impossible, which was a distressing experience. If the situation had been even worse, I might have missed school entirely. Some learners simply do not thrive in a traditional classroom setting and would prefer to study online or via video conferencing. Likewise, students who frequently encounter disciplinary issues may find a home environment more suitable, because they are not forced to interact with peers who cause trouble. At home there is no one to “fit in” with, allowing them to concentrate on their assignments and move forward without constant interruptions. Moreover, remote learning can reduce the time spent commuting, giving students extra moments for rest or extracurricular activities, which may improve their overall wellbeing and health.  

Parents often claim that going to school and the social aspect of schooling are beneficial, but I am not convinced that this is always true. I think students should be free to choose the learning mode that best fits their comfort, and parents ought to support that decision. The amount of work required is essentially the same for both settings; grades depend on the quality of the work, and deadlines must be met in either case. The only real difference is that remote learners do not physically attend a classroom.  

Some may wonder whether students who study from home ever cheat, but we cannot know for certain. I would like a definitive answer, yet I suspect none will ever be provided. There are numerous reasons why remote learning can be valuable, though I can only share the points that come to mind. It can be challenging for children and teenagers to endure the social pressures of a school environment, especially when they have to deal with difficult classmates. Not every peer is problematic, but the overall atmosphere can be stressful. Online instruction itself is not inherently negative; if given the opportunity, I would have embraced it.

Research indicates that studentswho decide on a future profession before entering high school tend to achieve greater success in that field compared with peers who choose later. Yet this early decision often brings considerable stress, because the youngster feels compelled to reach the goal more quickly than others. The mental burden of committing at a tender age is problematic and should be avoided, as it can increase anxiety and distract students from their overall development. My first argument is that early commitment creates unnecessary pressure during high school. While high school may appear to be a stable environment for pursuing a chosen path, it is far from simple. When a student fixes his or her sights on a single career, the expectation to progress rapidly becomes overwhelming. The belief that success will arrive sooner if one follows this plan creates a false sense of urgency, and the fear that failure to do so means the plan will never materialise puts the student in an inescapable trap. Consequently, the learner focuses so intensely on that one objective that other subjects become difficult to engage with or study. Although committing to a goal may seem straightforward, the reality is that high school is a period when education itself transforms the learner. Minds are not fixed; students frequently change their interests as they encounter new subjects and electives. Therefore, it is wiser not to bind oneself to a specific career too early, because the stress it generates can hinder learning and well‑being. Another major concern is the pervasive pressure that accompanies early career fixation. This pressure is not a source of enjoyment but a heavy burden that pushes students to act for the approval of parents, teachers, or school administrators rather than for personal satisfaction. As weeks pass, the intensity of this pressure rises, leading to feelings of depression, sadness, and a loss of self‑identity, since the student is pursuing the path for others instead of for himself or herself. High school itself reshapes attitudes. The transition from middle school to high school is stark: the curriculum becomes more demanding, a wider variety of electives becomes available, and the overall atmosphere shifts from the more homogenous environment of earlier schooling to a more diverse and independent setting. Because of this constant change, it would be unrealistic to expect a teenager to maintain an unaltered career choice made before entering high school. Without exposure to different subjects, a student cannot truly know what he or she enjoys. Thus, allowing flexibility and trying various fields is essential for genuine self‑discovery. In my view, students should avoid locking in a career at a young age. Instead, they ought to enroll in courses that spark interest, continue if the subject resonates, and switch if it does not. The images presented on television do not reflect the realities of most professions, so expectations must be tempered. Every individual is unique, and a career is merely a label. The best approach is to give oneself room to explore, rather than forcing a premature decision that may cause stress and limit personal growth.

They could graduate after one to two years of focused study in their chosen field, since they already have the knowledge from high school courses. Another example is that students can approach their future in a mature and serious way; these courses can motivate them to pursue a better future, helping them shift from not wanting to study for a career and become responsible for their own decisions. It can teach them that a career is an important step toward a successful life. While some people think this is a good idea, others disagree, and some think it is a waste of time. For example, students will have more things to worry about, such as studying more and taking extra classes, which can cause them to become mentally and physically tired, leading them to prefer waiting until college. However, waiting until college can be too late because students may not have enough time to consider a particular career they want. For example, once they enter college they must decide on the career they will study, and if they do not decide they might choose a field they are not passionate about, which can lead to more years in college or even dropping out, resulting in poor job prospects or an uncertain future. In conclusion, committing to a career at a young age is beneficial for students because it helps them prepare for the future, allows them to achieve their goals sooner, and gives them a clearer idea of what to expect in college.

Finding a career path whilestill in high school can give students a head start on their future plans. In some countries, young people are expected to decide what they will do for a living before they even start secondary education. I believe that committing to a profession at an early stage is beneficial. This early awareness can also help them set realistic expectations about education and work. First, early identification allows students to work toward their goals sooner. If a student begins to explore a specific field during high school, they may be able to finish college in less than the usual four years. By already being familiar with the subject through elective courses, they can enter university with some credits or basic knowledge, which can shorten the time needed to obtain a degree. Second, thinking about a future career at a young age encourages a more serious attitude toward studies. When students see that their high‑school classes are linked to a real job, they are often more motivated to work hard and take responsibility for their learning. This sense of purpose can replace a lack of interest in schoolwork. However, some argue that putting too much pressure on teenagers is counterproductive. They say that adding extra courses on top of the regular curriculum can cause stress, fatigue, and lower academic performance. In their view, it is better to wait until university to choose a major, because students then have more freedom to explore different interests. Nevertheless, delaying the decision can also be risky. When students reach college without a clear idea of what they want to study, they may select a program simply because it seems popular or easy, rather than because they are passionate about it. This indecision can lead to longer periods of study, repeated courses, or even dropping out, which ultimately harms their chances of obtaining a good job and building a stable future. In conclusion, committing to a career while still in high school is a positive step. It enables students to achieve their objectives more quickly, develop a mature outlook, and avoid the pitfalls of choosing a field later in life. For these reasons, early career planning should be encouraged.

Education plays a crucialrole in shaping individuals for the modern world. It influences how people behave at work, solve problems, and contribute to society. From basic mathematics to language, the knowledge acquired has helped humanity achieve great milestones such as landing on the Moon and managing global challenges. My position is that the school board should not lengthen the school day. The existing timetable already supplies roughly seven hours of combined physical and mental activity, and adding another one and a half hours would create several difficulties.

First, the present schedule already packs a great deal into a single day. Many students arrive late because the bus is delayed or because they get to school earlier than permitted. Once they are in class, they may be trying to grasp a new concept while also completing a homework assignment. After a lesson, they move to lunch and then deal with locker issues, and at the end of the day they often wonder how to fit a friend’s plans with their own pending projects. In short, a regular school day is already full of obstacles and stress for students.

If the day were extended, these existing difficulties would become more intense. More homework and additional assignments would be expected, and some lessons could become dull after prolonged focus, while others might be shortened to fit the extra time. New problems could also appear, such as teachers struggling to cover the curriculum and students feeling overwhelmed. Moreover, a longer day would clash with the schedules of families, coaches, and teachers. Students involved in extracurricular activities like baseball or swimming would need extra time to practice, and parents might find it harder to balance work commitments with their children’s new routine. Teachers would also have to stay longer to finish grading and prepare materials, which could affect their own well‑being.

There is also evidence that longer school days can reduce learning effectiveness. After several hours of instruction, students tend to experience fatigue, which hampers concentration and retention. Research shows that attention spans decline after about 45‑60 minutes of continuous teaching, so extending the day without adequate breaks would likely lower the quality of instruction rather than improve it. In addition, the extra time may lead to increased fatigue for both pupils and staff, making it harder to maintain motivation and enthusiasm for learning.

There are some potential advantages to a longer school day. More time in class could allow deeper study of subjects and give students a chance to finish homework during school hours. Lunch and physical‑education periods could be extended, providing more social interaction. However, these benefits do not erase the drawbacks. The added workload could increase anxiety for both pupils and staff, and the already packed day might become even more chaotic. In addition, the current schedule already contains many activities that demand attention; simply adding time does not solve the underlying issue of overload.

Parents who work outside the home would also feel the strain. A later dismissal time would require them to arrange extra childcare or adjust their work schedules, which can be costly and may force some to miss work. This added pressure can affect household stability and increase stress for families already juggling multiple responsibilities.

Balancing instructional time with adequate rest and extracurricular opportunities is essential for fostering healthy, motivated learners. A school day that is too long may undermine the very goals of education by causing burnout and reducing the enjoyment of learning.

In conclusion, I am opposed to extending the school day. The present seven‑hour schedule already presents numerous challenges, and lengthening it would likely amplify stress, increase homework demands, create scheduling conflicts for students, families, and teachers, and reduce the overall quality of learning. While there are some positive aspects to a longer day, the negative consequences outweigh them, and the change could have lasting, undesirable effects on the school community.

Therefore, preserving the current schedule supports both academic success and the well‑being of the whole school community. This decision helps ensure that learning remains effective and enjoyable for everyone involved.

Have you ever noticed that eighty percent of pupils who attend the after‑school support sessions achieve better results than those who do not? Such programs are designed to give extra assistance to students who need it most, raise their academic performance, and provide additional time for completing unfinished assignments. When a learner misses a lesson, staying after school lets them meet the teacher, review the missed material, and finish the work they could not do during class. Moreover, students can study together with peers and the instructor, receive targeted help on challenging topics, and thus improve their test scores, which contributes to long‑term success. Another advantage is that teachers can clarify concepts without interrupting the regular lesson, preventing confusion among the rest of the class. For students who find it difficult to finish tests or quizzes within the allotted time, the extra session offers the only realistic chance to complete them and avoid losing marks. Critics sometimes argue that staying after school is a waste of time and yields no benefit, while others show little concern for missed work or classes. However, these views overlook the fact that the additional sessions give teachers dedicated time to re‑explain material, ensure comprehension, and support learners in completing assignments with guidance. These sessions also give teachers insight into each student's difficulties, allowing them to tailor instruction and provide personalized support. This focused attention not only lifts grades but also builds confidence, making failure less likely. In summary, after‑school programs represent a valuable opportunity that many schools provide to help students catch up, improve their performance, and develop better study habits. Because the extra help directly contributes to higher achievement and overall success, encouraging all students to participate is essential. Therefore, schools should promote participation in these programs to ensure every learner has the chance to succeed. Their impact on student outcomes is clearly measurable.
