Allowing students to bring andoperate cellphones inside the classroom creates several problems that hinder learning. First, the devices pull students’ focus away from the lesson. When a pupil is busy checking messages or scrolling, they miss the teacher’s explanations and therefore do not absorb the material. The constant vibration and notifications make it hard to stay concentrated, and the temptation to look at the screen often leads to off‑task behaviour, which reduces comprehension and academic progress. Even when the device is silent, its mere presence can make students think about what they might be missing online, shrinking the mental bandwidth available for the lesson.

Second, cellphones are frequently used for non‑educational activities, which does not support learning. Instead of researching or completing assignments, students may play games, browse social media, or chat with friends. This misuse means they miss out on essential knowledge and can even face disciplinary issues for violating classroom rules. Moreover, the habit of constantly checking the phone can develop a short‑term attention span, making it harder for students to engage with longer texts or complex problems. Teachers should only permit phone use when it directly serves a class task, otherwise the device becomes a distraction rather than a tool.

Third, the presence of phones disturbs other learners. Ringing tones, vibrations, or the sight of a classmate looking at a screen interrupt the flow of instruction and force the teacher and peers to pause. When a phone rings, the whole class may stop working, and the teacher must spend time dealing with the disturbance instead of delivering content. Such interruptions make it difficult for everyone to follow the lesson and can lower the overall atmosphere of the class. When students are distracted by a ringing phone, they lose the chance to practice the skills they need for future success.

In summary, cellphones in the classroom mainly hinder learning by pulling attention away from the teacher, being employed for unrelated purposes, and breaking the concentration of classmates. For these reasons, schools should restrict phone use during lessons and allow it only when it directly supports educational objectives.

True self‑esteem doesnot come from constant praise alone, but from the encouragement that pushes a person forward and helps them follow their dreams. A friend once said, “Never let anyone put you down; always get back up.” This captures the idea that believing in yourself, rather than being swayed by others’ criticism, is essential. To feel good about yourself you need a thick skin that blocks negative voices, and courage, confidence, and trust act as the foundation of self‑esteem.  

First, confidence is the starting point for achieving any goal. I remember feeling uncertain about passing the state exam (SOL). My teacher encouraged me to stay positive and avoid over‑thinking. After I finished the test, she told me I had passed and reminded me to trust my abilities. This experience shows that when someone offers praise, it strengthens a person’s belief in themselves.  

Second, courage helps us overcome fears that can hold us back. Imagine a relay race where you fall behind early. It is easy to think, “I’m last, there’s no chance to catch up,” and give up. A teammate’s encouragement can lift your spirit, urging you not to quit and to keep running until the finish line. The support that comes from being praised gives the resolve to persist despite setbacks.  

Third, young people should listen to the advice of adults. Some argue that teenagers can do whatever they want, but that view ignores the need for guidance. When I was younger, I shoplifted with friends. My mother warned me not to associate with trouble‑making peers, but I ignored her. We were caught, the store demanded payment, and my parents had to intervene. This incident illustrates that adult guidance, when respected, can steer youths toward better decisions.  

In conclusion, encouragement, confidence, courage, and trust are key elements that boost self‑esteem. Whether taking a test, competing in a sport, or making everyday choices, positive support helps people feel capable, stay motivated, and make responsible decisions. Such encouragement not only lifts mood but also builds lasting confidence that carries into future challenges.

Is Emerson correct when he says that without attempting something beyond what we already master, we will never develop? I agree with this view, because it shows that anyone can strive for a higher level of achievement in his or her own life. Moreover, the quotation encourages readers to reflect on their own aspirations and consider whether they are willing to push past current limits.

First, a powerful statement such as Emerson’s can spark motivation in many people. When they hear it, they often feel a renewed confidence that they are capable of reaching farther goals. This newfound belief can inspire them to set more ambitious targets and to take actions they previously thought impossible. Consequently, individuals begin to trust their own abilities and to imagine themselves succeeding beyond what they once considered.

Second, stepping outside one’s comfort zone tends to produce tangible results. People who dare to go beyond their self‑imposed boundaries discover new skills and strengths. They learn what they are truly capable of handling, which makes them feel confident that they can accomplish any task that comes their way. This sense of competence often feels like a “weight‑lifting” rush, a clear sign that they have uncovered hidden potential. As a result, they become more willing to tackle fresh challenges, accumulate richer experience, and build a more resilient mindset.

Third, the experience gained from such attempts translates into practical advantages. Those who have repeatedly pushed past their limits tend to perform better at work and in other areas of life. Their accumulated know‑how allows them to handle new responsibilities quickly and with less hesitation. In contrast, people who avoid taking risks may remain stuck, uncertain about their capabilities and reluctant to pursue higher expectations.

In summary, Emerson’s assertion highlights an essential component of personal growth. By urging us to try what lies beyond our current mastery, it motivates us to develop confidence, acquire valuable experience, and become more capable of meeting future demands. The quote therefore stands as one of the most inspiring sayings, reminding us that true progress begins when we dare to go beyond what we already know.

People who prize independence oughtto seek the counsel of knowledgeable authorities when confronting crucial life choices. An expert can be thought of as a teacher who has mastered a particular field; just as a student relies on a teacher’s expertise in science, a person should rely on specialists for matters that demand deeper insight.

First, self‑reliance is a valuable trait, yet every individual is fallible. Adolescents, in particular, are vulnerable to strong external influences, and they benefit greatly from the guidance of parents or other qualified mentors. These figures have spent years studying their areas of competence and can show young people what truly matters, helping them develop sound judgment and grow into responsible adults. While some parents may be indifferent, many provide the support that enables their children to make wiser decisions.

Second, reckless choices can bring serious personal harm. Consider a person who wishes to open a restaurant using all of his savings. At first the idea seems promising, but without professional advice he may overlook essential costs, underestimate market demand, and jeopardize his finances. If the venture fails, the resulting debt can lead to depression or even despair. In such situations, consulting experts—who understand business planning, finance, and market dynamics—offers a safer route and protects the individual from avoidable mistakes.

Critics sometimes argue that making decisions alone fosters personal responsibility and prevents blame‑shifting. While learning from one’s own experiences is important, it is wiser to avoid costly errors by drawing on the knowledge of those who have already navigated similar challenges. Two heads are indeed better than one; expert input can streamline the decision‑making process and enhance the quality of the outcome.

In summary, although independence is commendable, the most effective way to handle significant decisions is to seek guidance from experts and trusted authorities. Their experience can prevent harmful mistakes, promote better choices, and ultimately contribute to personal growth. We should remain open to acting independently when appropriate, but we must also recognize the value of external advice in achieving a more successful and fulfilling life.

Do you think students should study online from home? In my view, they should not. Pupils who have jobs or other responsibilities often find it hard to attend virtual lessons because they are occupied. Moreover, many learners prefer to spend their leisure time doing activities they enjoy rather than sitting in front of a screen. School is meant for learning, while home is a place for relaxation and personal interests. Consequently, online classes can cut into the free time that students need to unwind and pursue hobbies. I personally would not choose online learning because I work during the evening and have little spare time. A friend of mine tried attending classes at home, but the sessions ate up a large part of his free hours. Some argue that online lessons help students concentrate better and prepare them for planning their future careers. This view is mistaken; life is not solely about focusing on future goals. It is also about enjoying the present and doing what one likes. While it is true that preparation for work is important, it should not come at the expense of a balanced, happy life. In the future, some students may combine classroom attendance with occasional online study during free periods, but the majority will still prefer traditional schooling because they value a fulfilling life over a strictly career‑oriented schedule. Therefore, online classes at home are unnecessary and can interfere with students’ well‑being and enjoyment of life. Students who lack free time often feel stressed, which can hurt their academic performance and personal happiness.

Technology has always acted as a compelling and mysterious field for me. Even as a child, I spent countless hours not playing my video-game consoles as intended, but rather meticulously studying every component of the device in an attempt to crack the mystery on how it operated. Despite the fact that I've grown older and many aspects of my life have changed, my passion for technology has not only remained, but undoubtedly grown stronger as well. Therefore, an internship in this field seems vital in feeding and nurturing this passion. Although I have not had previous experience in shadowing, an opportunity to shadow would be fitting due to my previous experience and ever-growing passion in this field.

My experience in the technological field proves fitting for this opportunity to shadow. In school, I am enrolled in the Center for Information Technology at Generic_School. This specialty center provides me with crucial access to exclusive technology-based courses and teachers that help me broaden my vision in the technology field. Classes such as IT Project Management, Programming, and AP Computer Science Principles are all courses that I have been graciously provided with through the center and received exceptional results in. This daily involvement in technology not only increased my knowledge in this field, but also my curiosity on the subject. Outside of school, I am a member of the Technology Student Association, a club dedicated to assisting students nurture their interests through rigorous competitions. Through this club I have been able to surround myself with peers with similar interests and aspirations. This club has also provided me with opportunities to exhibit my knowledge in the technological field through competitions, receiving first place in States in Mass Production, Junior Solar Sprint, and Biotechnology. My involvement and superior results in these events prove to show not only my interest in this field, but my capabilities as well. These experiences transfer directly over to the internship, allowing for a smooth transition without much confusion.

The passion I have for technology undeniably proves me to be fitting for this internship opportunity. A crucial action that proves my strong interest in technology occurred when high school specialty center results were published. I was accepted into the medical, IB, and the information technology centers. Despite the fact that the majority of my close friends chose to enroll into the medical center, I stuck with my passion and enrolled into the Information Technology center. The action of choosing my interest over my close friends of many years displays how much I value technology and wish to pursue it in the future. In addition, my strong passion for technology can be displayed through the utilization of my free time. While other kids may choose to spend this time by indulging themselves into video games, much of my time is spent educating myself on technology. Many enjoyable hours of activities such as reading on the history of computers or watching videos on the future of technology were spent during this time. This use of my limited free time shows that technology, in my mind, is not a merely a class in school, but rather a hobby or an enjoyable subject. This attitude would no doubt have a beneficial effect for the internship.

In conclusion, the heavy interest and years of experience I have in technology proves me to be exceptional candidate for this shadowing opportunity. Although my work experience is limited, my passion and expierence in technology may help me ease into the internship without trouble. The talent I have in technology mixed with the catalyst that is my preexisting passion for this field helps me understand the importance of this internship. Not only will this internship assist in broadening my horizons on technology, but it will also help nurture and grow this passion into something meaningful and of use to the real world. Therefore, I believe this internship is perfect for me.

Working byyourself tends to be more advantageous than collaborating in a team. When you work alone you can maintain a steady pace without interruptions, and you never have to wait for someone else’s opinion before proceeding. Moreover, many people feel uncomfortable being surrounded by others, so solitude removes that pressure.  

On the other hand, group work does have its merits, such as the exchange of ideas and the possibility of generating fresh perspectives. Nevertheless, the drawbacks often outweigh these benefits. The presence of multiple voices can increase stress, making it harder to concentrate and to develop original thoughts. In a noisy environment a stressed individual may find it difficult to think clearly, and the anxiety may persist even after leaving the workplace. Being alone allows a person to relax fully, and once relaxation sets in, ideas tend to flow more freely. A sudden insight can arise while you are focused on a task, and you can act on it immediately without needing to consult anyone. In a group setting, a proposal must be discussed, evaluated, and approved by everyone, which consumes time and may lead to disagreement. Consequently, solitary work saves time because you are not occupied with lengthy negotiations or waiting for consensus. Additionally, working in isolation reduces the chance of conflict and confusion that arise when several people speak at once. Disagreements can cause misunderstandings and waste valuable minutes. When each person handles their own responsibilities, the overall workflow becomes smoother and more efficient.  

Shy individuals especially benefit from working alone. They may find it difficult to speak up, share their thoughts, or feel judged by colleagues. In a group, the need to present ideas can become a source of anxiety, leading them to hide their contributions or simply agree with others. This not only hampers personal development but also results in lower‑quality output.  

Some argue that collaboration opens doors to new opportunities and diverse viewpoints. While sharing ideas can be valuable, the potential for stress, time loss, and interpersonal tension makes solitary work a more reliable path to productive and pleasant performance. A quiet, personal space lets you think deeply about every aspect of a task, analyze details without distraction, and enjoy a calm environment free from shyness or pressure.  

In conclusion, although group work offers the advantage of idea exchange, the overall benefits of working alone—greater relaxation, reduced stress, faster decision‑making, and suitability for introverted personalities—make it the preferable choice for most people. Therefore, for anyone seeking a calmer, more efficient work experience, working alone is the better option.

Setting an example through your ownactions can be a powerful way to influence others, but it isn’t always the most reliable method. People’s behavior can be inconsistent – some act responsibly while others act recklessly or engage in harmful habits. When the role model you follow makes poor choices, the impact can be negative rather than inspirational.  

I grew up in a city where drug use, gang activity and violence were visible, and the attitudes of many young people reflected those negative patterns. At the same time, I have also seen individuals who volunteer, help their neighbours and act with kindness, showing that positive influence is possible.  

A personal example that stays with me is a friend whose father took his own life after making a bad decision. That tragedy made the friend rethink his own path and motivated him to change. In high school I observed several students who put the needs of others before themselves, organizing volunteer work and community events, which encouraged their peers to follow suit. I even helped organize a Halloween party for children at a local church, an experience that brought joy and demonstrated how small acts can inspire others.  

I do not consider myself a perfect role model, nor do I claim to be a bad one. I make mistakes, and I have learned that the best way to grow is by recognizing errors, reflecting on them and using those lessons to improve. Only then can I genuinely inspire those around me.  

In conclusion, while setting an example can be effective, it is not universally positive because some people’s behavior is detrimental. Therefore, I believe the most reliable approach is to focus on becoming the best version of yourself. There is only one you, and by striving to be authentic and responsible, you naturally become a better influence for the many people around you.

Tobegin, a group can be defined as a set of individuals who join forces to achieve a common objective. The way such collections are organized, the processes they follow, and the dynamics that shape them are studied in the field of group dynamics, which is central to understanding organisational behaviour. Many theories have been proposed to explain why groups emerge and how they develop.  

Collaborating in a team often yields higher productivity than solitary effort. When several people contribute, a wider range of competencies can be applied to the task, and the exchange of ideas tends to deepen comprehension of the subject matter. Moreover, teamwork provides a platform for developing interpersonal abilities such as communication, listening, and leadership, as well as the capacity to motivate fellow members. These competencies are valuable throughout one’s academic journey and future career.  

However, group work also presents challenges. One frequent problem is the uneven distribution of effort: a few outspoken members may dominate the discussion while others remain passive, leading to an imbalanced contribution. This can hinder the learning of those who do not actively engage. Additionally, individuals in a group may feel they have less direct control over the assignment, since decisions are often made collectively rather than by a single person.  

On the other hand, working alone allows a person to retain full authority over the task and to set their own pace. Yet it may also limit exposure to diverse viewpoints and the chance to practice collaborative skills.  

In sum, both modes of working have distinct benefits and drawbacks. Effective management of group processes is essential to maximise the positive outcomes while mitigating the negative aspects.

Homework clubs are a practical solution for students who find it hard to complete assignments on their own. By gathering together after school, they can finish tasks more quickly, receive assistance from classmates, and improve their overall learning abilities. The calm atmosphere of a club helps students concentrate, which makes their study time more effective.  

First, working in a club lets students complete their work earlier in the day. When the assignment is done before evening, they have time for other activities and are less likely to submit late work. I remember in seventh grade I often postponed my homework, which resulted in a poor grade and a long grounding period. After I started attending a study group, I finished my tasks sooner and avoided those negative consequences. I arrived early and was able to finish my math worksheet before the school bell, giving me extra time to review before the next class.  

Second, the club creates an environment where peers can help one another. A student who struggles with a particular subject can receive explanations from a classmate, making the work easier to finish. For instance, I stayed after school with my English teacher, concentrating on the assignment and asking for help repeatedly. This focus allowed me to raise my grade from failing to passing. Seeing a classmate solve a difficult problem inspired me to try harder, and the group often discussed different approaches, which deepened my understanding of the material. The teacher’s guidance combined with peer support made the learning process more engaging.  

Third, participation in a club strengthens collaboration and communication skills. Working together encourages students to share ideas, listen, and speak confidently. In fourth grade I entered an English‑as‑Second‑Language program where I knew no words at first. Daily lessons introduced new vocabulary, and a fellow student named Etka, who was more proficient, assisted me in practicing conversation. Over time my speaking confidence grew, and I no longer needed the program. Through regular group discussions, I learned how to ask questions politely and give constructive feedback, which later helped me in team projects. Etka not only helped with language but also shared study tips that improved my overall academic performance.  

In conclusion, after‑school homework clubs provide students with the chance to finish assignments early, support each other, and develop essential learning and communication skills. For these reasons, such clubs are valuable for anyone who wants to improve academic performance. Overall, the combination of early completion, peer support, and skill development makes homework clubs a worthwhile option for students of all levels.

Most high‑school students choose to spend the full four years in school before moving on to college, applying during their senior year and receiving guidance from counselors and teachers. Finishing early can be challenging for teenagers because learners develop at different rates and some are naturally quicker than others. School districts ought to let each student decide whether to graduate early and give them the freedom to plan their own future. Those who follow the standard four‑year schedule do not adopt the early‑graduation route, mainly because it creates extra pressure and anxiety; they must handle additional assignments while still being able to select elective courses. Every student realizes the importance of passing classes and keeping track of credit requirements for graduation. Pursuing an early exit can be risky, as the combination of stress and demands often leads to mental‑health difficulties. Some parents constantly monitor grades, which can cause frustration for the youngsters; when grades slip, guardians may restrict privileges and exert greater control over their lives. The fear of falling behind and receiving poor marks is ever‑present, yet it is less pronounced for students who remain for the full four years. Teachers frequently advise taking additional courses in the summer or evenings to stay ahead, but completing four years means no extra coursework is required. Although assignments still need to be completed, students are not rushed and have time to balance regular work with optional classes. The extra time can be used for homework or extracurricular activities rather than for unnecessary additional courses. Schools offer the chance to study new subjects that students have not encountered before, and elective choices allow them to explore interests and keep motivation high. For those who graduate early, this flexibility is reduced, making the traditional four‑year path a more advantageous option. In summary, completing the conventional four years of high school provides stability, reduces anxiety, and preserves access to a broader curriculum, while still allowing support from teachers and counselors when needed.

Many schools have formed partnerships with local businesses and industry groups, arranging internships or job‑shadowing experiences that give students a realistic preview of different careers. I think this plan is worthwhile because it lets young people see if a particular job suits them and raises the chance of landing a well‑paid position later.  
Such partnerships connect schools with local companies, allowing students to try out real‑world work environments and help them build professional contacts and decide whether the field matches their interests and abilities.  

First, gettinghands‑on experience in a real job lets students clarify what they really want to do in life and sets a strong foundation for their future. For instance, one of my cousin’s children was selected to tour Liberty University several years ago. During the visit he explored the campus, attended a few lectures, and decided that the programs offered were interesting. He later enrolled, studied diligently, earned straight A’s, and today runs his own successful business, clearly satisfied with the direction he chose.  

Second, internships also raise the chances of securing a high‑earning position. My other cousin, whose name I’ll keep generic, serves in the Air Force. He joined because his family could not afford university tuition. After a demanding period of training, he later attended Liberty University as well, graduated in 2015, and is now employed by the FBI. He tells me the early hardship was worthwhile, that it gave him discipline and confidence, and that his salary now lets him dream of buying a house. His story shows how early exposure can lead to a prestigious government job and financial stability.  

Some students argue that college is unnecessary and that a job at a fast‑food restaurant is sufficient. A friend once told me that returning to school felt like “returning to hell” and that she preferred working at Wendy’s. Hearing such views made me study harder and aim for better grades, because I want a career that provides both security and personal fulfillment, rather than a job that offers only short‑term income.  

In short, providing students with internship or shadowing opportunities is a smart idea. It helps them discover what they truly want and improves their chances of landing a well‑paid job. The stories of my cousins show how early exposure can lead to entrepreneurship or a prestigious government job. I hope that, with such experiences, I can work hard, achieve my goals, and eventually provide a comfortable life for my own children.

A person can be teased for almost anything, which is very sad. Because of this, those who are bullied often lose confidence and wish they were someone else.  

I remember a time when I felt depressed. I was constantly teased about the size of my head and how thin I was. At first I laughed it off, but the hurt grew and I stopped wanting to go to school. I didn’t want to leave the house or talk to anyone, and it was a very lonely feeling.  

One day a close friend noticed my absence and asked why I wasn’t coming. I told him everything, and he said I should ignore the hurtful words and live my life to the fullest. From then on we became inseparable; he always had my back and I had his. He listened carefully and reminded me that everyone has the right to be themselves, which made me feel understood.  

His support gave me the courage to face the bullying again.  

Soon after, I told my mother what was happening. We talked for a long time about how life is short and I shouldn’t let anyone stop me. She also told me that taking small steps toward my goals would help me regain confidence. Her words changed my view of the world and gave me a new sense of purpose.  

Trying to be authentic in today’s world is difficult. Even a simple comment that someone’s shoes are ugly can make a person change their style, buy things they don’t like, or do things they don’t want to do just to fit in with others who have nice clothes and shoes. This pressure makes it hard for many to stay true to themselves. When people try to copy what they think others want, they often lose their own interests and feel empty inside.  

There should be more help available for people who are struggling with bullying and low self‑esteem. Everyone should be encouraged to love themselves and to be authentic, because harsh words from others can sometimes lead to serious outcomes such as suicide. We need to treat each other with respect, and parents ought to teach their children the value of respect from an early age. Schools and community groups can provide counseling and safe spaces for those who are struggling.  

People should not worry about what others think of them. They should live their lives fully, feel proud of who they are, and understand that negative comments are normal. Those remarks can make a person feel like trash, but they can also make us stronger and help us become better human beings. That strength should drive us to achieve great things and make us, and the people close to us, proud of who we are. Being yourself should be the greatest accomplishment we can achieve.

Winston Churchill’s point is that moving from failure toward success is a difficult journey in life. To reach a fulfilling career and achieve success, one must be willing to work hard, even if progress takes many years. Not every person will become successful, and everyone makes mistakes, but perseverance is essential. Failure is not a final verdict; it simply signals that a different approach may be needed. With the right potential and determination, a turnaround is possible. This journey requires patience, resilience, and a clear vision of the desired outcome.

First, many people argue that turning failure into success is a positive development. For instance, a friend who was discouraged from playing basketball was told it was not his sport, yet after months of practice his skills improved dramatically. The common saying “practice makes perfect” reflects this idea. Likewise, my sister was determined to attend the University of Virginia; despite her family’s doubts, she studied intensively and was eventually admitted, showing that effort can overcome initial obstacles. Life is inherently challenging, so we must accept that hard work is required to move forward.

Conversely, most individuals encounter difficulties at some point. No one lives without problems, and in academic settings it is rare to find a student who does not struggle with coursework. From birth, people are not inherently intelligent; they must invest effort to become smarter. In my own experience, my math and history grades are strong while my English and science scores are lower, illustrating that each person has distinct strengths and weaknesses. Recognizing these differences and committing to study and practice is the way to improve.

Some critics claim that the pursuit of success is a waste of time and will not benefit one’s career. They argue that the amount of information required in school, college, and later employment is overwhelming, and that earning money for housing, bills, insurance, and family obligations already demands considerable effort. Those who voice such opinions are often individuals who face homelessness or lack stable living conditions, suggesting that they may view the effort as unnecessary.

Nevertheless, striving for success offers personal satisfaction. Achieving one’s professional goals brings a sense of pride and reduces future stress, because the work is completed early rather than postponed. Learning and mastering required material also builds competence, and even if ultimate success is not reached, the dedication itself prevents regret later in life.

In conclusion, the path from failure to success is undoubtedly demanding, but it is attainable through persistent effort, recognition of individual strengths, and a willingness to learn. By embracing challenges and working diligently, people can improve their circumstances and feel fulfilled.

Emerson’s claim that some individuals never truly mature makes sense to me. If a person’s character is fundamentally childish, they are unlikely to transform significantly as they get older. People who never mature often lack the self‑awareness needed to recognize their own flaws.

There are three main factors that keep such people stuck. First, their attitude often remains unchanged. They may be unable or unwilling to modify how they feel toward others or how they behave in response. For instance, I sometimes act very irritably toward my sister, even when she simply asks me for something, despite her being three years younger. This shows that a bad attitude can persist regardless of the situation. Even when she apologizes, I still feel the same irritation, showing how stubborn my mindset can be. This stubbornness can affect not only family relationships but also friendships and work interactions.

Second, violent tendencies can be hard to curb. Some people cannot stop being aggressive, and this can lead to hurting those they care about most. I remember being a gentle student in middle school, but after a haircut that drew teasing, I became upset and reacted violently toward the classmates who mocked me. Although I try to keep my temper in check with friends who understand me, I constantly battle the impulse to lash out. I have learned to pause before reacting, but the habit of quick anger remains. When I finally stopped reacting, I realized that controlling anger is a daily effort that requires constant practice. My younger sister also displays this pattern; when her older sister becomes angry, she reacts with aggression, then works hard to restrain herself, much like I do.

Third, the company a person keeps can reinforce immature behavior. Some friends exploit others for money, buying only what they want, while others pretend to be friendly but speak cruelly behind their backs when they are not present. I recall a scene in a movie where a group of popular, mean girls act warm to a new student, yet once the newcomer leaves they whisper harsh remarks, ensuring she cannot hear them. These dynamics make it hard to develop trust and maturity. Such patterns make it difficult to build lasting, supportive relationships.

In conclusion, the way a person acts childish can prevent growth. I agree with Emerson because many people remain selfish, violent, and surrounded by disrespectful friends, making it difficult for them to change. The three reasons—unhelpful attitude, persistent violence, and harmful friendships—show why some never grow up. Only by reflecting on these habits can a person begin to change. Overall, these patterns illustrate why personal growth can be stalled in life.

Our relationship deepened, and I came to appreciate her character fully, realizing that my first judgment had been hasty.  

These experiences show that while a first impression may be strong, it is not immutable. Changing how someone perceives you usually requires patience and consistent behavior. If we act authentically and demonstrate positive qualities over time, the original view can be revised for the better. Conversely, if we act negatively, the impression may worsen.  

Even though the initial impression can affect how we interact, it does not lock us into a permanent label; people are capable of growth and change. Therefore, giving people a chance to show their true selves is essential for fair judgments.  

In summary, first impressions are not impossible to alter. They may take days, weeks, or even months to transform, depending on the interactions that follow. The key factor is the actions we take after the initial meeting, which gradually shape a more accurate and favorable perception.

Imagine stepping out of high school a year before the usual time and heading straight to college or a job. It feels rewarding because all the hard work has finally paid off, yet the price is that many enjoyable activities and free time are given up. For this reason I think it is unwise for students to finish high school in three years and start college or the workforce a year early.  

If a student accelerates through high school, the course load must be compressed into summer terms or evening classes. Summer employment becomes difficult, since school assignments and study time would occupy most of the season. Evening lessons also conflict with after‑school clubs or sports, making it hard to stay involved in those activities. In addition, the schedule would leave little space for elective courses such as art, music or photography. Graduation demands that all required subjects be completed, and trying to fit them together often squeezes out the optional classes that broaden a student’s experience.  

The workload would be intense. Learners would need to study each subject thoroughly, turn in homework at home, and keep up with notes to avoid falling behind. Moreover, projects and presentations add extra pressure, leaving few moments for relaxation or personal interests. Some people claim that graduating early provides a head start, but the heightened stress and limited extracurricular involvement outweigh any benefit. Therefore, schools should refrain from offering a three‑year high‑school track that pushes students into college or work a year sooner.  

Balancing summer classes with a part‑time job is challenging, and many students find they must sacrifice leisure time to keep up with the coursework. Without a summer job, students lose valuable income and may feel financial pressure, which can distract them from their studies. Missing out on sports or clubs can also affect a student’s sense of future college applications. Elective subjects such as visual arts, drama, or music give students a chance to explore personal interests and develop creative skills, which are often missing from a rigid schedule. Colleges look for a well‑rounded transcript, so missing out on electives may weaken an application, even if the required courses are completed. The intense workload can lead to burnout, affecting both academic performance and overall health. Students may need to manage their time more carefully, planning study sessions around homework and test preparation to stay on track. Balancing school with other responsibilities often leaves little room for rest, making it harder to maintain high grades. While some families view early graduation as a shortcut to success, the reality is that the added pressure can hinder a student’s overall development. Consequently, schools should avoid creating a three‑year high‑school track that forces students into college or the workforce a year sooner, as the drawbacks outweigh any potential benefits.

Most of the time, students finish high school early so they can start college right away. I think they should finish in three years and spend a year working instead, because this lets them save money for tuition, become more mature, and develop strong time‑management abilities. These advantages open many possibilities before they enter college.  

First, working gives students the chance to earn cash and avoid taking out loans. Many young people need financial help for college, and some families cannot cover the costs. If a student takes a loan, he or she will have to repay it after graduation, which creates a long‑term burden. By leaving school after three years and getting a job, the student can accumulate savings, so the family does not need to borrow money and the student learns to be financially independent. This responsibility also shows others that the student has grown up, and it makes parents proud.  

Second, a year of work makes students more mature. At seventeen, a recent graduate often feels young and inexperienced. Spending twelve months in the workforce forces them to rely on themselves, handle duties, and see how the real world operates. Maturity is important in college because it helps a student meet deadlines, interact professionally with professors, and avoid being treated as a joke or a target for bullying. When a student enters college at the same time as peers who have already worked, the transition feels less isolating.  

Third, a job teaches valuable time‑management skills. In school, some students turn in assignments late or miss classes. Working requires punctuality, completing tasks on schedule, and balancing different responsibilities. Those habits translate into better organization in college: turning work in on time, arriving to lectures promptly, and planning sleep and study periods. With a clear routine that includes studying, working, recreation, and rest, a student no longer worries about being late or forgetting deadlines.  

Moreover, working experience can provide valuable networking contacts, expose students to professional environments, and even qualify them for scholarships that require work history, further easing the financial load of college. These benefits help students enter university with a clearer sense of purpose and a stronger résumé, giving them an edge over peers who start directly after high school.  

Some people argue that students should go straight to college after high school. While that path works for many, it can be risky for those who are not yet mature enough; they may struggle academically and feel overwhelmed. Allowing a year of work first gives them a chance to mature, earn money, and build confidence, so they arrive on campus better prepared and more likely to succeed.  

In short, students who work before college gain financial independence, greater maturity, and stronger time‑management skills, all of which make the college experience smoother and more rewarding. They will not need to worry about repaying loans after graduation, and they will be ready to take full advantage of the opportunities that higher education offers.

Although this is a good point, it is wrong because it misses the fact that some students would be unhappy with this decision. These are some reasons on why changing the menu would be a bad idea for the school.

Changing the food served in schoolcafeterias would be like snatching a bone away from a dog. First, pupils would likely be displeased with such a shift. When students are upset about school changes, their parents often get involved, which can damage the board’s reputation. This tension often leads to heated debates at school board meetings. I once saw a program where a school altered its menu without asking anyone, and the reaction was huge; the students even staged a walk‑out and refused to attend classes.

Second, if the favorite dishes are removed, many pupils may simply stop eating lunch at school. For instance, at a family dinner my relatives served meat loaf, which I detested; I could not finish it and ended up throwing it away. A similar situation happened when my friends and I went to a buffet that offered only a few items, so we were forced to take chicken wings that tasted terrible and we could not finish them. People generally avoid foods they dislike, so they are unlikely to eat or even try new meals.

Third, a menu overhaul would reduce the variety of choices available. This would be unfair to students whose tastes do not match the new options; they would have nothing else to eat. Imagine going to your favorite clothing store and finding that all the garments you love have been replaced with styles you hate – you would feel very dissatisfied, just as students would feel if their lunch were changed.

Some argue that a healthier menu would benefit students, but this view overlooks the fact that many pupils would be unhappy with the new selections. Consequently, the intended health benefits may never be realized if students simply skip meals. Even if the food is nutritious, the lack of appealing options can lead to refusal to eat, which defeats the purpose.

In conclusion, altering the cafeteria menu would cause student dissatisfaction, possible parental conflict, reduced food intake, and an unfair situation for those with specific tastes. Therefore, changing the school lunch is a poor idea.

Your character is something you decide for yourself. The question is whether we can choose our own traits, or whether they are shaped by forces we cannot control. It is clear that some individuals are swayed by friends, family, or even strangers who may have a negative impact, while others manage to follow their own positive inclinations and achieve a more successful life. In the end, the decision rests with each person.  

First, many people acquire traits from the environment around them. Those raised in unhappy homes may develop harmful habits, whereas those brought up in supportive families often adopt constructive behaviors. However, spending time with individuals who have negative habits can undo the good influence of a caring upbringing. Thus, the people we associate with play a crucial role in shaping who we become.  

Second, the traits we display can also be reflected in our material achievements and relationships. Successful people who own a comfortable home or drive nice cars often credit their positive habits for this progress, while destructive habits may lead to a troubled existence. Even personal relationships, such as a romantic partnership, can either uplift us or drag us down, causing emotional pain or fostering growth, depending on how we handle conflicts and mutual respect.  

Finally, it is not true that we are completely powerless against outside influence. Some individuals try to undermine those who succeed, hoping to keep them from reaching their goals. We must recognize these attempts, stay firm, and distance ourselves from harmful influences. The best advice is to reflect on our own values, decide whether our traits are beneficial or harmful, and consciously choose the path that leads to a positive and fulfilling life.

Do you think schools should make the school day longer? I’m against that idea. First, if classes ended later, pupils would find it hard to stay focused; they would be tired after a long day and might need extra time for assignments, travel, or extra study, which would leave them drowsy in the next lesson. Staying up late to finish homework or revise for a test also reduces sleep, so both the student and classmates could feel sleepy during class. Second, a longer schedule would increase students’ stress. Knowing they must rise early and not finish until late creates pressure that can harm their mental well‑being. Third, the extra time could cut into the actual learning for some pupils. Athletes, for example, may have to leave class early to attend practice, missing a substantial portion of lessons, and other students who need to depart early for appointments would lose valuable instructional minutes. In my view, extending the school day would do more harm than good.

In several countries, youngpeople are pressured to decide on a profession as soon as they start high school, and their school subjects are arranged to steer them toward that specific job. However, most adolescents at that age simply do not possess the maturity or insight needed to make such a decisive choice. I therefore argue that students should not be forced to select a career when they first enter secondary school, because they lack the experience to know what they truly want, they may end up choosing incorrectly, and they could waste years pursuing a path they later regret.

When pupils begin secondary education they are typically around fourteen years old. At this stage they are still developing socially and emotionally, and thoughts about their future are rarely a primary concern. As they grow older and gain more knowledge about different occupations, their attitudes toward work shift. By the time they reach sixteen, many students become more reflective about their aspirations and start to view their future more realistically. This natural progression shows that a definitive career decision at the outset is unrealistic.

If a teenager is compelled to pick a profession immediately, the risk of selecting an unsuitable field becomes high. Choosing the wrong career can lead to long‑term dissatisfaction, because individuals who feel trapped in a job they dislike often lack motivation and perform poorly. Moreover, the time spent on an inappropriate career can be difficult to recover, causing wasted years that could have been devoted to more fitting pursuits.

Research and careful planning are essential before committing to a professional direction. Students who take the time to explore various options, understand the requirements of different jobs, and reflect on their interests are far more likely to make a satisfying choice. Without sufficient exposure and self‑knowledge, any decision is likely to be premature and may result in the need to start over later, which is both costly and discouraging.

Consequently, it is advisable that students postpone a firm career decision until they have accumulated more life experience and clearer insight into their own passions and abilities. Providing them with guidance, exposure to diverse fields, and the freedom to explore will help ensure that their eventual career choice aligns with their true interests and leads to greater fulfillment.

I oppose the proposal toextend the school day by an additional one and a half hours. My objection rests on the fact that the present schedule already meets the daily requirement for learning. Introducing more time would exhaust students, making it harder for them to absorb material throughout the day. When school lasts for many consecutive hours and homework is assigned, the workload creates considerable stress. At present, the existing timetable already imposes a heavy load on most learners. If the board adds another ninety minutes, many pupils will likely become disenchanted with school, might abandon their studies, or lose enthusiasm for assignments and tests. Students would also find it difficult to allocate sufficient time for revision, examinations, or large projects that must be completed at home, especially those who work part‑time jobs. Free time is essential not only for enjoyment but also for physical well‑being. As a middle‑school student I can attest that I manage my current schedule and still have moments for recreation and study. However, an extra one and a half hours would shrink the window for play, family gatherings, and socialising with friends, which could negatively affect my health and overall happiness. For youths who hold part‑time positions, the impact would be even more severe. They would struggle to balance work, school, family interaction, and adequate rest. Insufficient sleep and limited leisure time can deteriorate mental health, physical condition, and overall satisfaction with life. Teachers, many of whom already supplement their income with secondary employment, would face additional challenges. An extended day would leave them with less opportunity to prepare lessons, grade work, or provide extra assistance to students who need tutoring or wish to retake exams. Those who are married or responsible for aging parents would find it harder to fulfill familial duties without a higher salary or a reduction in their secondary work. Consequently, educators might be forced to resign or demand higher pay to compensate for the extra hours. Bus drivers also encounter safety concerns. They already navigate early‑morning routes in low‑light conditions while transporting a full complement of students. Adding an afternoon segment that stretches the day would push the end of the school day into darkness, making it hazardous for drivers and passengers alike. The after‑school program, which currently runs for two hours, would then extend to three and a half hours, creating an unsafe environment for all involved. The after‑school initiative serves a vital purpose: it allows students to complete missing assignments, retake tests, or improve grades through supervised study. If the school day is lengthened, the program may have to be discontinued because teachers, drivers, and learners would be too fatigued to participate. Without this support, students would lose a valuable resource for academic recovery and grade enhancement. In summary, the present school schedule is adequate; extending it by an additional one and a half hours would overburden students, diminish their free time, jeopardize their health, hinder teachers’ effectiveness, endanger bus drivers, and possibly eliminate the after‑school assistance that many rely on. Therefore, I firmly disagree with the proposed expansion.

People often look for independence because it lets them choose their own path and shape their lives according to personal values. They also value the sense of autonomy that comes from being able to set their own goals and pursue passions without constant supervision. The primary motivation is the desire to decide for themselves, and taking responsibility for those choices demonstrates maturity and self‑reliance. While some individuals make wise selections, others fall into poor habits that can harm both themselves and those around them.

Bad choices such as using illegal substances, driving while intoxicated, or becoming involved with gangs often lead to serious trouble. Drug use damages health and can strain relationships, sometimes resulting in addiction, loss of employment, or even overdose. Drunk driving puts the driver and innocent by‑standers at risk, frequently causing accidents that send victims to the hospital, ruin careers, or claim lives. Joining a gang raises the chance of violent death, involvement in criminal activity, and brings sorrow and fear to loved ones. The legal system often penalizes drunk driving with license suspension, fines, or imprisonment, and repeat offenses can lead to longer jail time. Drug offenses may result in criminal charges, loss of custody, or difficulty finding future employment. Gang involvement can expose youths to violent confrontations, police surveillance, and a cycle that is hard to break.

On the other hand, thoughtful decisions help shape a stable future. Deciding what career to pursue, which field of study to follow in college, or whether to start a family encourages planning and goal‑setting. When a person selects a profession after considering the required education, they increase their chances of finding steady work, earn a reliable income, and secure the financial means to support a family. This preparation also builds confidence, because knowing what steps to take reduces uncertainty and stress. When a person plans their education, they can choose courses that match their interests and career goals, making the learning process more engaging. Research shows that individuals who set clear objectives are more likely to achieve them, because they create a roadmap and stay motivated. Moreover, balancing work and family life often leads to greater overall satisfaction, as personal relationships provide emotional support and a sense of purpose.

Parents frequently allow their children to make their own choices, believing that this process teaches self‑thinking and personal growth. By giving youngsters the freedom to decide, parents show confidence that they can handle life independently, and they see the development of confidence and responsibility in their kids. This approach also strengthens the parent‑child bond, because the child feels trusted and valued, which often leads to better communication and mutual respect. When children are permitted to experience the consequences of their choices, they learn resilience and problem‑solving skills that serve them later in life. Parents often act as mentors, offering advice without imposing decisions, which helps youngsters develop critical thinking and a sense of ownership over their actions. Such guidance creates a supportive environment where mistakes are seen as learning opportunities rather than failures, encouraging a growth mindset.

All these points illustrate that making decisions is a challenging yet essential part of becoming independent. Independence is highly valued in today’s world, so the real question is how each person will use the freedom they have earned. When individuals choose wisely, they not only grow personally but also contribute positively to their families and communities, proving that the ability to decide is a cornerstone of a meaningful life. Choosing wisely also builds self‑esteem, because successful decisions reinforce the belief that one can shape their own destiny. Moreover, societies thrive when individuals take responsibility for their actions, as this fosters trust, cooperation, and progress. Therefore, the freedom to decide carries both opportunity and responsibility, and using it thoughtfully leads to a richer, more purposeful life.

Can morehours in school help conserve energy? I think extending the school day by adding two extra hours and changing the schedule to four days a week would be a poor decision. The extra time would create many problems for both pupils and teachers. First, students who work after school, attend sports, clubs or have to pick up younger siblings would find it hard to fit everything into a longer day. They would return home later, feel exhausted, and have little time left for friends or leisure. This fatigue could also affect their concentration and performance in class. Second, teachers may face difficulties. Many live far from the school, perhaps in another county, and would need to leave earlier to collect their children. The longer schedule could force them to alter their own routines, causing stress and possibly affecting the quality of their teaching. Proponents of a longer school day argue that more classroom time would allow students to finish assignments during school, reduce homework, and give teachers more opportunity to cover material, which might lead to better test results and faster graduation. They also claim that a four‑day week would provide three days off for rest. However, these potential benefits are outweighed by the practical obstacles. The extra hours would disrupt the daily rhythm of families, make it harder for students to balance work and extracurricular activities, and increase the burden on teachers who already have long commutes. Moreover, the claim that longer days save energy is not convincingly supported; the additional heating, lighting and transportation needs could cancel any energy savings. In conclusion, the disadvantages for students and staff are significant. Therefore, schools should not adopt a longer day or a four‑day week in the hope of conserving energy.

Dear Principal,

I believeour school would benefit from establishing a community center. Such a space would let students discover the needs of the neighbourhood, explore ways to improve it, and understand why the community matters to them. Having a centre would teach us how to make things better. Students could work on projects that address local issues, such as recycling programs or neighborhood clean‑ups, giving them real‑world experience.

Some pupils worry that a centre would take up their time, yet they must first learn what the community requires. We could organize groups of students to create a list of needed improvements; presenting that list would show what the community needs. Participants could earn extra credit, especially those with lower grades, which would encourage involvement. The extra credit would be recorded on their report cards, providing a clear incentive for those who need academic support.

A few students refuse because friends label the activity as pointless. When peers see the benefits, they are more inclined to join, turning a solitary activity into a collaborative effort. However, learning how the community can become a better place for us is not a waste of time. The programme concerns our own lives; if the neighbourhood struggles, our own wellbeing may suffer. When students see this connection, they are more likely to join and work toward a healthier environment.

Others may question the relevance of the community. When they become familiar with its realities, they will see its importance and feel motivated to take part. Grades would improve for those who engage, and their peers might be drawn in by their enthusiasm, creating a positive cycle.

In short, a community centre would give students valuable learning experiences, teach them how to enhance their surroundings, and highlight the significance of community involvement. Overall, the centre would serve as a hub for learning, service, and personal growth, preparing students for future civic engagement.

I think this idea is worthwhile for our school.

Sincerely,
STUDENT_NAME

Showing kindness to others is vital because it demonstrates that you possess a caring heart, enables the ripple effect of goodwill across communities, and paves the way for a more hopeful future. Kindness serves as a cornerstone for personal success and overall well‑being.  

Imagine a world where no one practiced kindness; it would feel empty and harsh, lacking the warmth that makes life meaningful.  

When you act kindly, others notice that you have a sincere and generous spirit.  

This perception builds trust, because people see that you genuinely care and are willing to help.  

Kindness feels uplifting and soothing, as it aligns with the best intentions we hold in life.  

It never harms anyone; rather, it aims to improve circumstances for all involved.  

Spreading kindness worldwide can reshape attitudes, making harmful actions seem out of place within a compassionate framework.  

A single act of generosity may travel far, influencing many without the giver even realizing the impact.  

Without kindness, concepts such as empathy, love, sharing, and humility would disappear.  

Each small gesture you offer alters another person’s mood, and those around you often mirror your behavior.  

In the long run, kindness supports your own development.  

It reveals your true character and can open doors to better employment prospects and academic achievement.  

When you consistently demonstrate consideration, you become more appealing to employers and teachers alike.  

Moreover, reflecting on the kindness you have extended over the years brings gratitude for the life you enjoy now.  

Kindness does not appear spontaneously; it must be created and shared deliberately.  

Although many people aspire to a better world, countless individuals hesitate to give kindness, often out of indifference or fear.  

Yet, those who choose to spread compassion do so with the hope of fostering a brighter future for everyone.  

Ultimately, kindness resides within each of us; we simply need to let it surface and spread it everywhere.  

Life waits patiently for us to embrace and share this virtue, knowing that a world filled with kindness is a world where everyone can thrive.  

It also teaches patience and humility, qualities that enrich personal relationships and professional collaborations.  

When you nurture kindness daily, you build a reputation that can open doors to new opportunities and supportive networks.  

Even small acts, like a friendly smile or a helpful word, can have a lasting influence on someone’s day.

Successmeans moving forward from one setback to the next while keeping one's enthusiasm alive, because achieving it demands great effort. It plays a vital role in life, and understanding that occasional failure is also valuable. Although success is not easily attained, it can be reached with steady calm and genuine excitement. It is essential for people in their studies, careers, and future aspirations, as it helps them build a better tomorrow. When people stay motivated, they are more likely to persist through difficulties and eventually achieve their desired outcomes.  

First, obtaining success in an academic setting is challenging, yet students should recognize that persistent effort can lead to improvement. They must continue to hope for a positive outcome, study extensively, and avoid losing confidence. Practising each step makes tasks easier and increases the chance of achieving better results. For instance, when a student receives a poor grade, reviewing the material and practicing repeatedly can restore confidence and lead to success with renewed enthusiasm. Regular review of mistakes helps students identify patterns and correct them more efficiently. Thus, learning through repeated failures is crucial for academic progress.  

Second, success at work relies on dedication and sustained effort. Employees who do not perform well may jeopardise the organization’s achievements and risk losing their positions. However, by maintaining composure and actively seeking new opportunities, they can secure new jobs with the same enthusiasm. An example is an employee who was dismissed for submitting a weak report; after dedicated practice and improvement, he obtained a new role and performed excellently. Even when a project fails, the lessons learned can improve future performance and increase the chance of success. While work success can be difficult, it is never unattainable.  

Finally, people often have many future goals, but obstacles may appear along the way. The objectives may seem hard to reach, yet they are achievable with consistent effort. Maintaining firm belief in one’s ideas and staying determined enables individuals to overcome setbacks. For example, a family that wishes to travel to the beach may lack sufficient funds, but by working hard and staying motivated, they can save enough and eventually enjoy the trip. All goals become reachable when supported by dedication and perseverance.  

In summary, success can be achieved by progressing from failure to failure while preserving enthusiasm. Whether in education, employment, or personal aspirations, the path is not impossible; the key is to keep enthusiasm alive and learn from each setback. Thus, perseverance and enthusiasm together create a powerful foundation for lasting achievement.

Scientist Albert Einstein once said, "Imagination is more important than knowledge." Now imagine yourself as a beginning engineer, sitting at your desk, aggravated because you can't come up with a new invention. All you have around you are textbooks but no image or thought of what your invention may be. If only you could imagine a new invention of some sort then maybe you could build something. But with no imagination, how can you build knowledge? I agree with Einstein's quote. I believe imagination is more important than knowledge.

I agree with Einstein's quote because having imagination is how we've had all our inventions yet. Without imagination how were many of the things we own invented? For example, the telephone. The telephone couldn't have been invented without someone imagining a device where you could communicate without leaving your home. You need imagination in order to make new things. Another example would be the camera. Whoever invented it, had to have imagination in order to think of a device that captures any moment almost in an instant. Even I, as a student, need imagination in order to make new things. For example, when making an essay, such as this one, I need to imagine of a good story hook that goes along with the prompt.

Furthermore, I believe in Einstein quote because without imagination, knowledge is almost useless. For example, when learning a new vocabulary list. You may know all the definitions but you can't put them in your own words or use the words in different instances. Why? Because you can't imagine it. You can't picture it, you just know the definitions. Another example is when reading a book. Knowing how to read isn't even near of what you need to fully comprehend a book. You need to imagine it. Picture the story in your mind in order to fully understand the book's theme, setting and tone.

Lastly, I agree in Einstein's quote because without imagination, all our decisions would be made carelessly. For instance, before you speak or move, most of the time you imagine what the outcome of that action will be. If not, the outcome won't be for the better. Another instance is when in an experiment, you hypothesize what the result of the experiment will be. That takes imagination. When signing a contract, it's needed to imagine the consequences of signing and not signing the contract. In other words, you need to imagine things before you decide to take them on. Knowledge isn't the only thing that will help you when making decisions.

In conclusion, Einstein's quote is correct in my perspective. Knowledge isn't the most important factor to have, imagination is key to everything you do and will do. You can't fully understand most things without imagining them. Can't go on inventing things before imagining them first. Also, you won't be able to make good decisions before imagining the outcome. All in all, imagination is also how you'll enjoy your life. Knowledge is great and all but it can't bring others as much happiness as imagination can. It's how we've been happy for all these years. Imagination is how we have gone so far in this world and how much we've survived.

Scientist Albert Einstein famously claimed that imagination outweighs knowledge. As a novice engineer staring at a blank page filled with textbooks, I felt stuck because I could not picture a fresh invention. The lack of a mental picture left me frustrated, suggesting that without imagination, building new knowledge is impossible. I stand by Einstein’s view: imagination surpasses knowledge.  

First, imagination fuels invention. The telephone emerged from a vision of speaking without leaving home, and the camera was born from picturing a device that could capture a fleeting instant. Even when drafting an essay, I rely on imagination to craft a compelling opening line that grabs the reader’s attention.  

Second, imagination gives meaning to knowledge. Knowing a word’s definition does not let you use it creatively; you must be able to picture its sense in context. Likewise, reading a text demands visualizing the plot, characters, and atmosphere to grasp its deeper themes, setting, and tone. Without that mental image, knowledge stays flat.  

Third, imagination guides thoughtful decisions. Before you speak, act, or sign a contract, you typically envision the possible outcomes. In research, you hypothesize by imagining what the experiment might reveal. When negotiating a contract, you picture the consequences of each choice. Hence, imagination sharpens decision‑making beyond raw facts.  

Finally, imagination drives enjoyment and progress. It is the spark behind countless breakthroughs and the well‑spring of lasting happiness. Knowledge supplies tools, yet imagination shapes how we live, grow, and find fulfillment.  

Therefore, Einstein’s claim remains valid; imagination is the essential catalyst for invention, understanding, choice, and fulfillment.

Is constant activity necessary for achievement?Yes, staying idle prevents any progress. Thomas Jefferson said, "Determine never to be idle... it is wonderful how much may be done if we are always doing." Inactivity does not help you achieve anything; standing or lying at home does nothing. On the contrary, staying active lets you learn more, meet new people, and reach your goals. For example, I joined a soccer team despite having no interest, and through it I learned to kick a ball, play as a goalkeeper, and increase my speed. When I faced a vocabulary test with many unknown words, I studied until I mastered them. Joining the team also gave me the chance to meet new teammates and coaches, helping me improve my teamwork, speed, and mindset. Another time I asked a math teacher for help with an equation I didn't understand, and his guidance let me solve similar problems on my own. Imagine the possibilities if we were always engaged in productive activities rather than staying home watching TV. Free moments can be used to work on projects that enhance future success and sharpen thinking. Even when we think we don't need assistance, asking for help expands our understanding. While some people may lack time, resources, or transportation, inactivity is not a solution. By continuously doing something that supports future goals, we can accomplish more.

Have you ever had a really important decision you had to make? Did you feel overwhelmed because you didn't know what you should do? Asking for help or advise from people such as friends and family around you can really help alleviate all that stress. Most people encounter big decisions often throughout their lives, so getting advise from numerous people can help you get more input on something, and may end up helping you make a final decision. Seeking multiple opinions can really help someone make a better choice when dealing with decision making.

One way seeking multiple opinions can help someone make a better choice is that by asking more than one person, they can get more input. Asking numerous people can be a huge help when making an important decision. Not only are people getting different ideas of what they may want to do, they can also get advise from people who may be more experienced than themselves. For example, if someone was debating on which college they should apply to, they may end up asking people such as older siblings or parents for advise because they may have more experience with that matter. By asking multiple people, you can get multiple ideas, each of them being different in their own way. By getting more people's input, you may be able to start to make your own choice about the matter because of the advise you've gotten.

Another way seeking multiple opinions can help someone make a better choice is by not getting any biased opinions. By asking more than one person for advise on a subject, they can get more than one new idea that isn't one of their own. This way, they can get more than one person's thoughts on the decision, and have different ideas on it. For example, if someone were trying to make a decision on what sport they may want to tryout for at school, they could possibly ask their friends and family about which they should choose. However, they should also ask people like classmates and teachers, as they may have their own ideas, and won't give the person any biased ideas or information. Friends and family can have a great deal of influence on people, so it's important to always get people's thoughts that are on the outside. This will make it to where there's a greater chance of the decision maker not being biased, as they've heard numerous people's thoughts, and can make their own decision off of that.

A final way seeking multiple opinions can help someone make a better choice is by being more prepared about the choice they're going to make. The decision maker can use all the advise they've gotten from different people to make their own choice, and feel better prepared. They will be more focused as they know what they want to do, and will feel more confident and less overwhelmed. Feeling less overwhelmed can be a big help as the person doesn't have to be so worried, so they won't have any distractions from making the best possible decision. For example, if someone is trying to decide what kind of car they want to get, and they've gotten advise from numerous people, they can make a better choice when picking. They'll know exactly what they want, as they've heard many thoughts from the people around them, and so they can make their final decision.

After getting advise from multiple people around them, the decision maker may be able to make the best choice possible, as they've gotten new thoughts and ideas. Asking for help or for some advise from those around you can help you make the best possible choice because you've gotten a lot of new information and opinions that you wouldn't have gotten if you had only asked one or no one at all for advise. Making an important choice can seem a little bit easier and less stressful after seeking advise from multiple people. Getting help from others around you can help you make the best choice you can.
