Thomas Jefferson maintained that taking action issuperior to remaining idle. He claimed that a life of constant activity yields more achievements than one of inactivity. Whether the goal is mastering a musical instrument, imagining travel through time, or simply tidying a room, the act of doing something creates progress. For instance, a person who wishes to play an instrument but lacks the skill will begin lessons, and someone dreaming of exploring other worlds might design a device to make it possible. Even routine tasks such as cooking, cleaning, or completing homework are forms of accomplishment that add up over time.  

Doing something, alone or together, expands what we can achieve. In sports, players coordinate their efforts to win a match, and a video‑game studio relies on many specialists to produce a finished product that others can enjoy. Online games also let friends collaborate or compete, showing how collective effort can lead to success. Likewise, everyday chores demonstrate that even modest actions contribute to a sense of achievement.  

It is important to recognize that rest and sleep are natural parts of life; they allow the mind and body to recover and release tension. However, rest should not be confused with laziness. Taking short breaks after focused work helps maintain motivation for the next day, whether that work is school, a job, or personal projects. A brief pause, a meal, or a short nap can restore energy without abandoning the habit of activity.  

Moreover, engaging in activities helps develop skills and confidence, which can be applied to larger challenges later in life. When we avoid doing anything, we miss chances to learn, to grow, and to contribute to our community.  

Conversely, a habit of laziness erodes motivation and encourages people to seek the easiest path whenever possible. Once this pattern forms, it becomes difficult to break free. Such a mindset not only limits personal progress but also weakens the collective effort needed to solve larger problems. Therefore, staying active and purposeful is the best way to accomplish goals and enjoy a fulfilling life.

I agree that individuality is valuable. I enjoy seeing people follow their own preferences, because life feels more interesting when each person chooses what they like. I have many friends who pursue different paths, and I like doing what I want rather than copying others. My family, however, is often negative; they rarely listen when I try to express myself, which makes me determined to be independent and to act according to my own wishes. They often dismiss my opinions, telling me to be quiet and to follow tradition, which makes me feel unheard and pushes me to prove myself. I believe that too many people rely on others, and that dependence is not healthy. The history lesson highlighted that in earlier times people were not truly individual, and I think modern society seeks more attention, which leads to greater dependence on others. My life changed dramatically when I moved from Puerto Rico two years ago. Since then I have learned to value every opportunity, recognizing the effort and sacrifice behind each achievement. I constantly strive to improve myself, even though mastering the language and adapting to new customs is challenging. Because I could not ask questions or get help, I often felt isolated and struggled to keep up with the lessons. I keep moving forward because I trust my abilities and I set goals that I accomplish each day. I have learned that perseverance and self‑belief are the keys to overcoming obstacles, and I try to keep a positive attitude even when the path is uncertain. Adjusting to a new environment has been difficult. I have met people from many backgrounds; some are kind, others less so, and I love discovering new things and places. The only source of frustration is that, although I am not undocumented and Puerto Ricans are part of the United States, many people treat us as if we were because our first language is Spanish. This situation makes me more determined to succeed. School has been my biggest obstacle. In the first few months after arriving, I began to fail classes because I had no one to help me at school or at home. Now I feel that I do not belong here; the only reason I stay is to support my mother, whom I want to see succeed and receive everything she deserves. She works hard to provide for our family, and her encouragement motivates me to study and to succeed. Overall, I believe that embracing individuality allows people to live authentically, to pursue their passions, and to grow despite difficulties. My own journey shows that perseverance, self‑belief, and the desire to improve can overcome language barriers and cultural differences. I hope that by sharing my story I can inspire others to value their own uniqueness and to keep moving forward despite obstacles. I have learned that perseverance and self‑belief are the keys to overcoming obstacles, and I try to keep a positive attitude even when the path is uncertain. I feel proud of my progress and to keep moving forward despite obstacles.

Many people argue that cellphones should be allowed in class because they can provide quick internet access for assignments, but I believe that students ought not to bring phones into the classroom. First, phones create disturbances that interrupt the learning environment. When a pupil plays music or watches a video, the sound distracts classmates and prevents them from concentrating on the teacher’s explanation. Such interruptions often lead to missed instruction and lower academic performance. In addition, the visual stimulus can pull attention away from the board, making it difficult for students to follow the lesson flow. Teachers often have to pause the lesson to address the noise, which reduces the amount of time available for teaching and can disrupt the flow of the class.

Second, the presence of a phone encourages students to chat with friends instead of paying attention. During a lesson, a learner may spend time texting or browsing, which means they are not listening to the teacher. This lack of focus not only harms the individual’s comprehension but also sets a poor example for peers, fostering a noisy and unproductive atmosphere. Moreover, frequent chatting can create social cliques that exclude other students and foster a hostile classroom atmosphere.

Third, phones facilitate cheating during examinations. If a student has a mobile device, they can look up answers or share information with others, obtaining an unfair advantage. This undermines the integrity of the test and demotivates classmates who must rely on their own knowledge. The temptation to cheat also reduces the incentive to study, which can weaken overall learning outcomes. When cheating becomes common, students lose trust in the fairness of grades and may feel demotivated to try their best.

Fourth, excessive use of phones reduces participation and can be harmful to health. Spending long periods watching videos or listening to music strains the eyes and limits mental flexibility, making it harder for students to engage in classroom activities or respond to questions. Moreover, constant distraction may lead to reduced attendance, as students may feel anxious or lose confidence in the school environment. Physical discomfort from prolonged screen time can also cause headaches and fatigue, further impairing academic performance. Students who rely on their phones may also miss out on developing essential social skills that are valuable for future teamwork and communication. This habit can hinder their overall personal growth.

In summary, cell phones should be prohibited in class because they disrupt lessons, encourage off‑task communication, enable dishonest practices, and negatively affect both learning and well‑being. Therefore, keeping cell phones out of the classroom helps maintain a focused, fair, and healthy learning environment.

Thomas Jefferson’s observationraises a useful question: does constant activity bring greater results, or can there be value in staying still? While some people maintain that doing nothing also has its place, I side with the view that continual effort creates more opportunities, whereas inactivity often leads to missed chances.

First, many individuals feel that they cannot expand their options because of financial constraints or other hardships. They argue that without money or resources, additional possibilities remain out of reach. Yet the reality is that ease is rare; even the simplest tasks demand effort. My grandfather, who grew up in extreme poverty and could barely feed his five children, used to tell me that “one day everything will change.” He never stopped believing that, and after a particularly difficult period he managed to find new ways to improve his family’s situation. His experience reminds me that persistent struggle can open doors that once seemed impossible.

Second, when we make productive use of our time, remarkable achievements become attainable. By working hard and seizing opportunities, we can turn aspirations into concrete reality—whether it is owning a beautiful car, a spacious home, or any other desired possession. The key is to exploit each moment, set clear goals, and apply consistent effort. Moreover, helping others while we strive creates a richer, more fulfilling life, because the act of giving back adds meaning beyond personal gain.

Third, the habit of constantly seeking new paths prevents stagnation. If we remain fixed on a single route, we limit ourselves to the same limited set of outcomes. Instead, we should stay curious, explore alternative routes, and remain open to fresh possibilities. For example, I once asked myself how to accelerate my own dreams. I realized that if I keep looking for different ways to achieve my goals, I am more likely to succeed. This mindset encourages continual growth and adaptation.

Finally, consider the practical example of wanting a car that costs one million. The price itself does not guarantee ownership; it is the result of sustained effort, disciplined saving, and hard work that eventually makes the purchase possible. Conversely, a life lived without purpose or activity may lead to regret and disappointment, as laziness can cause one to miss out on the many opportunities that arise each day. By staying active, embracing challenges, and continuously looking for new options, we increase the likelihood that our life will become easier, more rewarding, and filled with the achievements we desire.

Having a positive outlookis essential for achieving success in life. First, a positive attitude improves the quality of our work and study, which leads to better results. When we approach tasks with optimism, we are more focused and motivated, so we can perform more efficiently and achieve higher standards. Second, a positive mindset helps us build stronger relationships with other people. By staying calm and friendly, we can ease tension, show respect, and create a supportive environment that benefits both ourselves and those around us. Third, optimism fuels perseverance. When challenges arise, a positive attitude prevents us from giving up; instead, we keep trying, learning from each attempt until we finally reach our goals. It also builds resilience, allowing us to recover quickly from setbacks and maintain momentum toward our aspirations. Finally, a positive outlook enhances our performance at work. With confidence and enthusiasm we are more likely to acquire new skills, take on responsibilities, and advance in our careers, often resulting in better positions and higher pay. In contrast, a negative attitude limits our potential and makes it difficult to accomplish anything. Therefore, cultivating a positive attitude is crucial because it influences our relationships, our ability to achieve objectives, and our professional growth.

When you're looking for advice, you might not go to the same exact person. Hopefully you do talk to more than one person to make a better choice and give up the less opportunity cost. Seeking guidance often means you won’t rely on a single source. It is usually better to speak with several people so you can compare options and avoid the cost of a poor decision. Most individuals choose to get advice from more than one person rather than let one person’s view dominate their choice.  

When you hear many different takes, you can see the situation from angles you might never have considered, which helps you avoid blind spots. One advantage of gathering advice from a group is the variety of possibilities you receive. With many perspectives on the table, you have a broader set of choices to consider, which can lead to a more satisfactory outcome. However, the final decision may be swayed by the majority opinion, for better or for worse, and you will inevitably face an opportunity cost — either you make a wise move or you make a mistake that can affect many areas of your life, from your mood today to long‑term goals.  

Another benefit is that hearing different viewpoints lets you filter out advice that does not fit your situation. You can adopt suggestions that seem helpful and discard those that appear irrelevant, learning from both positive and negative examples. This process can sharpen your own judgment and even enable you to support others who face similar dilemmas, either by sharing what you have learned or by offering direct help.  

On the downside, consulting multiple people can also be problematic. The differing opinions may confuse you, causing you to question your original thinking and potentially choose a path that is not optimal. Moreover, the effort required to evaluate each suggestion can be time‑consuming and exhausting, especially if the sources are not reliable. The pressure of weighing several suggestions can increase stress, and the final choice may turn out to be either the best or the worst decision of your life. Deciding which advice to follow is therefore a difficult and sometimes overwhelming task.  

In summary, talking to several people when you need advice offers a richer selection of options and the chance to learn, but it also brings the risk of indecision, undue stress, and the possibility of an unsatisfactory outcome.

Several schoolsprovide the possibility for students to study from home using online platforms or video lessons, while other schools refuse to offer such an option, claiming that learning at a distance is ineffective. I disagree with the schools that do not provide distance learning, because I believe that attending classes in person generally leads to better outcomes for most learners. While it is true that online lessons can give students flexibility, the overall effectiveness of remote education is questionable for the majority of learners.

First, when a student encounters a concept that is difficult to understand, there is often no one nearby to explain it immediately. In a classroom the teacher can give instant clarification, whereas at home the learner must wait for a later conversation, search for information online, or rely on limited resources, which can slow comprehension. Moreover, teachers can use chat or email to answer questions, but these methods do not provide the same immediacy and personal connection as a face‑to‑face discussion.

Second, the school environment creates a structured setting that encourages concentration. Being physically present allows direct interaction with classmates, immediate questioning of the teacher, and a routine that helps maintain focus. In addition, peer interaction and group activities foster motivation and a sense of belonging that are harder to reproduce online. The presence of a teacher who can monitor progress also helps keep students on track.

When learning occurs at home, the lack of routine and the presence of household distractions can reduce focus. Although some learners, such as those who work after school or who have caregiving duties, might find the flexibility of distance learning advantageous, these cases are relatively rare. For many students, the ability to balance work and study without a fixed schedule leads to inconsistent study habits.

Nevertheless, the majority of students benefit from the physical presence of a school. The structured timetable, the ability to receive instant feedback, and the social atmosphere all contribute to sustained effort and better retention of material. Moreover, the guidance of experienced individuals reminds us that consistent discipline and responsibility are essential for success, and attending regular classes helps develop those habits. The advice of older, wiser people — who often tell students to keep going if they truly want to succeed — reinforces the idea that effort and perseverance are key, and school attendance supports those values.

In addition, while distance learning can be useful for a minority of learners, it should not be dismissed as the only or inferior method. Schools that reject it outright ignore the potential benefits for students who need flexibility, and they also overlook the fact that many learners thrive when they can combine online resources with face‑to‑face instruction. A blended approach could give students the best of both worlds.

In conclusion, the claim that distance learning is a poor method is not fully justified. Although it may not suit every student, the primary advantage of in‑person education remains clear for most learners. Therefore, schools should consider offering distance learning as an additional option rather than refusing it completely. Moreover, advances in internet connectivity and interactive software have made remote learning more reliable and engaging than it was a few years ago. Schools that embrace both traditional and face‑to‑face instruction can better meet the diverse needs of their students and prepare them for a world where flexible learning is increasingly common. Such an approach ensures that no learner is left behind for all students.

To save energy and cut costs, some companies have introduced a four‑day work schedule, working ten hours each day. The question is whether our school should adopt a similar plan by lengthening each school day by two hours. I disagree with this proposal. The four‑day week is used by companies to reduce electricity use and give employees a longer weekend, but a school is a different institution that must meet the educational needs of many students.  

First, adding two extra hours would make the school day too long for pupils. After a full day of lessons, students are already tired, and a longer session would reduce their ability to focus on what the teacher says. Moreover, they would have less time after school to finish homework, which could lead to lower grades. For example, I work part‑time after school and must arrive at four o’clock; if classes ended later, I would miss my shift and could lose the job, a situation that would also affect other students who have similar responsibilities. Many students also have family duties, such as caring for younger siblings, which would become even more difficult with a longer school day.  

Second, the extra hours would create additional problems for attendance and academic performance. When lessons become longer, students are more likely to feel exhausted, which may cause them to skip school or arrive late. Poor attendance is a serious issue because it directly influences whether a student can pass the year. When students are exhausted they may even fall asleep in class which reduces participation and makes it harder for teachers to assess understanding. Consequently, the proposed schedule would not improve learning; it would harm both concentration and attendance.  

In conclusion, extending the school day by two hours is not a suitable solution for conserving energy or resources. The added workload would make students more fatigued, limit their time for homework, and jeopardize their employment and attendance records. For these reasons, I believe our school should keep the regular timetable rather than adopt the four‑day, ten‑hour model. A balanced school day that respects students’ energy levels and personal responsibilities is essential indeed for effective learning and overall well‑being. This makes the plan impractical.

Many people believe that a student’ssense of worth depends on what they achieve, but I think both genuine effort and positive feedback are crucial. In schools, teachers often use comments to highlight progress, and students quickly notice whether their hard work is seen. When pupils work hard, even if the result is not perfect, they learn perseverance and develop a sense of responsibility. Recognising their effort with sincere praise reinforces confidence and encourages them to keep improving. Likewise, real achievements—whether a high grade, a successful project, or a personal milestone—provide concrete evidence that they are capable, which also strengthens self‑esteem. The combination of hard work and acknowledgment creates a positive cycle: praise motivates further effort, and successful effort produces pride that fuels future confidence. Specific comments that point out what a student did well help them see the connection between effort and result. When a pupil receives such clear feedback, they are more likely to repeat the successful strategies in future tasks. Students who receive regular encouragement tend to perform better not only for themselves but also as role models for classmates, fostering a supportive classroom atmosphere. Moreover, the feeling of being valued by teachers or peers makes learners more willing to take risks and try new challenges. Therefore, neither achievement alone nor praise alone is sufficient; each supports the other in building a healthy self‑image. In short, fostering both diligent effort and constructive feedback helps students develop lasting self‑esteem and a positive attitude toward learning. These combined experiences teach learners that growth comes from both personal effort and the support they receive from others. Consequently, students become more confident not only in school subjects but also in tackling challenges outside the classroom and overall well‑being today.

From what I have observed, the claim that first impressions are unchangeable is false. In my view, people often maintain that view because the person they are meeting shows little interest or seems disengaged, which can shape a negative initial impression. However, an initial impression does not lock a person into a permanent judgment; individuals are capable of growth and transformation.  

A key point is that a bad day or personal difficulties can temporarily affect how someone behaves, leading to a less favorable first impression. For instance, my best friend and I first met in a mathematics class. At that time he seemed reluctant to talk and ignored my questions about the material, giving me the impression that he was uninterested. Yet, over the following months we spent more time together, collaborated on assignments, and discovered shared interests. Today we are close friends, showing that the early impression was not permanent.  

Therefore, I disagree with the idea that first impressions are impossible to alter. The evidence from my own experience demonstrates that people can change their behavior, attitude, and relationship with others after an initial encounter. It is clear that flexibility in perception benefits both personal relationships and social interactions. Consequently, we should not judge someone solely on the basis of a first meeting, as circumstances and personal development can readily reshape those first impressions.

Inmy prompt I wanted to see how people behave when they get to know one another, and I think it is amazing how attitudes can shift once a connection is made. I have tried hard to get along with many people, but not everyone is kind; there are still those who bully or prejudice others without even meeting them. Because of this, I often feel isolated, since many people gossip about others and I dislike that habit.  

The individuals who threaten bullying usually do not say anything directly; they simply assume they can act aggressively. I try not to let their words affect me, because their chatter is their own problem. However, when someone becomes upset about this, they may get hurt, and then they come looking for me when they are in trouble.  

When I am angry or sad, I usually play soccer, which helps me forget my worries. If I could, I would organize soccer matches for anyone who wants to play, so they too could distract themselves from their problems. Sports are valuable because they let people have fun without resorting to violence.  

Besides soccer, there are many other ways to meet new people: going to the cinema with friends, watching a soccer, basketball or volleyball game, or simply spending time at the beach. All these activities give us a chance to connect and enjoy ourselves.  

I believe every problem has a solution, but the main obstacle is a lack of respect for one another. If we treated each other with respect, the situation would improve. We should involve families to help stop those who cause harm, and encourage young people to study hard so they can leave difficult backgrounds and secure better jobs. A high‑school education opens doors to decent employment.  

Feeling safe means having what you need and knowing you can call the police if someone tries to take it from you. People should not be frightened; showing fear can make others take advantage. We are all capable of smart decisions, and we should stay calm rather than angry, because anger can hurt both ourselves and others.  

To avoid conflict, it helps to invite people to play sports or spend time together at the beach. This keeps the mood light and can turn acquaintances into lasting friends. Finally, no one should reveal their most vulnerable point, because friends might use that information against you.

Failure is a crucial part of becoming successful. When we fail, we learn what not to repeat. To illustrate, picture a young athlete who wants to turn professional in soccer. He has played for elite clubs, was named the best player on his team, and has never been dropped from a roster. One afternoon his coach informed him that a professional trial is taking place the next week and gave him a detailed schedule to follow. The plan required a balanced diet and rigorous daily training. Some evenings he felt exhausted and tempted to eat junk food, but he resisted and kept to the regimen. The trial day arrived and he felt ready. The session began with warm‑up drills and then moved to skill exercises. He played confidently, even looking like the strongest participant on the field. At the conclusion the officials gathered everyone who had qualified and announced their names. He was not called, meaning he did not earn a spot on the team. He felt a mix of disappointment and frustration, but he refused to let the setback define his future. 

This moment highlights the importance of enthusiasm and perseverance. He could stop playing soccer and look for a different path, or he could stay determined and try again. Failure reveals how patient and resilient a person can be, and whether they are ready to face repeated setbacks. A compelling example is the narrative of a writer who was trying to sell a manuscript while living in a cramped flat with his child. He struggled to find a publisher, faced the risk of eviction because his bills were unpaid, and spent several weeks homeless. Nevertheless, he continued to promote his work. Eventually a buyer recognized the quality of his writing, began recommending it, and sales increased. His persistence turned rejection into success, proving that perseverance after failure leads to achievement. This story shows that even when circumstances are harsh, continued effort can eventually bring reward. Consequently, failure is the key to achieving success.

Ibelieve that a 10‑hour workday is superior to an 8‑hour one because it reduces energy use and frees up more personal time. If we work ten hours each day for four days, the weekly total reaches forty hours, still leaving Friday and Saturday free for extra overtime if needed. A schedule that runs from ten in the morning until ten at night is more convenient than the usual nine‑to‑five routine.

My suggestion for schools is to lengthen the daily period by two hours, turning the day into ten hours and keeping the week to four days. With this change, students would finish school earlier on the weekend, giving them more rest and more time to complete assignments at home or at part‑time jobs. Teachers would also benefit, gaining three days off each week, which could improve their wellbeing and productivity.

When pupils have sufficient sleep, they concentrate better in class and feel more energetic throughout the day. Extra evening hours mean they can finish homework without rushing, and they have the whole weekend to study or relax. Moreover, fewer school days mean lower consumption of electricity, water and other resources, helping the environment and cutting costs. In short, a ten‑hour day over four days can enhance learning, support families, and promote sustainability. Self‑confidence is essential for people to feel positive about themselves. For many students, developing this confidence is difficult because of how they were raised or how others treat them. Learners ought to nurture self‑esteem for their own benefit, even though the learning process can be tough at first; it is simply one obstacle that requires sustained effort. They must keep trying even when progress feels slow, because persistence is the key to real confidence. Some may argue that praising sub‑par work lowers academic standards. In my view, students should attempt tasks they can understand well enough, taking personal risks to prove their confidence. Critics might say that building self‑confidence is not easy, yet the real source of true self‑esteem lies in genuine achievements, not in empty praise. Empty praise can give a false sense of security and does not help students grow. Achievements are earned when individuals are willing to take risks and push themselves throughout their schooling. There will be moments when giving up seems inevitable, especially when personal problems arise, but overcoming those challenges reinforces confidence. The effort and perseverance required to succeed create a truly lasting sense of self‑belief that cannot be replaced by mere compliments.

Although many believe that doing nothingserves a purpose, everyone needs something to occupy their time. Having a purposeful activity is essential for a fulfilling life. People who remain inactive often lack direction, show little concern for others, and miss opportunities for success. An active individual can achieve greater achievements and improve the prospects of their family and future generations. In contrast, a lazy person who avoids effort may neglect responsibilities and even harm those around them.

Many people worldwide are unemployed yet refuse to seek work. They prefer to stay idle, wasting time instead of looking for a job, which contributes to persistent poverty. In several countries, the idle go to streets begging for money, missing the many chances available to them. Such behavior reflects a lack of motivation and a belief that life should be easy without effort.

The consequences of inactivity extend to families and children. When parents are inactive, children may be forced to work at a young age to compensate, exposing them to hardship and street begging. Inactive parents also fail to provide guidance, leading to a cycle of dependency.

In schools, students often display laziness during group tasks, preferring the easiest parts and avoiding responsibility. This attitude can hinder their development and create difficulties when they enter the workforce, where they may expect tasks to be simple and avoid challenges. Consequently, they may struggle to find employment and rely on easy, low‑skill jobs.

Being active brings clear benefits. An active person sets goals, works purposefully, and can improve their economic situation. Societies with lower levels of inactivity tend to experience stronger economies and fewer people living in poverty. By engaging in meaningful activities, individuals can support their families, contribute to their communities, and secure a better future.

Ralph Waldo Emerson claimedthat true greatness comes from being completely self‑reliant. I disagree with this view because throughout life we regularly depend on other people. Success often requires cooperation, and the ability to make good choices depends on the support we receive from others.  

First, consider the workplace. In many jobs you will encounter a colleague whose attitude or habits are difficult to get along with. Rather than insisting on complete independence, it is more productive to find ways to collaborate. By working together you may discover that the person can offer skills or information you need later on. Moreover, staying in a job that does not match your aspirations does not mean you cannot strive for a better position; the experience of working in an unsuitable role can actually motivate you to pursue your true goals. Numerous companies achieve their objectives through teamwork, showing that collective effort, not solitary effort, drives progress.  

Second, social life illustrates the same principle. Some individuals prefer to be alone because they feel comfortable without close contact, while others avoid crowds because they enjoy being the center of attention. Both types may be classified as asocial or attention‑seeking, yet neither group is immune to the need for connection. People can learn to interact more smoothly by observing one another, offering assistance, or simply being patient. When someone seeks help, the willingness to respond can transform a strained relationship into a constructive one.  

Finally, personal decisions shape the path we travel. We may choose to follow the expectations of society or to chart our own course. A president, for example, cannot accomplish major reforms alone; he must rely on the legislature and his advisors. Likewise, each person decides whether to let external pressures dictate his life or to set personal objectives and pursue them with determination. The easy route often means surrendering to the crowd, whereas taking responsibility means making deliberate choices that reflect one’s own values.  

In conclusion, Emerson’s ideal of constant self‑reliance overlooks the reality that human beings thrive through collaboration. Whether at work, in society, or when making life decisions, the ability to cooperate, seek help, and decide independently creates a fuller, more purposeful life. Therefore, individuality does not exclude the need for teamwork; rather, it includes the capacity to choose when and how to work with others.

I agree that a person’s attitude is the most important factor in shaping a successful and fulfilling life. The way we act toward others reveals our attitude, and when we meet someone who is friendly and humble, they usually see us as respectable and kind. A positive attitude makes other people feel comfortable, so they are more willing to talk with us and spend time together. For example, when a child first meets his father, the father’s first impression is based on the child’s attitude; a well‑mannered, respectful child makes his father proud and confident in him.

Respect and a good attitude are closely connected. To gain respect from others we must first show respect and keep a courteous demeanor. This principle applies not only in daily conversations but also in raising children. Parents should teach their kids to treat people kindly and to stay humble, because a good attitude helps youngsters become balanced individuals who appreciate the beauty of life. When children learn to be respectful and optimistic, they are more likely to grow into adults who are trusted and admired.

In modern society many people lack a proper attitude; they are rude, dismissive, and unwilling to listen. This shortage makes communication difficult and weakens social bonds. Therefore it is essential to promote kindness, respect, and humility in every area of life. Schools should include lessons on attitude, teaching students how to speak politely, how to listen attentively, and how to interact with people of any age. By learning these skills early, young people can build stronger relationships and achieve greater personal success.

Attitude also influences personal happiness and career advancement. A person who approaches work with a positive, respectful mindset is more likely to receive praise, gain trust, and progress in his or her profession. Moreover, a humble outlook reduces conflicts and creates a calmer environment at home and in the community. When we consistently show respect, we earn the confidence of friends, family, and colleagues, which in turn supports our overall well‑being.

Ultimately, attitude is the foundation of a meaningful life. John Lubbock, aBritish naturalist and politician, once said that a person’s character is shaped by the choices they make. I agree with this view, because although our past experiences influence us, the decisions we take each day determine who we become. For instance, a child raised in an abusive home may feel damaged, yet he or she can decide to respond with resilience rather than bitterness, thereby strengthening character. The power to choose lies in our actions, not in any fixed trait.

Some people argue that a person is simply “mean” or “unwilling to share,” suggesting that these labels describe innate character. In reality, such behavior often reflects personality traits that have been cultivated through personal decisions. When we recognize that we are the architects of our own character, we stop letting others define us. No one else can judge us until they understand our background and the choices we have made. Our character can lift us up and leave a lasting legacy.

Consider someone whose parent dies from illness; the grief may plunge them into sadness, but they can choose to honor that parent by living purposefully, turning sorrow into motivation. Each small step taken in that direction builds a stronger self‑image, and over time the person becomes a source of pride for family and community. Others may ask how they managed to become so strong or independent, and the answer lies in the deliberate choices they made. Even when circumstances seem unfavorable, the ability to choose our response remains a powerful tool. By deciding to act with courage, patience, or kindness, we transform obstacles into opportunities for growth. Such deliberate choices reinforce the notion that character is not a fixed trait but a dynamic construction shaped by daily actions. When we look back, we see that each decision, however small, has added a brick to the edifice of who we become.

Many of us experience doubt, thinking we are incapable of achieving certain goals. Negative thoughts may whisper that the task is impossible, but these mental barriers can be overcome by focusing on what we can control. Our character is not meant to keep us down; it is a force that pushes us past obstacles, like walls that life throws our way. By confronting those challenges, we prove to ourselves that we can break through. Therefore, we should not allow fear or external opinions to dictate our path. Trusting our intuition and following our heart leads us toward decisions that align with our values. When we act in accordance with what we know is right, we shape a character that stands out, because it is uniquely ours. Life does not offer a menu of pre‑selected options; it offers a canvas on which we paint our own story. As the quote reminds us, our character will be what we ourselves choose to make, and we should embrace that responsibility, enjoy the process, and let every action contribute to building a stronger, more authentic self. This is the true power of choice.

Doyou ever feel that spending extra hours at school after the regular day is pointless when you could be enjoying leisure activities? All the sports you love could be jeopardized if you join a homework club after school. Therefore, students ought not to attend after‑school homework clubs because they cut into family time, prevent participation in favorite sports, and make it impossible to play those sports.  

First, attending a club after school reduces the time you can spend with your family. Imagine a student whose parents plan to eat out for dinner, but the student must stay for the club. He calls his mother and says he cannot make it, and she reminds him they were supposed to go to their favorite restaurant, Red Lobster. He misses the meal because of the club, showing how the club interferes with family moments.  

Second, the club also disrupts participation in sports. Suppose a student plays basketball and is enrolled in an after‑school English club. On Wednesday he must attend the club, then go to basketball practice, arriving five minutes late. The coach marks this as the first strike, and after a third strike the student is removed from the team. Thus, the club can cost a student his spot on a team he is passionate about.  

Third, the club limits the time available for video gaming. A student who streams games on YouTube every day may find that after‑school club pushes his return home to around 7 p.m., leaving little time for both homework and gaming. Moreover, if he has just purchased a new game that can only be played on weekends, the club steals the weekdays when he could practice, causing him to lose many of his online followers. He ends up missing half of his audience because the club occupies his evenings.  

In conclusion, after‑school homework clubs are a waste of time for students who have other activities. Doing homework at home is more flexible, and sports or gaming should not be sacrificed for extra classroom hours. Therefore, students should avoid after‑school homework clubs if they do not want to spend additional time in school.

In my view, technology has essentially taken over modern society because many cannot imagine life without their phones.

Having a positive mindset is the most effective way to achieve success. Attitudes can be grouped into two categories: a constructive, optimistic outlook and a destructive, pessimistic one. When we approach situations with a constructive attitude, we are more likely to resolve conflicts, maintain good relationships, and stay motivated even during challenging periods. For instance, if we disagree with a supervisor about salary, speaking calmly and respectfully can lead to a mutually acceptable solution, whereas an aggressive tone may result in termination. Positive attitudes also help us get through dull or unpleasant moments; imagine a family road trip that feels tedious, but a cheerful outlook can lift the spirits of everyone in the car and make the journey enjoyable. There are many simple habits that foster a positive attitude: getting enough rest, enjoying sunny weather, receiving a thoughtful gift, eating a favorite dish at a preferred restaurant, spending time with close friends, visiting relatives, embarking on a pleasant trip, and countless other experiences. Conversely, a negative attitude can steer us onto an unproductive path. People who constantly display a bad attitude often struggle to form friendships and may find themselves isolated. A typical example is a student who arrives at school stressed and irritable; after a teacher’s seemingly minor action, the student erupts in anger, prompting the teacher to send the student to the guidance office and issue a disciplinary report. Another frequent manifestation is a desire to argue or fight, which can quickly escalate into serious trouble. Factors that contribute to a negative outlook include exhaustion, an overwhelming workload, bad weather that limits outdoor activity, exposure to another person’s hostility, feelings of anger toward someone, or hunger when the food is unsatisfactory. When I maintain a positive attitude, I experience the best moments in my life. Things that lift my mood include enjoying my favorite meals, receiving a present, or being surrounded by family. For example, yesterday my cousin celebrated his birthday at an exciting venue; I approached the day with enthusiasm, played games with him, and savored delicious food, which made the occasion memorable. I also feel upbeat when my family and I travel together, because exploring new places broadens our horizons and creates lasting memories. In another situation, my science teacher displayed a caring demeanor, granting us an extra day to submit a project. The advantages of cultivating a positive mindset are numerous. Before an important exam, studying with confidence and a calm outlook helps me wake up feeling assured, and I am more likely to perform well. The greatest benefit, however, is the sense of happiness that accompanies a positive attitude; feeling joyful is, in my view, the most rewarding experience a person can have. In summary, a constructive attitude supports success in various areas such as work, school, and family gatherings. Therefore, whenever we encounter difficulty or feel down, the most effective response is to adopt a positive attitude. Adopting a positive mindset can truly transform everyday life for us.

Partnerships between schools and businesses can be very useful for students who are looking for opportunities before they enter college. Through such collaborations, students can visit companies, observe daily activities, and discover which kinds of work interest them. When schools have formal ties with firms, many learners are able to clarify their career preferences.  

I believe I would be a good candidate for this program because I enjoy being around people, I want to find out what kind of job suits me, and I am eager to gain practical experience. Some people feel uncomfortable in social settings, but I find interacting with others uplifting. Whenever I am in a group, even with strangers, starting a conversation quickly creates a sense of familiarity.  

Many students already know what they want to study, yet I am still uncertain about my future direction. I often ask myself what I am good at and have not yet identified a specific strength. While some people end up in jobs they dislike because of family pressures, I think it is better to choose a career that brings personal satisfaction. Before committing to a particular role, it is wise to try it out so that I can understand what the job actually involves.  

For example, I once wanted to work in a restaurant but knew nothing about the tasks involved. I asked a friend who was already employed there, and that brief conversation gave me a clearer picture. In some professions, such as nursing, hands‑on experience is essential, whereas other fields may rely more on research. If I were selected for a partnership, I could explore nursing or other occupations and take part in real‑world activities, which would help me decide.  

Therefore, I think the school should choose me, not because I am the only one who wants this, but because I value teamwork, I am eager to discover suitable work, and I seek the chance to experience different jobs before making a final decision.

Dear Principal,

I believethat replacing the current cafeteria menu with healthier, more varied options would be a positive change for the whole school community. Introducing new, nutritious meals would give every student access to food they have not tried before, and it would help those who are tired of the same daily dishes. To make this transition smooth, I think the first step should be for you to speak with the cafeteria manager and request a list of the meals that students enjoy most and those that are eaten the least.

If we keep the dishes that are popular and replace the ones that see little consumption, the new menu will retain the favorites while offering fresh alternatives. This approach would likely increase student satisfaction, because they would still have the foods they like, and at the same time they would discover healthier choices. A more diverse menu could also make our school a model for other institutions, encouraging them to adopt similar improvements.

The benefits extend beyond student happiness. When the cafeteria provides appealing, wholesome meals, parents may spend less on buying snacks or meals outside of school, which can ease financial pressure. Moreover, students are less likely to skip class to purchase food from nearby shops, reducing safety concerns for both pupils and parents. By offering balanced meals that include more proteins, less fat, and essential nutrients, we can support better health and concentration in class.

Some students have food allergies that limit what they can eat in the current menu, leading them to rely on home‑cooked meals or to go without eating altogether. A broader selection of safe, healthy options would allow these students to eat at school without worry, improving attendance and overall well‑being. In addition, a nutritious diet can help reduce the risk of obesity and related health problems, contributing to a healthier school environment.

I understand that change can be challenging, especially for those who are attached to the existing menu. However, involving students in the decision‑making process — by gathering their preferences and adjusting the menu accordingly — will make the transition easier for everyone. The goal is not to discard the foods students love, but to enhance the menu with options that promote health and variety.

In conclusion, I strongly support a revised cafeteria menu that balances popular items with healthier, more diverse choices. By consulting the cafeteria manager, reviewing student preferences, and making informed adjustments, the school can create a meal program that satisfies students, supports parents, and fosters a positive reputation. Thank you for considering these ideas.

Sincerely,  
A Student

Most of usthink that failing to reach a high target is the biggest risk, yet the real problem is settling for a low target and thinking we have succeeded. I maintain that striving for an ambitious goal is not harmful; even if the goal seems out of reach, the attempt itself can be valuable. While Michelangelo suggested that effort alone can make anyone achieve anything, I disagree with the idea that one must lower the target to make progress. The height of the goal is irrelevant; what matters is that you can reach the intended result, no matter which route you choose. For instance, I am currently preparing for a school leaving exam; I could aim for the highest possible score or settle for the minimum required to pass, and in either case I can still obtain the diploma. Effort does not guarantee success, nor does it limit the outcome; you can reach any objective regardless of how hard you work or which path you follow. This pattern appears in many areas of life—work, education, and even within humanity as a whole. Moreover, many people deliberately lower their own expectations, believing that modest standards make life easier. In short, the greatest danger is not aiming too high, but aiming too low and assuming that achievement is assured.

In my opinion,the most valuable accomplishment is when someone tells you that you can be yourself, without pretending to be someone else. It is far better to live authentically than to constantly act a false role. When we hide our true nature, we are essentially lying to ourselves and to others, and that creates unnecessary problems.  

People often think that behaving in a way that does not reflect who they are is advantageous, but I strongly disagree. We should stop worrying about what others think and concentrate on our own values and on the individuals who accept us as we are. Those who do not judge us are the true friends, and their acceptance is the best gift we can receive. It shows that we are unique and that we do not need to change to fit someone else’s expectations.  

Ralph Waldo Emerson once suggested that we should strive to become better versions of ourselves, but I think his idea misses the point. The real achievement is not constantly trying to reshape ourselves for the world, but rather showing the world the genuine person we already are. Each person possesses a distinct quality that contributes to making the world richer, and that contribution is only possible when we stay true to ourselves.  

A personal experience illustrates this point. When I was sixteen, a friend constantly pretended to have a lot of money. She claimed she was wealthy, even though her family’s income was modest. Because of this lie, many of our classmates became close to her, while they stopped talking to me, urging me to join parties, drink, and smoke. I refused, and eventually they discovered that she was not as rich as she said. The revelation showed that pretending does not bring lasting respect; honesty does.  

Therefore, I always encourage people to be themselves, even when it is difficult. Acceptance from others begins with authenticity, and a world where people feel safe to express their true selves is a better world. The greatest accomplishment, then, is simply being honest and true to who we are.

Why should anyone tell others what trulymatters in life or which choices to make? Each person can choose how to live, and if they are self‑reliant they do not need someone else to dictate their path. It is better for individuals to decide for themselves, even when they feel uncertain, because any error they make becomes a lesson that improves future actions. Feeling confident in one’s own judgment also brings security when facing later decisions, and by figuring out what is important on their own, they discover personal values. Many people make mistakes by choosing poorly, but those errors are not failures; they are opportunities to learn how to do things correctly. Some turn to experts when a big decision looms, fearing a wrong choice, and that is understandable. Yet trusting oneself first, rather than immediately seeking another’s advice, is usually the wiser approach. When people rely on their own judgment they gain confidence, which helps them make better choices later, even if the initial decision turns out wrong. The experience of learning from those mistakes equips them to choose correctly next time, without needing outside help. Therefore, it is unnecessary for others to tell us what matters or what decisions to take. We should give ourselves time to reflect, consider what is important to each of us, and decide accordingly, because each person’s needs differ. By making their own choices, individuals also develop independence that benefits all areas of their lives. In short, taking personal responsibility for our choices builds security, promotes learning, and leads to a clearer understanding of what truly matters in life.

Sometimes the truth can be painful, yet I believe that being truthful is often the best policy. While there are moments when withholding information may be kinder, there are also situations where pointing out a mistake is necessary. When we are open with one another, we tend to receive honesty in return, which strengthens our relationships. Being truthful with our parents is especially valuable; if we are in trouble they can offer guidance and support, whereas secrecy prevents them from helping. If we hide our faults, trust erodes quickly; people will assume we are dishonest and may lose confidence in us forever. Admitting wrongdoing, even if it feels uncomfortable, usually leads to a more favorable resolution than trying to conceal it. Nevertheless, honesty can cause hurt, and some individuals prefer to avoid that pain. In such cases, we must weigh the benefit of protecting someone's feelings against the long‑term damage of a lie. I have found that being honest with friends is preferable because they will appreciate the candidness and value a relationship built on truth. If we keep secrets, they may feel deceived later, which can damage the friendship. Likewise, honesty with partners prevents misunderstandings and builds trust. From my experience, truthfulness is a useful skill in adult life. When we have a job, a family, or other responsibilities, we need to face reality as it is. Life can be unfair, and being prepared to accept the facts helps us cope better. Therefore, while honesty does not guarantee a painless path, I believe it is generally the better choice, and I would rather surround myself with people who tell the truth rather than those who keep secrets.

Manypeople argue that the summer vacation is too brief and should be altered, and they also suggest removing the spring break. They claim that the summer period should begin in June and finish in August, because May is often still cool and not suitable for a holiday, while June offers warm weather that is perfect for traveling with family and friends.

If the spring break were eliminated, students would gain an extra week that could be devoted to preparing for the SOL and reviewing material for the final exam. This additional time would allow teachers to provide more focused instruction, offer extra practice sessions, and give learners the opportunity to ask questions and receive help in class.

The week that would replace spring break could be used for a variety of engaging activities. Schools could organize sports events, workshops, and field trips to museums, concerts, or universities, making learning more enjoyable while still reinforcing academic skills. More extracurricular options would keep students motivated and help them develop new interests.

Overall, the community that supports changing the calendar believes that a longer summer break starting in June and ending in August, together with the removal of spring break, would give students more time to study, improve their test performance, and enjoy a richer school experience. Therefore, we agree with the view that the school schedule should be revised to provide three months of summer and no spring break, allowing greater preparation for the SOL and final assessments. This change would also give teachers more flexibility to plan lessons and assess progress throughout the year. Students would also benefit from a longer break to relax and recharge before the new school year.

One time I applied to aprivate school and had a conversation with its principal. He told me that a student should decide on a specific career before entering high school. I agree with this perspective because knowing what you want to study early helps you concentrate your efforts and become proficient in the future. Whenever I enjoy an activity, I want to do it constantly, so having a career I like means I can practice it regularly. Playing soccer not only keeps me fit but also teaches teamwork and discipline, qualities that are valuable in any profession. Another passion of mine is soccer; I play it frequently in the summer and hope to become a professional player, which shows how dedication to a beloved activity can shape a future career. She studied diligently, performed the duties that nurses carry out, and after six years of work she now works as a qualified nurse, fulfilling the ambition she had as a child. Her dedication shows that perseverance can overcome challenges and lead to success. This example demonstrates that persistent effort can lead to the desired profession, even when obstacles arise. I disagreewith the school districts that propose letting students earn their diploma in three years instead of the usual four. A three‑year program would not give students enough time to learn properly. In order to keep up, they would have to study intensely during the summer and in the evenings, which would tire their brains and leave no room for rest. Without regular breaks, they would also miss out on important elective courses that broaden their education.

One possible benefit of finishing early is that students could graduate sooner, but this advantage is outweighed by the drawbacks. The accelerated schedule forces learners to work hard all year round, reducing their ability to focus on what they truly want to study and to explore different career paths. Moreover, the extra pressure can harm their mental health and academic performance.

By contrast, a four‑year plan allows students to spread their workload more evenly, giving them time to recover during holidays and to engage in extracurricular activities. This extra year provides space to think about future goals, choose appropriate courses, and develop the skills needed for university or the workplace. It also gives them more free time for personal interests, which contributes to a healthier, more balanced life.

Therefore, the three‑year diploma is not a good idea. Students who finish early may also miss important social experiences and feel less prepared for the transition to higher education or work. Four years offers the necessary time for proper learning, reduces stress, and better prepares students for the challenges ahead.

Should we achieve more by stayingconstantly active? I believe that people who keep working constantly bring new inventions such as radios, televisions and cars. If nobody were occupied, technological progress would be much slower. Technology must be developed and refined, because it creates jobs and improves everyday life. The more people engage in productive activity, the more society changes for the better.  

Historical examples show this clearly. The radio was a major breakthrough; inventors struggled to tune it correctly, but their perseverance paid off. When the device finally worked, it became popular and sparked further innovation. That same drive pushed the development of television, which added visual images to the audio experience. The first television set was a novelty, offering something people could watch rather than only listen to a film. Its success motivated manufacturers to improve the product and to market it widely, which in turn created more jobs.  

The same pattern repeats with computers. Early computers had no sound and were used mainly for basic programming tasks. As enthusiasts worked to make them more user‑friendly, more people wanted to own them, and the market expanded. This demand encouraged further research, leading to modern machines that can perform complex calculations and even simulate real‑world situations.  

In each case, the key factor is determination to keep working. When individuals are occupied, they notice problems, devise solutions and push inventions forward. Constant activity therefore accelerates technological advancement, which reshapes how we live and creates new opportunities for employment. If we stopped moving, progress would stall, and the benefits of new technology would be delayed.

In my view, itis not advantageous for learners to attend lessons from home via online platforms. First, studying at home brings many distractions. A video game, a pet, or household chores can easily pull a student’s attention away from the lesson, and the presence of other family members makes it hard to concentrate. The home environment also contains television, mobile phones, and other devices that compete for attention, further reducing actual study time. In a classroom, the teacher stands directly in front of the pupil, offering immediate guidance that makes the learning process clearer and more efficient.

Second, remote learning is not suitable for all situations. For example, in my own house there are three brothers and a sister, so the environment is noisy and chaotic, which hinders focus. Moreover, research suggests that children retain information better when they study in the morning, when they are more alert, rather than in the evening after a long day. Teachers can observe each student’s progress directly and give personalized feedback, which is difficult to achieve through a screen. Therefore, relying on video conferences for daily lessons is not an effective solution.

In conclusion, students achieve better results when they attend school in person rather than learning from home. Parents share this opinion because face‑to‑face instruction is more effective than distance education.

Beingyourself wherever you are is, in my opinion, a sensible approach to life. I strongly believe that it is far superior to pretending to be someone else or feeling uncomfortable with your true nature. When you accept who you are, you base your actions on your own judgment rather than on the expectations of other people.  

This confidence allows you to stay steady while pursuing your objectives. Trusting yourself means you do not readily accept criticism or pressure from individuals who try to shape you, and you keep your focus on the goals you have set for yourself.  

For example, acting authentically shows those around you how strong and capable you are, which motivates you to continue improving. By staying true to your values, you demonstrate that personal growth is possible when you follow a path that reflects your own aspirations instead of the one suggested by society.  

Moreover, your example can encourage other people to rethink their own habits and to seek a better life on their own terms. When they observe someone living according to personal principles, they may realize that change is achievable even if the dominant culture pushes a different agenda.  

Of course, obstacles are inevitable. Some people or groups may try to block your progress, hoping you will fail or give up. In such situations, having a clear purpose and confidence in yourself becomes crucial, because it shields you from being swayed away from your intended target.  

Maintaining a strong sense of self also supports your mental health. When you rely on your own judgment, you are less likely to feel anxious or confused by external pressures. This inner stability helps you bounce back from setbacks and keeps you motivated to pursue your aspirations over the long term.  

When you trust yourself and keep a well‑defined goal in mind, obstacles become more manageable. Your self‑respect also attracts the respect of others, creating a positive feedback loop where you and those around you motivate each other to grow.  

When you show respect to yourself, you also demonstrate respect for others, which encourages mutual trust and cooperation. This reciprocal attitude not only builds stronger relationships but also helps you stay focused on your goals despite external distractions.  

In summary, staying authentic and working hard to improve your life is the right way to achieve happiness and personal growth. Even if society changes around you or others try to push you in another direction, maintaining your own identity and purpose enables you to succeed and to inspire others to do the same.  

By staying true to yourself, you not only achieve personal fulfillment but also contribute positively to the community, showing that authenticity can be a force for good and inspire others to do the same and inspire future generations.

This inner stability helps you bounce back from setbacks and keeps you motivated to pursue your aspirations over the long term.

Living in an environment that constantlydemands the highest quality is, for me, a crucial accomplishment. I share Emerson’s view that personal individuality enables us to achieve our objectives. Recognizing that we must pursue our goals through effort is essential, because hard work, competition, and the drive to be the best are the engines of progress.  

When I rely on my own abilities, I feel more confident that I can reach the standards I set for myself. Independence encourages me to explore different solutions and to trust my judgment, which in turn motivates me to work harder. Working alone forces me to perfect every detail, because there is no one else to rely on; I want my work to impress the people around me. For example, when I tackle a task without a partner, I strive to produce a flawless result that stands out among my colleagues. This sense of personal achievement often leads to recognition, such as awards or praise, which everyone desires for their effort.  

Many people, like me, find that solitary work creates a strong emotional drive to excel. The pride that comes from completing a project on my own boosts my motivation and increases the quantity and quality of my output. In factories, workers who operate independently tend to generate higher production levels, which benefits the whole organization.  

Competition, although it can undermine teamwork, also serves as a powerful catalyst for individual improvement. When a worker receives a higher salary or additional benefits for superior performance, others may become resentful, creating tension. Yet this rivalry often pushes employees to innovate, seek more efficient methods, and aim for greater output. For instance, a worker who finishes a task ahead of schedule might be granted extra free time, prompting fellow employees to search for ways to match or exceed that efficiency in order to earn the same reward. In this way, healthy competition stimulates higher productivity and personal growth.  

Companies often encourage such competition by offering monetary bonuses or additional leisure time to the most productive employees. In a setting where many workers operate separately, the desire to be the top performer can lead to a significant overall increase in output. Therefore, structured challenges that allow individuals to showcase their skills can be beneficial, provided they are balanced with cooperation.  

Beyond the workplace, the principle of self‑reliance applies to life in general. People everywhere seek recognition and success, and they must overcome criticism, bullying, or other obstacles. The most reliable path to distinction is to depend on our own efforts, especially when support from others is scarce. In society, competition is evident in fields such as sports; consider soccer, where a team of eleven players strives to be the leader on the field. The same drive exists in business, where a manager must compete with peers to attain the top position. In both cases, personal initiative and hard work are essential.  

Individuality also contributes to broader progress. In government, officials who bring unique perspectives and work independently can propose innovative policies that improve the nation. The same holds for factories, countries, and any organization that values competition: it drives advancement and raises the overall standard of performance. Consequently, I agree with Emerson that competition, when harnessed properly, yields positive benefits for individuals and for the institutions they belong to.  

In summary, a demanding environment pushes us to rely on our own capabilities, to work hard, and to view competition as a motivating force rather than a threat. By embracing individuality, putting in sustained effort, and using healthy rivalry to spur improvement, we can achieve our goals and contribute to the betterment of our communities.

Modern technology lets us finish many activities without meeting anyone else. We can order books, purchase items, and play video games online without speaking to another person. Consequently, face‑to‑face interaction has become less frequent. It is clear that humans are social beings; throughout history we have sought contact with others, and today we still rely on personal connections. For this reason, we should step back from excessive use of devices. While the internet makes shopping and gaming convenient, it also satisfies a basic need for human contact that cannot be replaced by a screen. Children are receiving tablets before they can walk, and they spend hours in class or at home glued to phones, which limits their chances to form new friendships and meet people. If we continue to replace real interaction with digital alternatives, our ability to communicate and build relationships will weaken. When we limit our screen time, we have more opportunities to talk with family, meet neighbors, and take part in community activities. This balance supports mental health and reduces feelings of isolation. Therefore, taking a break from constant technology use is essential for maintaining a healthy social life.

Iagree with Winston Churchill’s remark that true success means moving from one setback to another while keeping enthusiasm alive. It isn’t realistic to expect constant victories; obstacles are inevitable. My own experience illustrates this point. Last year I sat for an English exam in my school class. I had studied hard and aimed for an A or at least a B, yet I only managed to pass. Feeling disappointed, my teacher offered me a second chance, so I retook the test and this time earned an A‑. The disappointment turned into motivation, showing that persistence matters more than immediate perfection. Each time I faced a setback I learned how to improve my study habits which later helped me perform better in other subjects as well.

A similar situation occurred with my aunt, who wanted to travel to El Salvador. When she first inquired about a ticket, the fare was beyond her budget, so she postponed the trip for several months. After a few more attempts the price rose even higher, but she chose not to wait indefinitely. While finalising the purchase, she discovered that her passport had expired, preventing the transaction. Upset, she applied to renew her documents, but the processing took longer than expected; three months passed and the new passport still hadn’t arrived, leaving her unable to travel to see her grandmother. She kept checking the airline website daily and finally received the updated passport two weeks after the expected delivery date, allowing her to book the flight without further delay. Despite these repeated hurdles, she never lost her excitement for the journey.

Churchill’s observation is therefore well founded because no one is flawless, and each failure offers a lesson that makes us more resilient. Critics sometimes claim the quote is false, arguing that repeated failures label a person as a loser or a fool. When people lose hope, they often give up too soon, forgetting that many successful journeys include several stumbling blocks. In my view, such criticism stems from a loss of confidence rather than from the reality of the situation; when enthusiasm fades, people become weak, not the other way around.

In summary, success is built on the ability to endure setbacks without giving up. My experience with the English test and my aunt’s travel plans both demonstrate that staying motivated, even after multiple attempts, shapes a stronger character and ultimately leads to achievement. Therefore, embracing each failure with optimism is the true path to lasting success.

Some argue that a four‑day work week should be used as a model in schools, but I disagree. Extending the school day by two hours would mean students spend more time each day, which would increase energy use. In addition, longer days mean more electricity for computers, monitors and tablets, making it harder to conserve resources. Showing someonea concrete example is often the clearest way to teach them a better method. When a teacher demonstrates how a task should be done, the lesson feels more genuine and the student senses the instructor’s intention to help.  

In my own childhood my grandmother constantly showed me different ways to arrange objects and gave advice on many small chores. Because of her guidance I have grown to want to teach my friends and other people things they may not yet know, whether it is how to play soccer, how to locate information, or how to repair a broken toy. Throughout my life I have learned practical skills such as maintaining toys, fixing computers, and handling other everyday problems.  

I appreciate teachers who explain concepts clearly, because their approach makes learning easier for everyone. In contrast, some teachers are frequently angry or fail to teach effectively, which leads students to dislike them. Providing clear examples is, in my view, the most reliable way for students to grasp difficult ideas that they would otherwise never understand.  

Beyond academic matters, personal behavior plays a crucial role in life. The way we act in class or at home influences how others perceive us; good conduct can open doors to advice and support. When I observe someone behaving well, I am more likely to ask for guidance on how to improve my own actions.  

Watching other people also teaches me new tools that will be useful later. Although I have no specific plan after high school, I am passionate about technology and electricity, the two fields that fascinate me most. The future may bring unexpected changes, but I intend to keep learning and adapting.  

I recognize that everyone makes mistakes, and the best way to correct them is to acknowledge them and seek help for better behavior, whether at school or elsewhere. In addition to reading newspapers, watching news programs, and asking questions, many other avenues exist for gaining knowledge, and each person can contribute a small piece of wisdom according to what they know.  

People often approach me for advice because they trust my willingness to listen. I enjoy hearing others’ concerns and offering support when needed. Our lives are enriched by family, friends, neighbors, and many caring individuals who have big hearts. We all have a purpose, even if it is not yet clear, and the world our creator gave us offers countless opportunities to make a positive impact.  

My personal goal for this year is to arrive on time for every class, because punctuality reflects respect for others and for the learning environment. I also aim to pass the SOL exam and to perform well in all my subjects. My teacher, who consistently models effective communication and kindness, serves as an excellent example of how influence can be exercised through example, conversation, and encouragement. For these reasons, I truly value the school experience. I also hope to grow as a learner and a responsible citizen.

I think this is one of the best decisions you can make to enroll your child in an online school, or even yourself if you want to further your education.
