Thomas Jefferson, who served as president, expressed the idea that constant work helps people improve their abilities. When we repeat tasks regularly, they become simpler and we acquire knowledge more readily. Although the routine can sometimes feel tedious, the advantage is that persistent practice builds skill and confidence.  

I try to work, study, and exercise every day because the repetition helps me remember what I have learned and makes the tasks feel less difficult over time. For example, reading a book each day expands my understanding of many subjects, while people who never practice remain lazy and miss out on learning.  

The contrast between those who act consistently and those who do not is clear. Students who complete homework regularly, athletes who train on schedule, and workers who attend their jobs daily tend to perform better than peers who are irregular. By encouraging others to keep up their responsibilities, we can help them grow and succeed.  

My own experience illustrates this point. At the beginning of school I ignored my assignments and studied little, which hurt my progress. A friend reminded me to work steadily, and I soon found that doing my tasks every day made school easier and boosted my confidence. I now want everyone to adopt the same habit.  

Moreover, eating nutritious food on a regular basis keeps the body healthy, reducing the need for frequent medical visits. In short, maintaining a steady routine in work, study, sport, and diet leads to personal improvement and better overall well‑being.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once observed that 'unless you attempt something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow,' and his statement holds true. To grasp his meaning, we must recognize that claiming mastery means being able to perform a task flawlessly. Real development requires setting personal goals, even if the steps are modest, because each small effort moves you forward on the road to greater achievements.

Growth is not effortless; mastering a skill can take years, but confidence and belief in yourself make it possible. For example, someone who can ride a bicycle should then try a motorcycle, a person who bakes cupcakes ought to learn cake baking, and anyone who can float should teach themselves to swim. These incremental challenges reinforce existing abilities and expand your capabilities.

When you consistently push yourself, you are more likely to achieve the objectives you set, and sustained dedication enables you to surpass what you already know. It is also wrong to assume that failure in a single small task signals impossibility; perseverance and repeated effort are essential until true mastery is reached. Without continual self‑challenge, progress stalls.

Ultimately, the choice rests with you: decide whether you wish to evolve as an individual or remain unchanged and miss out on reaching your life goals. Your willingness to step outside your comfort zone determines whether you will continue to improve or stay static.

I think that a firstimpression is not set in stone; people can revise it over time. Everyone sees situations differently, so the way one person reacts may be completely unlike another’s. Some individuals do not alter their view because they simply do not care, while others change when they receive a negative impression that shakes their initial belief.  

When someone repeats the same actions day after day and ignores what others say about them, they may stay unchanged. However, a new perspective can make them reflect on their behavior, recognize mistakes, and decide to modify their attitude. Real change usually requires a strong motive; without it, people often remain stuck in old habits, repeating the same errors without much thought.  

Relationships illustrate this dynamic. Jealousy, toxicity, and negative influences are common sources of conflict. Adolescents sometimes suffer serious consequences when they believe a partner has been unfaithful, acting impulsively without considering how painful that betrayal will be for the other person. In a healthy partnership, the goal should not be to impress others or provoke jealousy; instead, personal growth and the willingness to change can strengthen the bond.  

From my own experience, I once felt that altering my self‑image was impossible. When someone told me I was a girl who let others down with my attitude, I became deeply discouraged, thinking I could never meet anyone’s expectations. I realized that I was comfortable with habits that suited me, even though they did not serve others. One day I resolved to transform myself, no matter how difficult the process might be, and I managed to do so with or without assistance.  

Changing after a first impression demonstrates that you are not the same person you once were, and it helps prevent repeating past mistakes. Although some claim that the past cannot be erased, consistent effort to move forward can lessen its impact. No one is perfect, but we can improve our attitudes, become more selective about whom we trust, and grow from each new impression we receive.

I believethe school principal should not force students to pick up trash or take part in community service, since they also have family responsibilities and other obligations such as homework and extracurricular activities. Younger children in elementary school likely have free time and can handle the task, while junior‑high pupils could help if their schedules are not too full, especially those who are not involved in sports and need time for rest. Some schools might decide to make every pupil do community work as a punishment for bad behaviour, but that seems unfair. I could volunteer on weekends to assist others, because I am occupied with school during the week. The principal ought to target only the students who misbehave, assigning them the work, which might make them reflect and become less willing to repeat the littering or other misconduct.

Choosing between collaborating withothers and working independently is a common dilemma. In my view, working by yourself is far more advantageous. When you work alone, nobody can take your ideas or duplicate your effort, which often happens in a team setting.  

Team projects can become frustrating because responsibilities are shared unevenly; members may do very little while others pick up the slack. This imbalance can make you feel uncertain of your own abilities and dependent on others for progress. Moreover, working with friends or classmates sometimes leads to plagiarism, as they may copy your work without contributing meaningfully. It is discouraging to see teammates rely on you while you receive little in return, and it feels unfair when credit is not evenly distributed.

In contrast, constant dependence on a group can erode self‑esteem, making me doubt my capabilities whenever I face a difficult assignment.

In my view, allowingstudents to join lessons from their own homes would give them clear advantages. First, they would arrive at the virtual session feeling prepared, which helps them stay concentrated. In a regular classroom many pupils feel embarrassed to show how capable they are, especially when they doubt their English skills. When they can study alone, they are less likely to worry about being judged and can concentrate on the material. Another important point is the chance to work independently. A learner who is at home can pause the lesson, look up information, or take a short break to get a snack without disturbing anyone. If a question arises, a quick message to the teacher can resolve it without the pressure of speaking in front of classmates. This independence also benefits students who are shy or who need extra help from the instructor on a one‑to‑one basis. Flexibility in timing is another strong argument. For those who find early mornings difficult, studying later in the day can be more comfortable, especially for pregnant students or young mothers who have additional responsibilities. A friend of mine continued attending school while pregnant; after giving birth she preferred to keep the lessons at home because it was far less stressful to manage a newborn while learning. Nevertheless, there are obstacles that must be considered. Not every family can afford the technology required for online classes, and some students may need to work to support themselves, which can limit their study time. However, these challenges can be addressed through school‑provided devices, subsidies, or flexible schedules that let learners balance work and study. The overall effect of home‑based learning would be positive. Students could spend more time on the computer, experience fewer distractions, and use mobile devices for research whenever needed. They would also avoid the discomfort of cold weather in winter or the pressure of dressing appropriately for school. Moreover, they would not have to interact with classmates they do not get along with, reducing the chance of conflict. In addition, studying from home may improve mental health. Many pupils suffer from anxiety or low mood, and a quieter, self‑controlled environment can help them feel calmer and more motivated. By allowing them to choose when and where they learn, schools can support their well‑being as well as their academic progress. To sum up, offering classes that students can attend from home would give them greater readiness, more focus, and a comfortable setting. While financial and logistical issues exist, they can be managed with appropriate support. The key is for students to stay determined, ask for help when needed, and put effort into their studies, proving that they can succeed regardless of the obstacles.

Many peopleargue that students should decide on a profession as soon as they start high school, because the curriculum is organized to steer them toward a particular path. I disagree with this view, since a teenager is not mature enough to make a permanent career choice. First, young people lack the experience and self‑knowledge needed to understand what a given occupation actually involves. High‑school students have never worked in a real job, so they cannot judge whether a field matches their interests or abilities. Second, adolescents often change their minds. A student may be enthusiastic about a subject in the first year, but later discover a new passion that makes the original plan obsolete. For example, a classmate who chose a technology course in his freshman year discovered that the salary expectations were far higher than he imagined, so he switched to a materials‑and‑process class and eventually pursued a career in construction. Third, the best decisions for a student are made when they have more life experience. In the senior year or during college, individuals have a clearer picture of their strengths, preferences, and the realities of the labour market, which allows them to select courses that truly prepare them for a chosen career. Therefore, the most sensible approach is to focus on achieving good grades throughout high school, while keeping an open mind about future occupations. During the early years of secondary school, students are still discovering themselves, and the subjects they study can only give a vague impression of a future profession. Without real‑world exposure, any decision made at that stage is likely to be based on incomplete information. Moreover, academic performance in high school influences the options available later; strong grades open doors to advanced programs or specialized tracks that can shape a career direction. If a student neglects his studies, he may find himself locked out of desirable fields later on. Consequently, the priority should be to excel academically while remaining open to different possibilities, and only after gaining some practical insight—perhaps through internships, extracurricular activities, or part‑time jobs—should a definitive career path be chosen. In short, postponing a career decision until later in schooling gives students the time and experience needed to choose a path that truly fits their abilities and interests.

Have youever spotted something lying on the pavement and wondered whether to pick it up? That moment, when you pretend the object belongs to you, is essentially a lie, and it is a bad habit because you cannot be sure whether the money, toy, or any other item actually belongs to someone else. When a child finds a lost item, the first impulse is often to keep it, but that is not a smart choice since the original owner may return looking for it, and the item could be taken by someone else.  

When I was a kid I frequently saw people drop things on the street. I would pick them up, return them, or tell the owner they had dropped something. In my elementary school, signs were posted everywhere reminding students to leave found objects where they were and not to take what isn’t theirs. Most children followed the rule, yet some ignored it, which is unacceptable because they might not need the item and simply want to possess it.  

Many people argue that we should leave found items where they are, because the owner will likely come back to look for them. It is rare for someone to abandon something and never notice its absence. Schools teach this lesson because children need to understand that taking something that does not belong to them is a form of theft. While it is true that a person can purchase a needed item from a nearby store, the difference between needing something and wanting something is important. Need means the object is essential for daily life or personal well‑being; wanting means you simply desire it for bragging rights, fun, or because you feel like taking it, even though you have the means to buy it.  

If you find an object, the responsible action is to refrain from keeping it. Instead, you should hand it back to the person who dropped it, be aware of your behavior, ignore peer pressure, and act with kindness and helpfulness. This lesson is vital because many adults today do not practice it, and when they do, they may cause harm to others. When a child drops a favorite toy and someone picks it up, the child could feel angry, sad, or upset, especially if the toy was expensive or cherished. Imagine the same scenario reversed: you drop your toy, and a stranger rushes to give it back. You would likely feel happy, proud, and delighted that the person acted with goodwill rather than selfish intent.  

I once lost my iPad a few years ago. A person who saw it picked it up and kept it, and I never discovered who took it. The loss left me upset, and I had to rely on my mother’s phone until my father could buy me a new device. That experience showed me how distressing it can be when something valuable is taken without the owner’s knowledge. Expensive items such as smartphones, which can cost more than a used car, become even more problematic when they are stolen. The owner may become frantic, searching everywhere for the device because it is essential for communication, navigation, or calling for help. The emotional impact of losing a costly phone is comparable to the feeling I experienced with my iPad.  

Therefore, teaching children to return found objects and to avoid taking what isn’t theirs is essential. When kids learn to be honest, helpful, and kind, they develop a sense of responsibility that benefits the whole community. Parents and teachers should reinforce these values, especially since some adults no longer model them. By instilling the habit of giving back what we find, we reduce theft, protect others’ belongings, and create a more trustworthy environment for everyone. By practicing honesty and returning lost items, we help build a community where trust is the norm and everyone feels safe.

At the heart of my viewpoint is the belief that contributing something valuable to other people is essential. First, when we create something that benefits others, we gain a steady source of motivation to support many individuals in achieving their dreams, goals and overall life purpose. This ongoing drive helps us stay committed even when challenges arise, because seeing the positive impact on others reinforces our dedication. For example, providing resources that help people grow and make their families proud can serve as a powerful incentive. Second, a clearly defined job that serves a large number of people gives us a concrete reason to move ahead and accomplish our own aspirations. Such a role can be found in fields like education, healthcare or community services, where the work directly influences many lives and opens doors to further career possibilities. In such a position we assist those who wish to fulfill their purpose, and the role itself can open many opportunities in various sectors. Thirdly, mastering a particular skill that allows us to produce something valuable for others represents the highest form of achievement we can offer. When we develop expertise, we not only improve our own capabilities but also create tangible benefits for the people we help. When we choose to help others, we become deeply engaged in the struggle to secure a meaningful accomplishment. For instance, my own strong capacity to guide people toward success can inspire both them and myself, leading to remarkable results in our lives. In summary, helping others discover their greatest achievements and life purpose brings lasting happiness, allows us to enjoy a satisfying career we love, and encourages us to keep moving forward while never stopping to dream big. Overall, this approach not only benefits the people we assist but also enriches our own journey, making life more meaningful and purposeful. By staying focused on helping others, we ensure continuous growth and fulfillment.

Can you remaintrue to yourself in every situation and achieve the highest goals? I believe that staying authentic and believing in yourself makes the impossible possible. When you trust your own abilities and keep faith, no barrier can stop you. When you are honest about your values and talents, you can focus your energy on what truly matters, which makes your path clearer and more rewarding.

First, self‑belief removes obstacles. If you have confidence in your own powers and a strong sense of purpose, you can overcome difficulties. This idea is illustrated by Martin Luther King Jr., who held a dream of racial equality. His confidence and persistent optimism drove him forward, and his vision was realized in Washington, D.C. Being authentic also helps you build genuine relationships, because people respect honesty and are drawn to those who know themselves.

Second, perseverance combined with self‑belief leads to success. Cristiano Ronaldo’s early life was marked by hardship; his father left the family and his mother struggled. Yet his passion for football never faded. He trained hard from a young age, eventually joining the national team and becoming one of the world’s greatest players. His story shows that believing in yourself, even when circumstances are tough, can turn dreams into reality. Ronaldo’s dedication to training every day, even after injuries, shows that consistent effort amplifies self‑belief and pushes you toward your goals. His rise from a modest neighborhood to global stardom inspires many to trust their own potential.

Finally, the message is clear: if you keep believing in yourself, any goal can be reached. Whether it is a social cause, a personal ambition, or a sporting career, the combination of authenticity, confidence, and steady effort makes everything achievable. When you stay true to yourself, you avoid the fatigue that comes from pretending to be someone else, allowing you to sustain motivation over the long term. So, nurture your self‑belief, stay true to who you are, and you will find that the limits of what you can accomplish are far beyond what you imagine.

Changing the cafeteria lunch menu is a bad idea because not every student will accept the new meals. Many pupils are extremely selective about what they eat; they inspect the appearance and smell of the food, and if it looks or smells odd they will throw it away or go without eating until they get home. In addition, a number of students have food allergies that they keep hidden out of fear of being teased, so the school often lacks the information needed to provide safe options. When the menu is altered, the risk of allergic reactions rises, and the waste of uneaten meals creates a financial burden for the institution. Consequently, schools should keep the existing menus, as this avoids unnecessary spending, prevents health hazards, and respects the preferences of the student body.

Students today are very picky, and they often examine their food carefully before deciding to eat it. If the new dishes look unappetizing or have an unfamiliar odor, they are likely to discard them, which means the school spends money preparing meals that end up in the trash. Moreover, the cost of producing food that most pupils reject can be significant, especially for schools that already operate on tight budgets. Instead of investing in menu changes that may not improve satisfaction, the saved funds could be directed toward activities that students truly enjoy, such as clubs, sports equipment, or upgraded technology.

Another concern is the lack of accurate data on students’ dietary needs. Schools may not know which children have allergies or other restrictions, and without this knowledge any new menu could put some pupils at risk. Keeping the current menu eliminates the chance of accidental exposure and the associated liability. It also spares the school from the embarrassment of serving food that most students refuse to eat.

In summary, altering the lunch menu would likely lead to low consumption, increased waste, potential health problems, and unnecessary financial loss. Therefore, the safest and most sensible course of action is for schools to leave the existing menus unchanged, ensuring both student wellbeing and fiscal responsibility.

Have youever wondered why some students finish their studies at a younger age? It might seem surprising, but they are often more intelligent than their peers who stay longer. While critics argue that completing school in three years is a poor choice, I believe it is actually beneficial because it fosters greater maturity and personal responsibility.  

One advantage of finishing early is that students become more accustomed to real‑life situations. Many teenagers today lack practical experience; they often drink and drive, causing accidents because their parents usually intervene and protect them. When parents constantly bail them out, young people do not consider the consequences of their actions and fail to develop a sense of accountability. By graduating after three years, a student is forced to confront the world on his own, learn from mistakes, and understand the impact of his choices. For instance, a teen who must arrange his own car insurance after breaking a law will quickly realize that he cannot rely on his parents to cover every mistake.  

A second reason to support early graduation is the development of financial independence. When a young person pays his own rent, utilities, or phone bill, he begins to manage his money carefully. In my family, my mother paid the phone bill, so I never thought about where the money came from. If I were responsible for that expense, I would monitor my usage more closely and avoid wasteful habits, such as leaving lights on or running water unnecessarily. Consequently, early graduates learn to budget, plan, and accept the outcomes of their financial decisions.  

Some may argue that finishing school early causes students to miss out on social experiences and become stressed. They claim that teenagers should enjoy their youth and have fun. However, the benefits of maturity and responsibility outweigh those temporary pleasures. A well‑prepared young adult is better equipped to handle the challenges of adulthood, both personally and professionally.  

In conclusion, graduating early is advantageous because it promotes maturity and full responsibility for one’s actions. It prepares young people for the realities of adult life and teaches them to manage their own affairs.

Self‑esteem, in my view, grows out of real accomplishment. The harder a student labors, the more chances for success appear, and each award or achievement reinforces a feeling of pride that nurtures genuine self‑esteem. Many pupils work diligently, finish assignments on time and even hold part‑time jobs after classes, yet they still lack a solid sense of self‑worth because they have not learned to trust themselves. Confidence is therefore the prerequisite for building true self‑esteem; without it, effort alone does not translate into self‑respect.  

On the other hand, some students go to school without any after‑school duties and already feel self‑confident, yet they struggle to develop authentic self‑esteem. For these learners, pursuing achievements becomes essential, since recognition of progress fuels confidence and, ultimately, self‑esteem. By striving for tangible results—whether academic grades, sports accolades, or artistic recognitions—students receive encouragement that strengthens their self‑belief.  

A practical way to foster this cycle is to work hard, arrive punctually, and follow a clear schedule or checklist that outlines daily tasks. Unfortunately, many young people today appear less industrious; technology seems to breed laziness, or perhaps they simply lack motivation to pursue goals at school. I grow weary of seeing such attitudes, because dedicating just two focused hours at home can produce numerous achievements that propel a student toward his or her objectives.  

When it comes to cultivating real self‑esteem, the first step is to earn achievements, then develop confidence, and finally become the best version of oneself. Teachers play a crucial role in this process, since they interact with students more frequently than parents do during a typical week. While teachers rarely give direct lessons on confidence, they can model effective ways to attain goals, demonstrate perseverance, and inspire students to seek success. When a teacher shows the path to achievement, learners are more likely to contemplate their own goals, build confidence, and consequently raise their self‑esteem.  

My own experience illustrates this dynamic. In 2017 I arrived in the United States with no English proficiency and no friends. The isolation and language barrier made me extremely shy; my face flushed whenever someone tried to speak to me, revealing a lack of confidence. Determined to improve, I worked hard to master the language and actively sought friendships, eventually attending classes, conversing comfortably, and forming a supportive circle. This progress boosted my confidence dramatically, allowing me to become a more capable and happy student.  

In sum, confidence and diligent effort to achieve are the twin keys to building self‑esteem, which itself stems from accomplishment. Students should concentrate on their studies or any learning environment, aim for meaningful achievements, and receive encouragement from both family and themselves—provided they are already confident. When these elements align, true self‑esteem can flourish.

I agreewith Emerson’s claim because when someone truly masters a task they perform it more effectively, which in turn opens up more chances and higher‑status positions than those who have not mastered it. Mastery also builds confidence and a solid reputation, which further enhances career advancement. Of course, not everyone shares this view; some argue that people without formal mastery can sometimes do a job better. 

First, a person who has mastered a job has spent years studying and practicing, so their work is more efficient. For instance, a chef who has mastered cooking only needs to recall recipes, while a less‑skilled worker must remember ingredients, utensils and equipment. 

Second, mastery gives better opportunities because it signals that the individual is already prepared for the role. Many employers require a proven mastery before hiring for a position, and in restaurants a manager role often demands such proof, resulting in higher pay. 

Third, a mastered person is viewed as more experienced, which leads to better job placement. In a kitchen, a skilled cook may become the manager, whereas someone without mastery is more likely to stay in a lower‑pay position such as dishwashing and will need more time and effort to advance. 

In short, those who have mastered a skill enjoy superior performance, more career prospects and higher status compared with those who have not. Therefore, I support Emerson’s statement that without mastery one cannot truly grow.

Thomas Jefferson once said that there is great wonder in what can be achieved when we keep moving. He meant that constant effort, whether for the benefit of others or for oneself, leads to greater results. This raises the question of whether a life spent continuously doing something yields more success than a life that also embraces periods of rest. Some people argue that inactivity is necessary because it allows the body and mind to recover and regain strength, enabling continued productivity. Others maintain that persistent work is superior, since hard effort brings personal goals closer and makes a person useful to society.  

Many individuals rise each morning to work, giving their best effort, yet the situation of those who are not employed deserves attention as well. Even without a formal job, a person can contribute through volunteer work, helping neighbors, or pursuing personal development activities that promote growth. While rest is essential for everyone, excessive idleness can hinder the realization of aspirations and dreams.  

It is clear that engaging in purposeful activity is advantageous when the actions are constructive. Hard work driven by passion often leads to achievement, and many people work to earn a living, support their families, or pursue interests they love. The motivation behind work varies: some seek financial stability, others seek personal fulfillment, and still others aim to make a broader societal impact. Regardless of the motive, the act of working provides direction and purpose.  

From a societal perspective, individuals must meet basic needs such as food, shelter, and bills, which requires a source of income. A job is therefore a practical necessity, but it is not the only way to stay active. When people feel that their efforts benefit the larger community, they experience a sense of belonging and purpose.  

Dreams and goals act as catalysts that drive people to act. A person who envisions a future goal is more likely to stay active, whereas prolonged inactivity may erode motivation and shift one’s mindset. In conclusion, the wisdom of Thomas Jefferson encourages us to stay active, but it also reminds us that rest is a vital component of a balanced life. Taking breaks is healthy, yet we should not allow them to become permanent obstacles to achieving our dreams.

It is essential to keep a hopeful outlook, especially when one lacks it, because a negative demeanor can make others feel uncomfortable. I fully support this view, as a hopeful attitude helps people find employment and contributes to a better life at home.  

From my experience working in a restaurant, I see that a friendly, upbeat attitude toward customers makes a big difference. For instance, I always greet guests with a smile, while a colleague who constantly appears irritable creates tension in the workplace. In my opinion, a good attitude is a key factor for getting and keeping a job, and it is also valued within a family setting.  

Moreover, the people around us shape our outlook. A cheerful demeanor also reduces stress and creates a more pleasant atmosphere for everyone involved. Some of my friends tend to be pessimistic, and I notice that their negativity often leads to poor decisions. My mother and grandmother constantly remind me not to be negative, emphasizing that a positive mindset is healthier and more productive. Consequently, I try to stay optimistic, believing that this habit was taught by my parents. These reminders from my family have guided my behavior throughout school and work, helping me develop confidence.  

Positive thinking is not only useful for personal well‑being but also for professional environments. When a person is happy, they naturally radiate positivity, which attracts opportunities. Conversely, someone without a hopeful attitude may struggle to secure a position, as employers look for employees who can interact constructively. Such an approach also encourages teamwork and reduces conflicts in the workplace. In my current job, a new employee who arrived with a doubtful expression quickly lost the trust of the manager during training, showing how crucial a constructive attitude is.  

This attitude also helps maintain good relationships with family and friends.  

In summary, everyone who wishes to obtain employment should cultivate a positive attitude, because it improves interpersonal relations, enhances performance, and supports a harmonious household. If a negative mindset appears, it is advisable to change it, as a hopeful outlook benefits both the individual and those around them.

Thomas Jefferson once declared that one should never remain idle, noting how much can be achieved when we keep moving. Staying active—whether by pursuing career ambitions, assisting others, or simply engaging in purposeful tasks—contrasts sharply with a sedentary lifestyle, which can cause numerous health issues. Is it true that people achieve more when they follow their own interests, or does inactivity also allow goals to be reached? While a lack of activity may bring some temporary comforts, it often results in poor physical condition, a sense of emptiness, and an unproductive life. Those who choose to stay indoors, avoid employment, drop out of education, and neglect their health may find themselves isolated from society and suffering from an unhealthy body. Conversely, being active gives life direction and offers many advantages: better health, progress toward professional and academic objectives, opportunities to help others, and personal growth through learning new skills. For example, obtaining employment demonstrates active participation, and dedicating time each day to pursue one's passions can lead to meaningful accomplishments. Engaging in activities, whether work‑related or recreational, contributes positively to overall well‑being. As Jefferson reminded us, “Determine never to be idle… it is wonderful how much can be done if we are always doing.” Although opinions vary, the evidence suggests that maintaining an active life is far more beneficial than remaining idle.

Adoptinga four‑day school week means replacing the usual five‑day schedule with only four days of classes. This change should be considered not only for the parents who work but also for every high school and university. By reducing the weekly school hours by ten, the missing time can be recovered by lengthening each school day by two hours and by extending the length of each lesson. Longer periods allow teachers to give more attention to each subject and give students extra time to finish projects or assignments. The additional two hours each day also give pupils more opportunity to meet with teachers for help when they are struggling in a class.  

The extra two hours can be used on the fourth day for activities such as reading in the library, playing sports, or any other after‑school interest. The fifth day of the week, which would be a regular school day, can instead be kept free for medical appointments, health‑related matters, or for parents to write a note explaining a student’s absence. This flexibility reduces the number of missed lessons because students can attend appointments during a non‑school day.  

Teachers, who are also parents, may need an additional day for family activities with their children. Seniors, who are at a critical stage in deciding their future, would benefit from extra time to explore university options, apply for scholarships, and look for weekend or part‑time jobs. Freshmen, transitioning from middle school, would need support in adjusting to new extracurricular activities and a different routine.  

The free day can also be used for community service, with parental permission and adult supervision, allowing students to clean streets, help the environment, or take part in other civic projects. Schools could partner with local companies to offer internships or part‑time positions on the free day, giving students practical work experience.  

One possible drawback is that students who hold part‑time jobs might find it harder to keep their work schedule, since extending the school day reduces the number of hours they can work. However, if the fifth day is kept free, those students could work full‑time on that day and still have three full days for employment.  

Although longer school days may be tiring, the four‑day schedule actually provides more time for rest, homework, and extracurricular projects after school, and the three free days can be used for relaxation, family time, or additional work. In my view, the advantages outweigh the disadvantages for the majority of students.  

Therefore, I conclude that everyone should have three days off from school and attend classes for only four days a week.

Some people believe that studentsshould be required to take an arts class. They say this will help students discover what they want to do, develop their skills, and gain opportunities. It will also benefit them in the future. It is important that students choose the electives they want. If they are forced to take a class they do not enjoy, they may feel lazy, skip class, receive poor grades, lose motivation, and miss out on the credit needed to graduate. Without a high school diploma, they cannot attend college or secure a good job, which could lead to homelessness. Therefore, it is important that students decide which electives they want to take.

Many peopleclaim that students must be forced to attend an arts or other elective class. I disagree. I think that learners should be allowed to choose the electives they prefer, because making a personal selection helps them discover what they truly enjoy, develop useful skills, and remain motivated in school.

First, when a student can pick a subject that interests them, they are more likely to attend each lesson willingly. Attendance improves grades, because engaged students listen, participate, and complete assignments. Moreover, choosing a course that matches their abilities lets them experience success, which builds confidence and reduces the tendency to skip classes. In contrast, a required class that feels irrelevant may cause boredom, absenteeism, lower performance, and a loss of the credits needed for graduation. Without enough credits, a pupil cannot finish high school, which limits future job prospects and can even lead to economic hardship.

Second, every individual possesses distinct talents. By enrolling in an elective where they excel, a student is more likely to enjoy the material, achieve higher marks, and acquire knowledge that will be valuable later. For example, a learner who is strong in drama may be hired by a production company, leading to a career in acting or filmmaking and the possibility of earning a good income. In addition, a student is not limited to a single skill; they may excel in several areas, and each additional competence broadens their future options and makes them more attractive to employers.

Third, the benefits of selecting preferred electives extend to the long term. When a pupil studies something they love, they are better prepared for the transition to college and adult life. They gain a clearer sense of direction, can pursue their aspirations with confidence, and are more likely to achieve the goals they set for themselves. The skills and experiences gathered during these years become a solid foundation for a successful career and a fulfilling future.

Finally, critics argue that students lack the motivation to choose their own courses and may treat electives as a joke. However, giving students autonomy actually enhances their enthusiasm and sense of responsibility. When learners feel that their opinions matter, they are more inclined to engage seriously with the material rather than dismiss it.

In conclusion, allowing students to select the electives they are interested in supports personal growth, academic achievement, and future success. By choosing courses that align with their passions and strengths, students stay motivated, earn the credits needed to graduate, and open doors to rewarding career opportunities. Therefore, the best policy is to let learners decide which electives they wish to take.

Seeking guidance from knowledgeable individuals is essential for effective learning and for avoiding unnecessary mistakes. When people rely on the advice of experts or authorities, they receive clearer direction, make wiser choices, and experience fewer setbacks in life. Therefore, it is far better for individuals to consult professionals rather than trying to decide everything on their own.

For example, a student who struggles to understand a mathematics lesson can approach the teacher or a subject specialist for clarification. The instructor can break down the concepts step by step, which helps the learner grasp the material more easily and continue progressing in the subject. In contrast, a student who avoids asking for help often falls behind and may even fail the course altogether.

Similarly, a person who starts a new job benefits greatly from an experienced colleague who explains the procedures and expectations. Without such instruction, the newcomer is prone to commit many mistakes, which can damage the organization’s performance and waste valuable time. Proper guidance therefore reduces errors and accelerates adaptation to the new role.

In my own school, a new student arrived without knowing the rules. He unintentionally broke a regulation and faced serious punishment. Had a teacher or senior student explained the expectations, the incident could have been avoided.

Many adolescents act without counsel because they have no trusted adult to advise them. Their decisions often result in daily difficulties or even harmful outcomes. On the other hand, youths who receive regular guidance from mentors tend to perform well in school, work, and personal life, showing the positive impact of support.

The broader consequences extend to society at large. If every person had access to knowledgeable advisors, the world would likely be safer and more stable. Moreover, governments led by competent experts would be better equipped to steer the nation, reducing the risks that citizens currently face. Additionally, when teenagers are not left to fend for themselves, they are less likely to engage in risky or destructive behavior, fostering a more peaceful environment. Such a supportive environment also reduces the financial burden on families, as fewer mistakes mean less need for remedial courses or job retraining.

In summary, having an expert to guide individuals throughout life promotes better learning, fewer mistakes, and greater overall well‑being. It enables people to make sound decisions, reduces danger, and creates a more harmonious world. Therefore, encouraging the use of professional advice for everyone, especially young people, would improve futures and bring lasting peace.

Beyond individual cases, schools and workplaces that embed mentorship programs see higher achievement rates and lower turnover. When teachers take time to explain expectations clearly, students feel more confident and are less likely to repeat errors. Likewise, companies that assign seasoned staff to newcomers notice faster integration and higher productivity, demonstrating that guidance benefits both learners and organizations.

When societies invest in mentorship and expert guidance, they experience lower crime rates, stronger economies, and a greater sense of community cohesion. Citizens feel more secure knowing that experienced leaders are there to advise them, which fosters trust and cooperation across different groups. Consequently, the overall quality of life improves for everyone.

Many schools assign summer projects to keepstudents engaged over the vacation, but the question remains whether these tasks should be set by teachers or created by the students themselves. I believe that allowing students to design their own projects is the better option. When learners plan and carry out their own work, they reinforce what they have already studied and acquire additional skills that will help them when the new term begins. For example, as an ESL student I often create my own summer assignments to review material from the previous year, ensuring that I do not forget what I have learned.

The first advantage of student‑designed projects is confidence. Because the learners themselves choose the topic and decide how to approach it, they feel more comfortable and motivated. If schools permit students to formulate their own assignments, they will know exactly what they are expected to do, making the work easier and more enjoyable.

A second benefit is retention. Continuing to work on a personal project during the break prevents the loss of knowledge that can occur when study stops completely. If a student abandons practice, laziness may set in, and the material may fade from memory. By keeping the project alive, the student revisits the content regularly and solidifies understanding. ESL learners, for instance, who do not engage in self‑directed summer tasks risk forgetting vocabulary and grammar rules.

Finally, student‑led projects promote activity and showcase individual abilities. Without a teacher directing every step, learners can be more creative, explore personal interests, and demonstrate what they have mastered. In this way, they not only avoid forgetting the previous year’s material but also develop independence and a deeper grasp of the subject.

In conclusion, giving students the freedom to design their own summer projects supports learning, retention, and personal growth, so schools should encourage rather than restrict this approach.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once observed that the highest achievement is to remain true to oneself despite a world that constantly pushes us toward other identities. I agree with this view because our deeds, attitudes and the way we present ourselves reveal who we really are, and they show whether we are merely following the crowd or daring to be different.  

First, when we stay authentic, other people tend to copy our behavior. For instance, a student who stays after class to explain a difficult equation to a peer, even though solving problems is the teacher’s responsibility, shows that helping others is valuable. Those who witness this generosity often become more willing to assist their classmates, creating a ripple effect of kindness.  

Second, being true to yourself makes you a source of inspiration in many areas of life—home, the neighborhood, school, college and even church. Imagine a neighbor who regularly mows his lawn, fixes a fence for a friend, and offers to carry groceries. Such actions motivate those around him to adopt similar helpful habits, turning ordinary deeds into a shared standard of care.  

Third, the achievements that stem from authenticity can change the outlook of many people. When we openly describe how we reached a goal, we give others a clear example to follow. In a family where one member runs his own business while another works a low‑pay job, the proactive attitude of the entrepreneur spreads optimism and encourages relatives to consider new possibilities. These examples show how personal authenticity can create a positive impact on many lives.  

In conclusion, Emerson’s statement remains meaningful today. More than half of the world’s people try to do extra things because they recognize the advantages of helping others. The most important accomplishment, therefore, is to be an authentic example that inspires and uplifts the people around us.

Oneof my strengths is drawing. When I put pencil to paper I enjoy sketching the night sky – stars, the moon, forests and the sea. I often experiment with charcoal, ink or watercolor to capture the atmosphere of each scene, which keeps my practice fresh. Drawing lets me show who I am through many styles of art, and I love the freedom it gives me to create anything I wish. If I make a mistake I can simply correct it.  

Another form of drawing that I love is painting. With paint I can express feelings – sadness, joy, anger or frustration – by choosing colors that match my mood. I choose cool blues for calm moments and bright reds for excitement, letting the palette speak for my feelings. Art is one of my favorite ways to create, and many people are willing to spend large sums for a piece they find beautiful, even if the price reaches billions.  

Although many have artistic talent, some creators doubt the value of their work and discard it. They do not realize that others may appreciate their art and be ready to pay for it. Some artists keep their pieces for personal memories or to show family, and while they may sell to relatives, they rarely expect huge financial returns. When I keep a piece for my family, it becomes a lasting reminder of shared moments and personal growth.  

I believe creators should try to sell their work, because it can bring in a good amount of money. Even a modest sale can be rewarding.  

Art is a demanding job that requires patience. A mistake may force you to start over, but you can also turn that error into something new and beautiful. Seeing something ugly and reshaping it into art is part of the process. Patience lets me work slowly, giving each stroke time to settle and each color to blend properly.  

Some people find art boring, yet if you truly love creating, it never feels dull. When I am excited to paint, I lose self‑control and let my hand move freely, not worrying about how the result will look. The joy of being absorbed in the activity makes the experience worthwhile. The excitement of creating can turn a simple sketch into a vibrant story that captures a moment in time.  

Creating art can also cause stress when the outcome does not match expectations, and I have felt that pressure myself. However, with practice and patience the task becomes less daunting. I consider myself skilled but still a learner, and I keep practicing because consistent effort improves my ability. Every error teaches me something new, and I welcome those lessons as part of my artistic journey.  

Practicing regularly helps me grow, and it shows that art, while challenging, can become more manageable over time. I enjoy drawing and painting, and I hope others will share the same passion and consider sharing their work with the world. Sharing my art online has also connected me with other creators, inspiring me to keep improving.

Is it true that studentsgain any advantage by attending lessons from home? I believe they do not. In my experience, a classmate who studied remotely stopped completing assignments and used the free time for personal tasks, so she gained nothing from the arrangement. Moreover, learners would exploit the flexibility to avoid their responsibilities, miss out on learning, and therefore receive no real benefit. The idea of studying from home sounds convenient because it removes travel time and allows a flexible schedule, yet the lack of direct supervision often leads to poor habits.  

First, the freedom to stay at home encourages students to attend to other matters instead of studying. For instance, they may submit assignments late or spend the class time chatting online. While not every remote learner behaves this way, those who view the situation as an opportunity often choose entertainment over coursework. They may watch videos, play games, or scroll through social media, turning a short lesson into a prolonged distraction.  

Second, they frequently invent reasons for not completing tasks. They might go out with friends, meet a partner, or engage in leisure activities, using the class time as an excuse to avoid work. Because the teacher is not physically present, they assume they will not be monitored, which reduces their sense of accountability. When deadlines approach, they often rush to finish the work, producing low‑quality submissions that do not reflect their true understanding.  

Third, many students become lazy when faced with assignments. Knowing that no one will remind them to work, they postpone or skip the tasks altogether, preferring to spend time on non‑academic pursuits rather than the work that will help them later. In some cases they share answers with classmates or download completed tasks, which undermines the purpose of the assignment and prevents genuine learning.  

Finally, the lack of actual learning is evident. Instead of studying, they party, hang out with friends or partners, and sometimes cheat by copying from others or searching the internet for answers. Consequently, they acquire little knowledge and miss the chance to develop skills that are essential for future success. Without solid comprehension, students are less prepared for exams, future courses, and the workplace, which ultimately harms their academic and professional growth.  

In summary, attending classes from home does not benefit students because it leads to distraction, procrastination, and superficial learning. They misuse the flexibility to do unrelated activities, neglect their assignments, and therefore gain nothing academically. Therefore, the supposed convenience of home‑based classes is outweighed by the negative effects on discipline, engagement, and academic achievement. Students deserve a learning environment that promotes real study, not distraction.

It is clear that many people hold the view that students should rely on self‑confidence and strive for achievement, while others point out the difficulties this perspective can create. From my point of view, confidence is indeed a vital ingredient for success, but it must be combined with hard work, a balanced lifestyle, and a realistic outlook toward the future.

First, believing in one’s own abilities gives students the courage to tackle challenges. When a learner trusts that they can accomplish a task, they are more likely to persist through setbacks and to put in the necessary effort. This inner conviction turns obstacles into opportunities for growth, and it is precisely the kind of mindset that leads to genuine achievement.

Second, achievement itself is not a mysterious force; it is the result of sustained effort and the development of skills. By working diligently, students acquire knowledge and competence that enable them to complete tasks successfully. The sense of satisfaction that follows a finished project is a powerful motivator, reinforcing the idea that hard work yields rewarding results.

Third, while academic effort is essential, students must also remember to enjoy life and plan for what lies ahead. It is important to balance study with moments of relaxation, especially time spent with family, because these relationships enrich the overall quality of life. At the same time, thinking about a future career helps students set meaningful goals and gives direction to their current efforts.

Fourth, pursuing a profession offers stability and a sense of purpose. A well‑chosen career, especially one that requires specialized training, can provide both financial security and personal fulfillment. However, many students feel they lack the experience needed to enter the workforce. Gaining practical exposure through internships, projects, or volunteer work can bridge this gap and make them more attractive to potential employers.

Fifth, sincerity and precaution play crucial roles in the learning process. Being honest about one’s strengths and weaknesses builds trust with teachers, peers, and future colleagues. Taking preventive measures — such as preparing thoroughly before an exam or safeguarding personal data online — helps avoid unnecessary difficulties later on.

Finally, tolerance and compassion are indispensable for a supportive educational environment. Accepting diverse opinions and behaviors, even when they differ from our own, fosters mutual respect and reduces conflict. When students feel that they are understood and valued, they are more inclined to engage actively and to develop confidence in their abilities.

In summary, students benefit greatly from self‑confidence and a commitment to hard work, but they also need a balanced lifestyle, practical experience, honesty, foresight, and a compassionate attitude toward others. By integrating these elements, learners can achieve their goals while enjoying a fulfilling life and preparing thoughtfully for the future.

Why do people need to follow their own instincts and ideas? I believe they should trust their own judgment and make their own choices. When you rely on yourself, you develop confidence, and others are more likely to trust you as well. First, making independent decisions reduces the need to constantly seek advice. If the ideas come from inside you rather than from other people, you do not have to ask for suggestions or wait for permission. This also means you can write or create without copying from the internet or from another person. By depending on your own thoughts, you save time and keep your work original. Second, following your inner voice gives you the ability to solve problems without waiting for help. When a difficulty appears, you can act immediately because you already trust your own abilities. This self‑confidence prevents you from looking for guidance unnecessarily and helps you become more resilient. Moreover, believing in yourself influences how others see you. For instance, imagine you have to give a presentation in class. If you doubt your own capability, the teacher may also doubt you, which can lower the grade you receive. By showing confidence, you convince the audience that you are competent, and the outcome improves. In conclusion, people should prioritize their own instincts and ideas because this builds self‑belief, promotes independence, and encourages others to trust them. Listening only to others while ignoring your inner voice diminishes personal worth. Therefore, trusting yourself first is essential for personal growth and for gaining the respect of those around you.

Some schools have created programmes that link younger learners with older students. The purpose of these schemes is to let both groups gain something useful and to show how they can help one another. The older pupils are given a chance to reflect on their responsibilities, while the younger ones can see what challenges they will face later on.  

In this setting the older student can point out common errors and show the younger learner how to act correctly. By sharing personal mistakes, the senior pupil helps the junior avoid similar problems. Conversely, the younger student can offer fresh insights that the older learner might have missed, and can assist with tasks such as language practice or navigating school life.  

When a conflict arises, the older student is often able to intervene and guide the younger one toward a peaceful solution, reminding them that everyone makes mistakes and that learning from them is essential. The relationship also provides emotional support: a younger pupil who feels uncertain can turn to an older peer for advice, just as an older student who feels unsure can seek guidance from a younger companion.  

Although some older students may be reluctant to help, the overall effect of these programmes is positive. They encourage mutual respect, promote harmony, and teach both groups valuable life lessons. In the end, the partnership benefits everyone, because the older student learns to share knowledge and the younger student gains confidence and direction.

Making thoughtful decisionscan turn everyday life into something more enjoyable and less complicated. When we act responsibly and consider the consequences before we move forward, the outcomes tend to be positive and rewarding. One effective habit is to pause, reflect, and plan before we begin any action.  

Unfortunately, many people rush into choices without thinking, and this often harms their future. For instance, a student who regularly skips classes may cause his teacher to contact his parents, resulting in disciplinary trouble. Moreover, missing lessons can lower his grades, limit his academic progress, and eventually reduce his chances of obtaining a well‑paid job after graduation. He may also miss out on the same advantages that peers who complete their studies receive.  

Similar patterns appear in other areas of life. In my own country, I once made a poor decision by skipping a lesson with a friend to play soccer. Because I failed to think ahead, I did not pass that subject, my grades suffered, and my parents were called to school. Another illustration comes from my brother’s experience. While in ninth grade he spent most of his time with friends and ignored the importance of the state exam (SOL). When he reached twelfth grade, he needed to pass the SOL to graduate, and the lack of preparation forced him to retake the test. He later told me not to repeat his mistake, emphasizing the need to consider future implications before acting.  

These examples show that careful thinking before deciding helps protect one’s goals and opportunities. If we ignore this principle, we risk setbacks that affect our education, career prospects, and overall well‑being. Therefore, cultivating a habit of thoughtful reflection can lead to a more successful and satisfying life, and even contribute to broader positive change in society.

Many people wonder whether successis built by moving from one failure to another while staying enthusiastic. Winston Churchill once claimed that this is exactly what success looks like. I disagree with that view. Although setbacks are inevitable, they do not define the path to achievement, and perseverance together with genuine enthusiasm is what truly matters.  

First, failure is a universal experience. Almost everyone makes mistakes in school, at work, or in personal relationships; it is rare for a person to go through life without any disappointment. For instance, my cousin has never let her parents down; she earned top grades, graduated with a scholarship and is now studying at Virginia Tech. Her success shows that it is possible to avoid major failures altogether.  

Second, reaching a goal requires effort and determination. When a person encounters a setback, the appropriate response is not to become discouraged but to stay resilient. Life is challenging for everyone; no one attains their ambitions without hard work. If an initial attempt fails, one should consider alternative plans and keep searching for new opportunities rather than giving up.  

Third, enthusiasm is a crucial ingredient. It fuels motivation and helps a person persist despite difficulty. Some individuals lack this inner drive, showing little interest or passion for any activity, which often leads to indifference about their future. Maintaining a strong feeling of excitement for what you pursue can keep you moving forward.  

Finally, Churchill’s statement oversimplifies the reality of achievement. While many people do experience multiple failures, success does not necessarily require a continuous cycle of setbacks. With persistent effort, a positive attitude, and unwavering enthusiasm, it is possible to reach one’s dreams without constantly stumbling. In my own life, I struggled with English after moving to the United States, but through dedicated study I improved and succeeded. Therefore, I do not agree that success must consist of moving from failure to failure; instead, hard work and sustained enthusiasm are the real keys to achievement.

Online courses are a valuable option for students who have a hectic schedule. People who work, have family duties, or lack transportationcan still attend classes without sacrificing their daily responsibilities. By studying from home, they can prepare meals, complete assignments, and attend lessons at times that fit their personal timetable. For instance, a parent can watch a lesson while caring for a child, and a worker can log in after the shift ends. Another advantage is that learners who live far from campus or do not own a vehicle can avoid long commutes and study in the comfort of their own room. Moreover, summer sessions become easier because students can continue their education through video‑conferencing rather than traveling to a physical classroom. In my view, online learning benefits many students; those who are occupied with work or other commitments, as well as anyone interested in flexible study, can readily enroll and succeed. Students can also replay recorded lectures, which helps them review material at their own pace. The flexibility allows them to balance study with other responsibilities, reducing stress and improving overall performance. Consequently, many learners find online education a practical solution for their busy lives.

Technology has undeniably changed the way we live, but it also weakens personal connections. I agree that, although many inventions are useful, technology is not the greatest creation of humanity because it often reduces face‑to‑face interaction. While it offers convenience and access to information, the overall impact on personal relationships tends to be negative.

One major problem is the growing dependence on mobile devices. People become glued to their screens, whether they are texting, gaming or scrolling through social media. This habit leaves less time for real conversation, and families may find themselves physically together yet mentally distant. Constant notifications further fragment attention, making it harder to engage deeply with those around us.

Another issue is the rise of online shopping addiction. While e‑commerce offers convenience, some individuals spend excessive amounts of time and money buying clothes or other goods. This compulsive behavior can replace meaningful activities and further isolate the person from others.

The lack of communication also affects empathy. When someone is constantly occupied with a phone or a game, they may ignore a friend who needs help or a family member who requires support. Even adults and children can become so absorbed in their devices that they prioritize virtual experiences over real‑world kindness.

In conclusion, we should strive for a balance that limits excessive use of technology. By setting clear boundaries and encouraging regular offline contact, we can protect our relationships and ensure that technology serves us rather than dominates our lives. Overall, mindful usage can help preserve human connection.

One of mystrongest abilities is reading aloud. When I speak the words, the meaning becomes clearer to me, and the ideas stay longer in my memory. Speaking the text also lets me notice where I stumble or lose focus, so I can pause and clarify unfamiliar terms. This habit makes it easier for me to explain the content to others, because I can describe scenes and details more vividly while I speak. I find that the rhythm of spoken words helps me notice repetitions and improves my fluency, which in turn makes the material easier to recall later.  

Reading out loud improves my comprehension. The act of vocalizing forces me to process each sentence, which deepens understanding. It also helps me remember what I have read; when I only think silently, I tend to forget many details, whereas speaking the passage keeps it firmly in mind. Because I can hear the natural pauses, I am better at structuring my own writing, matching the logical order of the original text.  

The benefit extends to writing tasks. Before drafting an essay, I often read the source material aloud. This practice allows me to hear the flow of the text, identify the main points, and organize my thoughts more logically. As a result, I feel less anxious when I begin to write, because the material is already familiar and well understood. When I practice reading aloud regularly, my confidence grows, and I become more willing to share my interpretations in class discussions.  

Moreover, speaking the text aloud can aid peers. When I read a passage to a classmate, they can follow the rhythm and grasp the meaning more easily than when they read silently.  

In conclusion, reading aloud is a valuable strategy for me. It enhances understanding, strengthens memory, supports clearer explanation, and makes the process of writing essays smoother. For these reasons, I rely on reading out loud whenever I study or create written work. Overall, this simple habit saves time and reduces the stress associated with studying and composing assignments.

Working in groups is generally moreadvantageous than studying alone. When students collaborate, they can support one another, combine their ideas, and develop a wider range of abilities. Group work also encourages friendships and improves communication, which are useful both inside and outside the classroom. For these reasons, teachers ought to give students more opportunities to learn together.

First, a group brings together more perspectives, which leads to richer ideas and more effective solutions. A student who is unsure how to approach a task can receive help from classmates, making the learning process clearer and more successful. Moreover, interacting with peers enhances communication skills; students learn to explain their thoughts, listen actively, and resolve misunderstandings. This collaborative environment also allows learners to meet classmates they might not otherwise know, fostering a sense of community.

Second, group work provides a practical setting for developing essential skills such as teamwork, negotiation, and written expression. When students discuss assignments, they practice articulating their points clearly and learn to give and receive constructive feedback. More capable learners can assist those who struggle, especially with language barriers, ensuring that everyone benefits from the shared effort. In this way, group tasks become a vehicle for mutual growth rather than a solitary burden.

Third, collaborative projects can strengthen personal relationships and improve academic outcomes. As students work side by side, they discover common interests and often form lasting friendships. These social bonds can boost motivation and create a supportive atmosphere that encourages higher achievement. The positive dynamics of a group also extend beyond school; the same cooperative attitudes are valuable at home and later in the workplace, where teamwork is frequently required.

Finally, effective communication is the cornerstone of successful group collaboration. When members speak openly and listen attentively, misunderstandings are minimized and objectives are reached more efficiently. A well‑communicating group can divide tasks according to each person’s strengths, ensuring that the final product is of higher quality. While some teachers prefer individual work to avoid distractions or copying, the advantages of group learning outweigh the occasional drawbacks, especially when students are guided to stay focused.

In conclusion, encouraging students to work in groups offers numerous benefits: richer ideas, enhanced communication, stronger social connections, and better academic performance. Teachers should therefore incorporate more group activities into their curricula, allowing learners to help one another and acquire skills that will serve them throughout their lives and careers. By embracing collaborative learning, students become more adaptable, confident, and prepared for the teamwork demanded in future professional and personal contexts.

Scientist Albert Einstein once said that imagination is more important than knowledge, and I completely agree with that statement. Imagination can make a person happier, can be useful for other people, and can help someone obtain a satisfying job.

First, imagination brings personal happiness. When you picture something you enjoy, such as soaring like a bird or looking at yourself as a centenarian, the mental picture creates positive feelings. Even though the scene is only in your mind, it can lift your spirits and give a sense of freedom or comfort. By visualising pleasant scenarios, you can improve your mood without any external cause.

Second, imagination can help others in difficult moments. Imagine a young girl crying in a shopping centre because her outfit looks unusual and draws attention. If you use your imagination, you can suggest that she view the onlookers as an audience admiring a princess, encouraging her to act elegantly and stop crying. This simple mental exercise can calm the child and change the atmosphere.

Third, imagination is essential for finding a good career. A person who wants to be a home designer but lacks imagination may produce unrealistic layouts, leading to criticism and dismissal, which prevents earning a steady income. Conversely, a writer who can imagine many ideas and write numerous successful books can generate substantial wealth, often surpassing that of a medical professional. Thus, imagination opens doors to rewarding professions.

In conclusion, I share Einstein’s opinion that imagination outweighs knowledge. It not only makes us happier, assists others, and facilitates desirable employment, but it also stands as the most vital element in our lives.

Every single student puts effort into their studies. They can keep working hard for months or even years without waiting for praise. Constantly rewarding a pupil each time they receive a good mark or finish a small assignment is not appropriate. I think that real self‑esteem is formed through effort because it shows that the student has relied on their own dedication, avoids arrogance, and does not come to expect rewards if praise stops. Occasionally a compliment after a notable achievement does feel pleasant. When a learner puts in hard work, that effort is evident both in the quality of their work and in their demeanor. Many pupils demonstrate their best effort without ever receiving acknowledgment. A student should focus on personal goals if they truly wish to succeed. If a learner is praised all the time, what have they actually learned about perseverance? They may come to believe that every positive action deserves a reward. Consequently, some students become conceited when they obtain high grades, while others who have worked just as hard but received lower marks feel overlooked. Those who constantly boast about their scores can hurt classmates’ feelings, especially when peers flaunt their grades. Such self‑centered, closed‑minded attitudes prevent helpful support. Some learners prefer to keep their results private. When praise is constant, students begin to anticipate benefits in return. They may act not for personal growth but to earn a prize, which undermines genuine effort. Real hard work should be its own reward; the satisfaction of knowing you have succeeded without external acknowledgment is rewarding. It builds confidence because the student realizes they can achieve goals independently. In conclusion, true self‑esteem arises from hard work and personal accomplishment, not from frequent praise. Students who rely on their own effort and value their own achievements are the ones who deserve recognition. This dedication shows that learning is a personal journey rather than a competition for external approval. When students see that effort alone can bring satisfaction, they become more motivated to improve.

In contrast, a science project can be very different; once I got to see a frog’s interior. It might sound disgusting to many readers, and honestly it did not smell good either. One activity I find genuinely enjoyable is carrying out science experiments. A key reason they appeal to me is that they are unlike typical school assignments. In contrast, a math task usually means solving countless equations, while a language‑arts assignment often requires writing a long essay. Science projects, however, let us see real objects and discover things that are not visible in everyday life.  

For instance, during a biology lesson we dissected a frog. At first the idea of looking inside a frog’s body seemed repulsive, and the specimen did not have a pleasant odor. What fascinated me was that a frog’s internal system contains far fewer organs than ours, and the ones that are present are not all red like human tissue. The organs were also tinted in unexpected shades such as blue and pink, which differ markedly from the red we normally see inside our own bodies. The bodies had been preserved in a frozen state, which made the tissue dry and allowed us to cut through them more easily. Because the teacher said we could explore any part we wanted, my group examined the specimen as thoroughly as possible.  

One particularly unsettling moment occurred when we noticed several flies trapped in the frog’s stomach. That sight was disturbing, yet it did not deter me from continuing the investigation. After we finished examining the frog, the teacher identified each organ and explained its function. One classmate jokingly poked the frog’s eye, and the eye, still not completely frozen, released fluid that splashed onto him. He got wet, while the liquid reached another student but not me. The teacher then sent the boy to wash up, and shortly after decided to end the activity. Despite the odd incident, the whole experience was very entertaining.  

Another project involved working in complete darkness as part of a unit on light. The task was simple: spray a mist in front of a flashlight and observe the light waves. After the teacher explained the principle, we carried out the experiment. At first I saw nothing, which was disappointing, but after a few seconds the waves became faintly visible for a short time. Although the demonstration was brief and the explanation took a long time, I found the activity intriguing.  

These examples show that science experiments are not inherently boring. Even when a project seems modest, it can still be interesting, and there are many different kinds of experiments to try. I believe they are the most enjoyable activities in school because they provide a hands‑on way of learning and make lessons more engaging.
