Working in a group ismore advantageous than working alone. When you are part of a team, members can share ideas, help with writing, provide examples and supply information that you might miss on your own. In contrast, a solitary worker has no one to review or improve a concept.  

One major benefit of group work is the ability to discuss the assignment openly. You can ask questions, talk through examples and receive feedback on how to proceed. This collaborative dialogue often makes the task feel less stressful. For instance, in a high‑school English class the teacher assigned groups of four to create a project. One student collected the sources, another drafted the text, a third gathered visual material, and the fourth prepared the oral presentation. Because the workload was divided, the final product was completed more smoothly and the presentation felt less anxiety‑provoking.  

On the other hand, working alone offers independence and the chance to use your own ideas without interruption. You must locate all the necessary information yourself and there is no one to validate your suggestions. This can make the process more difficult and may lead to gaps in the work.  

Some students prefer to work by themselves because they do not want to be disturbed and they enjoy having full control over their tasks. Yet, they miss out on the support that a group can provide, and there is no one to validate their ideas. This can make the process more difficult and may lead to gaps in the work.  

Some people avoid groups because of interpersonal issues, nervousness, or a preference for quiet environments. Many learners like group work because they feel comfortable discussing ideas with friends and can answer questions easily. Overall, the majority of students prefer teamwork over solitary study. While working alone has its advantages, the collaborative benefits of shared responsibilities, mutual support, and richer content make group work the more beneficial choice.

Working with a group is clearly moreadvantageous than handling an assignment by yourself. When several people collaborate, they share ideas, divide the workload, and finish the task more quickly. Each person can contribute according to their strengths, which lightens the burden on any single individual. In contrast, doing the whole job alone means you must take on all responsibilities, which makes the process slower and more demanding. A group also makes it easier to assign specific tasks; a designated leader can monitor progress, verify that each person has completed their portion, and reassign work if someone encounters a personal problem. This flexibility ensures that the assignment can still be finished even when one member is unavailable, something that is impossible when you are working alone. Additionally, the collective discussion deepens everyone's understanding of the material, because multiple viewpoints are examined and refined. One simple gesture, such as abrief smile or a helpful hand, can change someone’s day. Aesop, the ancient Greek storyteller, reminded us that no kindness, however tiny, is ever wasted. When we notice how a small act influences another person, we see that it can lift a gloomy mood, bring a genuine smile, and even improve physical well‑being.  

People often say that receiving kindness makes them feel valued and loved. That feeling comes from the sense that someone cares about them, which in turn creates warmth inside and outside. Such moments are described as among the most rewarding experiences in life, and they do not require any material gift – just a kind attitude.  

If we are shown kindness, the natural response is to pass it on. This does not mean we must give large presents; a small deed, like helping a neighbour tidy their home or offering a friendly greeting, shows that we appreciate the care we have received. By returning the favour, we create a cycle of goodwill that benefits everyone.  

Do we have small acts of kindness in our families? When a family member offers support, the others usually feel comforted and more connected. The same principle applies to friends, colleagues, or strangers. A smile directed at someone who looks stressed can brighten their mood, while a brief note of encouragement can lift their spirits. Even simple actions such as holding a door open or sharing a laugh can make a big difference.  

When we take time to notice these small moments, we realize how much they can brighten a day, reduce stress, and strengthen bonds. It is not necessary to plan grand gestures; a simple act of kindness can be as easy as offering a compliment, listening attentively, or helping someone carry groceries. By choosing to be kind, we not only help others but also feel more fulfilled ourselves. So, think about the small ways you can spread kindness today, and notice how it changes both your life and the lives of those around you.

Even if you shut off the water supply before starting, a misjudged twist of a pipe can cause a burst that spreads water across the kitchen. You then have to call the plumber again, paying extra for a problem that became more serious because of your intervention.  

Another illustration involves the death of a beloved pet. When a child’s dog dies, the family may try to comfort the child by getting a new animal. However, the child may find it difficult to accept the replacement, leading to loss of appetite, sleep disturbances, and even silence for an extended period. The child may feel isolated, refusing to play with friends, and the household atmosphere becomes tense as everyone tries to avoid reminding the youngster of the loss. The new pet cannot replace the original bond, so the attempt to help actually deepens the child’s grief.  

In a school setting, a teacher might notice a sad student and try to lift his mood by inviting him over after class to work on a project. If the student’s father had recently died in a car accident, this well‑meaning suggestion can remind him of his loss and intensify his sorrow, making his emotional state worse than before. The student may become withdrawn, avoid class participation, and experience a drop in academic performance, showing that the comment intensified his emotional pain.  

These examples show that well‑intentioned actions, when performed without proper understanding, can create additional difficulties rather than resolve the original ones indeed clearly.

Manypeople discover that consulting more than one person is helpful when they need to make a decision. Different voices can point out mistakes that a single opinion might miss, and together they increase the chance of choosing a wise course, such as avoiding theft or illegal trade. A single perspective may be narrow, while several viewpoints provide a fuller picture.

For example, a student who is stuck on a mathematics problem often finds that relying on just one difficult method does not succeed. By listening to various strategies, the student can select the one that fits best and solve the task more easily. In a classroom setting, children may ignore the teacher’s instructions, which can lead to disorder. Clear rules together with helpful suggestions guide them toward responsible behavior and keep the learning environment safe.

Sometimes individuals make reckless choices, like selling drugs or taking money from others. In these situations, advice can warn them about possible consequences and suggest better alternatives. Even youngsters, who may act impulsively at school, benefit from guidance that steers them toward appropriate conduct.

Although some people prefer to rely on a single trusted source, this can be risky if that person’s advice is incomplete or biased. When a decision involves serious matters—such as a person repeatedly stealing money—a broader discussion with several advisors can provide a clearer view and support a healthier choice.

When people gather opinions from several individuals, they can compare different experiences and avoid repeating the same mistakes that others have already made. For instance, a young adult deciding whether to accept a job offer can hear advice from a mentor, a family member, and a colleague, each highlighting different aspects such as growth opportunities, financial stability, and work‑life balance.

Although it might seem that unlessyou attempt something beyond what you already know, you will never develop, that view is mistaken. Mastering something does not guarantee that trying something new will lead to failure; rather, giving up is what prevents growth. For instance, adopting a healthier lifestyle—eating better and exercising—is challenging, yet many people still decide to give it a try. They do this because they want to push themselves into a new environment they never imagined would be difficult. Moreover, trying new activities often stems from a desire to find enjoyment or satisfaction. Learning to cook, for example, is something most people have never done before, but that doesn't stop them from giving it a go. In other words, we seek new challenges because we want to test our ability to solve problems we haven't faced before, or because we refuse to surrender.

Another motivation for seeking new experiences is curiosity. People may wonder whether they can master a new skill, such as raising a child and teaching them right from wrong. This curiosity drives us to attempt tasks that seem beyond our current capabilities. We believe that humans are capable of achieving things that machines cannot, simply because we are willing to explore and learn. History shows that societies have overcome great obstacles—gaining independence from colonial rule, abolishing slavery, and confronting racism—by persisting through difficulty. These achievements illustrate that mastery often requires effort, even when the goal seems impossible.

However, the greatest obstacle is not external difficulty but internal resistance. When we allow fear, doubt, or lack of motivation to dominate, we may label ourselves as failures or quitters, inflicting emotional pain upon ourselves without any physical harm. This emotional suffering is the most damaging challenge we face, because it blocks us from confronting and mastering our feelings. People who have succeeded in this area often seek therapy or self‑reflection to understand their emotional reactions. By confronting these inner struggles, we become more willing to try new things, driven by curiosity about what interests us and whether we can accomplish it. Thus, the key is to keep trying new challenges beyond our current mastery, as this is how we grow.

Many people say thatfirst impressions are hard to alter, and I agree for three main reasons. When we first meet someone, we instantly notice how they behave, and those observations create an immediate feeling of liking or disliking. Because a person might be seen only once, that single interaction often becomes the basis for a lasting judgment; there is little chance to see them in a different light. Even if we encounter the same individual repeatedly, the original emotional reaction tends to stay fixed, so our view of them remains unchanged. For example, I once met a man for the first time and, after a brief conversation, I found his manner of speaking and his demeanor unpleasant. That negative impression stayed with me, and I never revised it despite later seeing him again. Thus, the initial impression formed from a person’s actions is remarkably resistant to change. Therefore, once an initial judgment is made, it is difficult to alter one's opinion of that person. This makes first impressions especially powerful in social and professional settings.

Is it true that constantactivity leads to greater achievement, or can periods of inactivity also be valuable? I believe that remaining active is far more advantageous for progress, although brief moments of rest are sometimes necessary. When we keep ourselves occupied, we naturally produce more results. Staying busy forces us to plan, organize, and meet realistic, measurable objectives, which in turn accelerates our ability to reach goals. An active mindset also makes us better prepared for future challenges, because we are constantly practicing the skills needed for success. Conversely, a life devoid of activity is unhealthy and unproductive. Idleness encourages procrastination and prevents personal growth; it does not move us closer to the targets we set. While occasional pauses allow the mind to reflect and reassess strategies, they should be limited and purposeful rather than a permanent state of inaction. Thomas Jefferson captured this idea when he observed that great accomplishments arise from continual effort. His words remind us that sustained work, not perpetual laziness, drives achievement. Setting specific, attainable targets gives direction, while regular evaluation of progress ensures continuous improvement. Even short breaks can refresh the mind, provided they are used to regain focus rather than to avoid work. Therefore, cultivating a habit of purposeful activity, supported by clear goals and occasional, intentional rest, is the most reliable path to success.

My second point concerns the power of attitude to inspire others. My cousin spent three years in the final year of high school without passing, which lowered her confidence and made her doubt her goals. This year, after dedicating herself to studying and preparing for the exams, she is on track to graduate. Her story illustrates how a positive mindset can help someone overcome repeated disappointment and reach the desired outcome.

Some may argue that failure harms society, but I maintain that learning from the beginning is essential for any achievement. My third argument is that the experience gained from multiple failures equips us with the insight needed for eventual success. As the saying goes, “You can lose a battle but not the war,” meaning we may lose many things, yet our enthusiasm and determination should remain intact.

In conclusion, I agree with Churchill that failure is vital for success. Personal experience, the ability to motivate others, and the lessons drawn from repeated setbacks all demonstrate that persisting despite failure leads to lasting achievement.

Extending my skills in this way illustrates how surpassing what one can already do leads to new capabilities, higher positions, or richer pastimes.

Tryingsomething that lies outside the limits of what you already know is the only way to develop. It may sound like a simple piece of advice, yet in a world where many people cling to familiar habits, such wisdom often goes unheeded. I share this view, except for the fact that my physical growth has already plateaued; I feel I have reached my limit in that respect. Returning to the central idea, I fully endorse Ralph Waldo Emerson’s observation that without venturing beyond what we have mastered, true growth is impossible. In my seventeen years of life I have experimented with many activities, and I can attest that I have changed into the person I am today.  

Many individuals avoid new experiences simply because they judge the appearance of the opportunity or the person offering it before giving it a chance. If they were willing to try, the outcome could be either beneficial or detrimental, but the possibility of transformation is undeniable.  

When I speak of stepping beyond what I have mastered, I do not mean that I must constantly change; rather, I mean that a willingness to explore new paths is essential for personal advancement. I have made an effort to try new things, and I believe that doing so can help me become a better member of society. Conversely, if I chose to remain in a monotonous routine, I would eventually feel bored and stagnant.  

Some may argue that repeated, consistent practice was the key to their success. This point is valid in certain contexts. For example, athletes often repeat the same drills until they perfect a skill, and dancers rehearse the same movements until a performance is ready. In these cases, repetition is a necessary part of mastery.  

However, for other people, embracing a new routine can lead to unexpected achievements, even if talent varies.  

In conclusion, trying something new does change who you are, either by helping you grow or by causing harm.  

People may become wiser with age, but not everyone who grows older becomes wise; some remain youthful and reckless.  

Ralph Waldo Emerson, a thinker of great insight, captured this truth when he said that without reaching beyond existing abilities, growth cannot occur.  

Thank you for reading my thoughts.

During a council meeting, officials are considering a 10 p.m. curfew on weekdays and a midnight curfew on weekends for teenagers. I am convinced that implementing these curfews is a beneficial measure because they keep young people out of trouble. Firstly, teenagers are less likely to be on the streets after 10 p.m., a time when drug‑using adults and other hazards are common, so staying home reduces the risk of encountering danger. Secondly, being at home allows them to spend time with their families, complete schoolwork, and discuss positive matters, which supports their well‑being. Finally, obeying the curfew teaches responsibility; breaking it can lead to serious consequences, so the rule encourages respect for community regulations. When teenagers are required to be home early, parents can more easily supervise their activities and prevent them from getting involved in illegal behavior. In short, the proposed curfews protect teenagers from risky situations, keep them safe under parental supervision, and reinforce lawful behavior. Therefore, the council should adopt the weekday 10 p.m. and weekend midnight curfews for youths. These measures not only lower the chances of nighttime incidents but also give families peace of mind, making neighborhoods safer for everyone.

Ralph Waldo Emerson suggests that society often tries to shape us into something we are not. I believe that each person possesses the power to choose actions that improve themselves and become better members of society, although some choices can lead us astray. Therefore, we must establish clear objectives for the future and plan the steps needed to reach them.  

From my experience behind bars, I learned that self‑respect is essential. If we do not value ourselves, there is little reason to set goals that might simply gather dust. While people may claim that external forces are responsible for their decisions, this view is inaccurate; individuals often shift blame onto others when they know they have erred. We should take responsibility for our own actions.  

In today’s world, cooperation and mutual support are vital. We need to act as a family, lifting each other up when we fall and healing one another when we are hurt. Difficult periods are temporary; remembering how far we have come from past hardships gives us strength. The world may try to pressure, break, or discard us, but the goals we set and the supportive people around us can help us achieve our dreams. When we surround ourselves with positive influences, we find the courage to keep moving forward. Small acts of kindness reinforce our resolve and remind us that we are not alone on this journey. By staying focused on our personal vision, we can turn challenges into opportunities for growth.

In my view, students should enroll in activities at their own school because doing something they love builds confidence, keeps them active, prevents excessive screen time, and helps them become leaders rather than followers. First, pursuing a passion gives self‑belief and can turn dreams into reality; many youths doubt themselves, but commitment to a field they excel in shows they can succeed. Second, regular physical activity improves health, reduces stress, and can open pathways to professional opportunities, so an active lifestyle is essential. Third, spending too much time on electronic devices distracts from study, practice and social interaction, often leading to fatigue and reduced concentration, so balancing screen time with outdoor play and other pursuits is important. First, students should not be lazy because staying idle limits personal growth and can lead to boredom; participating in sports or clubs keeps the body healthy, improves mood, and can open doors to future opportunities such as professional athletics or scholarships. Second, excessive use of electronic devices distracts from studies and practice, causing fatigue and reduced concentration, which hinders academic performance and overall well‑being. Therefore, balancing screen time with outdoor activities, weekend plans with friends, or simple chores keeps energy levels high and mind focused. Trying new activities also helps students discover hidden talents, meet new friends, and develop resilience; life can be challenging, but the effort to pursue one’s passions builds character and prepares them for future responsibilities. Overall, living once means making the most of each day; by trying new activities, believing in your talents, staying active and limiting digital distractions, you grow personally and inspire others to do the same, becoming a leader rather than a follower. Signing up for a club or team also gives students chances to learn teamwork, leadership, and time‑management skills, which are valuable for later life. It creates a sense of belonging and can make school more enjoyable. Spending hours glued to a phone or computer not only reduces physical activity but also impairs concentration, makes it harder to finish homework, and can lead to sleep problems, all of which negatively affect academic success and personal health.

Success without anysetbacks is impossible. When a person never experiences failure, they remain unaware of their errors and therefore cannot improve. In my view, the saying by Ralph Waldo holds true: failure teaches us what went wrong and how to correct it, which ultimately leads to greater achievements. For instance, someone who only enjoys success will be lost when a problem arises because they have never practiced dealing with it. By confronting failure, we come to understand the effort required to reach a goal and we learn the conditions that make success possible. Consequently, we become more resilient and better prepared for future challenges. Although some may argue that constant success is preferable, I believe that failure and success work together; each provides the other with meaning. The unpredictable nature of life means that the ability to recover from failure is essential, and without having stumbled before, we would have no basis for growth. Thus, embracing failure is key to lifelong achievement.

Have you ever found that you understand something better when you see a concrete example, or do you prefer to learn through other means rather than being shown examples? Albert Schweitzer once remarked that “example is not the main thing to influence others,” suggesting that influence can occur through methods other than illustration. One such method is receiving direct assistance from a knowledgeable person, which often proves more effective than merely presenting examples.  

In my ceramics class, the instructor frequently demonstrates how to shape clay by showing a finished piece, yet she rarely offers personal guidance. Because she explains the process only once, many students, including myself, struggle to replicate the technique. When she does work closely with a student, that student’s project usually turns out superior to the rest of the class, indicating that hands‑on help can be more valuable than a single demonstration.  

Some argue that examples can be confusing. For instance, a teacher might ask students to draw whatever they imagine. If the teacher then supplies a sample picture, learners may feel compelled to copy the illustration rather than trust their own ideas, which can distort their creative thinking. This shows that examples are not universally beneficial, especially in subjects that rely on personal expression.  

Conversely, supporters of examples claim that they convey practical experience and clearly demonstrate how a task should be performed, thereby influencing learners more strongly. While it is true that some individuals learn more readily from visual models, I believe that there are several stronger approaches that can reduce the reliance on examples. Direct mentorship, step‑by‑step feedback, and guided practice often lead to deeper understanding and more lasting influence than a mere illustration.  

Therefore, I maintain that there are more powerful ways to affect others than simply providing examples. Direct support and personalized instruction tend to produce better outcomes and more lasting influence than isolated demonstrations.

Many students look forward to a longer summer vacation because it gives them extra time to be with family and friends. A longer break can also serve as a reward for those who have worked hard throughout the academic year and need a chance to relax away from assignments and grades. Recognizing their effort can reinforce the importance of education and motivate them to aim for better results later. It also helps prevent burnout by giving students a chance to recharge mentally and physically.

Some educators worry that students forget what they have learned when they return to class after a long break. While it is true that a vacation reduces stress and lets young people enjoy leisure activities such as reading or following the news, this does not mean learning stops. Research shows that a short period of rest can actually help consolidate memory, and younger learners are often quick to retain information after a break. Such consolidation can lead to better performance on tests after the break.

For many pupils, summer vacation is an opportunity to travel, either within their own country or abroad. An extended break provides enough time to explore new places, experience different cultures, and gain historical insights that they can later share with classmates and teachers, enriching classroom discussions. These experiences also broaden their worldview and foster cultural empathy.

A month away from school can affect anyone, depending on how the time is used. Some students use the vacation to earn money for personal expenses, while others devote themselves to community service or take part in various activities that keep them engaged. In either case, the extended break allows them to reconnect with relatives who live far away, strengthening family bonds that may be hard to maintain during the school year.

In summary, a longer summer vacation is advantageous. It offers a well‑deserved rest, supports personal development through travel and service, and helps students retain and even deepen their knowledge when they return to school. Overall, it benefits both learners and society for everyone.

Inmy view, a positive outlook is essential for achieving success in life. Many people claim that maintaining optimism can open doors and improve one's well‑being. I agree with this assessment because the way we think influences the chances we have to meet new people and seize opportunities. When we approach situations with confidence and hope, we are more likely to attract supportive contacts and to act decisively when possibilities appear. Having a positive mindset also helps you cope with stress and stay motivated during challenging times. It encourages resilience in the face of adversity.  

A constructive attitude also boosts personal performance. For instance, if you start work with optimism, you feel more energetic and can interact with colleagues in a friendly manner, which rarely harms your reputation. People who consistently show a hopeful demeanor tend to progress further in their careers and enjoy a more satisfying life.  

My own family illustrates this point. My grandparents, who have lived long and prosperous lives, attribute much of their success to an unwavering positive mindset. One of my grandfathers used to say that the only thing needed in any job or in life itself is a good attitude; with that, everything else can be attained. Whenever a difficult decision arises, they rely on their optimism to move forward rather than stay stuck.  

Moreover, a hopeful outlook shapes daily habits. A person who wakes up smiling at themselves is already setting a tone of confidence that can carry through the day. Conversely, those who lack such positivity may struggle to find direction and often feel uncertain about their actions.  

Looking ahead, the importance of a positive attitude will only grow. As societies become more competitive and complex, the ability to stay optimistic will be a valuable asset both personally and professionally. Therefore, cultivating a good attitude is one of the most effective steps anyone can take toward a successful life.

Some may argue that our behavior alone cannot change the world, but the evidence suggests otherwise. By consistently demonstrating helpfulness, a positive attitude, and reliability, we encourage others to reciprocate, creating a cycle of trust and support. This ripple effect can strengthen friendships, improve family bonds, enhance the reputation of teachers, and motivate public servants like firefighters to act even more responsibly. Ultimately, the way we behave shapes how others perceive and treat us, and it can lead to a more caring and supportive society.

Reading the statement, I understand that the speaker emphasizes the value of trying new activities throughout life. Many people spend their entire years doing the same thing, avoiding change because they think it isn’t necessary or they lack the motivation. In fact, staying in one role for decades can create a sense of stagnation, making it harder to see new possibilities or feel excited about the future. These new experiences also build adaptability and problem‑solving abilities, which are valuable in any career or personal project.  

However, accumulating diverse experiences helps a person develop and become more confident. For instance, when a young person begins to explore, they learn many skills that shape them into a better individual. Adults, who have already gathered considerable knowledge, recognize that growth often requires stepping outside one’s comfort zone. They also realize that responsibilities tied to what they already know influence their choices, yet embracing new challenges can broaden their horizons and relieve the pressure of routine.  

Going to school illustrates this idea. Education provides knowledge, and the more you learn, the more chances you have to succeed. School is only one part of lifelong learning; the skills and attitudes gained there continue to serve us in work and personal life. Beyond formal schooling, many people continue learning through work, travel, and online courses, showing that education does not stop at graduation.  

I agree with the speaker’s view for several reasons. First, people often become stuck in a single role; a teacher who has taught for five years might feel reluctant to change. Yet, exploring other professions or further studies can spark personal development and open new pathways. Sacrifices are inevitable—giving up hobbies, family time, or social events may be required—but the long‑term reward is a richer, more fulfilled life. The sense of achievement that comes from mastering new tasks can boost self‑esteem and reduce the feeling of being trapped.  

Consider someone who wishes to expand a small restaurant. By studying business, working as a manager, and applying sound financial practices and marketing strategies, the owner gains experience that drives growth. This not only improves the business but also contributes to personal advancement. Similarly, acquiring more experience generally leads to better job prospects and a higher quality of life, provided one is willing to move beyond familiar limits. Even small steps, such as learning a new software tool or volunteering, can accumulate into meaningful progress.  

In my own experience, the more I learn and the more I try, the more I grow. For example, I once decided to learn basic coding during my free time; the challenge pushed me to think differently and gave me confidence to take on new projects at work. Without venturing beyond what I already master, progress stalls and opportunities shrink.  

Therefore, I fully support the comment that expanding one’s experiences is essential for personal development and success. In short, embracing variety in life is not a luxury but a necessity for growth and fulfillment.

Many people find educational activities fun for several reasons. First, they provide opportunities to discover new information. Engaging in unfamiliar tasks does not harm you; instead, it offers benefits such as gaining fresh skills. For instance, trying a new dance style or experimenting with a creative project can become a personal interest, and the process itself expands what you know. These activities range from classroom lessons to extracurricular clubs, giving students varied chances to explore. Second, these activities are enjoyable because they let you share time with friends. Working together on a task encourages mutual support, and the friendship ties strengthen as you create memories together. Spending time together also strengthens teamwork skills that are useful later in life. Having friends nearby also means you can receive help when needed or simply talk about what concerns you, especially during difficult moments. Third, learning from errors makes the experience rewarding. As the saying goes, failure points the way to success; each mistake signals a chance to improve, prompting you to examine what went wrong and correct it. When you analyze a mistake, you learn not only the specific lesson but also how to approach future problems more wisely. This habit of reviewing and fixing errors sharpens your thinking and fuels imagination. Overall, these benefits make learning feel less like a chore and more like an enjoyable adventure. In short, educational activities are enjoyable because they let you do things you like, help you grow intellectually, and build stronger social connections. These experiences also boost confidence and prepare you for future challenges. Therefore, educational activities are not only fun but also valuable for personal development.

It is clear that summer vacationshould not be shortened. After months of attending classes, pupils need a prolonged break to relax and recharge. The long pause gives them a chance to step away from textbooks and enjoy activities that are impossible during the regular school year.

First, families can use this time to travel together. They can visit relatives who live far away, explore new places, and create shared memories without the pressure of homework or exams. Such trips strengthen family bonds and provide a mental reset.

Second, the extended break allows students to recover lost credits. Those who failed a subject can enroll in summer courses, earn back the necessary points, and stay on track for graduation. This flexibility supports academic progress rather than hindering it.

Third, athletes benefit from the extra time. Without the burden of school assignments, they can train more intensely, improve their fitness, and enjoy their sport without worrying about grades. This contributes to both physical health and personal satisfaction.

Fourth, readers gain ample opportunity to read. With fewer obligations, they can spend hours in libraries or at home, devouring books that broaden their knowledge and imagination.

Fifth, travelers and adventurers can explore the world, capture moments with photos, and write journals about their experiences, which they can later share with classmates. These activities enrich their education through real‑world learning.

If summer vacation were reduced, the negative consequences would be significant. More days spent in classrooms would limit leisure time, increase academic pressure, and raise stress levels among students. Families would have fewer chances to reunite, and the overall enjoyment of the break would diminish. The loss of a long vacation would make school life less balanced and could harm students’ well‑being.

In conclusion, keeping summer vacation intact is essential. It provides necessary rest, supports family connections, enables academic recovery, and offers diverse opportunities for personal growth. Therefore, school boards should maintain the current length of the summer break.

Overrecent years, students have increasingly relied on mobile phones, a trend that began only about fifteen years ago in today's digital age when these devices first became a regular part of daily life. At first, schools prohibited their use inside classrooms, but policies have since changed and pupils are now permitted to bring and operate their phones during lessons. This essay examines the consequences of allowing cellphones in class. Among the positive outcomes, teachers find it simpler to manage activities and share resources, while students benefit from quick access to information without waiting for a limited number of computers. Mobile phones also enable the use of specialized applications that may be difficult to run on school computers, giving both teachers and learners more flexibility. However, the same convenience brings notable drawbacks. Many pupils become distracted, checking messages or browsing the web while the teacher is speaking, and they may also use phones to disrupt classmates. Such interruptions can reduce concentration and hinder learning. In summary, permitting cellphones in the classroom offers clear advantages in terms of information access and instructional tools, yet it also raises serious concerns about distraction and classroom management. The overall impact therefore depends on how students and educators balance these competing factors.

Winston Churchill is often quoted as saying that failure is essential to achieving success. I agree that failure is crucial, but only for people who truly want to improve their lives. First, every failure teaches us something. When we make a mistake, we learn what went wrong and how to avoid it later. People who have experienced similar setbacks are often the best guides for those currently facing the same problem, because they have already walked that path. Since life is full of errors, learning from each one keeps us moving forward.  

Second, failure reveals who our real supporters are. Friends who stay with us during difficult times show their true character, while those who disappear may have only been interested in easy moments. Even someone we consider the least helpful can become the one who offers real assistance when we need it most.  

Third, we must avoid repeating the same mistake. If we keep making the same error, our enthusiasm fades and it becomes harder to stay motivated. By learning from the first failure, we can progress more quickly and tackle additional challenges without losing momentum.  

In conclusion, everyone encounters failure, but the most successful people are those who extract a lesson from each setback and refuse to repeat it. The ability to change one’s life depends on a strong desire and readiness to improve.

Having a positive mindset is essentialfor achieving success and enjoying a fulfilling life. When you treat yourself kindly and interact pleasantly with others, your days become brighter and more engaging. For instance, imagine working in customer service and a client criticizes you, claiming you are not performing well. Even in that situation, maintaining a calm and optimistic outlook is crucial; you understand that the client’s frustration is not directed at you personally, and your role requires you to stay professional and continue working with confidence. A positive outlook offers many benefits. Observing someone’s tired or angry expression often indicates that they are dealing with a negative environment, whereas presenting a friendly demeanor signals readiness to take action, generate positive energy, and make tasks easier. Pursuing your aspirations also demands self‑knowledge, mutual respect, and an attitude that demonstrates good conduct. A constructive attitude shapes how others perceive you, influencing whether you are considered a strong candidate for a desirable position. When you approach opportunities with optimism, you increase the likelihood of undertaking significant projects and achieving long‑term goals. In a job interview, showing your abilities clearly, speaking honestly, and remaining courteous helps the interviewer assess your suitability. A favorable attitude can lead to better employment, higher earnings, a comfortable home, and an improved future. Moreover, spreading positive vibes lifts the mood of those around you, including loved ones, and encourages everyone to strive for their best achievements with confidence. A positive attitude also strengthens relationships, because people are drawn to those who radiate optimism and support. When you consistently show kindness, friends and family feel valued and are more likely to reciprocate, creating a supportive network that enhances both personal and professional growth. Thus, a positive mindset not only improves individual well‑being but also contributes to a more harmonious community. For example, a manager who greets his team with a smile and encourages open communication often sees higher morale and productivity, demonstrating how attitude influences outcomes.

Docurfews keep teenagers out of trouble, or do they unfairly limit young people's freedom? I believe they are necessary because they protect youths, especially when they are still growing and out at night. The intention behind curfews is to keep them safe; the only group that gains from this rule is the teenagers themselves. If a teen is out in the middle of the night without supervision, they may act without restraint, which can lead to trouble. When a curfew is in place, they must obey the set time, just as adults are expected to respect community rules. In the evening most people are at home with family, so there are fewer opportunities for misbehavior on the streets. Moreover, nighttime is a time when theft or violent incidents are more likely, and a curfew reduces the chance that a teenager becomes a victim or a perpetrator. Some argue that staying out late is fun, but in my view nightlife can be dangerous; for instance, a shooting at a club in Las Vegas a few years ago showed how quickly a night out can turn tragic. In short, curfews serve a protective purpose for teenagers and therefore are a positive measure.

In fact, many people fail to achieve their objectives because they lack a positive outlook. A hopeful attitude is the foundation of success in life, since it brings optimism, helps confront difficulties, and builds confidence in oneself. For instance, Generic_Name always thinks positively about his studies, his job, and his personal life, which makes him unafraid to tackle new challenges. Can studentsgain advantages by studying from home? I believe that, although a few learners might find it useful, most students would profit more from attending school in person. For instance, they can take part in sports they enjoy, avoid boredom in a classroom, and enroll in elective courses or specialized programs. Nevertheless, not every pupil would choose remote learning as their sole option, since many lack the means to do so.  

First, schools provide opportunities for athletic activities. Many students love playing sports, and the school offers the facilities for them. When I feel down, joining a game such as soccer helps me distract myself, have fun, and share my enthusiasm with teammates. Regular participation in sports can keep young people away from drugs and gang involvement, giving them a constructive outlet and a chance to pursue their aspirations.  

Second, attending school prevents boredom. Learners feel motivated and happy when they interact with classmates and teachers, rather than staying alone at a computer at home. In school they can ask a teacher for help, study with a peer, visit museums or university campuses, and explore history together. These social experiences make learning more engaging.  

Third, schools offer elective classes and academies that let students discover their interests. Our country provides courses such as cooking, piano, cosmetology, art, fitness, medical assistance, dentistry, band, police work, detective work, electrical trades, and emergency services. These options help learners identify what they want to study later and give them credits that can be transferred to university or scholarship applications. For example, my school guided me toward a career path and assisted with university enrollment.  

In conclusion, while some students might prefer distance learning because of personal circumstances, the majority would benefit more from being present in school, where they can practice sports, stay motivated, avoid boredom, and take advantage of diverse elective programs. However, it is important to recognize that a minority cannot attend school due to family responsibilities, work commitments, or lack of transportation, and they may need alternative options such as online classes to complete their education.

First impressions matter because they shape how we are perceived and remembered. When we meet someone for the first time, that initial impression often determines how we are judged thereafter. A warm smile, steady eye contact, and confident posture signal openness and competence, while a closed posture or distracted demeanor can create a negative impression that is hard to reverse. Research shows that people form judgments within the first few seconds of meeting someone, and those first impressions tend to persist. Consequently, presenting oneself with confidence, genuine interest, and genuine respect for others increases the likelihood of making a positive, lasting impression.

Many argue that young peopleshould not decide on a career early because they lack the time and experience to make such a serious choice. I disagree; committing to a profession while still in school can be advantageous. If a student knows their desired field early, they can focus their studies and activities on that path, gaining deeper knowledge than someone who waits until later. This early commitment also prevents the need to try many different jobs just to discover a suitable occupation after graduation.

Conversely, some people believe that adolescents are too immature to choose a career and that they should wait until after high school. Yet, a student who has already identified a vocation can use the remaining years of secondary education to explore that field more thoroughly, perhaps through internships, specialized courses, or mentorships. By the time they finish school, they will have a clearer picture of what the career entails and be better prepared to make informed decisions about further education or training. This approach also helps students develop confidence in their choices and reduces the stress associated with uncertain future plans.

In conclusion, students ought to commit to a career at a young age. Doing so allows them to build relevant expertise early, reduces uncertainty later in life, and leads to more purposeful planning after they leave school.

It is often claimed that the initial impression of a person is virtually impossible to alter later on. While some may argue that they can reshape that first impression whenever they wish, this view is inaccurate because the moment of first contact occurs so rapidly that there is no time to think or to act differently. An impression forms in a fraction of a second, faster than a blink, and therefore cannot be deliberately modified in that instant. Nevertheless, certain impressions can be revised if the circumstances allow, whereas others remain fixed no matter what one does.  

An impression is an affective feeling or mental image that remains after an encounter. Some of these impressions have a strong impact on our lives. Consider a student who feels unwell in class and, without warning, produces a loud noise that everyone hears. His first impression is to act normally, but the embarrassment is immediate: his face turns red, his heart races, and he cannot hide the shame. Such moments are not part of everyday life, and the resulting feeling of discomfort can linger for a long time.  

When an embarrassing event happens only occasionally, the resulting sensation may be intense, bringing confusion, unease, or even pain. However, if the same type of situation occurs repeatedly, the emotional reaction gradually weakens. The person may start to answer normally, for example when a parent asks about a girlfriend or when friends inquire about a romantic interest. After sufficient practice, the initial shame disappears and the response becomes calm and ordinary.  

My own experience illustrates this change. After many occasions of being asked about a potential relationship, I no longer feel embarrassed; I simply smile or give a straightforward answer, behaving like any other student. The repeated exposure has allowed me to replace the initial negative impression with a neutral one.  

I hope that in the future, when someone poses an awkward question, the instant feeling of shame will not dominate. My past experiences should help me stay composed, so the moment does not become the most painful part of my life.

I oppose the claim that imagination alone is sufficient. In my view, imagination resembles dreaming, but it becomes powerful only when it is backed by knowledge. With knowledge, a person can focus their mind on a goal and turn ideas into concrete achievements, such as founding a business, hiring staff, and delivering products to customers. This transformation is not merely fantasy; it is a real possibility, though it requires completing school, attending college, earning a degree, and investing considerable time. Developing a determined mindset and self‑motivation is essential for success. Moreover, someone who has navigated these steps can assist others—offering guidance on finding employment or creating one’s own venture—and inspire them to set their own goals. The help spreads: each person who receives support can then aid another, creating an endless cycle of encouragement. Thus, while imagination may exist only during sleep or idle thought, it is knowledge that makes it a practical tool for shaping the future. Therefore, education and perseverance are the keys to turning dreams into reality.

I back the school board’s plan to add one and a half hours to the school day because it would give each class more time to learn. With a longer period, a worksheet or set of notes that a teacher hands out can be worked through fully while the lesson is still in session, rather than being left incomplete when the bell rings. At present, many classes end before students can finish their assignments, forcing them to work after school or rush through the material. The extra half hour would give teachers a buffer to address questions that arise during the lesson, rather than having to schedule separate help sessions.  

Another advantage is that teachers would have extra time to deliver their material without feeling rushed. They could finish lesson plans, grade assignments, or attend to other duties, which means they are less likely to cut short a topic because the clock is ticking. With more time, teachers could also incorporate short activities or reviews that reinforce learning without sacrificing the main content. This flexibility would reduce the stress of trying to squeeze everything into a short period.  

The extended schedule also gives students more chances to master difficult concepts. The longer schedule also gives students more chances to master difficult concepts. If a subject is unclear, the teacher can spend additional time revisiting it step by step, offering explanations and practice until the class feels confident, which often leads to better test performance. When teachers have the luxury of extra minutes, they can repeat key points, use examples, and check for understanding before moving on. Students who receive this additional support often feel more confident and are more likely to participate in class discussions.  

Moreover, the extra hour allows teachers to plan more effectively and to catch up on work that was not finished earlier. Teachers could also use the longer day to organize materials, update lesson plans, and prepare for upcoming units, which improves the overall quality of instruction. Students can also use the additional time to complete assignments they missed, reducing the pressure to rush the next day. Students who finish their work early can start on enrichment activities or review previous lessons, making the school day more productive.  

If the extension were not implemented, teachers would have limited time to cover the curriculum, and students would have difficulty obtaining help on topics they find challenging. Without the extra time, teachers may be forced to skip portions of the syllabus, and students may miss out on essential content, which can affect their overall academic progress. The lack of sufficient time for clarification can lead to frustration and lower motivation among learners.  

Overall, the additional half‑hour would benefit both learners and educators by providing more time for instruction, review, and completion of tasks, leading to improved understanding and higher achievement.

John Lubbock once said that a person’s character is shaped by the choices they make. This observation raises a worry: children sometimes alter their personalities because they feel insecure and spend a lot of time reflecting on themselves. While personal traits can dominate, I do not believe that we are completely powerless. The way others perceive us can make us feel uncertain, and we may try to modify ourselves to gain approval, just as the values we inherit from our families and the broader culture shape us. In today’s world, countless forces — especially the internet — exert influence that can go far beyond what we can control, offering both positive and negative examples.

Another possible outcome is that we can change our perspective on life, just as other people do. I have noticed a great shift in myself since moving to Virginia; I have been learning to behave in a way that feels normal to the locals. This adjustment shows that external factors, such as the media we consume or the music we listen to — like rap songs that talk about various topics — can affect our behavior. Young people, like adults, are vulnerable to these influences, and we may consciously decide which ideas to adopt.

Nevertheless, we also retain the ability to choose our own path. We decide which habits to follow, which values to embrace, and which direction to take. The world we live in is constantly changing, with new challenges appearing each year — conflicts, environmental degradation, and emerging diseases — all of which can be amplified by the opinions of others, leading to fear. Yet, thoughtful consideration can help us navigate these pressures.

In conclusion, while personal choice plays a crucial role in forming character, we are also surrounded by powerful external influences that can shape our behavior. Finding a balance between self‑direction and openness to beneficial influences allows us to move forward, even when we feel stuck.

People should seek guidance from experts and authorities about life's important matters. Those who try to make their own decisions often lack knowledge, follow only their instincts and ideas, and believe their actions are correct even when they are not and against the rules.  

Laws: the consumption of drugs and alcohol, the carrying of guns, and driving. The consumption of drugs is unlawful in many states and a permission to purchase them is required. Alcohol is legal but you need to be at least 21 years old to buy it, and you also need permission and be of a certain age to carry a gun. To obtain a driver's license, you must be at least 16, and if you get it at 16 you must have a more experienced copilot present, because they want to be sure you have the experience to drive alone.  

Work: when you have a job you must follow rules such as a schedule and duties. You have a specific schedule that tells you when to come to work and when to go home, which helps keep everything organized for the employer. If the employer could come to work whenever they want, it could affect the company; for example, if you are an accountant and the company needs you in the morning but you decide not to go because you make your own decision, you might go in the afternoon, causing problems with the accounts and making it your fault for not following the schedule. You also have specific duties that match your skills, so you cannot decide to do something else, because you could be fired.  

Society: you do not have the freedom to do everything you want outside, such as burning a library because you think it is brilliant, kicking or hitting others just to make your friends laugh, or taking a flower from private property that you like. You cannot make those decisions in your life.  

In conclusion, we cannot let people make all their own decisions. I am not saying that people cannot have rights to do or be something; I am saying that they cannot do everything they want, and they need guidance from experts and authorities, especially minors who lack the conscience to know what is right.

People ought to rely on the advice of experts and authorities when dealing with matters that affect their lives, because those who try to decide everything on their own often act only on impulse. Without a knowledgeable guide, a person depends on personal instincts and ideas, assuming that whatever feels right must be correct, even when it contradicts facts or established rules.  

For example, the law restricts the use of illegal substances, the carrying of firearms, and the operation of motor vehicles. Drugs are prohibited in most jurisdictions, and a special permit is required to obtain them. Alcohol may be legal, but sales are allowed only to individuals who are twenty‑one years old or older. Firearms are permitted only with a license, and a similar age restriction applies. Driving also demands a licence, which cannot be issued until the driver reaches sixteen; a novice must first practice with an experienced passenger until sufficient experience is gained.  

In the workplace, employees must follow set schedules and perform specific duties. An accountant, for instance, cannot decide to arrive at the office in the afternoon if the job requires a morning presence; doing so would disrupt the company's records and could lead to termination. These rules keep the organization orderly and ensure that each worker’s responsibilities match his or her skills.  

Similarly, society imposes limits on individual freedom. One cannot set fire to a library simply because the idea seems clever, nor can one assault others or trespass on private property to take a flower that has caught one’s eye. Such prohibitions show that people are not free to act without restraint.  

Consequently, it is unrealistic to expect everyone to make every decision independently. While individuals retain rights to choose certain actions, they also need the counsel of knowledgeable figures—teachers, mentors, officials—to help them discern what is truly appropriate, especially for younger people who have not yet developed a mature sense of right and wrong.

Adopting a positive mindset is crucial for achieving success in life. When individuals maintain an optimistic outlook, they not only enhance their own well‑being but also contribute to the betterment of the community around them. Although many people currently possess a negative attitude that hinders their progress, I firmly agree that shifting toward a more positive perspective is necessary, because it enables a happier family life, more productive work performance, and the capacity to uplift others.

First, a constructive attitude fosters healthier relationships within the family. People who approach their loved ones with patience and goodwill are more likely to experience mutual respect and emotional support. Conversely, those who carry a hostile or indifferent demeanor often struggle to maintain harmony at home, which can lead to conflict and dissatisfaction. By consciously improving their attitude, individuals can rebuild trust and create a more supportive domestic environment.

Second, a positive outlook significantly influences professional performance. Employees who greet colleagues and customers with a friendly smile and attentive listening tend to receive better evaluations and enjoy greater job satisfaction. For instance, a salesperson who remains calm and courteous when answering inquiries is more likely to close deals and build lasting client relationships. In contrast, a rude or impatient worker may alienate coworkers and customers, ultimately damaging his career prospects.

Moreover, a hopeful attitude enables individuals to assist others in need. When people approach problems with optimism, they are more inclined to offer help, share advice, or guide others toward better decisions. In educational settings, teachers who model a positive stance can encourage students to adopt similar behaviors, thereby improving classroom dynamics and academic outcomes. As students mature, this cultivated mindset equips them to make wiser choices in their future occupations and personal lives.

Nevertheless, many individuals persist in negative habits, such as impatience with children or disregard for societal responsibilities. These behaviors often stem from unresolved frustrations or a lack of self‑reflection. Recognizing the drawbacks of a pessimistic outlook is the first step toward change. Once people become aware that a negative attitude limits their ability to connect with family, perform effectively at work, or contribute positively to society, they are more likely to seek ways to modify their behavior.

In practice, cultivating a positive attitude involves simple yet powerful actions: practicing gratitude, listening actively, and responding with kindness even when faced with hostility. By controlling emotional reactions, individuals can maintain composure in challenging situations, such as dealing with an angry customer, and respond in a manner that de‑escalates tension rather than inflames it.

In summary, a positive attitude serves as the foundation for personal success and societal progress. It strengthens family bonds, enhances professional achievements, and empowers individuals to help others make better choices. While many currently struggle with negative perspectives, the transformative potential of optimism offers a clear pathway to a more fulfilling life and a healthier community.

I shareThomas Jefferson’s view that we can achieve a great deal when we work together. Often people stay idle, which causes them to miss many chances. It is far more effective to be part of a community, strive for the advantages we need, and remain active. Such behavior can bring about significant changes in our lives. To avoid putting off everyday duties, we should stay engaged and take part in activities that are useful to ourselves or others. When we regularly contribute, we help establish clear expectations for society and strengthen a person’s outlook. Achieving a result does not always mean reaching a specific target; it can also involve doing ordinary tasks well and gaining the most benefit from them. We must fight for what we want and never let an opportunity slip away. In my own life I have often been inactive and therefore lost many possibilities. The chances I had slipped through my fingers because I did not act. It is better to make an effort each day to pursue our goals and to keep moving forward. An active individual can assist others in reaching their objectives, which feels rewarding and makes good use of time. In a world where people have large ambitions, collective effort is essential. Simple deeds, such as helping a neighbor or joining a community project, may seem small but can create a big impact on society. Since the day is limited, we should use our time wisely by being active, working toward our aims, and supporting those who need assistance. In short, it does not matter who we are; by being sociable, staying active, and seizing every chance, we can reach our goals and make a positive difference.

Several schoolsnow provide distance learning as an alternative for students to attend lessons from home through online platforms or video conferencing. I believe this option would be advantageous for many learners, especially those who work during the evening or have other commitments that make attending regular classes difficult.  

Because many classes start at 7:30 a.m., students who have night‑time jobs often struggle to obtain enough rest. For instance, my friend works from 5 p.m. until midnight after school; he must rise at 5 a.m. to reach school, which leaves him exhausted during the first period. Lack of sleep not only affects his concentration but also jeopardizes his chance of earning a diploma, which he views as essential for a better future.  

Consequently, a distance‑learning programme would enable these students to keep their jobs while gaining additional sleep, which can improve academic performance. When they are not rushed, they have more time to complete homework, review material, and prepare for examinations, leading to higher grades and reduced stress caused by fatigue. This flexibility also allows them to maintain a more balanced daily routine, supporting both work and study responsibilities.  

Another group that could benefit are pregnant high‑school girls. Many of them avoid returning to school after giving birth because they feel judged by peers and teachers, or because caring for a newborn makes regular attendance difficult. With the option to study from home, they can continue their coursework without the need to attend classes in person, which reduces stress and increases the likelihood of completing their high‑school education.  

In summary, offering distance learning would support a wide range of students facing time constraints or family responsibilities. By allowing them to study from home, they can maintain employment, obtain sufficient rest, and ultimately achieve better educational outcomes, which benefits both the individuals and society. Such a programme would therefore be a practical solution to improve attendance, reduce dropout rates, and promote equity in education. It also prepares students for the increasingly digital workforce today.

I agree that being yourself can be challenging, yet it is essential for personal growth. In a world where many people feel isolated, choosing to act according to one’s own preferences is not easy, but it brings several advantages. When you rely on yourself, you have fewer distractions and can concentrate on tasks, which often leads to higher productivity. At the same time, allowing yourself time for enjoyment and socialising prevents burnout, so a balanced approach is ideal. Being true to yourself also means accepting your weaknesses and celebrating your strengths, which helps build a realistic self‑image.

First, spending time alone lets me develop my own ideas and evaluate what is truly valuable to me. By thinking twice before acting, I become more decisive and stronger. During my first year living in the United States without my family, I felt extremely sad and isolated because I did not speak the language and had no friends. That period taught me how difficult it is to stay true to oneself when external support is missing, and it showed me that self‑reliance is not a simple choice.

Second, after a few years I decided to stop comparing myself with others and to ignore the pressure from peers or relatives that made me feel unhappy. I stopped looking at what other people were doing and focused on my own path. This shift reduced my anxiety and gave me a sense of independence; I learned that I could manage my life without constantly seeking approval. Over time, I noticed that my decisions became quicker because I trusted my own judgment rather than waiting for external validation.

Third, recent years have shown that I am fully responsible for my own actions and decisions. My family recently reminded me that I must learn to handle things on my own before I turn eighteen. Although I was initially unable to do anything without their help, I have now mastered everyday tasks, managed my finances, and made my own choices. This self‑reliance has increased my confidence and prepared me for future challenges. These experiences have taught me that self‑acceptance is a continuous process, but it is worth the effort.

In conclusion, while being yourself is often hard and can feel lonely, the benefits—greater focus, personal insight, and independence—outweigh the difficulties. My experiences confirm that embracing one’s true self leads to a more fulfilling and balanced life.

Ralph WaldoEmerson wrote that ‘to be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment.’ I think this statement is wrong. To achieve real success you must seize control of your life instead of letting the world decide for you.  

First, you have to make your own choices. When you allow society or other people to choose your direction, you may end up feeling lost and dissatisfied. By deciding for yourself you understand why you selected a particular career, hobby or goal, and this clarity gives your life purpose. If you let others shape your future, you risk spending years in activities that feel empty.  

Second, genuine accomplishment comes from doing what you truly enjoy. When a task matches your interests, it never feels like a burden; you stay motivated and avoid fatigue. Choosing a profession or pastime that you love means you will not view it as mere work. Moreover, only you know your strengths, weaknesses and passions, so relying on your own judgment helps you pick the right field, set realistic goals and stay committed.  

Some people argue that following the crowd is safer, but history shows that those who submit to external expectations often regret their choices later. They may drift through life without direction, because they never exercised personal agency. In contrast, people who assert their independence create a life that reflects their values and aspirations.  

In summary, the path to the greatest accomplishment is not to submit to the world’s attempts to mould you, but to take responsibility for your own decisions and pursue what you love. By doing so you avoid boredom, maintain satisfaction and build a life that is truly yours.

I agree with Albert Einstein that imagination outweighs knowledge. Knowledge gives us facts, but imagination lets us picture possibilities and shape new ideas. When we let our imagination lead, we can discover ways to obtain knowledge that we might never have considered. However, imagination can also mislead us if we let it run too far, causing confusion or unrealistic expectations. For example, a student who daydreams about a subject far beyond what his mind can handle may become overwhelmed. In such moments, solid knowledge can be more useful because it grounds thinking and helps solve concrete problems, like the difficulty of a tricky math question on the test. Reading a book may expand your vocabulary while also sparking creative thoughts, showing how the two can complement each other. If someone wants to design a building but has no clear plan, imagination can suggest many designs, and then knowledge provides the technical details needed to turn the idea into reality. Both are valuable, yet there are situations where imagination can cause trouble. When a person feels down, imagination may tell them that nothing will bring happiness, which can be discouraging. In childhood, vivid imagination can make play unfair, leading to conflicts with friends, and a careless attitude toward knowledge in school can damage relationships, such as bragging about a high score that hurts a friend’s feelings. A teenage boy who is not the top student might rely on imagination to find a job, but without sufficient knowledge or effort his chances are low, and he may end up without work or become dependent on others for basic needs. This can lead to homelessness if he cannot repay the help he receives from friends. Young children naturally have the most imagination because they have few expectations. At night they may imagine monsters in closets and ask their parents to check, even though their parents insist there are none. The child may hear noises, become frightened, and scream for help, while the parents continue to deny the presence of any monster. Eventually the child discovers that the “monster” was just a parent making noise for fun, showing how imagination can both frighten and be clarified by reality. Moreover, imagination can motivate people to pursue learning, turning curiosity into a drive for acquiring knowledge. When a scientist envisions a new theory, the subsequent research relies on existing knowledge to test and refine the idea, demonstrating a partnership between the two faculties. In everyday life, people often use imagination to plan projects, and then apply knowledge of materials, measurements, and time management to bring those plans to completion. This interplay shows that neither faculty is superior in an absolute sense; rather, they each fulfill different roles that together enhance problem‑solving and creativity. Educators often encourage students to develop both imagination and knowledge, recognizing that creative thinking can spark interest in a subject, while factual understanding provides the foundation for deeper exploration. By balancing imagination with disciplined study, individuals can achieve both innovative ideas and reliable results. This balanced approach helps people grow personally and contributes to society. Overall, the balance between imagination and knowledge leads to richer personal growth and societal progress.

Modern technology enables us to accomplish many activities without meeting anyone face‑to‑face. We can borrow books, purchase goods, and play games while staying at home, avoiding direct conversation.  

However, this reduction in personal contact has produced several drawbacks. The constant reliance on devices has weakened the quality of our everyday lives.  

In the classroom, many schools now deliver lessons through online platforms, which often replace the teacher’s presence. Students watch recorded material instead of receiving live explanations, so the interaction between teacher and pupil diminishes. When I was younger, my teacher would write the task on the blackboard, clarify each point, and repeat the explanation until the whole class understood. That personal contact was essential for learning.  

Socially, the situation has also changed. In my childhood we gathered in the school cafeteria, shared stories about our day, and enjoyed each other’s company. Today, during lunch break, most students stare at their phones, and genuine conversation becomes rare.  

The loss of face‑to‑face interaction extends beyond school. Modern society tends to keep people inside their homes. People stream movies, read e‑books, and play video games because the technology is readily available, leading to a disengagement from the outside world. Even when nations clash with nuclear weapons, many stay glued to their screens, showing how technology can detach us from real‑world crises, and when tragedies occur nearby, many stay indifferent because the digital world shields them from real‑life emotions, making us feel weaker and less compassionate.  

Our dependence on gadgets also fosters laziness. Instead of walking to a library to fetch a book, we order it online and sit on the couch. Likewise, we used to meet friends at restaurants, talk while eating, and savor the company. Now many simply order food through an app, eat alone, and scroll on their phones, eliminating any personal connection.  

At work, technology is a double‑edged sword. It provides useful tools, yet it also creates constant distractions. Employees may watch a favorite team’s match on their phones, forget their responsibilities, and become less productive. Such neglect can lead to poor performance, loss of the job, and the need to find new employment.  

Moreover, the overuse of technology has contributed to a rise in accidents. Drivers who text while operating a vehicle often miss turns, collide with other cars, and cause fatal injuries. The resulting loss of a spouse, parent, or child underscores how careless reliance on devices can endanger lives.  

In summary, technology, while convenient, has produced several negative consequences. It reduces human interaction, encourages idleness, weakens emotional sensitivity, and even threatens safety. If we depended less on devices, we would likely enjoy richer social lives and maintain stronger connections with one another.
