Several years ago, before my uncle became a qualified physician, I watched him struggle with frequent anxiety attacks that resulted from an intense medical‑school study schedule. His experience showed me that balancing study with leisure is essential for maintaining mental health.

He soon realized that engaging in different, less demanding activities could give him a brief escape and help reduce his stress.

Allowing each student to take part in at least one extracurricular pursuit is a valuable idea. Such activities may include joining a sports team, becoming a member of a book club, or volunteering for community service. When every learner participates in some form of extra‑curricular involvement, their lives can become more varied and fulfilling, offering diverse experiences and reducing overall tension. These activities also foster social connections, allowing young people to meet peers with different interests and develop teamwork abilities that are essential in later life.

Physical activity is especially important for young people. Most students spend many hours seated in class and then remain seated at home on a couch, which limits movement. Regular exercise, even as little as twenty minutes per day, can improve cardiovascular health, boost metabolism, and support physical growth during adolescence. Even short bouts of activity can raise energy levels and improve concentration during classes. Incorporating sport into a daily routine therefore contributes significantly to a healthier body.

Reading also offers a useful mental break. A book can transport the reader to distant lands, imaginary worlds, or historical periods without leaving the chair. Through stories of adventure, drama, romance, or mystery, students can momentarily step away from their routine worries and refresh their minds. Book clubs enhance this experience by providing a space for discussion, where participants can share interpretations, discover new perspectives, and connect with peers who hold similar viewpoints. Such social interaction helps students feel less isolated and builds confidence, which can positively influence their classroom participation. These small breaks also help prevent the mental fatigue that often builds up during long study sessions.

Community service combines personal benefit with societal contribution. By helping others, students learn the value of teamwork, develop a sense of responsibility, and experience genuine happiness. Moreover, volunteer work often yields academic advantages, such as additional credits toward a diploma or eligibility for scholarships and college admissions. In addition, the discipline learned from regular practice often translates into better study habits and higher academic achievement.

In summary, engaging in any extracurricular activity after school gives both the body and the mind a productive respite. Students should select a pursuit that interests them and devote time to it once classes end. Whether through sport, reading, or community involvement, these activities promote well‑being, reduce stress, and enrich the overall school experience. Choosing an activity that matches personal passion ensures sustained motivation and makes the break from academics enjoyable rather than a chore. Research shows that students who participate in extracurriculars often achieve higher grades and display stronger leadership skills. These benefits extend beyond the classroom, fostering personal growth and preparing young people for future challenges. By encouraging diverse activities, schools can create a supportive environment where every student finds something they enjoy and can thrive. When students balance their studies with enjoyable pursuits, they experience less stress, greater motivation, and a more well‑rounded education. Such balance not only enhances academic performance but also builds resilience and confidence for life after school. Choosing an activity that matches personal passion ensures sustained motivation and makes the break from academics enjoyable rather than a chore. This holistic approach benefits everyone for all students.

This sense of purpose, combined with the prospect of a stable income, motivates me to pursue a career as a surgeon‑doctor.

I am confident that my dedication and compassion will enable me to succeed in this demanding but rewarding career.

Learning new languages can bean exciting test, and Vietnamese certainly fits that description. In the world there are roughly 67 spoken languages, and about 8.9 % of the population uses Vietnamese. It is listed among the ten most difficult languages to master. I am able to speak Vietnamese with full fluency, which lets me do many things: I can translate English into Vietnamese, teach my classmates how to speak it, and help them communicate with Vietnamese speakers.  

Because I know both Vietnamese and English, I can switch between the two and act as a bridge for translation. It is especially useful when I travel with my mother; she does not understand English, so I translate for her during our trips. My friends are enthusiastic about Vietnamese and often ask me to show them the basics. In class, a classmate greets me with “Xin Chào,” the Vietnamese word for “hello,” and I feel proud that they want to learn.  

I once taught an American friend how to speak Vietnamese, and now he can converse in the language as naturally as his native tongue. It is also advantageous when you are in Vietnam or in a community with many Vietnamese people; asking for assistance in Vietnamese can make a big difference. I remember a family reunion in Vietnam where I got separated from my parents. After shouting in English they could not understand me, but once I switched to Vietnamese I was able to ask for the police station and locate them.  

In short, Vietnamese makes an ideal language for anyone seeking a challenge. It can be especially useful for anyone planning a trip to Vietnam.

Albert Schweitzer claimed that the sole factor that shapes other people’s behavior is the example we set, not merely our words. In my view, this statement holds true because the way we act provides the clearest proof of who we are. When we demonstrate conduct through our deeds, others can see our values directly, which is more convincing than any spoken advice. People are constantly surrounded by influences, from family and school to the wider community and social‑media platforms. While some argue that individuals choose their own paths regardless of others’ examples, and others claim that mood and circumstances dictate reactions, I maintain that we are always being watched, often without realizing it. Consequently, the only reliable model we can offer is our own behavior. Words may explain a concept, but they lack the impact that observable actions have on a listener’s mind. A child will picture his future profession based on what he observes adults doing, not on what they say. Likewise, anyone who wishes to affect another’s life must first exhibit the qualities they hope to inspire. Our personal habits, attitudes, and choices therefore become powerful teaching tools. Even small gestures—such as helping a neighbor, speaking politely, or keeping a promise—can shape the attitudes of those around us. Because each person possesses a unique character, the specific actions we take can resonate with different observers, amplifying our influence. These observable deeds give credibility to our words and help build trust in our relationships. In short, the example we set through our conduct is the most effective means of influencing others. Albert Schweitzer’s assertion that “example is not the main thing in influencing others; it is the only thing” remains relevant, as our actions continuously demonstrate our true self and guide those who look up to us.

Everyone possessesa unique set of character traits, which makes it difficult to predict how others will act toward us. Often we quickly convince ourselves that we are in charge, yet many aspects of our lives—including the very qualities that define us—are beyond our control. From the moment a child enters the world, parents have no idea what kind of person that child will become. We can identify two kinds of personal traits: those that try to imitate others and those that remain authentic to the self. As people grow, they may be drawn to individuals with poor judgment and make bad choices by following such influences, gradually adopting their negative habits. Conversely, we can choose to embrace our true self, love who we are deep inside, and disregard the opinions of others. From the moment of creation, a higher power appears to know the distinctive traits each of us will develop as we age; when we accept ourselves, we inspire others to do the same. In short, we are not meant to follow the crowd; we are meant to stand out for ourselves. Every decision we make occurs within certain circumstances that shape its outcome.

Thomas Jefferson once said, “Determine never to be idle… it is wonderful how much may be done if we are always doing.” From this I understand that most achievements require persistent effort, and that idle behavior rarely leads to success. In my view, the quote is valid because real progress comes from continual activity, and because a life without work is unlikely to yield meaningful results.

First, the quote highlights the necessity of hard work. Jefferson suggests that we must constantly engage in tasks if we wish to obtain what we deserve. In practice, people who stay active are more likely to finish projects, acquire skills, and earn rewards. Conversely, those who remain idle often find that opportunities slip away. Therefore, the idea that effort is the engine of accomplishment is strongly supported by everyday experience.

The phrase “always doing” does not imply relentless hustle without pause, but rather keeping purposeful activity rather than abandoning tasks altogether. Even modest daily actions—such as reading a chapter, writing a short paragraph, or completing a small chore—accumulate over time and produce noticeable results. This steady momentum shows how small, consistent efforts can build toward larger goals.

Second, the statement reminds us that we cannot expect anything without putting in the required effort. Whether it is studying for an exam, working a job, or pursuing a personal goal, a steady level of activity is essential. Laziness creates a cycle in which nothing changes, while consistent effort breaks that cycle and opens new possibilities. By staying busy, we also avoid taking existing advantages for granted, because we recognize that they are the product of previous work.

Third, Jefferson’s words convey a broader truth about life’s conditions. They indicate that nothing is given freely; every benefit comes with a cost, and every outcome carries consequences. This perspective encourages gratitude: we appreciate what we have because we understand it is the result of our own actions. It also warns against complacency, urging us to keep moving forward rather than resting on past achievements.

When people ignore this principle, they often experience frustration, because the gap between desire and achievement widens without consistent effort. The quote therefore serves as a useful reminder that continual activity is the pathway to success. It shows that effort transforms possibilities into reality, that idle moments hinder progress, and that life’s rewards are tied to the work we invest. For anyone seeking motivation, the message is clear: keep doing, keep striving, and the outcomes will follow.

People everywhere form quick judgments about others based on what they say or do, and those first impressions often stay with us for a long time. Such initial views can shape how we feel, what we think, and the opinions we hold, and they may cause lasting hurt if we are not careful with our words. Once a negative impression is made, it is notoriously difficult to reverse, because the damage to someone’s feelings can be deep and the process of healing slow.

I experienced this myself yesterday while helping my sister choose a wedding dress. She is like a second mother to me, and I wanted her to look radiant on her big day. While browsing online, she spotted a gown she liked, but my instant reaction was that it was unflattering and that she would appear “like a skull” because of her slender figure. I voiced that thought without pausing to consider how it would affect her. The moment I spoke, her smile faded, and she seemed genuinely upset. I apologized, and after a brief conversation she accepted my remorse, but the sting of my words lingered. Since then she has kept a modest distance, showing how a single, thoughtless remark can alter a relationship.

A similar incident happened at a friend’s birthday party. A girl I’ll call Generic_Name invited me, and another attendee loudly declared that I looked “ugly and slow.” The comment was made in front of several others, and it wounded me deeply. Although the speaker later tried to explain that she was joking, the damage was already done; I left the celebration feeling sad, and the apology she offered at my home did little to erase the sting. This episode reinforces the idea that first impressions, once formed, are hard to shift.

My closest friend also illustrates this point. She once confided that her boyfriend seemed indifferent, and I expressed doubt after seeing him kiss another girl at school. She dismissed my concern as jealousy, insisting that he was the most handsome man she knew. However, months later I discovered that the man had a twin brother, and my initial judgment was mistaken. My friend’s trust in me eroded, and we have grown apart; she now avoids contact, and attempts to reconcile have failed. The episode shows how a hasty opinion can reshape an entire friendship.

Some people argue that first impressions can be altered instantly if the parties involved are willing to move past them, but experience suggests otherwise. When someone feels hurt, they tend to hold onto the initial judgment, especially if the speaker is perceived as uncaring or insensitive. Sensitive individuals may find it nearly impossible to forgive, and even sincere apologies sometimes fail to restore the original level of trust.

In sum, first impressions carry considerable weight because the words we utter can cause lasting emotional injury. Even when we recognize our mistakes and apologize, the original impact often remains, making it extremely difficult to change the way others view us. The evidence from my own life and the stories of those around me confirms that initial judgments are resilient and that repairing them requires more than a simple “sorry.”

This variation in learning capacity means that the ability to absorb and retain material differs from student to student. Therefore, having more time in high school may allow students to better understand their interests and future goals, especially since elective classes can foster creativity and expose them to new areas that might shape their future careers. For example, taking an art class can enhance creativity, while music classes can help students develop skills in the arts. Additionally, students who graduate quickly may do so because they want to enter the workforce immediately or pursue higher education without delay, while others may prefer the traditional timeline to explore options more thoroughly. Some students aim to earn an advanced diploma, which can open up better opportunities, whereas others may not be ready to decide on a career path right away. In such cases, having more time to reflect and explore through electives can be beneficial. For instance, students who take time to decide may avoid uncertainty after graduation, such as not knowing what to do next, which can lead to periods of inactivity. To support students who graduate early, having a clear plan—such as working to earn money or continuing education to gain more knowledge—is essential. Similarly, students who take longer to decide may still be exploring their interests, and this process can help them make more informed choices. Elective classes not only promote creativity but also provide opportunities to discover new interests that may not be covered in standard curriculum. For example, an art class can spark creativity, and a music class can lead to a passion for music production. Moreover, summer can be a valuable time to take a break from school or enroll in online courses to reinforce learning and prevent knowledge loss. In conclusion, while graduating in three years may suit students who already know their goals—such as entering the workforce or continuing their education—it is not inherently bad for others to take more time. Students with strong retention abilities may also benefit from an accelerated path. Ultimately, the key is for each student to create a clear future plan with defined goals and confidence in their choices.

In many schools, especially with younger children, older students are admired because they make activities feel cooler and more enjoyable. A program that pairs a younger learner with an older mentor can bring advantages for both parties.  

First, the partnership lets each student discover something new. The younger child can share fresh ideas or vocabulary he has just learned, while the older student explains the material he is studying in class. This exchange means both are exposed to concepts they might not encounter otherwise, and the younger learner gets help in areas where he needs support.  

Second, the older participant gains practical experience that will be useful later in life. By guiding a younger peer, he practices patience, leadership and classroom management—skills that are valuable for future employment. At the same time, the younger student feels a personal connection, which can develop into a lasting friendship; years later they may recognize each other and recall the time the older student helped them.  

Third, the program creates a safe space for self‑expression. Many students are reluctant to speak up in front of the whole class, but they are more comfortable talking one‑on‑one. This private dialogue encourages them to voice their opinions and ask questions, which builds confidence and makes learning feel more fun.  

Overall, the paired‑learning scheme helps students become more confident communicators, supports academic growth, and adds an element of enjoyment to school life. My own experience with reading buddies in sixth grade shows how such a arrangement can make schoolwork easier and more rewarding.

Many claim that failureis essential for achieving success, while others argue that it has no place in that journey. I believe that setbacks are a crucial part of the path to success because they teach us how to rise after each fall. When we encounter something we have never done before, the only way forward is to act differently. A big mistake can reveal deep lessons, and even a single failure forces us to try again.  

In everyday life we stumble, but that does not mean we cannot move forward. Each failure creates a chance to correct errors and grow. Although negative thoughts may appear—thinking we are useless or that we cannot succeed—there is always a drive inside that pushes toward achievement. Our abilities are not diminished by errors; they are refined through effort.  

We must take responsibility for our own progress and seek support from family, teachers, friends, or anyone willing to help. For example, I struggled with a biology exam that required a state assessment. I attempted it four times before finally passing, showing that persistence outweighs repeated setbacks.  

Failure also provides concrete lessons for tests: understanding the material, adopting new strategies, practicing repeatedly, and using available resources such as a dictionary. These steps turn a negative outcome into a stepping stone.  

Consequently, failure does play a significant role in the pursuit of success. It equips us with resilience, insight, and the motivation to keep moving forward.

I support thenew regulation that allows a late‑night weekend, but I oppose the 10 p.m. curfew that applies on weekdays. The policy was introduced to give young people more freedom after a long school week. Many young people under eighteen already have considerable duties. They must attend school from elementary through high school, help at home, and often contribute financially to their families. A stable home provides not only a place to rest but also a supportive environment where teenagers can discuss their problems with family members. 

In the coming years these youths will become the backbone of the economy, supporting the nation and the next generation. Because of this, earning money is a key concern for teenagers today. Having a job also teaches responsibility and prepares them for adult life. To obtain it they usually take part‑time jobs, typically about six hours a week. A schedule that runs from 4 p.m. to 9 p.m. works fine, but when the curfew forces them to work between 5 p.m. and 10 p.m. it creates a problem. They would be breaking the law simply by being at work during the restricted hours, which is an unjust interference by the authorities. 

Time is a valuable resource; teenagers need enough of it to study, work, and rest. Restricting their evening activities without considering their responsibilities is unfair. A home that provides comfort and security, combined with the ability to earn money, is what teenagers need now and in the future. Therefore, the curfew should be revised to allow reasonable evening freedom while still protecting public safety. The community should listen to the voices of its youth.

I fully agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s statement that “to be yourself in a world that constantly tries to make you somethingelse is the greatest accomplishment.” Embracing who you are, even when society pushes you in another direction, requires courage and perseverance. Life is never easy; it is a series of challenges that each person must face. No one is flawless, and true greatness is measured by the ability to overcome obstacles rather than by perfection.

Success does not appear instantly. It is the result of repeated effort, learning from setbacks, and refusing to quit. A soccer player, for example, wants to score a goal. To do that, he must first get past the opposing team, endure pressure, and keep trying until the moment arrives when the ball finally finds the net. The same principle applies to everyday life. When we fail, we may feel defeated, but that feeling does not mean the end of our journey. We still have hands, minds, and legs that can be used to move forward. One more attempt can turn a loss into a victory.

Time is a precious resource that should be managed wisely. Intelligent people use their time effectively, avoiding waste and resisting the temptation to blame circumstances or themselves when things go wrong. If we stumble, we should not give up; instead, we should keep trying, adjust our approach, and remember that time can offer new opportunities. Laziness, on the other hand, squanders time and leads to failure. As the saying goes, time never returns, so we must make the most of each moment.

Inspiration also plays a vital role. Reading about the lives of successful individuals can motivate us to follow similar paths. Their stories show that perseverance, hard work, and clear goals lead to achievement. For instance, the tale of Robert Bruce and the spider illustrates how repeated effort can lead to success. After seven failed attempts, the spider finally reached the top of the wall, encouraging Bruce to keep trying despite his own setbacks.

Understanding that failure is a natural part of life helps us stay resilient. If we never fail, it means we have never taken risks or tried anything new. Each failure provides valuable lessons and opens the possibility of starting again with renewed determination. Before giving up, we should ask ourselves whether we can make one more effort; that single additional try might be the key to success.

A clear aim guides our decisions and actions. Without a purpose, it is difficult to achieve anything meaningful. Establishing a routine for work or study creates structure that makes progress easier. In a student’s life, paying attention in class, completing assignments before attending lessons, and maintaining consistency can simplify the path to success. Hard work becomes a habit when we avoid laziness and stay committed to our goals.

External negativity should not derail our progress. Some people in our environment may try to discourage us, but ignoring their interference often causes them to lose interest over time. By focusing on our own efforts, we can silence critics and prove them wrong. Their eventual disappointment underscores the power of perseverance.

In conclusion, being true to ourselves, persisting through difficulties, managing time wisely, and maintaining a disciplined routine are the foundations of a successful life. When we keep trying, stay hopeful, and learn from each setback, we ultimately achieve the happiness and pride that come from overcoming obstacles. The journey may be long, but with steady effort and determination, a happy ending is within reach.

Life is full of setbacks, and the way we respond to them determines whether we move forward or stay stuck. When we meet difficulties with genuine enthusiasm, even the toughest obstacles become manageable, and our future can take a positive turn. This is why I agree with Winston Churchill that enthusiasm plays a vital role in achieving a smoother, more satisfying life.

First, enthusiasm creates a reservoir of energy that makes daily challenges feel less overwhelming. A person who approaches each task with excitement is more likely to stay focused, maintain steady effort, and enjoy the process. Because of this upbeat mindset, stress levels drop, patience grows, and happiness becomes a natural by‑product. In other words, a lively attitude transforms hard work into a source of fulfillment rather than a burden.

Second, the ability to keep enthusiasm alive after a failure is essential for long‑term success. When we stumble, it is easy to become discouraged, but retaining a hopeful outlook allows us to extract valuable lessons from the experience. Those lessons act as stepping stones that guide us toward new opportunities. For example, a student who dreams of attending college must first secure the necessary funds and develop a study routine. If laziness or negative thoughts take over, the goal remains out of reach. Conversely, a student who stays motivated, attends classes regularly, listens to teachers, and completes assignments on time can pass even the most difficult exams with far less anxiety.

The same principle applies to other aspirations, such as owning a home, a car, a pet, or traveling the world. Achieving these goals requires steady employment and disciplined saving. If one becomes complacent or loses vigor, the financial resources needed to realize these dreams may disappear. By contrast, enthusiasm fuels persistence, making it possible to work diligently, meet deadlines, and accumulate the means required for a better future.

Moreover, enthusiasm helps us bounce back from setbacks in academic or professional settings. Consider a learner who fails a mathematics exam. Rather than giving up, the student can seek extra help after school, review the material more thoroughly, and approach the next attempt with confidence. Teachers often provide additional support, such as after‑class sessions, which become effective only when the student remains eager to improve. Likewise, a person who does not graduate because a required course was missed can choose alternative pathways—re‑enrolling, attending a different institution, or finding supplemental courses—to eventually meet the graduation criteria. In the workplace, an employee who loses a job after an accidental mistake can leverage the experience gained from previous roles to secure new employment, provided they maintain a positive attitude and a strong work ethic.

These examples illustrate a broader truth: enthusiasm does not erase difficulties, but it equips us with the resilience needed to navigate them. When we keep our spirits high, we reduce stress, increase our energy, and cultivate patience, all of which create a more favorable environment for growth. Life may be inherently challenging, yet a hopeful outlook transforms obstacles into opportunities for learning and advancement.

In conclusion, the importance of enthusiasm in overcoming adversity cannot be overstated. By embracing a lively, determined mindset, we are better positioned to pursue our goals, endure setbacks, and ultimately achieve a more rewarding and less complicated existence. This aligns with Churchill’s assertion that enthusiasm is a key driver of a positive, successful life.

Schools are now offeringa way for students who cannot attend classes in person to continue their education from home. Many learners face serious obstacles that make regular attendance difficult, such as a lack of reliable transport or living far from the campus, and some have special circumstances that require additional support. When a school provides this option, the student must possess a device that can connect to the internet; without it, participation is impossible, because the only platform for remote study is an online connection.

The advantages of learning at home are clear. Students can follow the same curriculum as their peers, earn a credential, and apply to higher‑education institutions. Moreover, they can set their own pace and decide when to complete assignments, which can be helpful for those who need extra time or have other responsibilities. However, these benefits come with notable drawbacks. The most significant problem is the limited social interaction. Learners who study alone miss out on face‑to‑face conversations, which are essential for developing communication skills and emotional well‑being. This isolation can lead to feelings of exclusion and stress, and it may leave students unprepared for the collaborative environment of college or the workplace.

Another limitation is the difficulty of obtaining immediate help with questions or assignments. In a traditional classroom, a teacher can answer a query on the spot, but a student studying remotely must search for answers independently, which can be time‑consuming and frustrating. While some schools have special programs for students with chronic illnesses or other lifelong conditions, these services are not universally available. When a public school offers a home‑learning option, it usually requires a formal request, supporting documentation, and a review of the case before approval can be granted. Students cannot simply decide to stay home because they prefer not to attend; a legitimate reason must be presented.

The quality of the learning experience also differs from that of a regular school. Classroom settings provide a variety of resources—libraries, laboratories, extracurricular activities, and peer interaction—that enrich education beyond the core subjects. Remote learners miss many of these opportunities, and the lack of direct contact with teachers and classmates can hinder the development of teamwork and problem‑solving skills. Consequently, the overall educational journey may feel less comprehensive.

In summary, while distance learning offers a viable alternative for students who cannot physically attend school, it is not a seamless substitute for traditional schooling. Pros include flexibility, the ability to obtain a degree, and the possibility of applying to colleges. Cons involve reduced social contact, limited immediate academic support, and potential challenges for students with special needs who rely on on‑site services. Anyone considering this option should carefully weigh these factors, secure the necessary technology, and ensure that a valid, documented reason exists before committing to a remote‑learning path.

Technology makes manytasks easier, such as taking online courses, buying goods, and staying in touch with others. Yet, I contend that its overall influence on daily life is harmful. The main problem is that increasing reliance on digital devices reduces real‑world human contact, which can weaken social bonds and diminish the quality of our everyday experiences. While it saves time and offers new opportunities, the constant presence of screens reduces the quality of personal interactions and can lead to feelings of isolation.  

First, the rise of online shopping has caused numerous brick‑and‑mortar stores to shut down. Consumers now prefer platforms like Amazon, whose sales far exceed those of local retailers. For instance, two nearby shops named [store names] have been forced to close because shoppers choose to buy from home. The loss of these jobs and the disappearance of physical stores illustrate how technology can harm the economy and community. The closure of these shops not only eliminates jobs for sales staff and managers but also reduces foot traffic for neighboring businesses, creating a ripple effect throughout the local economy.  

Second, technology contributes to the emptiness of public venues such as parks, lakes, and shopping malls. People prefer staying at home to play video games or order items online, which means fewer visitors to these places. When public spaces become quiet, community interaction declines and the sense of shared environment fades. As a result, community events that once took place in parks or malls become rare, and the sense of belonging among residents weakens, making neighborhoods feel more fragmented.  

Third, the influence of technology reaches schools and children’s development. Students often distract themselves with mobile phones during lessons, making it difficult to answer teachers’ questions. Moreover, youngsters spend more time in front of screens and less time reading books or playing outdoors, which can lead to poorer academic performance and health issues. Such screen‑heavy routines also limit physical activity, contribute to sleep disturbances, and reduce opportunities for social play, which are crucial for developing social skills and emotional resilience. For example, my cousin, a middle‑school student, plays the video game Fortnite every day, stays up late, receives low grades, and rarely goes outside.  

Some argue that technology enables easy communication with family and friends and provides new ways to express ideas. While these benefits exist, they are outweighed by the reduction in face‑to‑face interaction and the loss of cultural activities. Real conversations and hands‑on creative pursuits, such as painting or dancing, are essential for personal growth, and their decline shows the overall negative impact of excessive reliance on devices. Even though digital platforms allow people to maintain long‑distance relationships, the superficial nature of many online interactions often replaces deeper, face‑to‑face conversations that nurture empathy and understanding.  

In conclusion, although technology offers convenience, its pervasive presence harms social connections, public life, education, and cultural vitality. The trend of reduced human contact, empty public spaces, and diminished curiosity threatens the well‑being of individuals and society. Therefore, it is crucial to balance digital use with real‑world interactions to preserve a healthy, vibrant lifestyle. By consciously setting limits on device usage and encouraging activities such as reading, sports, and face‑to‑face gatherings, individuals can mitigate the adverse effects and preserve a more balanced, fulfilling way of life.

Dear Principal, today I would like to discuss why most employers look for particular qualities in potential staff even when the applicant does not yet know the job. I agree with this view because a person does not always know how to do a job from the start, but they can learn it.

When someone begins a new position, they are often taught by a more experienced colleague, such as a manager or senior employee. For instance, when I first arrived in this country I worked with my stepfather to bake bread. I had never baked before, but over time I learned the process by watching him and practicing. Later, during a summer job as a cashier in a restaurant, I struggled to recognize the different coins because my home country used a different system. With the manager’s help, I quickly mastered the task and showed great enthusiasm to improve.

Many people who already know a job enjoy working hard because they want to deepen their knowledge, while those less familiar can still acquire new skills from coworkers or supervisors. In the United States, numerous workers put effort into their jobs not only for personal gain but also to provide a better future for their families. They hope their dedication will be seen by their children, who may follow in their footsteps and become more responsible individuals. This sense of responsibility is something to be proud of and often drives people to achieve their goals and secure a brighter tomorrow.

Responsibility is another crucial factor that employers value. A reliable employee who arrives on time and fulfills assigned tasks demonstrates accountability, which greatly increases the chance of being hired. In my home country, many attempts to open small shops failed because the staff were unreliable, missing shifts and neglecting duties, ultimately causing the businesses to close.

Moreover, employers need to consider patience when selecting managers. A patient manager is essential for training newcomers, whereas impatient supervisors may refuse to invest time in teaching, believing some workers will never learn or have more pressing matters. In many restaurants and stores, courteous managers who are willing to help create a positive environment and facilitate learning.

In conclusion, an applicant does not need prior experience if they are responsible, motivated, and eager to learn. Skills are acquired through challenges and mistakes, and a responsible attitude combined with a willingness to grow are the qualities most employers seek.

Many learners and educators argue that online classes are detrimental to students and schools. The primary concern is that pupils often fail to record what the instructor says. In a physical classroom, teachers can see whether a student is writing, which encourages note‑taking; online, the teacher cannot observe this, so students are less likely to bother with notes. Research shows that writing information down helps to encode it in memory, so the absence of notes can lead to weaker retention and poorer performance on tests.  

A second problem is distraction. In a real room, a student may glance around, but the teacher’s presence usually keeps attention focused. On a screen, the temptation to look away or switch tabs is stronger, causing missed explanations. Moreover, the home environment may introduce additional interruptions such as family members, notifications, or household chores. When information is skipped, students may feel lost, struggle with assignments, and become anxious about how to complete tasks.  

Because teachers cannot verify whether students are listening or taking notes, they remain unaware of the actual learning taking place. They also miss subtle cues like facial expressions or body language that signal confusion or disengagement. Without reliable feedback, the quality of online instruction suffers. Consequently, students do not gain the same advantages from virtual lessons as they would from face‑to‑face classes, where note‑taking and sustained attention are naturally supported.  

Some may argue that online platforms provide recordings that can be replayed, but this does not replace the active process of listening and writing during the lesson. Re‑watching a video still requires the student to be attentive at the moment of viewing, and the lack of immediate interaction can reduce motivation. Additionally, the inability of teachers to monitor participation means that struggling learners may fall behind unnoticed, widening achievement gaps.  

In summary, the lack of observable note‑taking and the higher risk of distraction make online classes less effective for learning. Without the natural checks that a physical classroom provides, students may miss critical information, leading to confusion, anxiety, and lower academic outcomes. Furthermore, the absence of face‑to‑face interaction limits opportunities for immediate clarification, making it harder for students to grasp complex concepts. Consequently, the overall effectiveness of remote learning is questioned by educators and parents alike indeed and therefore.

Online schooling can be a useful option, yet it is not suitable for every learner. Some students thrive when they study from home, while others find it impossible to succeed. Virtual classes are often demanding, and many learners are unable to pass them, which shows they are not meant for everyone.  

One major advantage of home‑based education is flexibility. Pupils do not have to rise early or follow a rigid timetable; they can decide when to work on assignments. This freedom can be pleasant, but it also means that the responsibility to start work immediately rests on the student, which can feel unrewarding. Moreover, without immediate assistance from a teacher, students may struggle to obtain help or ask questions, making the work much harder. If they fail, there is usually no chance to get extra credit or a makeup assignment, unlike in a traditional classroom.  

Another drawback is the loss of social experiences that regular schools provide. Students miss out on everyday interactions such as class discussions, school events, sports, dances, and even the occasional conflict or fire drill. These moments contribute to personal growth and friendship building. Consequently, many home‑schooled learners eventually return to conventional schools, and statistics suggest that roughly sixty percent either drop out or re‑enter regular education.  

In contrast, attending a physical school usually offers a higher probability of success. Working alongside peers allows students to receive and give assistance, fostering a collaborative environment. In life, effort and support are linked; giving your best and helping others often leads to better outcomes. Therefore, while online and home schooling have their merits, traditional schooling generally provides a more reliable path to achievement.

Do we decide our own character traits? The British naturalist and politician John Lubbock once remarked, “Your character will be what you yourself decide to become.” I strongly agree that each individual can shape their own character, because we possess enough independence to govern ourselves. We are free to choose the settings we place ourselves in and the way we react to both favorable and adverse situations, which means we ultimately decide who we become.  

First, everyone has the capacity to pick the kind of person they wish to be. We can select environments that support our desired values and avoid those that pull us away from them. Even when circumstances are harsh, we retain the freedom to choose an optimistic outlook or a pessimistic one; a smile or a tear is a matter of personal decision.  

My grandmother offers a vivid illustration. At seventy‑eight she had worked all her life, maintaining a relentless work ethicand a habit of never sitting still because she believed that idle time was wasted. One day she suffered a severe stroke that left half of her body paralyzed and took away her voice. The doctors said she would remain in a wheelchair permanently, a prospect that shocked and saddened our whole family. Yet she never allowed the loss of mobility to diminish her spirit. She deliberately chose to stay positive, refusing to let the tragedy dictate her attitude. This resolve showed me that, regardless of how difficult the situation, we retain the power to decide how we respond.  

Second, while the surrounding environment certainly influences our behavior, it does not determine it entirely. We can recognize toxic relationships, evaluate the impact of our surroundings, and actively transform a negative atmosphere into a constructive one. Our daily actions are shaped both by external factors and by the choices we make, but the final say always rests with us.  

Finally, how we react to others reveals the core of our character. Our responses expose both strengths and vulnerabilities, indicating whether we are calm or volatile. Although some people find it challenging to maintain a consistent character because mood swings can cloud judgment, we still retain the ability to decide whether to imitate others or to forge our own path. In the end, each person is free to determine the traits that define them, whether they face hardship or enjoy ease; the choice always belongs to the individual.

The goal that is required can be lesser, greater, or moderate, making no difference.  
The person who maintains it matters, not the size of the goal because anyone can be a president if he/she really wants it but cannot go to the gym a few times a week if he/she is lazy and lacks sufficient willingness in their heart.

Doesn't matter if it's short or long term goals.  
That enthusiasm can break after failures or become even stronger than before.

My skin turned red after an hour of practice.

Failureis a dreaded thing in our daily life that we try to avoid. Many people try to avoid any situation where they might fail, while a smaller group wants to face such challenges. Those people view failure as a learning process and achieve great outcomes in life. Fear controls every aspect of our life. How do we look? Did we make the right decision? In most cases we fear failure because we are unsure about the success or a positive outcome of a situation and the consequences of our actions. This idea divides people's minds into two sides, two ideologies: the shy, safety‑oriented player and the brave, risk‑taking player. Both sides have pros and cons.

Those who choose the safety game use their accumulated background knowledge, gained over many years, to feel certain they will not fail. The word “shy” does not accurately describe them when something new and unknown appears to learn. They avoid risk, so they do not try and therefore cannot fail. This can apply to any situation, such as answering a question in class, trying a sport, going to the gym, or wearing new clothes. The only barrier between them and action is fear. Because they do not take risks, they never know the outcome. If they fail, they view it as a loss. Perhaps the only perceived benefit is that they feel they will lose nothing, but their successes are fewer. This does not mean they are not risk‑takers or that they live in constant fear; they are simply more cautious. The steps they need to take may not be scary or may not require a big deal. These people have already made mistakes, which is why they fear trying again. They may have said something dumb in class and been laughed at, tried a sport and performed poorly, felt uncomfortable in the gym because they were not as strong as others, and so on.

The other side consists of those who try new things and gain experience, often achieving lasting success. Winston Churchill is a great example; his life demonstrates the importance of trying. It is easy to see that becoming Prime Minister of the United Kingdom was not simple for him. His biography shows that he tried many times, failed, yet ultimately succeeded. People like Churchill view failures as lessons. For them, learning is a process of perfecting ideas, making actions successful, deciding the right way, and answering questions correctly. When a failure occurs after a wrong move, they confront it, proud not of the failure itself but of the correction, the knowledge gained, and the drive to avoid similar mistakes. They may repeat the same mistake, but in the end they become winners. This is where enthusiasm enters. People pursue goals, and enthusiasm fuels them. Churchill won World War II because his goal was to avoid failing his people, humanity, and everything he built. Enthusiasm takes many forms: duty as a president, joy as an instrument player, or bringing happiness as a parent. Keeping enthusiasm depends on the person. The size of the goal matters less than the willingness to keep it; anyone can become president if they truly want it, but not everyone can go to the gym a few times a week if they are lazy and lack inner willingness. This connects closely to our life goals, whether short‑term or long‑term. Enthusiasm may wane after failure or grow stronger than before. My example involves martial arts. I learned to dual‑wield nunchaku, and the process was painful. Being right‑handed, using my left hand to spin the nunchaku hurt my forearm; I struck it thousands of times, leaving my skin red after an hour of practice. People asked why I kept trying and why I didn't give up. My persistence was driven by enthusiasm for mastering the nunchaku. After months of practice I succeeded, and though I am not yet a master, I no longer hit myself. Many people repeatedly fail, taking risks that could prevent them from trying again. In some cases, failure could be fatal. These are specific situations, but death is not the only thing that can stop us. There are also situations where a person becomes unable to do something they once did. Moreover, after tragedies we can become stronger than before. A boy who loved riding his bicycle and doing tricks had a car accident that cost him his leg. He spent months in a wheelchair, but doctors offered a plastic leg. After a long recovery, when he could move on his own, he wanted to return to his dream. For a long time he failed to ride his bike, feeling angry and broken, but he did not give up. After many more failures he finally rode again, now as before the accident because he never gave up. His story inspires me.

We need to fail in order to learn and enjoy what we achieve. We must try and train until we can no longer get it wrong, not just until we get it right. We also need a goal that fuels our enthusiasm, so we never lose it and can make it stronger after each failure. We can stay in our comfort zones and avoid failure, or we can face it and gain experience.

Failure is a feared experience that many people try to avoid in their everyday lives. Most of us prefer to stay in situations where success is guaranteed, because the possibility of not succeeding feels threatening. Consequently, a small group of individuals willingly confront potential failure, regarding it as a stepping‑stone toward improvement and achievement.  

The root of this fear lies in uncertainty. When we cannot be sure about the result of an action or the consequences that follow, anxiety rises. This mental split creates two opposite attitudes: the cautious, safety‑oriented person and the bold, risk‑taking individual. Both approaches have advantages and disadvantages.  

Those who choose the safe route rely heavily on what they have already learned. They use their accumulated knowledge to predict outcomes and to avoid any chance of mistake. This mindset shows up in everyday scenes such as answering a question in class, joining a new sport, going to the gym for the first time, or wearing unfamiliar clothing. The only barrier they face is fear itself; without risk there is no possible reward, and even if a failure occurs they simply accept it as a loss. While this protects them from immediate embarrassment, it also limits the amount of success they can achieve.  

In contrast, people who actively seek new challenges view failure as a valuable lesson. A well‑known illustration is Winston Churchill, the former British prime minister. His biography records numerous attempts and defeats before he finally led the United Kingdom during World War II. He did not shy away from difficulty; instead, he learned from each error and used that insight to refine his strategy. For Churchill, failure was not a stigma but a source of knowledge that propelled him forward.  

The same principle applies to anyone who persists despite setbacks. When a person makes a mistake, such as saying something foolish in front of classmates or struggling with a sport, the discomfort can be strong. Yet those who keep trying turn the embarrassment into motivation, studying the cause and adjusting their approach. Their perseverance eventually leads to competence and, often, to recognition.  

Enthusiasm drives the journey. It may appear as a sense of duty, as joy while playing an instrument, or as the love a parent feels for a child. The size of the goal is irrelevant; what counts is the willingness to keep the fire alive. A person might aim to become president or simply to attend the gym twice a week; the crucial factor is the inner drive that sustains effort. Even when the goal seems modest, the persistence it requires leads to achievement. Setbacks can dim the flame, but they often make it burn brighter. My own experience with martial arts illustrates this: I decided to learn nunchaku with my non‑dominant hand. The first sessions left my forearm red and bruised, yet my enthusiasm kept me training for months. Eventually I could spin the nunchaku without injuring myself, showing that steady effort transforms difficulty into ability.  

Not all failures are merely embarrassing. Some are life‑threatening or cause permanent physical change. A tragic example is a young boy who loved riding his bicycle and performing tricks. A car collision caused him to lose his leg. He spent months in a wheelchair, and doctors later offered him a prosthetic leg. He devoted time to recovery, and when he was able to move on his own he wanted to return to his dream. For a long period he could not ride his bike at all. He felt angry and broken, but he refused to give up. Eventually he got back on his bike and now rides with confidence, never giving up. His story inspires me.  

In summary, fear of failure pushes many people to avoid new experiences, which restricts their growth. Those who embrace risk, learn from each mistake, and maintain strong enthusiasm are the ones who achieve lasting success. As Winston Churchill showed, failure is not an end but a teacher; with a clear goal and unwavering motivation, we can turn every setback into a step toward victory.

Allowing students to enroll insummer courses with the goal of completing high school in three years is not a wise plan. One major concern is that many pupils still need additional credits before they can graduate, so they would be forced to take a heavier load of classes. Trying to fit extra subjects into a short period can create intense pressure and anxiety. In a typical four‑year schedule a teenager can join extracurricular activities, play sports, and attend regular classes without feeling swamped; compressing the timeline would make it difficult to balance these responsibilities and could hurt their college applications. Moreover, when students have to double up on courses to meet credit requirements, the workload often becomes unmanageable, leading to fatigue and reduced learning effectiveness.

Another issue is that a sizable portion of high‑school students work during the summer to earn money. Many use this period to save for a car, college tuition, or other expenses. If they are also attending classes, they would have far less time to work, which could reduce their ability to finance future goals. The summer break is often the only time they can focus solely on employment without the distraction of schoolwork, and losing that uninterrupted work period may limit their financial independence. Additionally, balancing a job with coursework can diminish the quality of both, as students may feel rushed and unable to give full attention to either task.

Finally, students usually appreciate a pause after the academic year ends. A summer or gap period gives them the chance to work full‑time, earn extra income, reflect on career choices, or simply recharge before the next stage of life. Rushing them into a three‑year program would eliminate this valuable break and might leave them feeling exhausted and less motivated. Without a proper interval to recover, they could experience burnout, which negatively impacts their mental health and overall well‑being. Moreover, a break provides time to explore interests, volunteer, or gain real‑world experience that complements classroom learning.

In short, graduating in three years instead of four is problematic. Students may lack sufficient credits, leading to a crowded curriculum and heightened stress; they often rely on summer jobs to fund their future, and taking classes would interfere with that earnings; and the desire for a post‑year break to work, save, or relax is an important part of growing up. For these reasons, the proposal to accelerate high‑school graduation by using summer courses does not make sense.

A British naturalist and politician John Lubbock wrote, "Your character will be what you yourself choose to make it." Do we choose our character traits, or does our character form from influences beyond our control? I think we can control our character traits because we can choose them, such as being quiet, being social, and being over ourselves. This is why I think we choose our character traits. For example, I think we choose traits like being quiet. Being quiet is not a good or bad thing; you can be quiet sometimes, not all the time, because you need to talk occasionally. You have to balance it out. I remember being a quiet kid in middle school, grades 6 to 7, with few friends and not talking to anyone. I felt alone, then I started talking to people and made many friends. So, I think we can control our character traits. That is why I choose traits like being quiet. Another example is being social. Being social is a great quality because talking to people helps you make friends, learn new things, and discover new things. I was a very talkative kid in grades 7 to 8, and I remember feeling like I was annoying because I talked a lot. I also learned how to approach and talk to people. I discovered that people can change over time; some become nice then moody or mean, others become mean then nice. Some people do not change, and that is how the world works. That is why I think we can control and choose traits like being social. My next example is being over ourselves, such as being confident or keeping yourself in check, which can be a good trait. It can also be a bad trait if you are overconfident and cocky. Some people dislike those kinds of people because they say there is no fun or they are party poopers. I confess that I was a little cocky and overconfident in sports because I was a very competitive kid. Sometimes I even screamed and yelled in happiness when I scored or won a game. Some people think our character traits are influenced beyond our control, and I see their point of view; when I screamed and yelled after scoring, I did not control it, I just yelled. I could have celebrated with my hands and looked up at the sky, but I did not. This is why I think we can choose traits like being over ourselves. Finally, I think when the British naturalist and politician John Lubbock wrote, "Your character will be what you yourself choose to make it," he thought that we choose our character traits, or that our character forms from influences beyond our control. I think he believed we choose traits like being quiet, being social, and being over yourself. This is why he thought we choose our character traits.

While external factors such as family, environment, and societal expectations play a role in shaping behavior, individuals still retain the ability to make conscious choices about their actions and attitudes. These choices reflect personal agency rather than passive acceptance of one’s upbringing. Moreover, people change over time, and so do their behaviors. Such transformations demonstrate that character is not fixed but evolves through deliberate choices. Even traits influenced by upbringing can be reshaped through intentional effort, such as practicing empathy or working on emotional regulation. Therefore, while external factors contribute to personality development, the power to choose remains with the individual. This aligns with John Lubbock’s assertion that character is shaped by personal choice rather than solely by external forces. Ultimately, character is not solely determined by upbringing or external conditions but is continuously shaped by conscious decisions.

I oppose extending the school day because it would make the day feel boring, stressful, and exhausting for students. First, extra periods would be dull; students prefer activities they enjoy and would rather spend free time on hobbies or play rather than sit through extra lessons. For example, a student might choose to go outside and play rather than sit through another class. Second, longer days increase stress levels. Prolonged classroom time can raise anxiety, raise blood pressure, and even trigger panic or depressive thoughts, which are harmful to young people. A student who feels nervous during a test may become overwhelmed and upset. Finally, longer days cause fatigue and dizziness. Without enough rest, students become tired and light‑headed, which hampers learning. Therefore, extending the school day is a poor idea; it would make the day dull, stressful, and exhausting for students. Keeping the current schedule helps students stay happy and healthy.

Many people debate whether a positive mindset is essential for achieving success in life. While some argue that attitude alone does not guarantee success, a positive outlook can indeed bring about significant changes in a person's life. First, when we stay optimistic, we tend to attract more friends; people are drawn to positivity and remember us more easily, which leads to a happier existence. Being positive also encourages us to engage with others, and the reciprocal conversations boost our mood and make us appear friendlier. Having a larger circle of friends reduces the chance of feeling isolated, because we are constantly surrounded by others and occupied with social activities, leaving little room for stress. Moreover, a positive first impression can open doors to personal and professional relationships. When we present ourselves with confidence and cheerfulness, others are more likely to recall us positively, creating opportunities at school or work. Research indicates that chronic stress harms health, so maintaining a positive attitude helps keep stress levels low. By staying upbeat, we are more likely to form good relationships with neighbors and acquaintances, giving us a support network to talk to and rely on. Consequently, individuals who cultivate optimism enjoy both a healthier body and a more joyful mind. In summary, a positive attitude serves as a key to success because it fosters friendships, improves how others perceive us, reduces stress, and promotes overall well‑being, leading to a happier and healthier life.

If I could decide, I would choose to attend school in order to meet more people. I can present three arguments supporting the idea that online learning can be carried out at home.

Moreover, a child with health issues might be reluctant to attend because they fear being mocked by classmates.

Second, other learners may dislike the regular school routine and prefer staying at home. They might feel judged or embarrassed, especially if they have a medical condition or if something distressing happened at school. Such feelings can make attending school difficult.

Finally, if I had to choose between staying at home or attending school, I would opt for attending school. I would want to help others understand why attending school matters and give them advice that there is no need to feel ashamed of their problems; they should not let bullying affect them.

In conclusion, while online learning offers flexibility and can address personal concerns, it is not necessary to ignore the advantages of attending school. People should not let the opinions of others dictate their choices.

Teenagers carry many responsibilities afterschool—homework, part‑time jobs, clubs, and other activities—so they naturally need to stay up later than adults. A curfew that forces them home before midnight would unnecessarily curb these duties and would ignore the fact that many teenagers already look after their own safety by managing homework, jobs, and extracurricular activities. Moreover, teenagers are capable of judging traffic conditions and can drive responsibly when they are alert; the real danger at night comes from impaired drivers and wildlife, not from teenagers who are generally attentive and capable of driving safely when they are alert.  

Therefore, imposing a curfew that forces teenagers home before midnight would be an unnecessary restriction that ignores their existing sense of responsibility and their ability to drive safely at night. Instead of imposing a curfew, the council should consider alternative safety measures such as increased police patrols, better street lighting, and campaigns that educate young drivers about the risks of nighttime driving. This approach would protect teens while respecting their growing independence and responsibilities.

Failures are essential for achieving successbecause they build confidence, prepare individuals for real-world challenges, and motivate persistence toward their goals. My mother often reminded me, "Be confident, I believe in you," which strengthened my resolve during difficult times. When I was in first grade in Honduras, my teacher told my mother I would fail because I struggled with math—I did fail, but my mother insisted it wasn't due to a lack of intelligence, only difficulty at that moment. The next year, I repeated the grade, and my new teacher was impressed by my rapid improvement in math and other subjects. This experience showed me that one failure doesn't mean giving up; it requires resilience and determination to keep moving forward. As a child, I dreamed of becoming a lawyer. During a school activity where we shared our future goals, I said I wanted to become a lawyer. A classmate doubted me, saying I wouldn't complete the path, but I replied, "You never know," stressing that no matter how many times I fail, I will never be a failure. Throughout my 18 years, I've faced many setbacks, but each has taught me valuable lessons for the real world. Some may disagree with my view, but they are mistaken—no one is perfect, and everyone makes mistakes. To succeed, one must take things step by step and persist no matter how many times they fall. I hope people never give up on their dreams because of a single setback, and that they prove their critics wrong by achieving their goals through perseverance.

Mythoughts on this are that it is a good time and should actually occur for many reasons. First, during weekdays young people have school every day, unless it is a holiday or they are sick. If this is implied, more young people will stay out of the streets late at night, so there is no need to be out that late in the first place.  

Second, 10 p.m. is a great time to be home on weekdays; it keeps you out of trouble and reduces the chances of young people encountering criminal activity at night. Most crimes occur late at night, so lowering these chances will improve safety.  

Third, many drug sellers operate at night; if young people must be home early, their chances of encountering drugs will decrease. If this becomes law, the curfew times are appropriate: Monday through Friday until 10 p.m., and Saturday and Sunday until midnight; no one should be on the streets later than these times.  

If they are out that late, there should be an extreme reason for breaking the law. This will most likely keep young people out of more trouble than they already experience. The curfew time is not unfair; it is generous. It should not interfere with anyone's life; you can still go out, but not stay out that late.  

I would understand if the law also applied to people over 18, since young adults like to party. But the law should target people under 18, which makes more sense; adults over 18 know right from wrong and what they should or should not do. The law is not meant to harm anyone; it aims to improve community curfews and keep teenagers out of trouble, which I agree with.  

However, young teenagers often act improperly, and adding a law may not change their behavior or keep them out of trouble. This law does not imply that young people cannot hang out with friends; it is intended to keep more people safe from street trouble. Many innocent people die each year after being out late at night in streets where dangerous individuals appear. They have after‑school activities, and this curfew will not prevent anyone from doing what they want. It is simply a way to keep young people out of trouble; there should be exceptions, such as attending a party, but also a reasonable limit.  

If they break the law, the consequence should start with a warning and then increase. My position on this curfew law is that I understand why people may object, yet teenagers generally know what they should and should not do. I have two viewpoints: why they should be worried and why they should not be.  

I know people enjoy sleepovers; the law should clarify whether they must stay at home or can stay at a friend's house. If they attend a weekend party when the curfew is midnight and return after 1 a.m., they may lose track of time. They are having fun with friends and may get caught if someone calls the police. Then police arrive, and they must face the law. What follows is a record of the incident, which can harm their future. This would be terrible, and they may also face parental trouble for the mistake. If they want to attend a good college, this record could hurt their chances of acceptance. This is a downside; a law violation goes on their record and may affect permits or future opportunities, which is unfortunate. Colleges consider all actions; a violation could hurt acceptance prospects for a high‑achieving student, causing lasting guilt.  

Currently there is no curfew for when teenagers should be home, but there is a curfew for drivers with permits. This creates a restriction: teenagers are rarely seen in cars late at night, only when leaving school.  

There are pros and cons, but I believe the benefits outweigh the drawbacks, and the proposal is reasonable. The main drawback I see is that being caught results in a record, which is undesirable. Overall, there are many benefits, and this law should be seriously implemented nationwide, not just in one city.  

This will keep more people safe; although some may treat it as a joke, young people should take it seriously. In conclusion, this curfew could prevent thieves from stealing young people and selling them, and could reduce rape incidents, which are harder to detect in the dark. It will likely lower the frequency of these negative events for anyone. It will also keep young people out of many dangerous situations that occur late at night.

Frommy perspective, a curfew that limits how late minors may stay out is a sensible measure and I support it for several reasons. First, on weekdays most young people attend school, so they are occupied during the day and only venture out after classes end or when they are ill. If they must be home earlier, they will spend less time wandering the streets after dark, which reduces the likelihood of encountering trouble. Second, a 10 p.m. deadline on school nights is a practical cut‑off. At that hour most youths are already at home, which keeps them away from situations where they could become victims of violence or other criminal activity. Since many offenses occur late at night, imposing this boundary lowers the chances of such incidents. Third, a large number of drug dealers target teenagers; by forcing them to be home earlier, the opportunity for them to obtain or use drugs diminishes considerably. The proposed schedule—Monday through Friday until 10 p.m., and Saturday and Sunday until midnight—covers the entire week while still allowing reasonable evening activities. If someone wishes to be out later, there must be a compelling justification; otherwise they would be breaking the rule. This approach is not unfair; it simply gives a generous window for most daily routines. I also think the law should apply only to people under eighteen, because individuals over that age are generally capable of deciding what is right or wrong and can manage their own behavior. The intention of the measure is not to restrict adults, but to protect teenagers who may lack experience and judgment. I fully agree that such a curfew would improve community safety. Beyond personal safety, a curfew can ease the burden on police and emergency services, allowing them to focus on genuine emergencies rather than responding to youthful disturbances late at night. It also helps hospitals and families, since fewer nighttime incidents mean reduced injuries and less stress for parents. The policy can be enforced by local authorities through routine checks and community outreach, ensuring that young people are aware of the rules and have the opportunity to plan safe activities before the cutoff. Adults who are already responsible for their own schedules often view the curfew as a reasonable safeguard, and many municipalities have adopted similar measures with positive results. The regulation can be flexible, allowing exceptions for special events when proper supervision is guaranteed, thus balancing protection with personal freedom. Overall, the benefits of a well‑designed curfew outweigh the minor inconveniences, making it a worthwhile measure for the safety of teenagers and the broader community. It also reinforces responsible behavior and helps prevent future problems and supports a safer environment for everyone.

To beginwith, a few companies have introduced a four‑day working schedule, each day lasting eight hours. Some schools are even considering cutting their timetable to just two hours per week. The main drawbacks of such a reduction for education are clear. First, shortening the school day would mean fewer instructional hours, which could hinder students’ ability to absorb the curriculum. If lessons are limited to only two hours weekly, teaching time is insufficient and learning may be disrupted. Second, teachers would receive payment only for the hours they actually work, rather than a fixed salary. This hourly wage model would force educators to seek additional employment to meet their financial needs. Third, the broader economy could suffer as well. When employers cut employee hours to lower energy consumption, household incomes decline, making it harder for families to cover expenses such as credit‑card bills, insurance, and rising food prices. In short, reducing the length of the school week is not a viable solution for saving energy. It jeopardizes the quality of education, destabilises teachers’ earnings, and places extra financial pressure on families. Therefore, schools should retain their standard eight‑hour day, and businesses ought to explore other ways to reduce energy use without cutting working hours.

From my pointof view, collaborating with classmates is far more advantageous than tackling assignments solo. First, working together lets us complete tasks much more quickly. When several people share the load, the work is divided and finished in less time. Second, each member can focus on a different aspect of the project, so we cover more ground and bring varied perspectives. Third, if someone encounters difficulty, the others can offer assistance, which makes problem‑solving easier.  

On the other hand, group work does have drawbacks. The main problem is that it can become noisy, with many voices and ideas competing for attention, which sometimes distracts from the main goal. Moreover, everyone may want their own approach included, leading to disagreements about the final product.  

In contrast, studying alone eliminates most of those interruptions. You have the freedom to work at your own pace without others pulling you off track. You also decide how the assignment should look, and you can ask the teacher for clarification on the requirements, ensuring that your work meets the expected standards. However, the downside is that you must do everything yourself, which often takes longer, and you bear the entire responsibility for finishing the task.  

In summary, although working by yourself removes some distractions and lets you control the style of the work, the advantages of group collaboration—speed, division of labor, and mutual support—outweigh the disadvantages. Therefore, as a student who finds it hard to finish tasks independently, I prefer to work in a team because teamwork makes the job easier. When I work with others, I feel more motivated and less stressed, and the final result usually reflects a balanced effort from everyone involved in school.
