Do you think confidence comes from achievement or from praise? I believe that confidence must come first; you need a strong sense of self‑confidence before you can truly achieve anything.

First, confidence allows people to work hard and keep learning every day. For example, a doctor never stops studying because new diseases appear and new treatments are developed. Learning a foreign language, such as moving from Spanish to English, is difficult because the same word can have several meanings and some words are completely unrelated. Even native speakers never finish learning a language, but the knowledge that you are constantly improving builds confidence inside you, showing that you will keep growing no matter what.

Second, being confident and positive helps you stay focused and finish tasks, especially when pressure builds up. When the school year ends and exams approach, a student who feels unprepared may become anxious, but the confidence you cultivate each day—showing up to class even when you feel low—keeps your mind clear and your knowledge fresh. If you study consistently, you will feel ready when the test day arrives.

Third, confidence means being sure of what you are about to do. When you look for a new job, the unknown nature of the interview can be frightening. Yet if you trust yourself and let confidence cover the fear, you present yourself with assurance; interviewers are more likely to hire someone who appears sure of their abilities. Without that confidence, you have no clear picture of what might happen and you are unlikely to be chosen.

Some people argue that self‑esteem grows after you achieve something. They say that once you accomplish a goal, the satisfaction of having fought for it creates confidence. While it is true that succeeding can boost your belief in yourself, it is also true that without initial confidence you may never begin the effort required to reach the goal. Consider the driving test: a student who studies hard the night before may feel certain of passing, but if they lack confidence they may doubt their skills and perform poorly. If they fail, the same effort must be repeated, showing that confidence is needed before the attempt, not after.

Moreover, a positive attitude fuels confidence. Positive people believe that they can master a new job even if they know nothing at the start. They tell themselves that perseverance will lead to competence, because they trust their ability to succeed. Learning to walk as a baby illustrates this point: repeated falls and effort eventually let the child move independently, which builds belief in their own capabilities. That belief is essentially confidence.

In summary, confidence is the foundation that enables hard work, continuous learning, focused effort, and decisive action. It reduces fear, increases certainty, and remains even after achievements are reached. Therefore, cultivating confidence in yourself is essential; let it cover your doubts, guide your actions, and sustain your success.

Working on your own is more challenging than collaborating with a team, yet it offers greater learning opportunities. Whether you work alone or in a group, you still complete assignments, but solo effort encourages you to discover information as you go. In a group, each member brings their own ideas and facts, which can enrich the discussion. However, some people use teamwork merely as a shortcut to copy answers and finish the task without truly understanding it. Relying on others’ work does not promote genuine learning; it only helps you get the job done.

I prefer to work independently because it allows me to learn more effectively. Although it may take longer, I spend time examining small details, which deepens my comprehension. When I finish a task on my own, I feel a sense of relief and satisfaction, knowing that I have accomplished it without relying on anyone else’s help. Completing work solo also means I have performed the task correctly, since I am the only one responsible for the outcome. When you work alone, you have the freedom to set your own pace and decide which aspects to explore in depth. This slower pace allows you to reflect on each step, which reinforces memory and understanding.

Group work is not inherently bad; it can be easier because responsibilities are shared and ideas are exchanged. Yet, it often leads to distractions. Listening to teammates, hearing different opinions, or simply being part of a conversation can pull your attention away from your own thinking. Moreover, the ideas contributed by others might be inaccurate, and adopting them could cause you to make mistakes. In contrast, working alone lets you follow your own method, concentrate on your own reasoning, and develop your own solutions. Moreover, you can review your work without worrying about coordinating with others, making revisions more straightforward.

People who are accustomed to teamwork may find independent study uncomfortable at first, but it pushes them to seek out additional information, facts, and clues that they might otherwise overlook. If you encounter difficulties, you can always ask a teacher or another knowledgeable person for assistance; this support does not diminish the benefit of self‑directed learning. Even though it may feel isolating at times, the personal growth you gain from independent effort is long‑lasting.

Overall, while collaboration can simplify certain tasks, independent work provides stronger educational benefits. It helps you build confidence, improve focus, and truly understand the material rather than merely copying what others have done. For these reasons, I believe that learning is more effective when you tackle assignments on your own. Consequently, students who practice self‑reliance tend to become more confident learners and perform better in the long run. Therefore, encouraging independent study in schools and workplaces can lead to deeper understanding and lasting competence. Such a shift would benefit both individual growth and collective achievement.

Attending classes from home is not a good idea. I believe it is better to attend classes at school for many reasons based on my own experience at home. It is not enjoyable because there is no teacher present to explain concepts you don't understand (even though there is a teacher, they are not physically present), and you receive no assistance if you are taking an online course. Additionally, students will not benefit because they will become off track and instead of focusing on their work, they will spend time browsing the internet. I definitely do not agree that students will benefit from attending classes at home. Having a teacher with you in class is wonderful. There will come a time when you have many questions about the topic being discussed. When you are in class at school, you learn a great deal from teachers who provide examples and explain concepts to you. However, if you are taking an online course, it is much more difficult to understand the main idea of the lesson. You won't have a teacher right beside you. You have to work independently, without a friend's help. This is different from being in class, where you can ask a friend for help, and they will gladly assist you. In an online class, there is no friend to help you. You have to take many notes to understand the lesson's objective. I personally struggled with online classes, attending 3-5 lessons each day, writing notes for each, and completing at least five quizzes daily. I had to re-read lessons three times to understand and capture important facts. Honestly, you learn to become more organized and independent each day. I personally believe students should attend classes at school. It is not a good idea to do online classes and take so many notes. In class, teachers are strict when students have their electronic devices out during teaching or when working on classwork. At home, while doing classwork and being on your phone, you are not fully engaged in your class. Since you are at home and don't have a teacher, you feel you have the right to be on your phone and laptop and do whatever you want instead of doing your work. That shouldn't be the case. If you stay home and take online classes, there is a purpose. If you don't pay attention and focus more on your phone, you will never learn anything about the course, which could cause you to fail. Then, you would have to retake the class. In my opinion, I agree with some students who want to take online classes because you can wake up late and take your time eating breakfast. It's not like going to school, where you have to get up early, rush to eat, and chase the school bus. I am that type of person who loves to sleep. But it is our responsibility to do our work and submit it on time before the deadline. If you don't want to fail the class, you have to save time for your class and for your school work. Not all the time it will be about you. There needs to be time for something more important. In conclusion, I think students will not benefit from attending classes at home. It requires a lot of responsibility to remind yourself to attend class at home, complete all your work, and submit it on time. We won't have a teacher with us personally, and we have to do all our work independently. That's why I think it's not a good idea for students to attend classes at home.

It is truly rewardingto express gratitude, whether by saying “thank you” or “you’re welcome.” When we speak kindly and use good manners, we show appreciation for the actions of others and create a positive atmosphere. This simple habit encourages people to return the courtesy, fostering a cycle of mutual respect. By consistently being considerate and polite, we invite others to behave similarly, which makes social interactions smoother and more pleasant.

First, expressing thanks after someone helps us or does something for us acknowledges their effort. A sincere “thank you” can brighten someone’s day and signals that we value their contribution. Likewise, responding with “you’re welcome” when someone thanks us reinforces the exchange and strengthens the connection between individuals. This reciprocal pattern builds trust and goodwill, making it more likely that people will continue to be helpful and courteous.

Second, maintaining manners in everyday situations demonstrates respect for others. For example, greeting a shop clerk with a friendly “how are you today?” and thanking them after a purchase shows appreciation for their work. Even a modest tip can convey kindness and acknowledgment of the service provided. When we treat service workers with politeness, they are more inclined to respond positively, creating a pleasant experience for both parties.

Third, kindness and good manners are essential for forming new friendships. When we are approachable and considerate, people feel comfortable around us and are more likely to engage in conversation. Simple gestures—such as helping someone pick up something they dropped, offering a sincere compliment, or asking about their day—can open the door to lasting relationships. These actions show that we care about others’ well‑being, which in turn encourages them to reciprocate with friendliness and support.

Moreover, being courteous extends beyond verbal exchanges. Helping a person who is struggling, offering assistance without being asked, or simply listening attentively are all expressions of good character. When we act with empathy and respect, we signal that we are reliable and trustworthy, qualities that people naturally want to return.

Finally, the principle of reciprocity underlies the importance of manners. If we consistently say “thank you,” “you’re welcome,” or “sorry” when appropriate, others are more likely to do the same for us. This creates a harmonious environment where courtesy is shared rather than taken for granted. In essence, good manners are not merely formalities; they are practical tools that promote kindness, happiness, and mutual respect in our daily lives.

In conclusion, saying thank you, being polite, and showing kindness are simple yet powerful ways to improve our interactions with others. By consistently practicing these habits, we invite the same courtesy back to ourselves, foster stronger connections, and contribute to a more compassionate community.

It would bepointless to change the school lunch to healthier options, because the menu has remained unchanged for years. Students have tried to persuade the administration to improve the food, yet no noticeable difference has appeared. Often the cafeteria presents two selections, such as pizza and a rice‑with‑chicken dish, and the majority of pupils automatically choose the pizza. This pattern shows that even when healthier alternatives are offered, the appeal of familiar, less nutritious foods dominates.  

Considering the eating habits of the student body, many children do not eat at all during the day, skipping meals entirely. If the school were to replace the unhealthy items pizza, hot dogs and chicken nuggets with more nutritious choices like rice with chicken, a pasta salad containing tomatoes, onions and spinach, and a veggie burger for vegetarians, the overall diet could improve. At the same time, the budget allocated for new floor tiles would be better spent on better food options, since no one really cares how the meals look; the condition of the floors is not a priority.  

In reality, the situation does not compel any major reform. Some students complain about the taste of the food, but they still prefer to eat it rather than bring a packed lunch from home. Occasionally a decent meal appears, yet this does not justify a complete overhaul of the menu. The most logical step is for each student to take responsibility for their own meals, preparing food at home and taking it to school. By doing so, they avoid the uncertainty of the cafeteria menu and ensure they receive food they enjoy and that suits their dietary needs. Therefore, rather than spending time and money on changing the school lunch, it is wiser to bring our own meals and stop worrying about the existing options.

She helped me create a daily study routine, and one afternoon I stayed after school for extra tutoring. By concentrating on the meaning of each question and paying attention in class, I passed the exam with a score above eighty‑nine and improved my overall grade.  

Third, I learned that failing a test the first time is not a disaster; it signals that I need to work harder. One evening I came home in tears, and my mother explained that failure simply shows where my mistakes lie. She reminded me that she herself had struggled in school but persisted, and now she is successful. She told me to keep trying my best, even if the result is not perfect, and promised she would always be proud of my effort.  

Some may argue that failure is unnecessary because there are other ways to succeed without struggling. They claim that one can achieve goals without hard work or making mistakes. However, this view is mistaken; failure is the most powerful teacher, forcing us to try harder, learn from errors, and persist until we reach our objectives.  

In short, failure is an essential part of life that drives improvement and eventual success. By embracing mistakes, studying diligently, and staying motivated, anyone can turn setbacks into stepping stones toward their goals.  

Beyond the classroom, experiencing failure has helped me become more confident and better prepared for future challenges. When I faced a difficult math problem that I could not solve, I spent extra time reviewing similar exercises, asking my teacher for hints, and eventually mastered the concept. This experience showed me that setbacks are not final; they are opportunities to develop problem‑solving skills and a stronger work ethic.  

my mother’s own story of overcoming academic difficulties reinforced my belief in the value of perseverance. She told me that when she was a teenager she repeatedly failed her exams, but she never gave up; instead, she studied late at night, sought help from classmates, and finally earned a scholarship that allowed her to continue her education. Her determination inspired me to view my own failures as temporary setbacks rather than permanent defeats.  

Many well‑known individuals have also turned failure into success. Thomas Edison was fired from his first job and experienced countless failed experiments before inventing the light bulb. J.K. Rowling’s early manuscripts were rejected by numerous publishers, yet she kept writing and eventually achieved worldwide fame. These stories show that failure does not define a person; it is a stepping stone toward achievement.  

In conclusion, failure is not something to fear but a vital part of the journey toward success. When we accept our mistakes, study harder, and keep trying, we turn every setback into a lesson that brings us closer to our goals. Therefore, everyone should welcome failure as an essential teacher in life.  

Preparation is key; when I review my answers before submitting a test, I notice careless errors that could have been avoided. By taking a few minutes to read each question carefully and to plan my response, I reduce the chance of misunderstanding what is asked. This habit, combined with regular study sessions, has helped me improve my grades consistently and feel more confident during exams.  

I have learned that each failure pushes me to work smarter, not just harder, and this mindset will serve me well in the future.

Keeping teenagers away from troubleis valuable for many reasons, and imposing a curfew that bars them from being out after 10 p.m. can bring noticeable benefits in their studies, social life, health, and finances.  

First, a nighttime curfew gives adolescents more rest. When they are not wandering the streets late at night, they are more likely to go to bed earlier, which improves the quality of their sleep. A well‑rested teenager can stay alert in class, concentrate better, and therefore learn more effectively. In addition, the extra hours spent at home provide ample time to complete assignments, review lessons, and prepare for upcoming tests, all of which contribute to higher academic achievement.  

Second, staying indoors during the evening promotes healthier social interactions. When teens are out on the streets after dark, passers‑by may feel uneasy, assuming the youths are involved in gangs or other risky behavior. This perception can lead to avoidance and isolation. By contrast, when teenagers remain at home, they can engage in positive activities with family or friends, build genuine friendships, and communicate more openly, fostering a more supportive social environment.  

Third, a curfew reduces the likelihood of violent encounters and the associated medical consequences. Late‑night gatherings often lead to arguments that can quickly turn physical, resulting in injuries that require hospital treatment. Keeping teens at home eliminates many of these confrontations, allowing them to stay safe and avoid unnecessary medical expenses.  

Fourth, the policy can have economic advantages. If a teenager wishes to be out after dark, a curfew encourages them to seek legitimate night‑time employment rather than engaging in unsafe activities. Working not only provides income but also teaches responsibility and time‑management skills. The earnings can be saved for future needs, such as education or emergencies, thereby improving the teen’s financial stability.  

Finally, the overall security of adolescents is enhanced by a curfew. With fewer young people on the streets late at night, the risk of accidents, crime, and other dangerous situations diminishes. Moreover, the combined effect of better sleep, more study time, healthier social ties, reduced health hazards, and increased earning potential helps teenagers develop holistically, supporting their academic progress, personal growth, and future prospects.  

In sum, implementing a nighttime curfew for teenagers offers a practical means to protect them from trouble while simultaneously boosting their academic performance, social well‑being, physical health, and economic outlook.

People ought to decidefor themselves, though seeking advice from those who have already walked the path can be valuable. My parents have lived through many experiences and know what is truly beneficial, so their counsel can help shape choices. For instance, when I consider buying a car, I would listen to their perspective because they have already faced similar decisions. Yet, the ultimate choice remains mine; I must decide what career I pursue, whether I want a spacious home or a reliable vehicle, and how hard I work to achieve these goals. 

In my family, my older brother serves as a role model. He moved out at twenty‑one with the aim of owning a car and an apartment while attending school part‑time. His determination shows that personal ambition, backed by self‑confidence, can drive success. He often reminds me that taking calculated risks is essential, and that no one can force you to act except yourself. 

Mistakes are inevitable, and they should be viewed as opportunities for growth. My parents, too, have erred, and those experiences have taught them valuable lessons. By reflecting on my own missteps, I can improve and become stronger. 

Having someone to look up to—whether a parent, sibling, or mentor—provides motivation, but it does not replace personal effort. Life will present obstacles, yet perseverance, like “keeping on swimming,” enables us to move forward. Therefore, while guidance is welcome, the responsibility for our decisions must rest with us, because it is our life and we should follow our hearts.

Many people prefer towork alone, but I believe that collaborating in a group is far more advantageous. When you are part of a team, tasks are completed more quickly and efficiently. You can discuss your progress with classmates, receive useful feedback, and adjust your work on the spot. This interaction also prevents the isolation that sometimes comes with working by yourself. In addition, group work helps you stay motivated and accountable, which further enhances productivity.

One common concern about group work is the possibility of a free‑rider who contributes little. While such a person can be a nuisance, the overall speed of a group usually outweighs that drawback. For example, if you have a short assignment and a presentation due in a week, choosing a team means you can split the work, finish each part faster, and still have time to polish the final product.

Another strong point of group collaboration is the variety of ideas that each member brings. Instead of struggling alone to generate concepts, you can share different perspectives, combine them, and create a richer result. Whether you are working on a school project or a professional assignment, the ability to merge multiple thoughts often leads to an impressive outcome.

Finally, working together allows you to learn from others, improve your communication skills, and develop a sense of shared responsibility. In my view, the benefits of teamwork—greater speed, better quality, and more creative solutions—make it the preferable choice over working alone.

One issue often debated is whetherschools should regulate students’ involvement in activities outside class. Some argue that schools should manage extracurricular time, claiming it would enrich students’ knowledge. I disagree; students should decide how to spend their free time after school, because many must work, care for siblings, or pursue personal interests such as sports, art, or extra study.  

First, numerous students work to support their families. A job after school leaves them exhausted, making it hard to prepare for quizzes, tests, or homework. Although a study hall could let them finish assignments, they often cannot attend after‑school programs due to work schedules. Moreover, the money they earn is meant for future college costs, an investment in their own education, so they may have to forgo some activities they enjoy.  

Second, some pupils must return home early to look after younger siblings while their parents work, and they cannot afford a babysitter. Their responsibilities limit the time available for clubs, especially when a parent is occasionally free. They may use brief moments to complete schoolwork or household chores, which is challenging when combined with their academic duties.  

Third, other students simply want to engage in activities they enjoy, such as playing sports, creating art, or learning a new language. They freely choose clubs that match their interests, and the school should not dictate their choices. These students participate voluntarily, not because a school imposes rules.  

In conclusion, the reasons presented show that schools should not control students’ after‑school activities. Recognizing each person’s goals and challenges will help us understand the effort people invest in achieving success and happiness.

Have you ever felt bored or stuck? Thomas Jefferson once wrote, “Determine never to be idle… It is wonderful how much may be done if we are always doing.” I completely agree with his view, because when I feel idle I tend to become sad or depressed, so staying active is essential. There are many ways to avoid idleness and keep the mind occupied. For instance, during the summer my father invited me to work with him as a carpenter. While not everyone has such an opportunity, there are other options: joining a gym, taking regular walks, or finding paid employment.  

Going to a gym may seem obvious, but it offers both physical and mental benefits; regular exercise can improve mood, boost confidence, and even enhance appearance. This is the first strategy I use to combat boredom. My second suggestion is walking. A simple stroll lets me clear my thoughts, enjoy fresh air, and appreciate the world around me. I often walk alone, with a friend, or while walking my dog, and it always brings a sense of calm.  

The third idea is to obtain a job. Working alongside my father has given me earnings that let me buy nice shoes, clothing, and gifts for my family. Yet the advantages go beyond money; the experience has taught me a new perspective on life, motivated me to change my habits, and shown me that real life involves challenges. Watching the building we constructed evolve from a rough framework to a finished structure has been rewarding and reminds me how much can be achieved through constant activity.

Is it wisefor young people to choose a profession early? In certain countries, students are pressured to decide on a career before they even finish secondary school, so the main issue is whether committing to a job at such a tender age is advisable. I believe it can be beneficial for those who are certain about a long‑term field such as medicine, law, teaching or nursing. By beginning their studies early, they acquire specialised knowledge sooner, which can lead to a stronger contribution to the nation’s development. Moreover, starting early gives them more time to progress, change direction, or pursue further qualifications, because youth provides the flexibility to adapt.  

On the other hand, there are drawbacks. Young learners may become fatigued by intensive schooling and could later discover that the chosen path does not suit their interests, leading to regret. Without sufficient maturity, they might also lack the insight needed to make a well‑informed decision.  

In summary, committing to a career at a young age can be a good strategy for motivated students who are clear about their goals, as it offers early expertise and greater opportunities for advancement. Therefore, teachers, counselors and parents should actively guide and encourage youths in selecting a suitable profession that aligns with their abilities and aspirations.

Some people claim that staying within a familiar skill set is the best way to reach one’s goals, while others argue that taking on more difficult tasks leads to greater achievement. I agree with the latter view: pushing yourself beyond what you already master can open new opportunities, make your work or hobbies more exciting, and broaden your education.  

When you doubt your abilities, confidence wanes, and progress stalls. Believing in yourself is the essential first step toward any goal and true happiness. By setting your mind to do more than you imagined, you begin to move forward in life, engage with the world around you, and take purposeful action. In my opinion, advancing further is a privilege not everyone enjoys, so making the most of it is worthwhile.  

A clear illustration is a student who once doubted whether she could handle chemistry. At first she thought she could not succeed, but after committing to the course she eventually passed and gained confidence that extended beyond the classroom. Likewise, many people feel dissatisfied with their jobs and perform poorly; finding something you enjoy and then setting a new challenge each week can transform work into a source of joy. Treat each challenge like a game, because most people are drawn to a good contest, and the effort becomes rewarding.  

Education remains a constant part of our lives, and there are many ways to learn — by watching others, reading, or practicing directly. To benefit from any situation, be mentally, emotionally, and physically prepared; life’s surprises will teach you both positive and negative lessons. Strive to do your best and extract something valuable from every event.  

In short, Emerson was correct: challenge yourself beyond what you already know. Believe in your own capacity, improve a little each day, and view life as a game that shapes you into a better person.

Finally, the initiative benefits the whole community. It encourages cooperation, develops leadership skills among seniors, and provides extra help for younger students, strengthening the school environment for everyone.

In short, this mentoring program is valuable for both older and younger learners and contributes positively to the broader community.

Ralph Waldo Emerson argued thattrue greatness lies in staying true to oneself despite a world that tries to shape you otherwise. I disagree with his view. In today’s society, many young people choose to stay close to peers who behave, speak, and act in the same way. This tendency to cluster with like‑minded individuals creates an atmosphere that feels unsettling, yet it reflects a strong desire to belong and to gain acceptance from others, even when such acceptance is unnecessary.  

A second reason for my dissent is the dominance of digital devices in the current generation. Youngsters spend countless hours online, often preferring virtual contact to real‑world interaction. Because of this, they are more inclined to follow popular trends rather than chart their own course, which undermines the very idea of individuality that Emerson championed.  

Finally, the pursuit of a diploma illustrates another form of conformity. Students frequently attend classes, listen to instructors, and take tests not to acquire knowledge but to obtain a credential that looks impressive on a résumé. In doing so, they sacrifice genuine curiosity for the sake of meeting societal expectations, further demonstrating that many are more concerned with fitting in than with being authentic.

Is it difficult to stay true to oneself in a world that constantly pushes a different identity? I want you to consider this question. Our planet is full of pressure to conform, and many of us end up losing the chance to simply be who we are and feel content. In this essay I will explain how society is constantly trying to reshape us, how external influences lead us to change, and why each passing year makes the situation worse for our generation.  

Every day the world offers new ways to alter our behavior, appearance, and beliefs. It asks us to reflect on what we truly desire for the future: Do we want to fit the mold of a wealthy individual, or to achieve all the goals set by others? These are the deep questions we should ask ourselves, because success does not come from imitating the crowd; it comes from embracing our own values. The world will not grant us authenticity; we must create it ourselves.  

We are heavily swayed by the attitudes, speech patterns, fashion choices, religious practices, and countless other aspects of daily life. If we do not adopt the latest trends in clothing or music, we may be labeled as uncool by society. Sometimes the barrier is financial, time constraints, or simply a lack of interest, but the judgment remains: not following the prevailing style makes us seem inferior. This pressure can lead to bullying, low self‑esteem, and even depression for those who cannot afford the demanded items.  

Moreover, the younger generation is deteriorating further because of the negative impact of the world around us. New substances that cause fatal addiction, ongoing conflicts between nations, and artists whose lyrics glorify drugs, violence, and explicit sexuality spread harmful messages. If we do not choose to be authentic and pursue positive actions, we risk ending up in a state of serious decline.  

Some argue that the world itself is the source of these ills, but that view is incomplete. The real responsibility lies in our willingness to accept or reject harmful influences. When we allow ourselves to be drawn into detrimental habits, we shift the blame onto society rather than acknowledging our own choices. Therefore, the solution begins with personal determination to stay true to ourselves.  

Looking ahead, I hope the world will transform into a more supportive and friendly place. If the upcoming generation finds the courage to reject negative trends and champion positive values, we can reshape the future for the better.

Is a positive mindset essentialfor anyone who wants to succeed in life? I firmly believe that it is, because a hopeful outlook can boost performance at work, inspire others to give their best even when tasks are difficult, strengthen personal relationships, and reinforce confidence in one’s own abilities. When we approach challenges with optimism, we are more likely to find solutions, stay motivated, and maintain healthy connections with the people around us, which together create a foundation for long‑term achievement and personal fulfillment.  

When I was employed at Mango Paradise, my supervisor was a harsh, perpetually irritable man who seemed angry with everyone. Yet I chose not to let his negativity affect me; I greeted each day with a broad smile, regardless of how he behaved toward the staff. One afternoon he appeared unusually downcast, because a close relative had been admitted to the hospital in critical condition. He looked devastated, worried that his wife, who was battling cancer, might not recover. I asked if we could speak privately, and he agreed. I told him that we were ready to support him in any way he needed. Unfortunately his wife passed away, and throughout the ensuing weeks we kept a hopeful attitude, assuring him that everything would be alright and that his wife would find peace away from suffering. His gratitude was evident; he later agreed to a salary increase for the whole team, a change that many of us welcomed while others did not. He transformed after that period, and we have remained at the company, earning considerably more than before, while the overall workplace atmosphere became noticeably calmer and more collaborative.  

In every life there are difficult moments that can make us want to give up, but a person who maintains a positive stance can encourage us to rise again and keep moving forward. When we choose optimism, we give ourselves the mental space to think creatively and to recover more quickly from setbacks. Hardships are inevitable, yet a hopeful outlook acts as a catalyst that lifts others out of despair and inspires perseverance.  

A similar situation occurred in my own family. My father lost his job, and for almost four months we could not pay the rent, threatening our home. He was crushed, searching for work for three months without success, which left us fearing the loss of our house. My mother, like a typical caring wife, told him not to worry, promising that they would overcome the difficulty together and that she would stand by him. He instantly brightened, gave her a warm smile, thanked her for her unwavering support, took the car keys, and began looking for another job. The search took months, and many rejections made him doubt himself, but his wife’s belief in him kept his hope alive. Our family's relief was not only financial; it restored a sense of security and hope that had been missing for months. When he finally received a call for an interview and secured the new position, the whole family celebrated the return of stability, and our financial strain disappeared.

Yet there is often a caring individual who helps us see how capable we are and reminds us of what we can achieve. In the tenth grade I had an algebra teacher who constantly encouraged us to trust our abilities. At first many of us ignored her advice, skipped the assignments, and ended the term with failing grades, convinced that our scores would never improve. Later she spoke with us individually, convincing us that we were capable of mastering any challenge we set for ourselves. She used encouraging words, offered extra help after class, and praised even small improvements, which gradually rebuilt our confidence. Her dedication inspired several of my classmates to pursue teaching careers, showing how one positive influence can ripple through generations. The shift in our attitudes was not immediate, but over weeks we began to ask questions, seek clarification, and take pride in our progress. By the end of the term, the once‑struggling class was thriving, and many of us continued to apply the same mindset in other subjects. I remain thankful to that teacher, because she not only raised our academic performance but also became a trusted friend who continuously supported and encouraged us.  

Consequently, a consistently positive attitude is vital in every human life. It should not be reserved for special occasions or happy moments; rather, it must be maintained even during the most difficult periods. In families, older generations such as grandparents, siblings and parents ought to set a positive example, allowing children to absorb confidence and optimism. When we cultivate a hopeful outlook at all times, we increase our chances of succeeding and finding happiness. By keeping a positive attitude, we not only improve our own well‑being but also inspire those around us to adopt the same mindset, creating a ripple effect of optimism.  

Thus, a positive mindset is an indispensable key to success in life, and it must be kept alive continuously.

Maintaining a constructive demeanor wherever you go can make a big difference in how smoothly your day proceeds, allowing you to finish tasks quickly and return home to relax.  

I work in a restaurant, and I have noticed that when I approach my shift with a negative attitude, the hours seem to drag on, making the work feel endless. Conversely, when I stay upbeat and friendly, the same shift feels much shorter, and I’m able to wrap up and unwind more easily. This personal observation highlights how a positive outlook can literally speed up the passage of time in a professional setting.  

A strong first impression, driven by a positive attitude, also benefits you over the long term. People are more likely to remember and trust someone who presents themselves confidently and cheerfully, which can open doors in both personal and professional contexts. Imagine a scenario where a hundred people start with a negative vibe and then shift to a positive one; the contrast shows how quickly attitudes can transform outcomes.  

Beyond the immediate workplace, a positive attitude can have lasting benefits. It may help you meet a future partner, connect with influential individuals, or discover opportunities that others never consider. Many people overlook how a constructive outlook can lead to better job prospects, promotions, and ultimately higher earnings—goals that resonate with a large portion of the population.  

It is also important to recognize that most people tend to be negative, especially when they feel stuck in poverty or lack direction. Keeping your head high, staying hopeful, and refusing to let circumstances dictate a pessimistic view can change the trajectory of your life.  

Being kind
kind to others and sharing a smile can uplift many people, fostering a more grateful and compassionate society. Humans naturally seek connection, so spreading positivity helps combat loneliness and promotes collective well‑being.  

In summary, cultivating a positive attitude is highly beneficial for work performance, personal relationships, and long‑term success. While many individuals carry negative mindsets, adopting optimism can lead to faster progress, better opportunities, and a more fulfilling life. Everyone should strive to understand what is best for themselves and nurture a constructive outlook, because it truly makes a difference.

Many peoplethink that changing one’s life is almost impossible, but I believe that change is both possible and necessary for reaching our goals. Throughout history we see individuals and societies reshaping themselves to pursue new ambitions, and the process of transformation can open fresh opportunities for personal growth. Many feel that the effort required is too great, that habits are deeply rooted, and that the future is uncertain, which leads them to believe that alteration is futile. However, these perceptions ignore the fact that even small adjustments can accumulate into significant results over time.

When we decide to modify our habits, career direction, or lifestyle, we create a clearer path toward the dreams we hold. For example, a student who switches from a broad study program to a specialized field gains skills that increase the chance of landing a desired job. Likewise, a professional who learns a new technology expands the range of projects he can undertake. In this way, change works like a window that lets in more light and new possibilities. These new possibilities can appear as doors that open onto different career paths, educational programs, or social networks, giving us the chance to explore options we previously considered out of reach. The sense of hope that comes from seeing a clear route forward motivates us to persist even when difficulties arise.

Although the process may seem difficult, it is not impossible. People often feel discouraged because they focus on obstacles rather than benefits. By breaking a large goal into smaller steps, the task becomes manageable, and the rapid development of technology provides tools that make learning faster and more accessible. Platforms such as Coursera, Khan Academy, and YouTube provide free or low‑cost courses that cover everything from basic computer skills to advanced data analysis. When learners use these resources consistently, they can acquire competence that was once reserved for specialists, making the transition to new fields smoother and less intimidating. Moreover, change encourages us to reflect on our mistakes and to plan more effectively. When we encounter setbacks, the constructive response is to examine what went wrong, learn from it, and adjust our strategy. A useful approach is to set SMART goals — specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time‑bound — and to keep a journal of daily reflections. This practice not only clarifies what needs to be done but also reinforces a habit of continuous improvement, helping us to recover from errors more quickly.

The ripple effect of personal change also benefits the wider community. As individuals acquire new abilities, they contribute more productively to their workplaces and to society at large. A more skilled workforce boosts economic growth, and innovative ideas that arise from diverse experiences foster social development. When more people upgrade their skills, new businesses emerge, and existing companies become more competitive, which in turn creates jobs and raises living standards. Communities that support lifelong learning tend to be more resilient and socially cohesive, because individuals feel empowered to contribute meaningfully to the collective good.

In conclusion, while the journey of transformation can be challenging, it is far from impossible. By embracing change, setting clear goals, learning continuously, and planning wisely, we can enhance our capabilities, achieve our aspirations, and positively influence the world around us. It is true that change demands effort, courage, and patience, but the long‑term rewards — greater confidence, expanded horizons, and a sense of purpose — make the journey worthwhile. Ultimately, the capacity to reshape our lives is a valuable asset that, when nurtured, leads to a richer and more successful future.

Imagine you are facedwith a decision and wonder whether it is better to seek guidance from a single individual or from several people. In my view, consulting more than one person usually brings greater benefits. When you hear different perspectives, you can compare the suggestions and choose the one that seems most reliable. For example, a famous athlete once said that it is wise to ask several people before deciding, because one opinion may be correct while another may be misleading. This encourages you not to be afraid of gathering advice from multiple sources.  

Nevertheless, there are situations where speaking with just one person makes sense. If you prefer privacy or feel uncomfortable sharing personal matters with many, you can turn to someone you trust completely. A trusted friend or mentor can offer thoughtful feedback without the risk of your information spreading. In such cases, the single source may be sufficient, especially when the issue is straightforward.  

Choosing the right person is crucial. It is best to approach someone who is known for sound judgment and sensible decisions, because their input is more likely to steer you away from mistakes. Bad advice, whether from one or many, can lead to poor outcomes, so it is important to verify the credibility of the advice‑giver.  

Privacy is another factor to consider. Revealing sensitive details to several people increases the chance that the information could be misused or cause embarrassment. Conversely, confiding in a single reliable individual, such as a counselor or a trusted adult, can keep your affairs private. A consular officer, for instance, is obligated to protect your confidentiality and may relate to your situation personally, making the advice more comforting.  

Finally, the quality of the guidance matters more than the number of people involved. Good advice has the power to transform lives, so whether you seek it from one trusted source or from a small group, the key is to ensure that the guidance is sound and trustworthy. Therefore, take the time to choose advisors whose opinions you respect and who can keep your confidence.

At first glance, people disagree about whether we should stay within what we already know or venture beyond it. Some think that once we have mastered a skill we can stop, but that view limits growth. I argue that we must keep learning and trying new things throughout life; without new experiences we cannot develop.

When we limit ourselves to familiar tasks, we miss chances to discover new passions and talents. One reason to keep learning is that it brings practical experience, which is more valuable than money. Imagine applying for a job with only a high‑school certificate, while another candidate also holds a plumbing diploma and has worked as a tradesperson. The second applicant clearly has more hands‑on experience and therefore a better chance of getting hired. Being ambitious in this way – seeking additional qualifications – helps us succeed.

A second benefit is personal maturity. When we confront challenges and learn from our mistakes, we become wiser and more confident than someone who avoids difficulty. Many give up after the first attempt, but persevering through the first, second, or even third try builds resilience. This inner strength makes future tasks easier for us.

Moreover, pursuing new goals expands our opportunities in society. Our reputation and the privileges we receive often depend on what we have achieved. For instance, I aim to become a police officer; after reaching that position I will continue to seek higher ranks. Each step not only improves my salary, physical condition and mental health, but also demonstrates continual growth while I am working toward the next target. As we climb higher, we gain confidence that influences our decisions and relationships in positive ways.

In short, many people prefer the easy path because it feels safe, yet the easy route offers little value. Obstacles may appear and make us think we have reached a dead end, but the more we try, the more chances we create for advancement. I believe it is never too late to keep learning, because the more we acquire, the more we understand, and the more we grow. This continuous journey keeps us relevant and fulfilled.

Do you believe that schools should offer courses that prepare students for a particular profession? I maintain that students ought to enroll in classes that point them toward a specific career. Considering a future job early is sensible because, as people grow older, they are less likely to end up in low‑pay, unsatisfying work. I am currently a junior and already know that I want to become a United States Marine. The course I am taking now that will help me reach that goal is JROTC. This program teaches students about the United States Armed Forces. In addition, I am also enrolled in Economics and the senior‑year English class, both of which are required for graduation but which I find useful for my future career. If we wait until after high school to think about our profession, we may feel lost, confused, and financially strained. In my family, none of my relatives pursued the jobs they originally wanted; my mother once dreamed of becoming an artist but could not because her school lacked art classes and she left school to support her family. These experiences show that early guidance can prevent wasted time and money. By choosing relevant classes now, students can build a clear path toward their desired profession. Work is inevitable for everyone. Therefore, I agree that it is beneficial to begin exploring career interests while still in high school. When I grow up I hope to serve as a United States Marine, and I am confident that the classes I am taking will equip me with the skills needed to achieve that ambition.

The school’s online learningoption can bring both advantages and drawbacks. Some schools offer this format, while others do not, and opinions about it vary widely. On the plus side, online lessons let you work at your own speed and avoid waiting for classmates, giving you more control over your study schedule. However, a poor or unreliable internet connection can interrupt your lessons, and the absence of a shared learning space with peers your age may leave you feeling isolated. Without immediate teacher assistance, you might struggle to grasp difficult concepts, and many online resources offer unclear explanations or limited video tutorials that cover only a narrow range of topics. In a traditional classroom, a teacher can demonstrate solutions directly, which usually enhances understanding, whereas virtual lessons may lack live support when you need it most. Moreover, the lack of nearby classmates reduces opportunities for collaborative study or peer encouragement, potentially lowering motivation and social interaction. Online courses can also assign a heavy workload in a short period, making it hard to keep up if the material is unclear, and students may become easily distracted by personal responsibilities, leading to procrastination and lower grades. While the flexibility of online learning saves time and offers freedom, success depends on strong self‑discipline, reliable technology, and the ability to manage distractions.

I believe Emersonwas correct when he suggested that true maturity is not measured by years but by the ability to take care of oneself. After finishing school and earning a degree, many people return home to live with their parents, keep a job, and try to save for a house. If they remain under their parents’ roof, they may still be seen as a child, no matter how old they become, because their parents continue to treat them as they did when they were young. Emerson’s point, I think, is that a grown person should have his own car, home, and family, and be willing to support them just as his parents once supported him. The story is the same, only the perspective changes. My older sister, for example, cared for her daughter, which made me see life from another angle. Although I was not yet fully independent, I moved out at fifteen, which was difficult but taught me responsibility. In my view, personal growth begins when you focus on yourself and your family first, rather than worrying about the wider world. You do not need to wait for a certain age; you need to act for yourself and your loved ones.

I believe that schools should create an after‑school homework club because many students find homework confusing and are unsure how to proceed. In such a club, learners could receive help, finish their assignments, and improve their overall performance. Although some people think homework is unimportant, it actually counts for about ten percent of the final grade, which can make a noticeable difference in a student's overall mark. Completing homework also prepares pupils for upcoming tests; the material practiced in those tasks often appears on exams, so a single completed assignment might be the reason a student passes a quiz instead of failing it.

Many middle‑school students are overwhelmed by the amount of work they must complete for each subject. A typical day may involve homework from seven different classes, and teachers frequently give more than one task per lesson. This heavy load makes it difficult for pupils to keep up, especially when they do not fully understand the material presented in class. An after‑school club would give them a dedicated time to ask questions, receive explanations, and work through problems with teacher support, rather than struggling alone at home.

The club would also assist students who lack time. Some have busy schedules and cannot finish assignments after school, so an organized session would allow them to complete their work before going home. Moreover, the club would focus on understanding rather than simply providing answers; students would learn the concepts instead of copying solutions, which leads to deeper knowledge and better exam results. Consequently, grades could rise, for example moving a borderline B to an A.

Beyond individual benefits, the school itself would look better if more students submit completed homework on time. Teachers would see that pupils are actively engaged and not merely copying answers, which improves the overall learning environment. Additionally, students who are capable of doing the work but struggle with deadlines would benefit from a structured setting that guarantees they turn in their assignments promptly.

In summary, an after‑school homework club would address the main problems associated with homework: confusion, lack of understanding, time constraints, and poor grades. By offering guidance and a quiet place to work, the club would reduce student stress, free up afternoons for other activities, and ultimately improve academic outcomes for both learners and the school. If the school implements this club, students will feel more confident, teachers will have clearer insight into student progress, and the community will benefit from higher achievement levels. Overall, the club would make homework less daunting and more productive for everyone involved. Parents would also appreciate seeing their children complete assignments without the evening rush. This support would help students develop better study habits that they can use throughout their academic careers.

Many people today spend most of their time on social‑media platforms rather than meeting face‑to‑face. Research indicates that prolonged use of digital devices is linked to depressive symptoms. Because of this, we ought to reduce recreational technology use, as it can lead to a healthier lifestyle and protect our eyesight from needing glasses. For example, a friend of mine received spectacles at the age of five after spending countless hours staring at a television screen.  

While technology can be useful—such as sending photos to relatives far away, completing assignments, checking the time, or contacting family and friends abroad—it also brings several drawbacks. It consumes a lot of money, and excessive screen time can strain the brain and diminish concentration. When students rely on phones instead of studying for quizzes or exams, their grades often suffer. I recall a classmate who cheated on a test by using his phone, while the teacher, distracted by his own device, failed to notice. Moreover, many gym sessions are now spent scrolling on phones rather than exercising, and even some teachers admit to using their phones during class.  

Spending hours in front of screens reduces face‑to‑face conversation, which weakens personal relationships and can increase feelings of loneliness. In addition, prolonged exposure to bright screens strains the eyes and may accelerate the need for corrective lenses, as illustrated by my friend’s early onset of glasses. The financial burden also grows, because constant upgrades and data plans drain household budgets.  

In my own life I enjoy soccer, baseball and basketball, which keep me active and away from constant device use. The prevalence of this problem is evident everywhere, affecting students and adults alike. If we do not limit our reliance on technology, we risk harming our mental health, vision, finances, and academic performance. Therefore, curbing unnecessary technology use is essential for a better, more balanced life.

Even if you stumble, it isn’t a reason to belittle yourself. As Winston Churchill once observed, “Success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm.” I agree with this view because achieving any goal demands persistent effort and the willingness to keep trying, even when the first attempts fall short. In most cases, the initial outcome is not what we hope for, so we must repeat the process until the desired result appears. However, success is not simply a string of failures kept together by sheer optimism. It also belongs to those who actively pursue it, rather than to anyone who merely experiences setbacks. Maintaining enthusiasm is crucial; when we become impatient, our motivation wanes and interest fades, making it harder to stay committed. Enthusiasm can be described as a strong, warm feeling of interest that fuels continued effort. Mistakes are inevitable on the road to achievement, and each one offers a lesson that helps us improve. Repeating the attempt, learning from the error, and moving forward are essential steps. Research indicates that a large majority—about 78 %—of people fail to succeed because they prefer comfort over self‑motivation. Therefore, being decisive about wanting success and adopting a mindset that anticipates obstacles can prevent repeated disappointment. In short, the quote captures the idea that true progress comes from persisting through failures while keeping enthusiasm alive, and that this perseverance, combined with proactive effort, leads to genuine achievement.

The central question thathas been debated for a long time is whether it is preferable to work by yourself or to collaborate with others. In my view, working together is usually the better choice. When people join forces, they bring a variety of perspectives that can be especially useful when facing a tough problem. For instance, while organizing a school celebration or preparing a simple class presentation, a group can supply several ideas that one person might never think of, preventing the frustration of being stuck like a driver on a dead‑end road. These varied viewpoints often lead to more innovative and well‑rounded solutions, because each member can point out strengths and weaknesses that a solitary thinker might miss.  

A group also creates a more relaxed atmosphere. Members can share a laugh, encourage each other, and keep spirits high even when stress builds up. The friendly environment also helps to lower anxiety, making it easier for members to stay focused and motivated. Because there is always something to discuss, the work never feels dull, and the experience turns into a pleasant memory that people look back on with a smile.  

Another advantage is speed. With more hands on deck, tasks are divided and completed more quickly than when a single person handles everything. When tasks are shared, the overall quality tends to improve, because multiple perspectives catch errors and suggest refinements that a single mind may overlook. This extra manpower not only saves time but also opens space for creative thinking, allowing participants to experiment, add details, or invent new solutions.  

Moreover, teamwork shifts the focus from “I” to “we”. By cooperating, individuals learn to listen, negotiate, and combine their strengths, which prepares them for real‑world situations where collaboration is essential. This collaborative habit not only strengthens the group during the project but also equips members with skills that are valuable throughout their professional lives. Collaborating also helps people develop communication skills that are essential in any profession. When team members discuss ideas openly, they learn to express their thoughts clearly and to listen actively, which reduces misunderstandings and improves overall efficiency. These abilities become valuable assets when individuals enter the workforce or pursue further education.  

Finally, working in a group teaches valuable interpersonal skills. Dealing with different characters and viewpoints forces one to communicate clearly and to respect others, fostering personal growth and stronger character. For these reasons, many people agree that group work brings greater benefits than working alone. Therefore, the advantages of teamwork make it the preferred approach for most tasks.

I agree that first impressions arevirtually impossible to erase, because they are formed in a single moment and become linked to the emotions we felt at that time. Once a feeling is created, we tend to cling to it, especially if it was pleasant, and we rarely wish to alter that memory. For example, when someone walks down a street wearing clothing that starkly differs from what most people wear, they instantly draw the gaze of everyone nearby, since such attire is rarely seen. This immediate reaction shows how novelty triggers swift judgments. People encounter these rapid judgments all the time, because we are constantly surrounded by a variety of individuals—family, friends, strangers, and even ourselves. Every setting, whether at home, at work, or in public spaces, exposes us to countless first impressions, making the phenomenon pervasive. The fact that we meet many different situations means the feeling of an initial impression can arise anywhere, even when we are alone. Moreover, first impressions can serve as a catalyst for personal growth. Observing a person who stands out may inspire us to modify aspects of ourselves, such as adopting new styles or habits, in order to emulate what we found appealing. In this way, the initial view can motivate positive change. In summary, first impressions are fundamentally resistant to change because they are unique and deeply rooted in our emotional experience. Although we may later rethink our view or notice that a repeated encounter differs from the original, the original feeling remains distinct and largely unalterable.

I believethat distance learning would be a great advantage for students everywhere. It would let them take classes from any school regardless of where they live, which is especially helpful for those who are far from a physical school or who cannot get a ride to class. Learning from home also makes the experience more comfortable because students are in a familiar environment with their family, and they do not have to endure long walks or risky travel. During the recent pandemic, many schools were forced to close, and online classes allowed education to continue.

Students who live in remote areas, such as mountain villages where a four‑hour trek is required each day, would no longer need to spend that time commuting. The same applies to children in cold or isolated regions where schools are scarce; online lessons can bring education directly to their screens, ensuring they do not miss out because of geography. In many countries, long distances and poor road conditions make daily travel impossible, so online lessons become the only realistic way to receive instruction.

In addition, learning from home creates a safer environment. Many students feel uneasy at school because they face bullying, peer pressure, or simply feel uncomfortable interacting with teachers and classmates. Studying at home lets them be around people they trust, which can lower anxiety and improve concentration. This supportive setting also benefits mental health by reducing stress that often stems from a hostile school climate.

Another strong point is the ability to access courses that their own country does not offer. For example, a French student could enrol in a program run by a university in the United States, experiencing a different teaching style and gaining perspectives that differ from the national curriculum. Such courses can include advanced subjects like computer programming, data science, or foreign languages, which broaden students' skill sets. Temporary residents, such as expatriates or refugees, also benefit because they can continue their studies without interruption while they are away from their home nation.

Some people argue that distance learning isolates students and limits social interaction, which may affect their ability to develop communication skills. While it is true that face‑to‑face contact is important, the model can be combined with occasional in‑person meetings, online social platforms, or virtual group projects, allowing students to maintain relationships. My friend was home‑schooled for several years; when he entered a regular high school he was shy and found it hard to make friends, showing that the lack of daily contact can have lasting effects.

Overall, distance learning offers a flexible, comfortable, and accessible option for many learners, especially those who cannot travel to school, feel unsafe, or need courses unavailable locally. While social interaction remains important, the benefits outweigh the drawbacks when the system is used thoughtfully, making it a valuable addition to education worldwide. Policymakers and educators should view it as a complementary option rather than a replacement for traditional schooling.

Online classes can help us in many ways. Not only it will save our time but also it can give us opportunity to do a lot of extra activities and enjoy the day.

Last week I sat for amath exam during the first period. I had studied thoroughly, but on the morning of the test I overslept, realized I was late, and missed the school bus. Consequently, I had to walk the entire distance to school, feeling exhausted and anxious. Because of that, my performance suffered, and I did not achieve the grade I expected. Had the class been conducted online, I could have taken the exam from home and avoided all of those inconveniences. Online learning would therefore protect students from similar disruptions and also free up their time.

Some people argue that students would not benefit from attending classes remotely, claiming that they might miss important parts of the lecture or struggle with assignments, which could lower their grades. However, this view overlooks several advantages. First, students often stay home because of illness or because they are away from their house, and online lessons let them continue their studies without missing school. For example, if I become ill, I can stay at home and still attend the lesson, rather than losing a day of instruction. Second, the flexibility of online classes enables students to manage their schedules more efficiently. By eliminating the commute, a high‑school student can use the saved hours for a part‑time job, additional coursework, or other extracurricular pursuits. This extra time can translate into higher earnings, better preparation for college, or the chance to explore interests that enrich future career prospects. Third, the ability to study from any location—whether at a relative’s house, a friend’s place, or even while traveling—means that education is no longer tied to a single physical location. This accessibility supports learners who have commitments outside school, such as family responsibilities or work shifts.

Moreover, the claim that remote learning reduces academic performance ignores the fact that many students already struggle with attendance due to health issues or transportation problems; online options remove those barriers entirely.

Online classes can help us in many ways. Not only it will save our time but also it can give us opportunity to do a lot of extra activities and enjoy the day. Overall, online learning provides a practical solution that fits modern student life and supports academic success. In many cases, young people have no alternative but to accept a profession chosen for them, which limits their autonomy.

Today, teenagers possess the legal right to decide which field of study they wish to pursue. In secondary school they acquire a range of subjects and develop practical abilities; mastering several skills is advantageous because it equips them for diverse jobs and helps them cope with unexpected challenges. Acquiring varied competencies also enhances problem‑solving abilities and makes graduates more attractive to employers. When students are guided toward their passions early on, their confidence grows and their way of thinking becomes more flexible. For instance, they can seek information online, talk with professionals who already work in the field they consider, and gain realistic insight.

After completing middle and high school, learners are ready to enter higher education and should be responsible for choosing the direction that best suits them. In contrast, in several regions of the world young people lack access to schooling. In countries such as Honduras, El Salvador, Guatemala and parts of Africa, many adolescents must work instead of attending classes because the quality of education is poor. Without adequate schooling, many youths end up in low‑paid jobs or become involved in criminal activities, undermining community development. Consequently, a large number of them migrate to the United States, where they believe a solid education will open better prospects for their future.

In those societies, families often discourage schooling, claiming that education will not lead to meaningful employment. This attitude can extinguish a child’s ambition and, in some cases, contribute to social problems such as violence and terrorism. When parents actively discuss future possibilities with their children, the youngsters are more likely to set realistic and ambitious goals. Therefore, parents ought to give their children the freedom to study and to explore career options at an early age, emphasizing the value of learning and encouraging them to think about their future.

The ability to contemplate one’s future at a young age has become increasingly significant. While many youths around the globe ignore school, jobs, and family responsibilities, teenagers in the United States benefit from numerous opportunities to secure stable employment, enjoy good health, and receive a high‑quality education. Students who plan early are also more resilient when facing economic changes or job market fluctuations later in life. When students have a clear career goal by the time they start high school, they are better prepared for college, can acquire deeper knowledge, and may serve as role models for peers, inspiring others to value education and career planning.

In summary, providing students with the freedom to choose their own professional path, while supporting them with diverse skill development, is essential. Early guidance fosters confidence, improves adaptability, and helps young people achieve personal and societal progress. Overall, empowering young people to choose their own careers not only enriches their lives but also strengthens the social and economic fabric of nations.

When we conserve energy we are better rested, which improves our overall wellbeing and helps us perform tasks more efficiently, whether in a job or in class, so we can meet deadlines and graduate on time.  

Lately some companies have tried to save energy by reducing the number of working days, yet extending each shift to ten hours. In my view this approach is flawed; while it may increase earnings and open career possibilities, it does not truly promote health or personal satisfaction. Most businesses – such as retail stores, service firms or schools – normally operate on eight‑hour shifts, including public sector positions. Switching to four ten‑hour days would likelydamage workers' health and their lives outside work.

Second, personal life suffers. With such long days there is hardly any time left for family, friends or leisure activities. The absence of social interaction can lead to isolation and reduced happiness, making the supposed benefits of higher income less appealing.

It can harm physical health, create emotional strain and limit the time needed for family, social contacts and extracurricular commitments. Therefore, preserving energy through reasonable work hours is the better path for a balanced and productive life. Overall, a balanced schedule supports long‑term achievement and personal fulfillment and reduces the risk of burnout.

Has anyone ever been pressured to decide on a career before finishing high school? I have, and I believe teenagers should take their time rather than rush this major choice. The decision shapes a person’s future, yet it is not something that should be forced too early. Every young person has the right to decide whether to pursue a profession or not, because it remains optional.  

First, I oppose the idea that adolescents must pick a career right away, since they tend to follow adult advice without questioning it. This often leads them to choose paths they dislike, which can waste their ambitions, financial resources, and time. Young people need inspiration for the future; examples such as doctors, architects, teachers, or other professions can motivate them. Having supportive figures—parents, relatives, or mentors—also encourages them to follow a chosen direction. When teens lack adult guidance or family backing, they may avoid pursuing any career at all.  

Second, teenagers should broaden their understanding of the working world. Watching videos or hearing from professionals who explain their daily tasks can provide realistic insight. It would be valuable to present two contrasting role models: one who has completed his education, enjoys a stable job and income, and another who dropped out and now struggles financially. Life after work can be challenging, whether the weather is hot or cold, and achieving a good future for one’s family—spouse, children, and relatives—requires careful planning.  

Finally, having a clear idea of a career while still in high school is beneficial, especially for those who enjoy drawing or designing, because architecture links creativity with building. Many young people abandon school because they feel there are limited opportunities, while others need to work to support their families. A structured program or event that encourages study and apprenticeship would help them make informed choices.

Whether individuals should decide for themselves orrely on others is a question worth considering. In everyday life we often make choices that turn out poorly, both at work and in personal matters, and these mistakes are not simply the result of feeling certain that something is right. Our emotions and the circumstances surrounding each situation shape how we think, feel and ultimately decide, which is a normal part of being human. Having the freedom to choose is a defining characteristic of humanity. It allows us to express our wishes, demonstrate what we can accomplish, and pursue the goals we imagine. Autonomy does not mean we must act without any guidance; rather, it means we have the capacity to decide while also recognizing when assistance is necessary. When people are trusted to decide for themselves, they develop confidence and independence, qualities that are essential for personal development and for contributing positively to society. This autonomy encourages creativity, as individuals are free to explore different possibilities without fear of external judgment. At the same time, it is realistic to acknowledge that no one makes perfect choices every time; therefore, support from mentors, family, or professionals can play a crucial role in guiding decisions that affect others or involve complex issues. In such cases, seeking advice does not diminish personal freedom but rather enriches it by providing additional perspectives. For instance, legal proceedings, workplace responsibilities, academic settings, or situations involving minors often require external input or constraints, because the stakes are high or the individual lacks full maturity. I maintain that people should be allowed to make their own decisions because doing so enables them to shape their lives and accept the consequences. When we follow the rules that surround us, we can exercise genuine choice and take responsibility for the outcomes, whether they are successes or failures. Mistakes are inevitable, but they provide valuable lessons; likewise, correct choices bring satisfaction. The essential point is that the ability to decide empowers us to construct our own path, learn from experience, and remain free.
