Dear Manager,

I am writing to ask whether I could arrange a visit to your company in order to see if a future career with you would be a good fit. If the tasks and environment look appealing, I would like to learn more about how the business operates and what is required to run it effectively.

Your organization is large, with many employees, which means work can be completed quickly. It would be valuable for students to experience what it feels like to be inside a real company, to observe daily routines, and to understand what it is like to hold a managerial position. By spending a typical workday—approximately seven hours—I could show them how schedules are organized, when breaks such as lunch are taken, and how tasks are coordinated so that products are ready for sale.

People often wonder how a company functions from the inside, and it can be demanding, especially during night shifts. There is also the question of how extensive a company’s facilities can become; are there limits to the amount of space that can be allocated? What are the financial requirements for constructing a new company, and must existing buildings be renovated and inspected regularly, for example every five or six years?

Location is another important factor. Where can a company be situated in an urban area versus a rural one? When do suppliers deliver raw materials so that production can continue and the business can generate revenue for further investment? What are the ongoing expenses for equipment, utilities, and maintenance, and how can a company avoid financial strain while ensuring smooth operation?

Visiting a company could also benefit those who are considering a career change or simply want to see what work feels like. Some individuals are eager to experience managerial responsibilities and the time commitment involved. If a company were to run out of money or essential supplies, would it need to be sold, or could it find other solutions? How much does a company typically spend on electricity and other utility bills, and what happens if the products it manufactures are found to be defective? Could poor quality lead to legal trouble?

Companies vary in size, and those that sell their products quickly often accumulate more profit, allowing them to invest in better equipment and expand their workforce. Each company produces its own goods and cannot simply appropriate another’s supplies or claim credit for a manager’s decisions. What are the consequences if a company steals an idea from another firm—would a large fine be imposed, or could criminal charges lead to imprisonment?

Do companies operate every day of the year, including holidays such as Christmas or New Year’s? Do employees receive vacation time after a certain period of service? On festive days, are machines switched off, and how is work continuity maintained? If an employee becomes ill, must they inform a manager before staying home, or is it acceptable to wait for a call? If sickness occurs while on the job, is a replacement worker provided, or is the employee expected to continue until they recover?

In the event of a fire, would the company receive compensation for lost or damaged assets? It would be beneficial for students to tour the premises, observe managerial and employee roles, and learn how financial resources are managed to prevent future insolvency. Experiencing these aspects firsthand would help everyone understand the responsibilities of leadership and the realities of various jobs.

Overall, a company visit would provide practical insight into operations, financial planning, and the day‑to‑day challenges of running a business, and it would give students a realistic preview of what a career in this field entails.

Sincerely,  
[Your Name]

I first became interested in skateboarding when I was nine. At that time many of my friends were already riding, and I watched them with fascination. Their constant practice and the way they performed tricks everywhere sparked my curiosity, and one day I decided to give it a try. I told my parents I wanted to start, and my mother was worried about possible injuries, while my father encouraged me to go for it. The next day after school I asked my mom if we could visit the nearest skate shop, and she agreed.  

Inside the shop I felt overwhelmed by the variety of decks, wheels, trucks and other components I didn't know about. The staff member asked if I had a specific need, and I explained that I was a complete beginner and had never ridden a board before. He showed me the parts of a skateboard – the deck, the grip tape, the trucks, the wheels and the hardware – and we began assembling my first board. After choosing all the pieces we paid, and the employee put the board together. We left the shop as it was getting dark, so I couldn't ride that evening.  

The following day, after returning home from school, I took my backpack off, went outside and tried the new board. My first attempt was just to roll, but I quickly fell in love with the feeling of gliding on the wheels. Since then I have been skating almost every day, or at least every other day, and the routine has become a central part of my life. Although it is not the safest sport, I have no intention of stopping, because each session brings me joy, builds my confidence and teaches me perseverance. It also gives me a sense of freedom and a way to express myself creatively, which keeps me motivated.

Online schooling can bea great option for many students who struggle with low grades and frequent lateness caused by oversleeping or missing the bus. Attending a physical school consumes a lot of time that could otherwise be spent on hobbies such as sports or simply relaxing at home. I support online classes because they let learners study from the comfort of their own rooms, which often feels more pleasant than a traditional classroom. One major advantage is the flexible schedule. Some pupils have trouble waking up early; the lack of sleep makes them miss the bus and arrive late. An online lesson usually begins later in the day, making it easier for these students to be on time. With more rest they have more energy, stay focused, and work more efficiently during class. Another benefit concerns health and attendance. When a student falls ill, missing a day in a regular school can put them behind on assignments and increase stress, especially if grades drop. With online lessons they can continue studying from home, and even while traveling with a laptop they rarely fall behind, which helps improve their academic performance. Critics may point out that prolonged screen time can strain the eyes and that cheating might be easier in a virtual environment since teachers cannot constantly monitor what students are doing. While eye fatigue is a valid concern, it can be reduced by taking regular breaks and using adjustable lighting. As for cheating, schools can employ proctoring software and timed assessments to minimize the risk, showing that the advantages of online learning still outweigh these drawbacks.

Winston Churchill, aformer British prime minister, once claimed that success means moving from one failure to the next while keeping one's enthusiasm alive. I agree with this view because everyone encounters setbacks, yet perseverance is essential for reaching one's goals. When we fail, we should work harder, keep trying different approaches, and never declare that we are finished. Only then can we discover what opportunities lie ahead.  

Some argue that success is achieved by progressing through failures without losing enthusiasm. For example, a person who aspires to become prime minister may be told it is impossible, but continued effort and belief in oneself can make the dream attainable. This perspective shows that persistence, not avoidance of failure, leads to achievement.  

Others maintain that success involves repeating the same failures, even if enthusiasm wanes. They suggest that trying the same thing over and over, regardless of results, builds skill and eventually yields improvement. In this view, the willingness to endure repeated setbacks, even at the cost of enthusiasm, is part of the process.  

In my opinion, the most valuable form of success is the one Churchill described: advancing through failure while maintaining enthusiasm. It encourages resilience and a positive attitude, which are crucial for long‑term progress. Nevertheless, there are moments when a temporary loss of enthusiasm can be beneficial, prompting reflection and a fresh approach. Therefore, success can be seen both as a continual drive forward and as a learning experience that sometimes requires a pause.

Should students be allowed to finishhigh school in just three years, go straight to college and start working sooner? Many young people, their parents and some teachers support this idea, and I share that view. I believe that a three‑year secondary program would let pupils graduate earlier, obtain a job more quickly and enjoy a more independent life at a younger age. In my country, El Salvador, secondary education already lasts three years. My older sister left school at seventeen, entered university and is now completing a nursing degree at twenty‑one. If I follow the same path, I will finish high school at nineteen and, after an eight‑year university course, I could be a professional by twenty‑seven. This schedule shortens the time needed to start a career. A recent poll at my school asked students, parents and teachers whether the secondary program should be reduced to three years. About 70 % of the participants voted in favour, showing strong support. Some teachers also argue that a shorter programme gives students who struggle academically a chance to finish before they fall further behind. For example, my brother did not pass his ninth‑grade year, so he had to repeat it and will now spend five years in school instead of four. My mother provides another illustration. She completed high school at seventeen, became a doctor at twenty‑five and secured a good position at a hospital. While working, she attended night classes and later earned a specialization, ending up with two rewarding jobs and a better standard of living. Her success shows that finishing secondary education early does not limit future opportunities. Critics claim that a three‑year high school is too short and may lower the quality of learning. However, they overlook the fact that students can still acquire solid knowledge in a condensed schedule, especially when schools adopt effective teaching methods. Moreover, the ability to enter the workforce or higher education sooner can be a clear advantage. I hope that, in the coming years, more schools will adopt the three‑year model, allowing students to move forward with their lives more quickly.

Can failure lead to success? Winston Churchill, the former British prime minister, once claimed that true success means moving from one failure to another while keeping enthusiasm alive. Many people with ambitions share this view. When setbacks appear on the path to achievement, they can serve as a catalyst for motivation, inspire self‑improvement, and provide valuable experience.

First, failure often supplies the drive needed to keep going. A student who has just received a poor grade may realize that she must study harder and try again. Without that initial disappointment, she might simply give up after a single setback. Likewise, anyone who aims for an ambitious target should expect obstacles; when the first difficulty arises, the resulting motivation is essential for reaching the desired outcome. When a person feels discouraged, the memory of a past failure can remind them that they have overcome difficulties before, which fuels determination to press on.

Second, failure offers a chance to reflect and improve. The common saying “you learn from your mistakes” captures this idea. If a project fails because of a specific error, the same mistake is unlikely to repeat once the problem is recognized. By analysing what went wrong, individuals can pinpoint weak points and adjust their approach, which moves them closer to success. This reflective process also helps to build confidence, because seeing tangible progress after correcting errors reinforces belief in one's abilities.

Third, failure builds practical experience. Without encountering difficulties, there would be no lessons to draw upon for future goals. The stories of well‑known achievers often highlight that their breakthroughs followed periods of trial and error. Moreover, the resilience gained from dealing with setbacks equips individuals to handle future challenges more effectively, creating a cycle of continual growth. Sharing these experiences can inspire others who are facing similar doubts, showing that failure does not seal the door to achievement.

In summary, failure can be a powerful stepping stone toward success when it is used wisely. It can spark motivation, promote constructive reflection, and generate the experience needed for future progress. Rather than surrendering after a setback, one should view it as a signal that the goal is nearer and continue with renewed effort. In this way, failure becomes not an obstacle but a valuable component of the journey to success. I personally agree with Ralph WaldoEmerson’s quote, “Unless you try to do something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow.” I believe that you must set your goals higher after you have mastered something, because striving for a higher challenge is essential for growth. It is perfectly acceptable to fail while pursuing a goal, since no one is perfect. Moreover, trying different goals allows you to become proficient in several areas.  

The first reason I support is that you should set a higher goal after you have already mastered something, because continuing the same activity you have already mastered will not produce any further development. For example, imagine I am on a rec soccer team—no tryouts, just sign‑ups. If I score almost every game and consistently outplay my opponents, I will not grow as a soccer player because the opponents are easy and there is no challenge; I would have to set a higher goal. A higher goal might be to move up to a travel team, which would provide the challenge needed for growth.  

Some people disagree with Emerson, fearing that setting higher goals after mastery will lead to embarrassment and failure. They are reluctant to fail, yet failure is a natural part of reaching any objective. When I reach a goal, such as scoring three goals in a soccer game, I work hard to accomplish it. I may fail to score three goals, but I tell myself it is alright because when you are reaching a goal you will fail at least once, and probably more than once. These failures teach me about my mistakes and help me avoid repeating them, so I work harder.  

Nobody is perfect, and it is always a good thing to fail so that I can learn from my mistakes. This is why I agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s quote.

I share the view of Ralph Waldo Emerson that one must venture beyond what one already knows in order to develop. My reasoning is that once a skill or objective has been fully mastered, the next step should be to aim higher. It is natural to stumble when pushing limits, and such setbacks are part of learning because no one is flawless. Moreover, pursuing several distinct goals helps you become proficient in multiple areas. The first justification for raising the bar after mastery is that repeating the same task offers little opportunity for improvement. If you constantly play on a recreational soccer team where you score easily and dominate opponents, your abilities will stagnate; the competition is too weak to challenge you. To see real progress you would need to move to a more competitive league or travel to face tougher rivals, which would force you to grow as a player. Some people oppose Emerson’s idea because they are afraid of failing once they have already achieved a level of competence. They worry about looking incompetent and therefore avoid taking on harder targets. In my own experience, when I set a target of scoring three goals in a match, I train hard and sometimes fall short. Yet I remind myself that occasional failure is inevitable when striving for excellence, and each mistake provides valuable lessons that make me work harder. A further point is that mastering various pursuits enriches your life. Sticking exclusively to one area after you have become expert in it limits the range of skills you possess. Having diverse strengths allows you to tackle different challenges and opens doors to new opportunities. Even if you eventually lose interest in one goal, having other competencies to fall back on is beneficial, as many people shift their focus over time. Consequently, I agree with Emerson’s statement. Raising your goals after you have mastered something ensures continual personal growth. The process may involve setbacks, but these are not reasons for discouragement; they serve as feedback that guides improvement. Additionally, exploring multiple objectives keeps you adaptable and well‑rounded. This is why I support the sentiment expressed by Emerson.

Summer is a season of scorchingheat, and schools traditionally give students a long vacation of about two months. Some teachers argue that the break is too extended and propose a year‑round schedule with a shorter summer and a longer winter holiday. I disagree with this idea because the extreme summer temperatures make attending school difficult, and the break provides valuable time for families to travel and for students to earn money.  

During summer the weather is often unbearable; temperatures can rise above 96 °C, which is far too hot for anyone to study comfortably. In such conditions students tend to sweat, suffer severe headaches, and lose concentration, all of which negatively affect their performance and grades. Moreover, people who work in hot climates find it harder to carry out even simple tasks, so learning in that environment is especially challenging.  

Conversely, the two‑month vacation allows students to enjoy a range of activities. Many families plan trips to the beach or travel abroad, taking advantage of the school‑free period to spend quality time together. Others use the break to work part‑time jobs, gaining experience and earning income. Because no classes are in session, students do not miss any instructional days when they travel, making the vacation both enjoyable and practical.  

In summary, the intense heat of summer makes regular school attendance impractical, while the extended break offers students the chance to relax, travel, and work. Therefore, the government should preserve the current summer vacation and not eliminate it.

An excellentprofessional often begins his journey when a young student selects a field he is passionate about and commits to studying it for many years. Research shows that children acquire knowledge more rapidly than older learners, and many parents encourage their kids to name future occupations such as doctor, teacher, dentist, police officer, or engineer. In schools, teachers ask pupils to draw pictures of their dream jobs, and even young children already have a clear idea of what they want to become. Therefore, it is beneficial for students to decide on a career early, because they need time to prepare properly and increase their chances of success.  

Preparing for a chosen profession requires time and effort. Every field involves specific subjects that must be mastered, and students may lack the necessary credits, forcing them to repeat courses. Aspiring doctors, for instance, face many years of study and considerable financial costs. They must save money to cover tuition, although in some cases the government funds the education of qualified students. The length of training and the depth of knowledge required make it essential to start early in order to achieve excellence in the chosen career.  

Students also have the chance to explore several occupations before settling on the one that suits them best. They may switch paths if they discover a new interest, giving them flexibility to select the career that aligns with their strengths and preferences. Early exposure to multiple fields expands their options and helps them make a more informed decision. In fact, starting early allows them to adjust their plans, correct mistakes, and acquire the necessary qualifications before entering the workforce.  

In summary, students should be encouraged to decide on a career while they are still young. Early commitment provides ample time for preparation, financial planning, and skill development, and it offers greater flexibility to change direction if needed. High schools can support this process by guiding students toward realistic goals and helping them explore various professions. A person who begins working toward his desired profession early is more likely to achieve a stable job and a promising future.

Prime Minister Churchill once said that success is built on failure, and I completely agree with this view. To me, success does not simply mean achieving a desired result; it is the continual effort to solve problems, face obstacles, and grow as a person. When we encounter setbacks, they are not signs to quit but opportunities to push our limits and develop the confidence needed to move forward.  

Success, in my opinion, is a habit of daily engagement rather than a distant dream. It requires us to look ahead, plan future steps, and avoid falling back into old, comfortable routines that hinder progress. Failure, therefore, is not the end of a journey but a test of our resolve, skills, and willingness to improve. It can spark motivation, prepare us for upcoming challenges, and encourage us to support others who need help.  

I remember taking an exam where I felt nervous, yet I was confident I could pass rather than fearing failure. This mindset showed me that confidence can outweigh anxiety, and that viewing a test as a chance to prove oneself is more empowering than seeing it as a threat. Some people chase success to achieve happiness, while others seek it to help those around them improve their abilities. For these individuals, thinking about the future and planning the next steps is essential.  

Conversely, many give up quickly, much like a player who, after losing a video game, throws the console away and never plays again. Such attitudes abandon enthusiasm and prevent growth. In contrast, those who welcome challenges view each level as a chance to discover weaknesses, refine skills, and strive to stay at the top. They understand that overcoming obstacles is what keeps them moving forward.  

In summary, success is not a static achievement but a dynamic process that embraces failure as a stepping stone. By staying dedicated, looking forward, and learning from setbacks, we can motivate ourselves and others, ultimately turning difficulties into opportunities for personal development.

I completely agree that a positive mindset can guide anyone toward success. When we keep hope alive, even if we have lost everything, a hopeful outlook makes challenges seem manageable and helps us recover. Working hard with confidence today or tomorrow will eventually bring the results we want. Conversely, a negative outlook can hinder progress and may lead to failure. For instance, Steve Jobs was forced out of the company he founded, yet his optimism never wavered. He returned three years later, rebuilt the business, and continued innovating despite serious health problems that once threatened his life. Similarly, Cristiano Ronaldo faced prejudice because of his skin colour, but he responded with a constant smile and steadfast confidence, eventually becoming one of the greatest footballers ever. In today’s fast‑paced world, a single loss can make us feel that success is out of reach, but this attitude is unrealistic. Every person, from a toddler to an elderly individual, encounters difficulties. By staying upbeat, we can approach each problem with a solution‑focused mindset, which makes the obstacles easier to overcome. Instead of giving up, we should breathe deeply, stay calm, and maintain a positive outlook. In this way, optimism becomes a powerful tool that transforms any situation into an opportunity for growth. A positive attitude also helps us stay resilient during setbacks, allowing us to learn from mistakes and keep moving forward. When we believe in ourselves, we are more likely to take risks and seize new chances, which often lead to personal and professional growth. Therefore, cultivating optimism is not just a feel‑good habit; it is a practical strategy that can change the course of our lives for all people worldwide.

Imagination is a basic human capacity that underpins the way we acquire knowledge. It serves as the foundation upon which all ideas are built, and without it we would lack the ability to understand the world. In everyday activities—whether at work, at school, at home or in the community—people constantly use imagination to picture the steps needed for a task, to decide how to act, and to select the skills required.  

From the moment a person conceives a new product, an idea, or a solution, imagination is the first mental model that guides the process. It allows us to anticipate needs, to design objects that meet those needs, and to imagine how they will function. Even when we possess strong skills in mathematics, science or other fields, those abilities remain unused unless imagination first supplies a purpose for them.  

It also fuels creativity in art, literature and science, allowing people to see beyond the obvious. Consequently, societies that nurture imagination tend to advance more quickly.  

Thus, imagination is not merely a creative pastime; it is the engine of progress. It has driven human development throughout history, enabling us to adapt to changing circumstances and to invent new ways of living. Every profession, every family interaction, every educational pursuit relies on the capacity to imagine possibilities before they become reality.  

In short, imagination is the seed of knowledge and the catalyst for action. It is the first step in any idea, task, or decision, and it shapes the way we apply our existing skills and information. Without imagination, the knowledge we possess would remain inert, and the world would lack the continual evolution that defines human life.

In the future I hope to achieve several major goals. First, I would like to become a billionaire, because that would give me the freedom to provide a comfortable life for myself and my family. One of my first wishes would be to purchase a spacious house of my own. It would include a private swimming pool, so I could enjoy the water whenever I want without traveling to a public pool. I would also love to host gatherings for friends, which would keep the noise down for my mother and avoid any complaints. Having a pool would satisfy a long‑standing desire and give me a place to relax after a busy day.  

Second, I would use my wealth to improve my mother’s life. She has worked hard for many years and deserves a new home, a reliable car, and fresh clothing. I plan to sell the house we currently live in, give the proceeds to her, and then take her to choose a vehicle she prefers, replacing her old, problematic car. Afterwards we could visit a mall together so she can select the outfits she likes, and I would make sure she receives the best care and attention she has always given me.  

Third, I would establish a hospital that offers affordable care. Many people are deterred by high fees, and some facilities are unfair toward patients based on appearance. My hospital would be staffed by skilled doctors and nurses, would treat everyone regardless of race or background, and would keep charges reasonable so that even low‑income individuals can receive treatment. I would also ensure that the environment is welcoming and that no one is turned away because of how they look.  

Finally, I want to assist the homeless. Rather than keeping all the money for myself, I would allocate a portion to provide food, clothing, and shelter. I envision buying an entire city block and constructing apartment buildings specifically for those without homes. Seeing people sleeping on sidewalks or begging for food would no longer be acceptable; everyone deserves a safe place to live. By offering stable housing, I hope to give the homeless dignity and a chance to improve their lives.  

These are the main reasons I aspire to become a billionaire: to secure a home with a pool, to give my mother a better life, to create a fair hospital, and to help the homeless find housing.

Itis clear that there are many ways to affect other people. What matters is not the way someone behaves, but how their deeds, objectives and enthusiasm are presented. Even a negative attitude can be persuasive if it is shown through concrete actions. The Disney film *The Princess and the Frog* illustrates this point: the heroine’s ambition to open a restaurant, driven by her father’s wish, kept her working until she finally secured the needed funds. Her persistence turned a seemingly impossible dream into reality, proving that determination combined with concrete steps can move people.

First, the way we act can shape others’ behaviour. For instance, regularly giving food to a local pantry may seem small, but a steady habit draws attention. When the media reports on such consistent generosity, more people are likely to contribute, strengthening the whole community. When people see consistent effort, they begin to trust the doer and are more willing to follow the example.

Second, having a clear goal motivates both ourselves and those around us. Imagine wanting to buy a video game that costs $80. With no money, you start doing chores, washing a car or mowing lawns, and even offering services to neighbours. By persisting, you eventually earn enough to purchase the game. This shows that setting a target and working toward it can inspire others to follow the same pattern.

Third, personal motivation is contagious. If you appear discouraged, it is hard to convince others to act. Conversely, showing energy and optimism signals purpose and willingness to work hard, encouraging others to adopt a similar attitude.

Some argue that personal behaviour alone sets the right mood for motivation. While a positive demeanor can help, it does not by itself show how someone can be persuaded to act. Therefore, the most effective way to influence others is to combine concrete actions, defined goals and genuine enthusiasm. These three elements together create a powerful influence on others daily. In summary, showing what you do, what you aim for and how eager you are to achieve it are the key tools for influencing people.

It is a good planfor students to finish high school in three years and go straight to college. Some learners prefer to leave school earlier than their classmates. Several reasons explain why they might choose this option.

First, many want to start earning money sooner so they can pay for tuition or support their families. Others see a short break as a chance to travel and spend time with relatives. In some cases, older Hispanic students who have family duties feel that a high‑school diploma is enough to get a well‑paid job, so they prefer to finish early. Also, high‑achieving pupils who already meet all graduation requirements can graduate ahead of schedule.

Students who decide to graduate early must work harder. For a 16‑year‑old in eleventh grade, the usual path means lacking enough credits, so they need extra courses or summer classes. When a learner has all the necessary credits, they can finish in three years by taking additional classes or using online courses.

Some students have jobs, family responsibilities, or extracurricular activities after school. Schools often provide after‑school programs, tutoring, or evening sessions that help students earn the credits they need. Some schools even run accelerated programs that let pupils complete high school in three years, usually during summer or evenings. Not every student can join these programs, but online courses offer another flexible option.

The main benefit of finishing high school early is that it shortens the time before college, allowing students to start their higher‑education journey sooner. It also gives them the chance to earn income earlier, which can relieve financial pressure. However, the fast pace can be exhausting. Students may also miss out on typical high‑school experiences such as sports, clubs, and senior events, which can affect their social development. They should also discuss their plans with parents and academic advisors to ensure that the accelerated path fits their long‑term goals and does not limit future opportunities. Colleges often look at the completeness of a student's high‑school record, so early graduation may require extra documentation or a stronger transcript to demonstrate readiness. School counselors can help students map out the necessary courses and choose the best summer or online options. If they do not manage their workload carefully, they risk falling behind and not completing the required credits.

In short, graduating high school in three years can be a sensible choice for motivated students who have the necessary credits and the stamina to handle extra work. Students must also be ready to handle the pressure of faster coursework and maintain motivation throughout the shortened timeline. The availability of summer, evening, or online courses makes the goal reachable for many, while the personal effort required determines whether the plan succeeds. Overall, early graduation can be a viable pathway for ambitious learners, provided they plan carefully, stay motivated, and seek support when needed. Students should also talk with their teachers and family members to make sure the plan aligns with their personal aspirations.

Dear diary, in today’s English lesson my friends said that first impressions in life are practically unchangeable. I think they are wrong, because a person’s initial appearance can be altered by the situation they are in, by the way they are treated, and by personal difficulties that affect their behavior.

One reason is that people may be going through a rough patch. When I moved to a new city a few years ago, I felt lonely and upset, which made me reluctant to attend school and to enjoy anything. A classmate once told me that his family had just lost a member, and his sadness made him seem distant. In my own life, my parents change jobs frequently, so we move every year. Even though we have not moved this year, the thought of possibly relocating next January makes me uneasy, because I feel at home at Generic School where teachers are supportive and classmates are friendly. For example, when I arrived in a new town last year, I missed my old friends and my family, and I found it hard to concentrate in class. The teachers noticed my sadness and offered extra help, which made me feel more comfortable. Even though I have not moved this year, the possibility of leaving my current school in January still makes me uneasy because I have grown attached to the staff and classmates who care about me.

Another point is that people do not always treat everyone the same way. At a recent party I wanted to join a group of friends, but they ignored me. I felt embarrassed and confused at first, but after talking with the girls, I explained that I have a twin sister and that I never meant to upset anyone. They listened, apologized, and invited me to join them, and we ended up dancing and laughing together. This shows that first impressions can be misleading when others act based on incomplete information.

A third reason is that some individuals struggle to control their emotions or actions. A boy in my class is usually helpful and kind, but he can become very angry and say hurtful things when he is upset. He has a condition that makes emotional regulation difficult, and his teachers take the time to explain his situation so that classmates understand him better. He told me that his condition is called ADHD, which makes it hard for him to stay calm, and the school provides a counselor who works with him regularly. Because of this support, his classmates have learned to be more patient with him. This example demonstrates that a person’s behavior may change depending on internal challenges rather than on a fixed personality.

In conclusion, first impressions are not permanent. People can be in difficult circumstances, may be treated unfairly, or may have personal issues that affect how they act. Because everyone makes mistakes or faces hardships, it is unfair to judge someone permanently based on a single encounter. I therefore stand by my view that first impressions can be changed. Therefore, first impressions are only a brief snapshot, and with understanding and empathy, we can see the whole person beyond that initial moment. I believe that taking the time to understand others can turn a wrong first impression into a lasting friendship. Everyone deserves a second chance.

Dear reader, it is a pleasure to share my thoughts on this topic. Thank you for giving me the chance to express my opinion based on my own experience. Although some people claim that first impressions are almost impossible to alter, I disagree. I believe that while an initial impression may be strong, it can be reshaped over time, and I will explain why.  

First, the importance of a first impression is often emphasized, yet it is not an immutable fact. The impact of that first meeting depends on the individuals involved. For example, when we meet someone we are interested in, we may strive to make a positive impression, but as we spend more time together, our perception can shift. The brief moment that forms the first impression is only a snapshot; as we learn more about the person, we can revise our view. Therefore, the claim that first impressions cannot change is overly simplistic.  

Second, impressions are not solely based on a single factor such as appearance or facial expression. They are also shaped by behavior, conversation, and the context in which we meet. A person might initially appear serious because of a frown, but as the interaction continues and the person shows warmth, the earlier impression can be overturned. In my own experience, I once thought a colleague was unfriendly because she seemed distant at first; after several weeks of collaboration, I realized she was simply shy and became very supportive. This shows that impressions can evolve.  

Third, time plays a crucial role in modifying first impressions. As days, weeks, or months pass, we accumulate evidence that either confirms or contradicts our initial judgment. If the evidence is positive, the original view tends to fade or transform. Conversely, negative experiences can reinforce the initial impression, but the key point is that change remains possible. Hence, it is inaccurate to say that first impressions are beyond alteration.  

In conclusion, while the first impression is important, it is not fixed. With time, new interactions, and a willingness to look beyond the initial snapshot, we can change how we perceive others. Therefore, I affirm that first impressions can be modified, and it is both realistic and beneficial to remain open to revising them.

In my view, Iunderstand the purpose behind Thomas Jefferson’s writing for his fellow citizens. He wanted to see whether they could take responsibility for their own tasks and avoid getting caught up in trivial matters, so that they might finally realize their own aspirations. At the time he wrote, many people were still haunted by the legacy of slavery, a system that had existed before Abraham Lincoln assumed the presidency of the United States. Jefferson’s piece can be summed up in three main points.

First, Jefferson hoped to observe how well his compatriots actually followed the principles he set out. Numerous individuals do not give much thought to what they can achieve in life; they while away time socializing instead of working toward personal goals. Some feel shy or fearful about pursuing their dreams because they worry about what others might say, or because they doubt the feasibility of their ambitions. Others cannot reach their goals simply because they never make the effort, assuming the obstacles are too great.

Second, a careful reading of the text reveals a call for genuine commitment to one’s aspirations. Many students attend school merely because they are required to, without recognizing the future opportunities that education can unlock. If we take Jefferson’s message to heart, we learn that hard work, focused study, and good grades are essential steps toward turning our desired future into reality.

Third, although we now enjoy a great deal of freedom and spare time, many people choose to spend it on parties, outings, and casual gatherings rather than on pursuits that could improve their lives. This lack of dedication prevents progress. To move forward, we must cultivate a stronger resolve to chase what we truly want for the future.

In conclusion, young people have the energy and potential to outperform others, provided they develop better thinking habits, maintain concentration, and draw support from their families. Jefferson’s writing serves as a reminder to stay steadfast in our dreams and never surrender, no matter the challenges we face.

To tell myteacher which way I prefer to work, I would say I work best alone. When I am by myself I can explore ideas that others might never consider, and I can develop them at my own pace, which helps me think more clearly. In a group, distractions are common; the constant discussion can break the flow of concentration, making it hard to finish tasks. Some learners appreciate working alone because they can submit their assignments on time, avoid the risk of failing, and escape the stress of coordinating with others, which can delay completion. Shy or quiet students also choose solitude so they do not have to keep up with classmates who may not be doing their share, and they feel more comfortable without the pressure of speaking in front of the class. In many group settings, the help from peers is minimal, and the workload is often uneven, with a few members taking on most of the effort while the rest contribute little. This uneven effort can make the project feel unfair and stressful, and it can lower motivation among the group members. Moreover, some students avoid discussing their work with friends because they fear that their parents will blame the peers for any poor result, and a teacher’s call could make the family feel guilty, which stops them from seeking help when needed. In my view, the advantages of working alone outweigh the drawbacks of group work. By focusing on my own ideas and managing my time, I can achieve better results and keep my responsibilities clear. Working alone also lets me set my own schedule and focus on the parts of the assignment that interest me the most. When I am not distracted by group chatter, I can plan my work step by step and check my progress regularly, which reduces mistakes and improves the quality of the final product. Because I am responsible for my own work, I feel confident that the grade I receive truly reflects my effort. I find that I can also use the time saved from not waiting for others to review my drafts, which makes the whole process smoother and more enjoyable. Overall, independence leads to better learning outcomes and personal growth.

Anyonewho wishes to achieve success must be prepared to stumble more than once while keeping their enthusiasm alive. Enthusiasm fuels persistence; it is the driving force that makes us continue pursuing our goals. I fully agree with the view expressed by Winston Churchill that perseverance through setbacks is essential. In everyday life we face highs and lows. For instance, when I received poor grades I examined what I was doing wrong and decided to improve. This shows that failure can be a valuable teacher, provided we do not let it diminish our excitement. To reach our objectives we must endure several setbacks but we should also recognize that obstacles will try to hold us back. The key is to focus on what we ultimately want to achieve and not allow difficulties to stop us. If a person stops caring about a pursuit, they will inevitably quit. Therefore, maintaining interest is crucial for long‑term progress. Falling down and getting back up repeatedly is part of the journey toward any meaningful goal. When enthusiasm fades, success becomes unlikely. Even when a goal seems distant and many challenges appear, staying engaged in what we love helps us move forward. There will always be attempts to hold us back, but we must refuse to be stopped. A positive mindset and constructive actions enable us to demonstrate our capabilities and prove what we can become if we keep our enthusiasm alive. Each failure offers a lesson that can be learned, guiding us toward the desired outcome. In short, repeated failure combined with sustained enthusiasm is the pathway to achieving our ambitions.

Numerous schools have formed collaborations with nearby enterprises. Through these ties, pupils can experience different occupations and get a clearer picture of potential career paths.  

Such alliances are essential because they equip learners with the resources needed to thrive in life. By working alongside professionals, students can sharpen practical abilities and deepen their intellectual understanding, which together prepare them for future success.  

One major benefit of a school‑business partnership is the distribution of risk. When a venture does not go as planned, thefinancial and personal burden is shared among all participants rather than falling on a single individual. Embarking on an entrepreneurial journey alone is extraordinarily challenging; it can feel like trying to reach the clouds, and the possibility of ending up without shelter or losing everything is unsettling. Having companions in the endeavor makes the experience far less daunting.  

Beyond the practical advantages, partnership promotes social well‑being. Collaborating with others reduces isolation, creates a sense of belonging, and makes the work more enjoyable. Regular interaction with teammates encourages mutual trust and strengthens relationships, turning the work environment into a source of happiness rather than boredom.  

Critics sometimes argue that partnerships may lead to disagreements and eventual failure. While it is true that conflicts can arise, they are often the result of poor member selection or insufficient communication. By carefully choosing compatible partners and establishing clear expectations, these obstacles can be minimized. Moreover, the exchange of ideas and shared responsibilities foster continuous learning, which is a core strength of any collaborative business.  

In conclusion, integrating business partnerships into school programs offers students a valuable platform to explore professions, develop essential skills, share risks, and experience greater fulfillment. Consequently, educational institutions should prioritize the creation of such collaborations to support every learner in achieving their aspirations and succeeding in life.  

When schools partner with local companies, students get the chance to visit workplaces, attend workshops, and even take part in short internships. This hands‑on exposure helps them see how classroom concepts are applied in real life, making their learning more relevant and motivating them to set clear career goals. Such experiences also build confidence and teamwork skills that are valuable beyond the classroom. These benefits make partnerships a practical and effective way for schools to prepare students for the future.

McDonald’s is a well‑known fast‑food chain where employees earn modest wages. If pupils were able to tour the restaurant, they could witness firsthand the daily routine of workers who have little formal schooling and are paid only a little. Seeing this might make them realize that neglecting their studies could lead to a similar fate.  

By observing the fast‑paced, demanding work environment, teenagers could understand that a low‑pay job requires hard effort every day. This awareness could motivate them to concentrate more in class and avoid lazy behaviour, aiming instead for a career that offers better compensation and stability.  

Many families lack the financial resources to keep their children in school, so some young people are forced to take up demanding jobs early. When students have the opportunity to receive an education, they should seize it, because it opens doors to higher‑paying positions and a more secure future. In contrast, those who ignore their studies may end up working in low‑wage establishments, repeating the cycle of limited earnings. Parents often sacrifice their limited income to fund their children's schooling, expecting a better future. When a student disregards his classes, that investment yields no return, and the family sees no benefit from the tuition fees they have paid.  

If a student does not treat his schooling seriously, the money his parents invest becomes wasted; he will acquire little knowledge and struggle to secure a rewarding career. Visiting a place like McDonald’s can serve as a wake‑up call, showing the connection between academic effort and future earnings.  

Therefore, I would write to McDonald’s to request that they host student visits, giving young people a clear picture of what awaits them if they do not apply themselves in school. Such an experience could encourage them to value education, work harder, and ultimately pursue a well‑paid, successful profession rather than settling for a low‑salary job.

People often debate whether technologyimproves or harms our lives. Some argue that it lets us finish many tasks without meeting others, while others claim it reduces face‑to‑face interaction. In my view, technology brings more benefits than drawbacks and is a great aid in everyday life.  

Today our schedules are packed with work, school assignments, part‑time jobs and other responsibilities. Teenagers, for instance, juggle heavy homework loads and after‑school employment, leaving only a short window of free time at night. Thanks to modern tools, activities that once required a trip to a library—gathering paper, supplies, books and waiting for assistance—can now be done quickly online. Without these tools we would spend far more time and money on basic tasks, and the overall pace of life would become even slower.  

Critics, however, point out that technology can isolate people, especially when family members sit together but stare at their phones instead of talking. This behavior may weaken personal bonds. Nevertheless, the same technology also connects us with relatives and friends who live far away. Through video calls, messaging apps and social media, we can see and speak with loved ones regardless of distance, which makes long‑distance relationships feel much closer and helps maintain emotional support.  

Technology also simplifies travel and navigation. When we need to reach an unfamiliar location, GPS applications provide instant directions, saving time and reducing stress. For example, my mother uses a map program to pick up my father after his work shift, ensuring they arrive on time and avoid unnecessary delays. Such tools illustrate how digital solutions enhance everyday convenience and give us greater independence.  

Beyond daily chores, technology supports professional fields. Scientists, doctors and researchers rely on advanced equipment to develop cures for diseases, improve diagnostics and extend lives. The same innovations that help us locate a restaurant also enable breakthroughs in medicine, showing the broad impact of technology on health and science. In addition, modern communication devices allow us to share information instantly, collaborate on projects across continents, and access educational resources that were previously out of reach.  

Moreover, technology has transformed education. Online platforms provide access to courses, tutorials and interactive simulations that allow students to learn at their own pace, regardless of geographic location. This flexibility helps those who work or have family commitments, making learning more inclusive and adaptable.  

In conclusion, technology is largely beneficial when used responsibly. It saves time, facilitates communication across borders, assists in navigation and underpins many scientific advances. While it can create distractions, the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, and people should continue to employ it wisely to improve their lives. Therefore, by balancing screen time with real‑world interactions, we can enjoy the many advantages technology offers while minimizing its potential downsides.

Distance learning is a valuable option formany students because it uses the internet to deliver classes and allow communication with teachers without the need to be physically present in a school building. Learners can attend lessons from home or any other location, receiving exactly the same curriculum that they would follow in a traditional classroom. This means that academic standards are maintained while the setting becomes more convenient.  

One of the strongest arguments in favour of distance learning is that it can help reduce bullying. In many schools, harassment creates a hostile atmosphere that affects students’ well‑being. By giving learners the possibility to study remotely, teachers can limit the opportunities for such behaviour to occur, and students who are vulnerable may avoid the daily pressure of confrontations. This safer environment can improve both confidence and academic performance.  

Students also face many responsibilities after the regular school day, such as caring for younger siblings, working part‑time jobs, or attending extra courses. Home‑based study lets them organise their time more freely, so they can complete assignments without neglecting these other duties. When learning can be fitted around personal commitments, the overall workload feels less overwhelming and students are more likely to stay motivated.  

Another advantage is the reduction of stress that many learners experience in a conventional setting. When classes are scheduled at fixed times, students often feel rushed, especially if they have not had enough sleep or if they must balance school with work. Studying from home allows them to set a pace that matches their energy levels, which can lead to better concentration and higher quality work. Moreover, the ability to pause or review material at will helps prevent the frustration that builds up when a concept is not immediately understood.  

In a typical classroom, a number of students behave disruptively, talk to friends, or act as negative influences, which can distract their peers and lower overall achievement. When these individuals are removed from the physical space, teachers do not need to spend time issuing referrals or suspensions. Instead, the focus can stay on instruction, and the learning environment becomes more stable. This stability benefits not only the student who stays at home but also the classmates who remain in school.  

Technology also plays a big role in making remote learning attractive. A variety of online platforms, interactive videos, and educational apps provide resources that are often more engaging than a standard lecture. Learners can choose the times that best fit their personal schedules, which is especially useful for those who work evenings or who need extra rest after a long day. This flexibility makes it easier to keep up with coursework without feeling pressured by a rigid timetable.  

Finally, distance learning can be a financially sensible choice. Students who work can earn money while they study, and they avoid expenses such as transportation, meals, or uniform costs. This means that families can allocate resources to other needs, and learners can focus on their education without the added financial pressure. In sum, the remote learning option offers a practical, safer, and more adaptable way for students to gain knowledge while managing their personal responsibilities.

Many individuals feel that theycannot manage the important choices in their lives without external help, while others argue that relying on experts is unnecessary. The debate asks whether people should decide for themselves or look to authorities for guidance on major matters. Some people claim that it is safer to let a knowledgeable person make all decisions, because then they would not have to worry about mistakes. Others maintain that it is unreasonable to hand over personal choices to strangers, since those people do not understand the individual's circumstances or preferences. This issue attracts strong opinions from both sides, but I firmly disagree with the idea of surrendering decision‑making. In my view, life is personal and each person must learn to handle its challenges. Even if my situation feels difficult, I prefer to take responsibility for my own choices. I may ask an older or more experienced friend for advice, but that is only a suggestion; no authority can legally or ethically take over my decisions. The ability to decide for oneself is essential, because only the individual truly knows what is best for his or her own path. Making your own choices also builds confidence and helps you grow as a person. Therefore, I believe that everyone should make their own decisions, regardless of how hard they may be.

Moststudents look forward to summer vacation, but some teachers argue that the break is excessively long and that, when school resumes in the fall, pupils become lazy and find it harder to retain what they learned. I disagree with that view for three main reasons.  

First, during the regular school year students are often occupied with heavy homework loads and frequent tests, leaving little time for part‑time jobs or other enriching activities. Summer provides roughly three months of free time, allowing young people to take on work, volunteer, or explore hobbies that they cannot fit into a busy academic schedule. Such experiences broaden their horizons, add valuable résumé entries, and can make future employment prospects stronger.  

Second, the school year is mentally exhausting. The constant pressure of assignments, quizzes, and exams can lead to stress and burnout. A prolonged break gives the brain a chance to relax and recover. During summer, students can travel to the beach, spend time with family, meet friends, or simply enjoy leisure activities without the constant reminder of upcoming coursework. This downtime helps reduce fatigue and prepares them for the next academic term.  

Third, the shorter breaks that occur in fall, winter, or spring are not truly restful. Teachers usually assign projects, reviews, or tests to be completed during or immediately after these short holidays, so students spend the limited time catching up rather than genuinely relaxing. In contrast, the long summer vacation offers uninterrupted time for rest, recreation, and personal growth, which is essential for maintaining motivation and mental well‑being.  

Some may argue that having more frequent breaks throughout the year would be beneficial, but those intervals are often followed by school‑related tasks that prevent true relaxation. Consequently, they do not give students the opportunity to recharge their minds.  

In conclusion, summer break is the only extended period that allows students to unwind, gain practical experience, and enjoy a variety of activities that are impossible during the school year. Therefore, the summer vacation should remain unchanged, as it is the best season for students to have fun, relax, and return to school refreshed.

Imaginethe school cafeteria suddenly offering a completely different menu. Most students would probably feel disappointed because the new dishes would replace the familiar, tasty meals they enjoy. The fact that these foods are appealing does not automatically mean they are nutritious. The United States, for instance, is known for widespread fast‑food consumption and a high rate of cholesterol‑related illnesses. Nowadays, modern technology makes it easy for people to stay sedentary: we drive everywhere instead of walking, we send texts instead of meeting face‑to‑face, we check the weather on our phones rather than stepping outside, and many of us prefer streaming services at home instead of going to the cinema. All of these habits contribute to a growing number of overweight individuals and related health problems such as heart attacks and high cholesterol. If nothing changes, the situation will only worsen in the coming years.  

One effective way to protect the health of future generations, especially the children attending our school, is to educate them about nutrition and to expose them to healthier food choices that can be just as enjoyable as fast food. For example, foods like avocado, fresh fruit juice, Caesar salad, and grilled fish are not only nutritious but also flavorful. By incorporating such options into the school menu, we can give students the chance to discover meals that are lower in fat and richer in essential nutrients. A menu that includes unfamiliar, wholesome dishes could replace some of the high‑calorie items currently offered, such as pizza or fried snacks.  

When students become accustomed to a broader variety of foods, they are less likely to limit themselves to burgers, fried chicken, or Chinese take‑out as they grow older. This early exposure helps build lifelong habits that support a balanced diet and reduce the risk of chronic disease. Therefore, I believe that the school cafeteria should adopt a healthier menu. Doing so aligns with our responsibility as members of the school community, and it promotes the well‑being of every student. We do not want to face future health issues caused by poor dietary choices. Thank you for your attention.

Imaginean old saying that honesty is the best policy. Suppose someone employed honesty in a harmful way—would you still agree or disagree? I agree, because honest actions can bring great benefit to others. The proverb teaches that truthfulness is the foundation of trust and can also foster new friendships. I support this view, yet I also recognize that misusing honesty can damage relationships and erode trust.  

When honesty is applied thoughtlessly, it may become destructive. I have observed a car accident where the driver who caused the crash avoided admitting fault; the court later ruled in his favor because he refused to be truthful. My father often reminds me that honesty plays a vital role in people’s lives. He recounts how his friends witnessed a robbery, and their truthful statements enabled the police to identify the perpetrator and secure a conviction. Even a small amount of honesty can make a difference.  

Nevertheless, honesty should never be used in a way that harms another person’s feelings. For example, during a team game the opposing side was dishonest, which upset several teammates. While truthfulness is valuable, it must be balanced with sensitivity.  

People’s attitudes toward honesty can change over time. I knew a friend who was habitually dishonest, but after many years he realized the importance of truth and became more open and sincere. Through my own candid behavior, I have formed new friendships and earned respect from others. When I am consistently honest, people tend to trust and admire me, and a positive atmosphere surrounds me, which helps build strong relationships.  

Conversely, when honesty is weaponized to hurt someone, the impact can be painful, like being struck by a train or feeling betrayed. I remember walking down my street and noticing many police cars outside a neighbor’s house. She had been robbed a few months earlier, and a truthful witness cooperated with the police, leading to the arrest of the thief. This illustrates how honesty can contribute to justice.  

In summary, honesty remains the most reliable policy. It guides us to act correctly, creates a constructive environment, and enhances our self‑esteem over the long term. Even future actions can be justified by the trust earned through honesty. Therefore, regardless of the situation, we should strive to be honest, because truthfulness benefits both the individual and the community.

Many diligent workers areconstantly searching for new jobs and a hopeful future. Most of them are responsible and confident that they can improve their work and make it better than before, yet they often fail to find a position because they lack experience and employers are reluctant to hire them for that reason. Some people argue that work experience is essential, but this view is mistaken. Numerous individuals have obtained jobs and achieved success without any prior experience; all they need is perseverance and belief.

For instance, my father struggled to find employment while my mother was ill and I was young. He had never worked in any field, yet he needed a job urgently to cover rent and my grandmother’s medical expenses. He kept trying, never gave up, and eventually became one of Morocco’s most renowned journalists, despite having no prior experience.

First, a person does not require prior experience to obtain a job. What matters is dedication, hard work, and honesty. By showing genuine commitment and treating colleagues with respect, an employee can raise the quality of his work and foster a respectful atmosphere. This principle applies not only to jobs but also to other pursuits such as acting, sports, or any activity one wishes to pursue. As Muhammad Ali once said, “Everyone starts as a beginner,” and the key is to demonstrate to employers that you deserve the position and can contribute positively.

Second, people without experience are often the most diligent and innovative. They frequently bring fresh ideas that elevate a workplace and maintain an optimistic outlook that supervisors appreciate more than that of seasoned staff.

Third, many employers refuse to give inexperienced candidates a chance, which is unfair. My French friend wanted to work as a teaching assistant for a French class in the United States, but schools rejected her because she lacked teaching experience, even though she is a native speaker and could teach the language more effectively. This illustrates the unfairness of demanding experience when it is irrelevant.

Finally, lacking experience should not hinder anyone. If you believe in yourself and keep working hard, you can obtain any job you desire. Employers who cling to the notion that experience is essential will eventually regret their decision when they see you excel at the top. In my view, what matters is the work you are prepared to do, not the work you have already done; those without experience often perform better than those who have it.

Winston Churchill once said that true success means moving from one setback to another while keeping enthusiasm alive. Some people think that failing will crush confidence and make them question their abilities, yet I believe that failure is a vital part of growth. This continuous cycle of trying, failing, and trying again shapes the determination needed for long‑term achievement. It pushes us forward, offers new strategies for reaching our aims, and builds a stronger character than before. Failure is constantly present, and we often view it as a negative outcome. In reality, it prepares us for more demanding challenges; without experiencing setbacks, how could we ever develop? Mistakes teach us lessons that success alone cannot convey, and they show that the path is not easy. By putting extra effort into what we value, the errors we make become stepping stones toward progress. When we encounter obstacles, they force us to consider alternative solutions. A failure reveals what does not work, giving us choices about future actions and helping us avoid repeating the same errors. For example, when I first began playing soccer, I only knew one way to strike the ball and missed the target many times. Instead of quitting, I experimented with different foot placements, learning to generate power or precision as needed. Each new technique I discovered not only improved my kicking ability but also taught me to adapt quickly to other situations. Those repeated attempts showed me that multiple techniques exist, not just a single method. Being knocked down by failure can also make us more resilient. Each time we rise after a defeat, we become a different, tougher individual who refuses to surrender over a simple mistake. That added confidence enables us to return stronger and avoid the same error in the future. Thomas Edison illustrated this when asked how he felt after failing a hundred times; he replied that he had not failed, but rather taken one hundred steps toward completing the light‑bulb invention. Therefore, embracing failure transforms obstacles into opportunities for personal development. In short, failure and the mistakes that accompany it are essential for learning, for discovering new ways to achieve goals, and for strengthening us beyond our previous limits. People should not fear failure; they ought to embrace it, because the satisfaction of reaching a goal feels far greater when it follows a series of persevering attempts.

In myview, allowing school pupils to study from home is not advisable. Many students would take advantage of the flexibility, preferring to stay in bed rather than rise early for a seven‑o’clock class. Some children simply lack the motivation to get up early, while others have enough discipline to attend school regularly. First, the risk of laziness is high. When learning takes place at home, a pupil may postpone the assignment, fall asleep, or simply procrastinate, completing the work much later. Although teachers and parents are available to offer assistance, the presence of a classroom ensures that help is more immediate and structured. Second, learning styles differ. Visual learners benefit from seeing a teacher’s explanations in real time, whereas some students concentrate better when they can work alone, and others thrive in a group setting with a partner. A school environment accommodates these varied preferences, while remote study often limits interaction. Third, access to resources is another concern. Not every student has reliable internet at home, which makes online lessons difficult or impossible. In a school, a wide range of materials—books, labs, libraries, and supportive staff—are readily available, giving every learner an equal chance to succeed. Finally, face‑to‑face contact reduces the likelihood of distraction. In a classroom, peers and teachers can monitor progress, keep students on task, and prevent them from goofing off. Although some pupils may manage online learning well, the overall evidence shows that in‑person schooling leads to more consistent effort and better outcomes. Therefore, while a few students might find online education useful, the majority would not benefit from working from home. Traditional school attendance remains the more effective option for most learners. Besides academic reasons, staying at home can affect a student’s social development. In school, children interact with classmates, learn teamwork, and develop communication skills that are essential for future workplaces. Remote learning limits these face‑to‑face experiences, which may lead to feelings of isolation and reduced confidence. Moreover, parents often have to take extra time to supervise home lessons, which can reduce the quality of support they can give at work or at home. This makes school the better choice.

First impressionsare extremely hard to change because when we meet a new person, the only data we have initially is their appearance, and we tend to stick with that initial view. As a result, people rarely manage to alter their first impression.

First, we often make rapid judgments based solely on looks. For instance, a student sees a classmate who does not appear physically fit and assumes the boy cannot take part in any sport, even though the student later watches him play and discovers he is actually the team’s best performer. The visual cue remains powerful, so the original belief stays intact despite contrary evidence.

Second, individuals tend to preserve their first impression because it reflects their personal opinion and they want to keep it in mind. Consider a man who is very quiet and gives the impression that he does not wish to speak with anyone; others therefore avoid him. Later, he shows a different side with his friends and reveals that he enjoys conversation, yet the early judgment continues to shape how people interact with him.

Nevertheless, there are situations in which a first impression can be revised. For example, a man who looks large and has a stern expression may be avoided by strangers, but a student who strikes up a conversation discovers that he is actually very pleasant. Likewise, a person who once behaved badly toward friends can change how they are seen by consistently showing kindness and helpfulness; the friends then update their view, leading to a more positive and lasting friendship.

Even with these occasional successes, the overall difficulty of changing first impressions remains. The initial visual or behavioral cue creates a strong mental shortcut that is not easily overwritten. Consequently, it is wise not to place too much emphasis on first impressions, as they are often resistant to change. Therefore, while it is possible to alter an early perception with effort, the process is usually slow and requires sustained interaction, so people should be cautious about forming judgments too quickly. In everyday life, taking the time to learn more about someone can prevent misunderstandings and foster better relationships.

Ralph WaldoEmerson once said that being true to yourself in a world that constantly pressures you to become someone else is the highest achievement. I agree with this view; maintaining your own identity rather than letting others reshape you is a remarkable accomplishment.  

First, many people try to convince you to follow paths that do not suit your interests. They may offer advice that seems logical but often leads you away from what you truly desire. Therefore, it is essential to reflect on your own goals and trust your inner preferences instead of blindly accepting external suggestions. When you rely on yourself, you avoid the common pitfall of receiving inaccurate guidance.  

Second, believing in your own abilities gives you confidence to pursue what you value. If you are convinced that you can achieve great things by staying true to your passions, you are more likely to act decisively and persist despite obstacles. This self‑assurance is a key component of personal success.  

Nevertheless, some argue that allowing others to influence you can also be a form of achievement, especially when the change brings positive outcomes. For instance, a person who repeatedly makes poor choices—such as breaking laws or causing trouble—may benefit from constructive feedback that steers them toward better behavior. In similar vein, offering thoughtful counsel to someone struggling can help them improve their situation. These examples show that transformation can be beneficial, but only when it genuinely serves the individual’s well‑being.  

Overall, the central message remains that staying authentic and knowing what you want to do is the most rewarding accomplishment. While external input can be helpful in certain contexts, the greatest success comes from trusting your own judgment and refusing to let others dictate the direction of your life. In addition, when you stay true to yourself, you develop a stronger sense of purpose that guides your decisions and gives meaning to your actions. This inner clarity helps you remain steady even when circumstances change or when others voice criticism.

First impressions are oftenthought to be fixed, but I disagree with that view because people are constantly changing and a single impression does not capture a person’s true nature. For instance, I once met a man who, at our first encounter, appeared angry, never smiled, and seemed very shy. As days passed, his demeanor softened; he began to smile and his irritability faded. My view of him shifted completely, showing that the original picture was only a temporary snapshot.  

A similar situation can be seen with a teacher. In the opening weeks of school, the instructor may be kind, assign little homework, and be patient. Yet, over time his attitude may alter: he becomes strict, gives heavy assignments, and raises his voice. Consequently, the impression formed at the start no longer reflects his current behavior, and the initial impression is proven wrong.  

The idea that a first impression defines a person is comparable to judging a book by its cover. The cover offers little insight into the story inside. Likewise, people may present a certain face initially, but their inner character can differ markedly. My own experience illustrates this point. Friends once told me that when they first met me they disliked me because I seemed angry and silent, speaking only to them. However, after spending time together they realized I was different from their first impression, and they eventually became my friends.  

Sometimes a poor first impression arises simply because the person is having a bad day. Suppose you meet someone while they are stressed and irritable; they may seem unfriendly. If the other person takes the opportunity to get to know you better, the negative impression can be revised. The key factor is the amount of time and interaction needed to form a more accurate picture. Generally, more than two encounters are required before a reliable judgment can be made, since a single impression is too limited.  

In conclusion, first impressions are not immutable; they can evolve as people change and as we learn more about them. Therefore, a single impression should not be taken as the definitive description of who someone is.
