People hold various views on community service. In my opinion, it is a valuable activity that can benefit the community. However, it should not be compulsory; participation must remain a personal choice. Some individuals argue that mandatory service feels like a penalty and therefore oppose it. They believe that forcing people to help undermines the spirit of volunteerism. On the other hand, those who are willing to contribute see great advantages for society and for themselves. Community service can also teach responsibility and teamwork, skills that are useful in later life. Allowing individuals to decide whether to take part respects their freedom and encourages genuine commitment. Consequently, the most sensible approach is to make community service optional, so that those who genuinely wish to assist can do so, while others are free to decline without penalty. This ensures fairness for everyone.

Working together with a groupof people is, in my opinion, far more beneficial. The task moves forward more quickly because the workload is divided, and the atmosphere feels more pleasant and less stressful. When we collaborate, we can support each other and also make new friends, which makes the whole experience more enjoyable. In contrast, working alone often leads to boredom and a slower pace; there is no one to discuss ideas with, so time seems to drag and motivation wanes. For example, in a group of four, each member can take charge of a specific part of the project and present it. If someone forgets a detail, another teammate can fill in the gap, ensuring the work stays on track. If I were to prepare a presentation by myself, I would have to read everything, explain all points, and handle any confusion without assistance, which is far more demanding. With a group, we can exchange ideas, refine our approach, and finish the project faster. Besides speed, working in a team helps us learn from each other's strengths, builds confidence, and creates a supportive environment that keeps us motivated throughout the project. Overall, the collaborative approach not only saves time but also enriches the learning experience for everyone involved. Therefore, I believe that collaborating in a team is the better option.

Many people think that praising a student’s work, even when it is not the best they can do, helps raise their self‑esteem. I agree; a confident learner is more likely to develop and succeed. When a student doubts his or her abilities, the chance of competing in later life diminishes, and a negative mindset can hold them back. Confidence therefore creates a foundation for continuous improvement. When students receive encouragement, they feel valued and are more motivated to engage in class activities, which further reinforces their learning.  

A student who believes in his or her own potential is more willing to try new challenges. This belief removes self‑imposed limits; with effort and practice the learner can expand their skills beyond what they imagined. If confidence is missing, the student may stay static, and self‑esteem may decline. By fostering a positive attitude, teachers and parents encourage students to keep moving forward and to view setbacks as opportunities for a second try. There are no inherent limits to what a student can achieve when they believe in themselves and work hard. These goals give direction and a sense of purpose, helping the student stay focused despite obstacles.  

Setting clear goals is another way to strengthen self‑esteem. When a learner writes down what they want to achieve, they can see concrete evidence of their abilities and decide which objective to pursue first. Support from friends or family, together with a strong personal desire to succeed, adds motivation. Even if the first attempt is not perfect, the student should understand that improvement is possible and that persistence is essential.  

In short, praising effort and celebrating progress, regardless of the initial quality of the work, gives students the confidence they need to grow. Believing in one’s capabilities, establishing realistic goals, and maintaining a resilient mindset are key to a successful life. Therefore, encouraging self‑esteem through praise is a valuable practice for any learner. Overall, the habit of acknowledging effort builds a stronger self‑image and prepares learners for future challenges. Such encouragement helps students develop confidence that lasts beyond the classroom.

Many people believe thata student should decide on a future career as soon as they begin high school. Although some claim that there is no need to make a decision until later, I think that choosing a profession early, particularly while still in secondary school, brings clear benefits.  

First, committing to a career at a young age helps students develop a sense of responsibility for their future. When a student knows what they want to study, they can focus their efforts, set goals, and prepare the necessary background. For example, a student who decides on medicine during high school can take relevant courses and gain experience, which improves their chances of being ready for university and later success in the field.  

Second, making a career choice while in high school provides more time to explore different options and, if needed, to change direction without wasting time or money. A student who discovers that a chosen path is unsuitable can switch to another field before entering university, avoiding the financial loss that comes from studying a discipline they later dislike. This flexibility also allows them to acquire broader knowledge and skills that are valuable regardless of the final profession.  

In conclusion, expecting students to identify a career by the time they enter high school is reasonable, and doing so during the high‑school years enhances preparation for university and offers the freedom to adjust one’s path without compromising time or resources.

Learning from home is not a good idea. First, attending a physical school provides more possibilities for study. In a classroom we can ask the teacher for clarification and receive explanations repeatedly if a concept is unclear. Moreover, being present allows us to interact with classmates, which enriches the learning experience and makes it easier to stay motivated. 

Sometimes circumstances such as illness or other obligations force a student to study online, and in those cases distance education can be useful. It offers flexibility in scheduling and can help a learner maintain focus because they can study at any hour that suits them. However, the lack of direct contact with the instructor means that questions cannot be answered instantly, and the student must rely on recorded material or delayed responses. 

Another drawback of remote learning is that it limits the number of courses a student can take. In a school we can enroll in several subjects and progress together with peers, which often leads to a higher chance of graduation. While video‑conferencing attempts to recreate the classroom atmosphere, it still falls short of face‑to‑face instruction. 

In my view, attending school is more important than distance learning because it provides greater opportunities to acquire knowledge, receive immediate help, and engage with others. Therefore, I believe that regular school attendance is essential for achieving our academic goals.

People who regard self‑reliance as a core value believe that each person should follow his or her own judgment when dealing with important life decisions, rather than depending on the advice of experts or authorities. They argue that personal responsibility goes hand in hand with caring for what one owns. For example, someone who spends a lot of money on a pair of high‑priced sneakers will be upset if the shoes become dirty or damaged, because the purchase represents a significant personal investment. In their view, the best way to protect such items is to match the cost of the goods with the type of work one does: if a person expects to work in muddy or rough conditions, it makes sense to choose less expensive, more durable footwear instead of risking a costly pair.

The essay also stresses that earning money oneself helps people understand the true worth of the things they acquire. When teenagers start working, they learn how much effort is needed to buy the items they desire, which reduces the tendency to constantly request expensive goods from parents. This practical experience, they claim, fosters a sense of appreciation and encourages careful handling of possessions.

Another point is the personal meaning attached to gifts. When a young person buys a pair of AirPods for a friend, the act of using his own earnings gives the gift additional value. The recipient feels appreciated, and the giver gains a sense of responsibility and pride. Such exchanges illustrate how self‑generated resources can strengthen relationships and reinforce the idea that one’s own effort carries weight.

Overall, the writer maintains that self‑reliance—defined by earning, protecting, and making decisions about one’s own belongings—should be preferred to seeking guidance from external experts. By taking charge of one’s own choices and resources, individuals develop a deeper respect for what they have and become more capable of handling life’s challenges independently.

Many pupils believethat a lengthy summer vacation is beneficial because it gives them time to be with friends. In my view, schools should operate throughout the year, offering a short three‑ to four‑week summer recess, an extended winter holiday, and a one‑week break in both spring and autumn. This schedule would prevent the monotony that comes from continuous study and give students regular moments to recover. Regular breaks also give teachers time to plan lessons more effectively and to provide additional support to students who need it. Some argue that a long break lets children travel abroad to see relatives in their home countries. While visiting family can be valuable, a short summer interval is sufficient for such trips, and the rest of the year can still provide ample time for personal activities. Without periodic pauses, learners tend to feel increasingly stressed as they repeat the same tasks day after day. A year‑round system would distribute the workload more evenly, reducing the mental load on students. Moreover, after a prolonged vacation pupils often return to school unmotivated and lethargic; shorter, more frequent breaks keep them more engaged and ready to learn. These periodic intervals help maintain a balanced lifestyle, allowing young people to pursue hobbies, sports, or community service without overwhelming their studies. These varied breaks also give families the chance to spend quality time together, reinforcing social bonds that support academic motivation. Students benefit from this balanced approach. In addition, a continuous calendar allows students to experience a variety of activities during the year rather than concentrating all leisure time into one extended period. The proposed schedule therefore promotes better well‑being, reduces fatigue, and supports sustained academic performance. Consequently, adopting a year‑round school model with modest summer holidays, a longer winter break, and brief spring and fall interludes is a sensible approach.

Many schools have considered using mobile phones as teaching aids, but I believe they should be prohibited inside the classroom. Students are already glued to their devices all day, and allowing phones during lessons only worsens their lack of focus. When a phone is in hand, attention shifts from the teacher to the screen, which means that learning suffers.

For instance, a pupil might search for information that could be useful, yet the same device is quickly used to send messages, play games, stream videos, or listen to music. These activities split concentration and make it difficult to retain what is being taught. Moreover, phones are often employed to capture photos or record videos for social‑media sharing, and some students even use them to harass classmates. Such behavior not only distracts the owner but also disturbs the whole class.

Some argue that phones can help with homework, research, or clarifying doubts, but the temptation to browse unrelated apps usually wins. A student who is supposed to work on an assignment may end up texting or video‑chatting, causing unfinished tasks and lower grades—sometimes even a zero. The constant interruption prevents students from fully engaging with the material, which defeats the purpose of education.

Research shows that students who keep phones nearby score lower on exams because they are constantly interrupted by notifications. Teachers report spending extra time trying to regain order, which reduces instructional time. Moreover, the presence of phones encourages cheating, as students can quickly look up answers or share answers with peers. All these factors undermine the learning atmosphere that schools aim to create. Consequently, banning phones helps maintain a focused environment where education can truly take place for every student alike. In short, while some claim that mobile phones are versatile tools, the reality is that they become major sources of distraction, misuse, and academic decline. Therefore, schools should ban cell phones from classrooms to ensure that students can concentrate on learning and achieve better results.

Trying something new that you have never done before can be scary for humans, no matter your age or how brave you are. If you have faced many difficulties doing it, you will likely be scared to do it again, even if you already know how to do it. For example, I have worked at a Japanese restaurant for about one and a half years, and it was my first time serving. I was scared, and the reason I decided to do it was the money. I was surprised when I succeeded; my boss told me I was doing a really good job, and I felt proud, even though my English wasn't perfect. Later, I had problems with him about money, which created too many issues, so I decided to get another job. My friend told me her boss was looking for new servers, so I applied. The problem was that the restaurant was much larger than the others, and the menu seemed very different, and I kept thinking, "You will fail." I felt terrible that day, and the progress was long and painful because of the many mistakes I made. However, I tried again, and now I think that what I went through wasn't that difficult. I'm not a master, but I'm still learning.

Many people are conformist and don't want to learn more, and unfortunately I include myself in that group. I often fail because I think I already know everything, even more than others. For example, one day I took a Spanish test and felt confident because Spanish is my first language, while most of my classmates were studying for it. I failed because the questions were ones I had never imagined, and getting a credit was very important. That day taught me that even if you know many things, it's always good to learn more.

In conclusion, you must be better every day and remember that there is always more to learn, even if you already know the material. Trying something new shouldn't scare you, because every human can learn and achieve what they want; the only obstacle is the one you put in front of yourself.

Is it not obvious thatwe should constantly strive to improve ourselves? I completely agree that without seeking new knowledge we cannot achieve lasting success. When we stop learning, we limit our potential and end up wasting time.  

Continuous learning not only expands our skill set but also keeps our mind active and adaptable. In a world that changes rapidly, the ability to acquire new information and adjust our behavior is crucial for personal and professional fulfillment. When we ignore this need, we risk becoming stagnant and miss out on opportunities that could enhance our lives.  

Working as a server in that restaurant was a steep learning curve. At first I struggled with the fast pace, taking orders correctly and handling tables with confidence. My nervousness turned into determination as I practiced taking notes, greeting guests politely, and remembering regular customers' preferences. Each mistake, whether a wrong drink order or a miscommunication with the kitchen, taught me to stay focused and ask for clarification when needed. Over time, my confidence grew, and I began to enjoy the interaction with people from diverse backgrounds. This experience showed me that perseverance and a willingness to learn from errors are essential for any new role.  

Later, when I sat for a Spanish exam, I entered the room confident that my native language would give me an advantage. The test, however, contained vocabulary and structures that I had never studied, such as idiomatic expressions and nuanced grammar points. My lack of preparation became evident when I could not answer several questions, and I received a lower grade than expected. This moment reinforced the idea that even when we think we have mastered a subject, there is always more depth to explore, and continual learning is essential. That experience taught me that confidence alone is insufficient; continual curiosity and practice are necessary to stay competent in any field.  

Beyond the specific examples I have shared, I have noticed that the habit of seeking new challenges shapes my overall outlook. Each time I step outside my comfort zone, I discover hidden strengths and develop a more resilient mindset. This growth does not happen instantly; it requires patience, self‑reflection, and the willingness to accept failure as a stepping stone. When I view obstacles as opportunities to learn, I become less afraid of the unknown and more motivated to pursue goals that once seemed impossible. In this way, the simple act of trying something new becomes a catalyst for continuous personal development.  

The patience I cultivated while learning to serve quickly in a busy restaurant taught me that steady effort, even when progress seems slow, eventually leads to mastery and satisfaction. This lesson reminds me that growth is a lifelong journey.  

In short, we must commit to daily improvement, embracing new tasks regardless of age or perceived bravery. The only real barrier is the one we create inside ourselves. By confronting fear and seeking extra knowledge, we open doors to more opportunities and personal growth.  

Therefore, embracing change and committing to lifelong learning are the keys to a truly fulfilling life.

Many students study from homebecause they live far away or lack transportation, and they may use video or online lessons. However, I believe that learning online is not advantageous; attending a physical school is preferable. In a classroom the teacher can see whether each student understands and can give immediate feedback, whereas at home the learner often becomes distracted by household noises and cannot focus on the lesson. Consequently, the teacher’s instruction is less effective and the student’s comprehension suffers.

Some learners live in remote areas and must travel long distances or use buses and trains to reach school, yet they still attend because they want to prepare for their future. Others, such as working immigrants, may have jobs that prevent them from going to school during the day, so they enroll in online courses to learn English or acquire new skills. While these circumstances make online study necessary for some, it does not replace the benefits of in‑person education. The classroom environment forces students to pay attention, reduces distractions, and allows teachers to monitor progress closely, which leads to better learning outcomes. When students have clear goals and are motivated, they are more likely to succeed, and a school setting provides the structure and support needed to maintain that motivation. Without such support, a learner at home may lose interest and abandon their studies.

It is true that not everyone has the same opportunities; some families cannot afford transportation or must balance work and study. Nevertheless, the core message remains that school provides a more reliable and effective setting for education than a home‑based online class. Moreover, classroom interactions with peers create a collaborative atmosphere that enriches learning, something that cannot be fully replicated through a screen. If a student truly wishes to achieve their goals, they should seek the structured environment that a school offers, rather than relying solely on remote lessons.

Never staying idle is a principle Thomas Jefferson expressed when he said that great things happen when we keep moving. I fully agree with his view. Many people claim they can accomplish nothing, yet the real reason is that they never make an effort; they prefer to remain inactive. When we stay constantly occupied, we achieve far more. For instance, if you work on a report, finish it, and then immediately begin another task, you keep building progress instead of stopping and thinking you can now relax for the rest of your life. Continuous work brings its own reward; you are not doing it for no purpose. Jefferson himself never rested, producing a large amount of work throughout his life, which shows that staying busy is essential. His main message is to encourage people to stay active all the time, because constant activity drives change in the world.

First impressions matter a lotbecause they are difficult to alter. For instance, if you see a dish that looks unappetizing, you are unlikely to eat it, even if it might taste good. Likewise, when someone gives a negative impression, you may avoid talking to that person. When you go shopping, you often read reviews before deciding where to go.

This quick judgment helps us save time, but it can also lead to mistakes when the appearance does not reflect the reality.

First, consider a restaurant visit. You expect a tasty meal. If you wait fifteen minutes and the dish arrives looking strange, you become disappointed and think the food is bad, even before tasting it. If the food looks appealing on your plate, you are more willing to try it regardless of any doubts.

Second, a parent may introduce a friend who talks nonstop. Because you prefer quiet, you may feel uncomfortable and develop a dislike for that person. The initial impression can lead you to avoid the individual altogether.

Third, imagine going to a new shopping area with a friend. You use your phone to locate a store. You notice the items look attractive, but the reviews are mostly negative, with only a few positive comments. In that case you are likely to choose another shop, believing the quality is poor.

In conclusion, first impressions are powerful and persistent. Once formed, they stay in your mind and influence your judgments, making it hard to change them later. Because of this, people often need repeated positive encounters to reshape their first impression.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once said that the greatest achievement is to be yourself in a world that constantly tries to turn you into someone else. I disagree with this view. In reality many people do not succeed in being authentic; instead they spend their lives trying to become what others expect, and this prevents them from reaching their own goals.

First, people often lack clear personal objectives. When they do have a aim, the surrounding culture pressures them to pursue a different path, so they end up chasing their own goals. Without a genuine purpose, they feel lost and may adopt a false identity simply to fit in.

Second, people often lack clear personal objectives. When they do have a aim, the surrounding culture pressures them to pursue a different path, so they end up chasing their own goals. Without a genuine purpose, they feel lost and may adopt a false identity simply to fit in.

As a result, they live a double life, presenting a façade to the world while their inner desires remain unexpressed. This constant disguise makes them dissatisfied, even though they appear to belong.

Finally, the notion that being yourself is the highest accomplishment ignores the difficulty of maintaining authenticity in a society that rewards conformity. People are not naturally inclined to be themselves; they must consciously resist the powerful urge to blend in. Overall, the website allows students to visit each year before the school year begins, making it easy to share opinions and change the menu in public or private schools. Every school, whether private orpublic, should introduce a simple online platform that lets students choose their meals. By giving pupils the chance to vote for dishes, suggest alternatives, and mark any allergies, the system creates a direct line between the canteen and the learners. When the menu is updated each academic year based on this feedback, students receive a more appealing and balanced diet, which in turn supports concentration, energy levels, and overall wellbeing.

At present many schools serve the same few items day after day. The repetition makes the food look boring, and a large share of pupils prefer to bring meals from home or skip lunch altogether. This habit reduces the intake of essential nutrients and can lower the stamina needed for classroom work. Moreover, the queues at the serving counter are often long, discouraging students from taking the time to eat properly. Consequently, they may feel tired, lose focus, and experience poorer academic results.

A web‑based menu system can solve these problems. First, it allows the school to collect real‑time opinions from the entire student body. Teachers and nutritionists can see which dishes are popular, which are rejected, and where allergies are common. Second, the platform can propose a rotating selection of options each semester. For example, a morning snack of fresh fruit or a light yoghurt, followed by lunch choices such as tacos, grilled chicken, vegetarian wraps, or a modest serving of fast‑food items like chicken nuggets. Such variety keeps the menu interesting and encourages students to try new foods, which expands their dietary range.

Third, the ability to modify the menu annually based on student input promotes healthier eating habits. When learners see that their preferences influence the offerings, they are more likely to select nutritious options and to eat the meals provided on site rather than relying on less healthy alternatives from home. Adequate nutrition supplies the glucose needed for brain function, so a more varied diet helps students stay mentally sharp and physically active throughout the day.

Finally, the implementation of this system benefits teachers as well. Classes run more smoothly when pupils are well‑fed and attentive, and the reduced need for students to leave the premises for food eliminates a source of distraction. In addition, the website can provide information about water intake and the importance of fresh fruit, reinforcing a culture of health that extends beyond the cafeteria.

In conclusion, creating an online portal for menu selection and yearly revision is a practical and effective way for schools to improve the quality of student meals. By listening to pupils, offering diverse and balanced food choices, and ensuring quick, hygienic service, schools can boost concentration, energy, and overall happiness. The result is a healthier, more engaged student community and a more positive learning environment for everyone.

Because working with a group offers more ideas about projects and allows for collaborative effort without distraction, with all members contributing to the project's ideas, tasks, and discussions, as well as the teacher's guidance. This collaborative effort ensures everyone participates in creating the best possible work, leading to improved grades. However, not all students consistently contribute, which can affect the group's overall grade, but this situation also provides an opportunity to improve scores. Sometimes, students working alone struggle to maintain focus and may not choose the best ideas, whereas group work allows for shared decision-making, where students can agree on the best approach. Some students prefer working with others, while others prefer working independently. When students work together, they can express their ideas to create the best possible work, and many students achieve good or poor grades when working alone, often due to lack of focus or distraction from phones or other distractions. Group work allows students to discuss class material, the type of project, and the teacher's guidance, leading to improved grades and a more positive learning experience. However, group work requires students to express their ideas, support each other, and ensure everyone participates, as one student's lack of effort can negatively impact the group's grade. This situation also provides an opportunity to improve grades and learn more about the teacher's expectations throughout the class.

In myopinion, working in a group offers more advantages than working alone. When we collaborate, we gather many ideas for a project, which makes the task easier and more interesting. Each member can contribute, discuss the assignment, decide on the type of work, and follow the teacher’s instructions together. This shared effort helps us produce a higher‑quality product and often leads to a better grade for the whole team.  

Even though some students may not always participate fully, the group setting gives everyone a chance to speak up and share thoughts. If one person has a strong idea, the others can support it or suggest improvements, resulting in a more balanced final product. Moreover, group work reduces the likelihood of distraction; classmates keep each other focused and can remind one another of the teacher’s directions.  

Students who work alone sometimes struggle to keep the best idea to themselves, and they may feel uncertain about how to proceed. In contrast, a group allows members to test different approaches, vote on the most suitable one, and collectively decide who will write the title or present the work. This collaborative decision‑making process makes the task less stressful and more enjoyable.  

Additionally, group work promotes learning of communication skills that are useful beyond the classroom. By explaining concepts, listening to peers, and negotiating roles, students develop confidence in expressing themselves and in cooperating toward a common goal. Even if a few members do not contribute perfectly, the overall effort is usually higher, and the teacher’s feedback can be applied more effectively when the whole team reviews the work together.  

Therefore, I firmly believe that group work is more beneficial than working alone. It brings diverse ideas, shared responsibility, better academic outcomes, and valuable social skills, all of which contribute to a more successful learning experience.

In my view, the first impressionmatters a lot because it is difficult to alter later. When people meet us briefly, they form an opinion that often stays with them. Many individuals try to appear more appealing than they really are, hoping to be liked, but eventually their true nature shows and the initial goodwill fades.

I think that being open about who we are helps others accept us for who we truly are and builds trust. My approach is to be honest with myself and with others; I never pretend to be someone I am not. I try to present myself as friendly, warm, humorous and charismatic to everyone I meet, and I also offer help using my knowledge and abilities.

At my workplace, new staff arrive daily. I take the time to show them how the store should look and I greet customers with a smile, which creates a positive first impression. When they see me smiling, they often say hello and tell me about their day, which makes me feel good. Although they may not know me well yet, they begin to trust me and share personal details. Among my colleagues we get along like a family, supporting each other.

In school the situation is different. I tend to be shy and only speak with my closest friends, but I still express my feelings to new classmates. Sometimes they act friendly at first, yet their attitude changes over time. For example, a girl I met in ninth grade seemed close at first, but later she and her sister spread rumors about me and my sister. I remained honest and friendly, but she behaved differently afterward. Another girl, jealous of my sister’s and my good grades and activity, tried to get our help but refused, so we gradually distanced ourselves because, although she was polite, she was not a reliable friend.

I believe we should always stay true to ourselves, regardless of what others think. Change can be beneficial, but it must not alter our core identity. I regularly reflect on my weaknesses and look for ways to improve them positively.

Finally, a strong first impression can open many doors in life. People who show a positive attitude when we first meet them are often the ones we can rely on, and feeling that trust makes us happy. Even if others judge me only by my appearance, I try to empathize with everyone and make an effort to connect, hoping that genuine effort will lead to lasting friendships.

The manual discusseswhether students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home. I believe they would, because online learning offers flexibility that fits many learners’ lives.  

First, students who work or help support their families can study without losing income. For example, a person who has a job to aid his or her household can attend lessons after work or early in the morning, something that would be difficult with a fixed school schedule.  

Second, many learners live far from their schools, so traveling each day takes a long time and costs money. If teachers could deliver lessons from home, students would not need to walk long distances or spend on transport. This is especially true for those who lack the financial resources to pay for travel.  

Third, some students cannot attend school regularly because of health issues, lack of transportation, or other responsibilities. Online classes let them continue their studies without missing essential content. In my community, a few classmates only come to school a few days a week because they need to work; they say they would learn more if they could study from home.  

Finally, online education can be combined with other activities. A learner who works during the day or cares for family members can still complete coursework in the evening or at night, making it possible to finish high school or earn additional qualifications.  

In conclusion, giving students the option to attend classes from home would help those with work commitments, financial constraints, long commutes, or other obligations. It provides a more inclusive and adaptable way to achieve academic goals.

The school board wants to lengthen each school day by one and a half hours. In my view, this is a poor idea. Adding that much time would put extra pressure on students, push back after‑school programs, and raise the district’s electricity bill, all of which would harm the learning environment. Teachers might think more class time helps, but the negative effects on students and the budget are too great.

First, the longer schedule would create a great deal of stress for pupils. After a full day of lessons many students feel exhausted, lose motivation to study, and may even develop symptoms of depression. The extra workload leaves little time for homework, causing some to skip assignments altogether, and the overall interest in school declines. Lack of sleep and constant fatigue can also affect their mental health and overall well‑being.

Second, extending the day would push back all after‑school activities. Students who rely on transportation, especially those living in remote areas, would have to wake up very early and might not be able to return home before evening, making it hard to finish homework. The delayed schedule could also reduce participation in clubs and limit opportunities for extracurricular development.

Finally, the extra hours would dramatically increase electricity expenses. The district currently spends more than six million dollars each year on power; adding another one and a half hours daily would raise that amount, leaving fewer resources for school upgrades, staff development, or facility maintenance. A larger utility bill could force the board to cut back on materials, technology, or extracurricular programs, which would lower the quality of education.

For these reasons, the school board should keep the regular day length and look for other ways to improve learning without lengthening the schedule.

By preventing obesity, the cafeteria will help us take care of our bodies and achieve a healthier, more active lifestyle. Therefore, supporting this plan will benefit the whole school community and improve overall well‑being.

In my opinion, doctorsshould be permitted to work fewer hours in the hospital so that they can rest and deliver better care. A reasonable schedule – for instance, a limit of seven to eight hours per day – would allow them to conserve energy and maintain a proper diet during their shift. In addition, a four‑day work week would give physicians extra time to prepare lessons, study, and attend to personal responsibilities such as family life. When doctors have adequate leisure, they are more capable of handling emergencies and providing high‑quality treatment to patients. The reduced workload also results in higher salaries and more career opportunities, because a rested professional can work more efficiently and avoid burnout. Consequently, shortening hospital hours and introducing a shorter week benefit both the doctors, who need rest and dedication, and the patients who depend on their expertise. Being a doctor requires great responsibility and constant learning; therefore, adequate rest is essential for maintaining the knowledge needed for medical practice. Moreover, students who observe a balanced schedule can see the value of work‑life balance, which may inspire them to pursue healthier careers.

In my view, technology isbeneficial. It lets us accomplish many tasks that would otherwise be time‑consuming. For instance, instead of driving to a store, we can order groceries online and have them delivered to our door, which is especially convenient when someone is ill or short on time. The ability to work remotely is another advantage; a laptop lets a person who normally works in an office perform his or her duties from home. Online services also simplify transportation. By downloading a ride‑sharing app such as Uber, a person without a car can request a ride to any destination. Shopping for clothing is likewise easier because we can browse items on the internet, compare prices, and purchase without leaving home. Even reading and borrowing books no longer require a trip to a physical store, since e‑books can be accessed instantly. Video communication provides another benefit. My grandmother lives in a different city, and we can speak with her face‑to‑face through a video call, keeping our family connected despite the distance. Air travel has become smoother as well; my sister checks us in online before we arrive at the airport, which saves us from long queues and guarantees our seats. These conveniences show how technology improves everyday life. However, there are some drawbacks. When people rely on deliveries and avoid going out, they may become less active and miss out on physical exercise. Moreover, excessive use of phones and texting can reduce face‑to‑face interaction; I have noticed that relatives often sit together at holidays but spend most of their time on their devices rather than talking. Overall, the positive contributions of technology outweigh the negatives. From online shopping and remote work to digital payments and virtual contact, modern tools make many aspects of life more convenient and efficient.

I completelyagree that a person cannot develop unless they step beyond what they already master. Some claim that growth can happen automatically over time, but that view is mistaken. As Emerson observed, true progress requires believing in yourself and daring to try something new; only then can you reach your aspirations and feel yourself growing.  

From my own experience I am constantly pushing myself, working hard, and encouraging my peers to do the same. We all want a better world, and we believe that personal development is the way to achieve it. If we remain closed‑minded, we will never improve, no matter what circumstances surround us.  

To grow, we must be organized, stay true to ourselves, and reject the pressure to conform to others’ expectations. The crucial moment comes when we face a choice: keep staying where we are, or actively seek growth. Choosing growth opens many doors for us and can also benefit those around us.  

The advantages of developing oneself are clear. A person who continually learns can handle a wide range of tasks, become more confident, and build stronger social connections. Emerson’s statement reminds us to value his insight: we should venture beyond our comfort zone, try new things, and trust that effort will bring success.  

I have noticed that when I set clear goals and keep a schedule, my progress becomes measurable and motivating. This habit shows that discipline and self‑reflection are essential parts of growth, and they help us stay focused even when challenges arise. Therefore, the decision to grow is personal, but its rewards extend to family, friends, and the wider community.  

In short, growth does not happen by waiting; it requires deliberate effort, self‑belief, and the courage to step outside familiar limits. When we do so, we not only improve our own lives but also create a positive impact on the people around us.

Meetingnew people can be done in many ways, both on the internet and in real life. While some may feel uncomfortable talking to strangers in a shop, library, or while doing outdoor activities, there are plenty of opportunities to connect with others. Some individuals are more open to making friends by speaking to anyone, while others keep to themselves because they find it hard to start a conversation with someone they do not know. If you want to meet a person you have never spoken to before, it is helpful to look at them first, show a friendly attitude, and be polite. Before you speak, think about what you might say and try to form a clear idea of yourself.

I enjoy making friends whenever possible, and I believe that being kind and approachable makes it easier for others to accept me as a friend. There are many situations where friendships can develop: working together in a group, attending a class, joining a club, or even meeting someone while walking a dog. In a classroom, for example, you can meet new classmates, and outside of class you may encounter people during extracurricular activities. Some people become withdrawn and avoid talking to anyone because they think it is unnecessary, but this limits their social life. A balanced approach—doing activities you enjoy while staying open to conversation—offers the best chance to build a wide circle of friends. Having many friends brings positive experiences, whereas isolation can lead to loneliness; even a pet can provide companionship, but human interaction remains valuable.

In everyday places such as a store or a park, a brief chat with a shop assistant or a fellow parent can turn into a friendly exchange. Likewise, when I go to school I meet new people both inside and outside the classroom. Positive people tend to be easygoing and kind, while those who are irritable may react quickly to conflict. Overall, being friendly, willing to talk, and participating in group activities are effective ways to meet new people and form lasting relationships.

Many people claim that first impressions are permanent, yet I believe they can be altered. To begin with, someone may appear indifferent or uncaring at first glance, but as you interact more, your view of them often shifts. Secondly, I experienced a situation where my initial view of a person was completely opposite to reality: I once thought a woman was kind and suitable for a lifelong relationship, but after getting to know her I discovered she was cruel and filled with resentment, constantly blaming me for things that were not my fault, which gradually eroded my affection. Moreover, people’s behavior can evolve as they gain new experiences, and this transformation can completely change how we perceive them. In short, first impressions are not immutable; even family members or close relatives can change, showing that these initial judgments can be revised. Therefore, it is possible to move beyond the first impression and develop a more accurate understanding of a person.

Staying active all the time is essential for good health. People who move regularly are less prone to illness because they have more energy. In daily life most of us have tasks to accomplish, whether at work or elsewhere, and many choose to keep their bodies moving throughout the day. When the body is constantly active, the muscles become accustomed to the effort, and after finishing the day a period of rest is all that is needed. An active body tends to be healthier and less likely to develop sickness, which is especially important for those who are used to staying busy; if they become ill, recovery can be more difficult. Adequate vitamins and nutrients are also required to support continuous activity. A well‑fed body can sustain the effort, while a weak one may struggle and even become dangerous. Therefore, any plan that keeps us moving should be carried out with care and moderation. It is not necessary to push the body beyond its limits; knowing when to stop is just as important as the activity itself. Being constantly on the move does not mean staying in one spot; many people remain seated for long periods, so incorporating regular movement is beneficial for both mind and body. Physical activity helps clear the mind, improves circulation, and contributes to overall well‑being. While it is wonderful to pursue our goals, we must remember that everything has a limit and excessive striving can harm health. Balancing activity with proper rest and nutrition will keep us healthy and productive. Regular movement also supports a strong heart and improves stamina.

Emerson once said that the greatest achievement is constantly striving to become something new each day. I fully agree with this view. When we accept who we are, we still feel a desire to explore fresh possibilities, which reveals how much we are capable of. By looking inward, our days become smoother and more enjoyable, because we are unique individuals who make the best choices for ourselves. The world often tries to shape us into something else, but recognizing that this effort is itself a valuable gift motivates us to nurture our own growth.  

When we deliberately seek new experiences, we discover abilities we never imagined. The surprise of realizing we can do something previously unknown fuels confidence, and it encourages us to act spontaneously, which feels exciting and impressive. Trying fresh activities regularly helps us improve continuously, and it also equips us to assist others when they need support. In situations where someone is struggling, our encouragement can show them that nothing is impossible, especially for those who have lost confidence due to bullying or constant negative remarks. Many people doubt themselves because harsh words have eroded their belief in their own worth. In such moments, speaking kindly, showing respect, and offering courtesy can lift their spirits and open the door to healing.  

Bullying, depression, anxiety, prejudice and racism are serious problems that affect many lives, sometimes leading to tragic outcomes such as suicide. We do not have to wait for these crises to arise; we can work to stop bullying and discrimination, thereby creating a more supportive environment. Helping others not only benefits them but also makes us better people, allowing us to view life from different perspectives and find solutions where none seemed possible.  

Taking care of ourselves is essential. It means listening to our inner voice, honoring our feelings, and pursuing what truly matters to us rather than seeking approval from others. When we focus on our own happiness, we cultivate confidence, optimism, and a sense of achievement. It is important to share positive words with those who matter, while discarding harmful comments that could damage our self‑esteem. At the same time, we should avoid announcing every ambition to everyone, because envy can turn into resentment when others become jealous of our successes. Instead, we should celebrate our milestones with the people who genuinely care about us.  

Working on your own lets you keep your own opinions, strategies, and solutions, which often leads to higher quality results. In a group, you must combine ideas and choose the one that seems most interesting or important, which can dilute your personal input. For me, individual effort is preferable because it allows me to express my unique ideas without compromise.  

The drive to become something different is the highest achievement, since it teaches us new skills and enables us to reshape the world despite negative expectations. Each day we should be mindful of the words we use, ensuring they do not harm anyone, because everyone deserves respect. Young people today often feel pressured by parental demands, yet they should be free to pursue what they truly want.  

Yourself is a core part of who you are and the values you hold, making it essential to nurture. You need people who uplift you daily, who stay by your side in both good and difficult times, and who genuinely celebrate your successes. Understanding who truly cares for you helps you identify real friends.  

A true friend is someone who genuinely wants the best for you, offers support, and encourages you to act with integrity. A friend does not abandon you or ignore what matters to you. Everyone should look closely to recognize who is truly a friend.  

Happiness is an emotional state that you can share with family, close friends, and other important people. When you feel comfortable in your own body, you are more at peace, even though many people struggle with body image.  

When you trust yourself and believe in who you are, you experience happiness and a sense of peace. It is important to nurture this feeling and avoid letting negativity affect you when others oppose your actions.  

When you have confidence in yourself, the people around you feel uplifted at every moment, hour, minute, and second.

Having apositive outlook is essential for success in life. Without it, achieving goals becomes difficult and earning the respect of others is unlikely. Therefore, cultivating optimism should be a priority not only in public places but also at home, in school, and at work, as well as in every environment we encounter. We must treat our parents, siblings, teachers, and neighbors with kindness and respect, because a constructive attitude encourages mutual respect and strengthens relationships.  

When we approach others with positivity, we become more approachable and trustworthy. People are naturally drawn to those who radiate optimism, while those who lack it are often perceived as disrespectful, self‑centered, or unwilling to cooperate. Consequently, a positive mindset helps us build lasting friendships and creates a supportive network that makes collaboration easier.  

From my experience as a student, I have seen how an optimistic attitude improves interactions with classmates and teachers, leading to better teamwork and a more harmonious classroom atmosphere. A person who maintains optimism is more likely to believe in his or her own abilities, set realistic goals, and persist despite obstacles. This confidence acts like a superpower, enabling the individual to turn aspirations into reality and to illuminate a brighter future.  

In short, a positive attitude is the key that unlocks personal growth, successful achievement of dreams, and harmonious social connections. By consciously choosing optimism in every situation, we can become better individuals and inspire those around us to do the same.

In my opinion, it is betterto work in a group because it offers many benefits. One example is that the group helps members think more clearly and quickly. Second, the work helps earn more money for both the company and the workers. The first reason is that the group can find information—through the internet, books, or other resources—when someone has a problem, such as a member being sick; others can substitute and solve the issue because they are professional. Although a group may occasionally face inconveniences like disagreements, they can usually resolve any problem. The second reason is that working in a group is more beneficial for the company and for workers: the company pays better when the work is excellent, and the group can achieve extra hours and more efficient work, which also helps earn more business with other companies and countries. In conclusion, I think it is more beneficial to work in a group for several reasons: it is easier to think and help each other when work is difficult, and it is more practical for earning money for both the company and the workers, as well as for collaborating with other companies.

In myview, working in a group is preferable because it offers numerous advantages. Firstly, a team enables members to think more clearly and solve problems more quickly, since each person can contribute ideas and support the others. Secondly, group work tends to generate higher earnings for both the company and the employees; when the team performs well, the organization can pay better wages and provide additional hours. Moreover, colleagues can locate information—such as online resources or reference books—and cover for one another when a member is ill, ensuring continuity of work. Although occasional disagreements may arise, the professional nature of the group usually allows them to be resolved efficiently. In addition, collaborative effort makes tasks more efficient, which in turn helps the firm secure more business with other companies and even in foreign markets. Consequently, I believe that working in groups is more advantageous than working alone, as it facilitates mutual support, improves productivity, and benefits both the employer and the staff.

Why is it not a beneficial idea to conserve energy and resources in schools? Some students claimed that it is a beneficial suggestion, because it would conserve less energy and we could conserve more resources, but I think that when we have assignments and lack computers at home, we must complete them in school, the library, free periods, or the classroom, and what would occur if computers lacked power? We can lose points in this class for failing to submit homework on time. Did this occur within a two‑hour school day, imagined over four school days? This can be a problem for students because we lack resources to complete homework on time, and we can feel considerable distress about it, possibly causing conflict with parents. Some students possess resources at home because their parents can afford them, which is why they consider it acceptable to conserve energy and resources in schools, whereas other students lack such resources because their parents cannot afford them, or for other reasons such as not having parental support, living with only their mother who has several other children and must cover rent, transportation, and bills; we are unaware of many factors that prevent them from paying for internet. I believe that energy and resources in schools are not detrimental, yet for some students it offers a viable means to complete assignments and enjoy them with accessible confidence; if energy is unavailable for four school days, completing tasks simultaneously becomes challenging, as many students share limited computers, making it difficult to locate the appropriate device for each assignment and requiring more time than others, which is why I consider it not a truly beneficial idea for all students, Other students argue that it is not the case because some students use the internet merely to browse Facebook or play video games, thereby wasting time that others could use, yet they cannot speak for everyone since some students rely on the internet for genuine purposes such as homework, reading books, and other activities. In benefits, we can conserve more energy by using it sparingly; the school's energy bill can be lower than before, allowing us to allocate more resources, and we can offer different extracurricular activities. In my view, it isnot a good idea to conserve energy and resources in the school. Some students argue that saving electricity would reduce costs and preserve resources, but I believe that without reliable power many pupils will be unable to complete their assignments. If the school runs out of electricity, students who have to do homework on computers in the library, classroom or during free periods will lose valuable time, and they may receive lower marks for late work. Imagine trying to finish four days’ worth of tasks when the computers are offline – it would be extremely difficult, especially for the many students who do not have computers or internet access at home.  

Students from families with limited financial means often cannot afford home internet or devices; they depend on the school’s facilities. If the school cuts power, they cannot finish their work, which can cause stress and even create tension with their parents. Moreover, some pupils claim that the internet is used mainly for social media or games, yet many others need it for research, reading, and completing assignments.  

Another concern is the air‑conditioning system. If the power is turned off, the classroom may become too hot or too cold, which can affect students’ concentration and health, especially when the weather is extreme. In addition, without electricity phones cannot be charged, preventing students from contacting their families or calling for help in emergencies.  

While conserving energy could lower the school’s utility bill and free up funds for other activities, the practical problems it creates for learning and safety are significant. Therefore, I conclude that it is not advisable to conserve energy and resources in schools, because the disadvantages outweigh any potential savings.

Everyone makes mistakes in life. When a person keeps failing without losing enthusiasm, they fail to learn from those errors. Often, feeling upset about a wrongdoing is essential, because without that discomfort we tend to repeat the same mistake and never improve. In my own experience, this lesson became clear during a difficult IB Mathematics course I took with a friend last year. One day she told me that my grades were poor and that I should change my approach or I would have to repeat the class next year. The comment stressed me for about an hour, and later I realized she was right. I did not study for the upcoming exam, and on the day of the test I felt calm, even happy that it was Friday. Both of us failed, but I felt terrible when I got home. My father asked about my result, and when I explained that I had not passed because I found the subject hard, he became angry and reminded me that my lack of effort was the real mistake. He said that nothing is impossible if you try your best.  

That conversation motivated me to become a dedicated student in that class. I resolved to study every weekend, giving my utmost effort. On Monday I asked the teacher if I could sit a retake, and after intensive preparation I succeeded; my friend, however, did not change her habits. She continued to experience repeated failures without any loss of enthusiasm, which is why she had to retake the course the following year. This illustrates my point: failure must have a negative impact, otherwise people ignore their mistakes and repeat them. When the pain of failure is felt, it pushes us to improve. If we were indifferent to our shortcomings, we would never strive for better performance.

Technology has brought clear benefits to everyday life. It speeds up work by allowing us to complete tasks more quickly, and it reduces the amount of time spent on communication. With email and other digital tools we can exchange important files with colleagues or partners without traveling to an office or arranging a meeting, which saves a lot of time. Because we no longer need to print and file paper documents, we also help protect the environment.  

Many people find face‑to‑face conversation difficult, especially when they must discuss tasks or critical information. Technology offers a simple alternative: sending an email or a message lets them share the same details without the pressure of speaking directly. This avoids nervousness and the discomfort that can arise from in‑person interaction.  

Digital storage also makes it easy to keep projects, presentations, data and other files safe. We can save them on a USB drive, on a personal computer, or in cloud services such as Office 365, which is especially useful for students who need to store assignments and letters without fear of loss.  

Some critics argue that technology has a harmful impact on people’s lives, but this view is mistaken. Modern tools increase efficiency: PowerPoint lets us create professional presentations, the internet provides instant access to information, and online shopping eliminates the need to visit physical stores. Moreover, the internet enables anyone to start a business, publish job advertisements, and search for employment opportunities.  

Overall, the advantages of technology outweigh any perceived drawbacks, making it an essential part of contemporary life.

They tend to send messages whenever the teacher looks away, and when a question is posed they reply that they missed it or ask for it to be repeated. Consequently, their academic performance suffers, as their grades drop due to constant conversation with peers.

Whenever people choose to adopta positive posture and outlook, their lives tend to improve. Even though some individuals maintain a pessimistic view, they often miss opportunities to act and make errors, yet many continue to hold a constructive attitude. For instance, when faced with unwelcome news, a person who remains calm and adopts a hopeful stance can say that everything will be okay and move forward. A positive posture also influences how others perceive you, often encouraging them to adopt a similar mindset. Maintaining such an attitude in school is especially valuable; even if a student struggles with a difficult assignment, a confident mindset can motivate peers to encourage them, and the student may eventually succeed. This belief in eventual success brings satisfaction, because the effort feels meaningful and the outcome is rewarding. The same principle applies in a medical setting. If a doctor informs a patient about an illness, the patient can choose not to dwell on worst‑case scenarios, but instead accept that the condition is manageable and will pass with time, leading to a slightly altered but still hopeful life. Embracing a positive perspective makes it possible to see that any situation can be handled, regardless of its size. By focusing on optimism rather than fear, one can stay happy, avoid excessive worry, and approach problems with confidence. In this way, a good attitude transforms challenges into opportunities for growth and happiness. It also strengthens resilience and hope.

When olderpupils collaborate with younger ones, they can form friendships and also benefit each other. Their teamwork also builds trust, which is essential for long‑term friendships. Working side by side requires them to listen and speak, which naturally leads to a bond and encourages cooperation, enhancing their communication skills. This shared activity teaches them how to negotiate roles and respect each other's ideas. They learn to coordinate tasks and support each other, which improves their sense of responsibility. Through conversation they discover each other's interests and dislikes, gaining insight from one another’s perspectives. The exchange of ideas broadens their horizons and helps them appreciate different viewpoints. This kind of partnership also supports the younger child’s learning. If a concept is unclear, the older peer can explain it in a way that is easier to grasp, allowing the younger student to ask for clarification whenever needed, which speeds up understanding. When the younger student receives timely feedback, the learning process becomes more efficient. Because the age gap is modest, often only a few years, the younger child feels comfortable sharing opinions without feeling intimidated. The modest age difference also means they share similar experiences, making conversation easier. Because they are close in age, they can relate to each other's challenges and offer relevant advice. Older students also gain advantages. They must speak slowly and avoid anger, which helps them stay calm and reduces stress, benefiting their mental well‑being. Explaining ideas in simple terms forces them to think clearly and reinforces their own understanding. Moreover, revisiting a lesson while teaching it helps the older pupil retain the material more firmly, as the act of explaining solidifies memory. The older student can also model good study habits, which further strengthens their own learning and boosts confidence. The younger student receives academic help and a supportive friend, while the older student develops patience, clarity, and confidence. These social and academic advantages show why it is important for small and older children to work together, fostering teamwork and lifelong learning. Consequently, schools and families should encourage such pairings to promote inclusive education. Overall, the benefits extend beyond academics to personal growth and community building.

I disagree with the statement “Unless you try to do something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow,” because even when you make a mistake you retain another opportunity to improve. Growth is possible at any time, and the presence of a second chance is essential for development.  

First, consider a typical classroom group project. All participants have different ideas, but only one person assumes the leadership role. The leader declares the work unacceptable because it is incomplete, prompting the group to discuss the issue, address the shortcomings, and resume work. The team never refuses to continue; instead, they recognize that they still have the chance to redo the task and improve it. This illustrates that individuals are not permanently blocked from progress; they simply need another opportunity to act.  

Second, a person who has committed a crime may seek education as a path to personal growth. Even while incarcerated, providing access to study materials and learning opportunities allows that individual to evolve into a better human being. The fact that someone is in jail does not eliminate the possibility of change, and denying educational chances would contradict the principle that everyone deserves a second chance.  

Some may object, arguing that a criminal should not receive another opportunity, but the broader view is that all people benefit from the ability to learn and improve. If we restrict second chances only to certain groups, we undermine the universal potential for development.  

In conclusion, people always have a second chance to grow, whether in collaborative work settings or personal circumstances such as criminal rehabilitation. By recognizing and providing these opportunities, we enable individuals to become better versions of themselves and contribute positively to society.

Based on my own experience, I agree that one should ground decisions in what they have actually lived through. When a person relies on genuine experience, they gain confidence and are better prepared for future challenges. Experience acts as a support system that enables them to move upward, assume new responsibilities, and acquire deeper knowledge. The more situations one has faced, the easier it becomes to evaluate risks and to seize opportunities.  

In contrast, without solid experience or adequate support, progress is difficult. A lack of practice prevents advancement and can keep a person stuck in the same position. This is why ongoing learning and seeking counsel from mentors, teachers, or supervisors is vital. By asking questions and receiving guidance, one can fill gaps in understanding and avoid repeating mistakes.  

Moreover, reading alone is insufficient; practical application is essential. Only through trying, reflecting, and obtaining feedback can true growth occur. When a person has accumulated enough experience, they become more attractive to employers or collaborators because they can demonstrate proven results. This often leads to better job offers, promotions, or the chance to lead projects. Moreover, the confidence gained from past successes helps them face new, uncertain situations without fear. Therefore, nurturing experience through deliberate practice and seeking guidance is not just beneficial but necessary for long‑term success. Consequently, combining personal experience with continuous practice and advice from others builds a stronger foundation for advancement and readiness for whatever comes next.

Student life feels unenjoyable, difficult, and strenuous; we constantly think about enjoying the day and going to new places, and some think about learning new subjects. Third, family waits for children because some are under 18 and need parental supervision when they take the school bus and return home. Parents may go to work while the class is long, but they return home when the children arrive. Occasionally, parents call in emergencies and cannot attend school because they worry about the children being late, so they go outside and take a fair route. Some students work, while others do not. Should our school adopt a four‑day week? In my view, the answer is no. First, a longer school day would leave little time for families. Children would stay at school all day, missing evenings spent with parents and siblings. After classes they would prefer to go outside and play, and telling them they cannot go would only make them upset.  

Second, the schedule would increase the amount of homework. With extra class time, teachers would assign more tasks, and students would have to work at home after a full day, leaving no time to eat or relax. This creates a stressful routine that makes the school day feel endless.  

Third, families, especially those with children under eighteen, would be affected. Parents would need to be present when their kids travel to and from school, which is difficult when they are at work. An emergency call could force a parent to leave the workplace, disrupting both work and school attendance.  

Fourth, the four‑day model could impact students who have part‑time jobs. Those who work would lose an extra day of income, while others might find it harder to balance work and study. The additional day off could also lead to boredom; students might spend free time on phones, watching videos or chatting, which does not contribute to learning.  

Finally, prolonged exposure to school may reduce motivation. When students are in class for many hours, they become tired and lose interest. Although some enjoy technology, the constant use of phones and computers can harm eyesight and concentration. Moreover, learning is not limited to the classroom; time spent with family and friends also provides valuable knowledge.  

In conclusion, a four‑day school week would not improve education. It would cut family interaction, increase homework load, stress parents, disrupt work schedules, and possibly lower student engagement. Therefore, schools should keep the traditional five‑day schedule.

On the positive side, it acts like a constant companion for many people, allowing them to stay in touch with friends and relatives who live far away. I disagree with the claim that first impressions are unchangeable. While it is true that initial perceptions can be strong, they are not fixed. People often feel certain about their first view of a person, an object, or an animal, yet this certainty does not mean the view cannot be revised. Many people believe that the first impression they form is the only one that matters, because the brain quickly categorizes information to save energy. This mental shortcut, known as a bias, can make it seem as though the initial view is permanent, even when later facts contradict it. Consequently, giving ourselves time to reassess can lead to a more balanced view. When we approach each new encounter with curiosity rather than certainty, the chance of revising our first impression becomes much easier. For example, I once formed a harsh impression that my girlfriend was being unfaithful with my best friend. The feeling was intense and hard to dismiss. Nevertheless, I decided to test whether my impression was accurate. I called her and we talked for a long time, trying to express what was on my mind without sounding accusatory. During that conversation I realized that my suspicion was unfounded; the impression I had was wrong. This experience shows that a first impression can be altered when new information is considered. It is important to verify one’s initial judgment before acting on it. When a negative impression arises, taking a moment to reflect and perhaps seeking clarification can prevent unnecessary conflict. Sometimes the best course is simply to wait and observe; over time the truth becomes clearer and the original impression may shift. In my view, keeping an open mind is the most effective way to change a first impression. By allowing additional evidence to surface, we can move beyond the initial snapshot and form a more accurate picture. Therefore, the statement that first impressions are impossible to change is false; they can be revised with careful thought and communication.

First, learning from home eliminates the daily commute, allowing pupils extra time with their families and removing the need to rise early. This also makes the morning routine safer, because there is no risk of traffic accidents on the way to school, and students can start the day with a relaxed breakfast together with relatives. Second, in the present era many health threats surround us, for example the spread of the coronavirus. By studying online, students can remain at home, which lowers the chance of catching illness and helps them stay healthier. They also have more control over their environment, such as temperature and noise, which can improve concentration. Third, when classes are conducted at home, parents are more likely to know where their children are. Some pupils skip school or leave the premises without permission; a home‑based lesson lets a mother see that her child is actually present, helping to prevent truancy and giving families peace of mind. Finally, although some learners may dislike using a computer or feel insecure about technology, the overall advantages outweigh these concerns. They can spend more quality time with relatives, avoid the stress of early mornings and crowded buses, and continue their studies safely from home, while also having the flexibility to review material at their own pace. This approach also prepares students for future digital learning environments today.

By choosing subjects outside his main field, he acquires additional knowledge that broadens his understanding and makes him more competitive in the job market. If a student decides to focus only on the required curriculum, he may become complacent and miss the chance to develop useful skills, which is why many people argue that studying only the mandatory courses is unwise. In my view, selecting electives is the better option because it allows one to learn more information and prepares the individual for future challenges.

For example, in my home country most people speak Spanish; when I traveled to El Salvador I was able to use both Spanish and English, which made me feel proud despite my limited English. Continuous practice is essential, and learning something new each day contributes to personal growth. Moreover, a student who does not take electives may be perceived as lazy, and his family might be disappointed if he lacks a strong academic title. A good qualification often leads to better employment opportunities, while a lack of education can result in unemployment and financial difficulty. Therefore, taking electives during the regular academic year is advantageous, because the regular academic year offers more material and depth than a short summer period.

Winston Churchill once said that life inevitably involves setbacks, and that one should not let those small failures diminish enthusiasm. I share this view because success is not a straight line; it is built on repeated attempts, mistakes, and the willingness to keep going. When we fail, we gain insight that helps us improve our abilities and become better at what we do. Each mistake teaches us something, allowing us to solve problems more effectively and to see how far we can progress by persisting. Learning from failure also means gaining experience that cannot be obtained otherwise. If we ignore a setback, we stop trying and stop stretching ourselves, which limits our growth. By confronting the difficulty, pushing ourselves further, and trying again and again, we gradually reduce the same errors. Over time the next attempt becomes easier because we have already identified the cause of the problem and found a way around it. Moreover, the habit of persisting cultivates resilience, which is valuable not only in personal projects but also in professional settings. Failure, therefore, is not a sign that the goal is unreachable; it signals that we have not yet discovered the right approach. The real obstacle is giving up, not the setback itself. In conclusion, achieving success requires passing through many obstacles and learning from each mistake. If we never challenge ourselves, we will never know what the underlying issue is, nor how to resolve it. This ongoing effort not only strengthens our personal growth but also equips us with the confidence to tackle future challenges. When we share our experiences with others, we create a supportive environment that encourages further learning and collective problem‑solving. Indeed, by persisting, learning, and adapting, we not only solve our own problems but also become capable of helping others, as the saying goes that two heads are better than one indeed.
