In this world, everyone has twenty-four hours in a day. What are you doing for a day? Do you accomplish something? Every day you want to do something, maybe you are inactive. Sometimes you do one thing and want to do another at the same time. I am a student; sometimes I have homework to do. Determine never to idle? For example, after school I need to think about a project to do, I want to relax and do nothing, and I want to eat dinner. Is it a struggle in my mind? Which do I want to do first? If I finish my project, after that I can decide what I want to do, which is the purpose of the day. My position is that if I always focus on one thing, I will accomplish more. If I am idle, it wastes my time and I cannot achieve my purpose. You do anything; it has a process. Never be idle for life? I think maybe, but I feel it is impossible, because you can be idle; this is your life, and you can decide to be idle or to do something completely. I believe that doing something you like helps you accomplish quickly. If I have a problem, during idle time I can think about finding a solution. Think about how I can achieve my purpose. When you are purposeful, I will accomplish much. Life is what you want to do—do more, or idle for time?

Every person has a full dayof twenty‑four hours. What do you fill those hours with? Do you manage to achieve anything? Throughout the day we often have many wishes, yet we may end up doing nothing. At times we start one activity and then want another simultaneously. As a student, I sometimes have homework to complete. I ask myself whether I should never waste time. For instance, after classes I must work on a project, I also feel like relaxing and not doing anything, and I want to have dinner. This creates an inner conflict about which task to tackle first. If I finish the project, then I am free to pursue whatever I want, giving the day a clear purpose. My view is that concentrating on a single task lets me accomplish more. Remaining idle only wastes time and prevents me from reaching my goals. Life does not run without some kind of activity. It may be impossible to stay constantly busy, because we can always choose to rest, but that choice is part of life. I think that when we engage in something we enjoy, we finish it more quickly. Even during idle moments we can think about solving problems and planning how to achieve our aims. By staying purposeful, we can get a lot done. The question is whether we prefer to be active or simply idle.

Influence,whether from peers or popular individuals, plays a big role in our lives. Many people believe that being able to attract money, make more friends, and enjoy good relationships is a sign of wealth and success. They think that such influence can also open doors to better jobs and a more stable life for their families, so that they no longer need help from others.  

However, influence can also have a darker side. When friends encourage risky or illegal actions, such as robbery or violence, the consequences can be severe. Some young people end up in prison because they followed the bad advice of their so‑called friends. This shows that not every influence is beneficial.  

The key to using influence wisely is to choose positive role models. If a person surrounds himself with friends who value honesty, hard work, and helping others, the impact is usually good. These friends can motivate one to study, get a decent job, and support the family. In contrast, friends who push bad behavior may lead to trouble with the police, school disciplinary actions, or even imprisonment.  

One should be careful and think before acting. Decisions should not be rushed, because hasty choices can create long‑term problems. It is important to ask why a certain behavior is being suggested and to consider the possible outcomes. If the answer is unclear or the action is illegal, it is better to refuse.  

Changing oneself for the better is another important aspect of positive influence. When a person decides to adopt good habits, such as punctuality, respect for others, and continuous learning, this not only improves personal life but also attracts people who share similar values. Employers often look for candidates who demonstrate reliability and a strong work ethic, so a good influence can help in finding a desired job, even in another country.  

In addition, a positive influence extends to helping others. By doing good deeds for friends, family, or the community, a person builds trust and creates a network of support. This kind of influence can lead to opportunities for cooperation, collaboration, and mutual benefit.  

To sum up, influence is neither inherently good nor bad; it depends on the source and the choices we make. By surrounding ourselves with people who promote honest and constructive behavior, thinking carefully before acting, and striving to improve ourselves, we can use influence to achieve wealth, meaningful relationships, and a successful future while avoiding the pitfalls that lead to crime or personal loss.

Many schools run after‑school programs in which older pupils assist younger ones. When a child struggles with a subject—whether inside the classroom or outside of it—having an older student nearby can provide the extra guidance needed. The older student may have recently mastered the material themselves, so they can explain concepts that were once difficult for them, and they can also model effective study habits. This arrangement benefits the younger learners, who receive more challenging material than they might encounter at home or in regular classes, helping them stay motivated and complete assignments more readily.  

Because the work is finished under supervision, students return to the regular school day with their tasks already completed, reducing the likelihood of late submissions and allowing them to stay organized. When they get home, they can relax, play, or enjoy outdoor activities without the pressure of unfinished homework. Over time, this support structure can contribute to better academic performance and, ultimately, more successful career prospects.  

The program also encourages peer‑to‑peer learning: younger children who have finished their work can help even younger peers, while older students reinforce their own knowledge by teaching. If a student excels in a subject such as mathematics but finds later assignments more difficult, the older helper can spend additional time reviewing previous work, ensuring the younger learner fully understands each problem.  

Moreover, the balanced schedule—combining study time with recreational activities—prevents children from feeling exhausted. After an active play period, they return to their tasks with renewed energy, rather than remaining listless throughout the day. In sum, expanding after‑school mentorship programs would give more students the chance to study effectively, receive assistance when needed, and maintain a healthy balance between work and play, leading to improved outcomes and brighter futures. These experiences also nurture responsibility, teamwork, and leadership, equipping young people for the collaborative settings they will face in higher education and future careers.

Many people believethat true success means moving from one failure to another while keeping enthusiasm alive, because each setback teaches us how to prepare better and understand others more clearly. However, others argue that this view is wrong, pointing out that a failure does not automatically lead to improvement; sometimes the same mistake is repeated. Since nobody is perfect, everyone possesses both weaknesses and strengths, and a single failure does not alter how others perceive us. Some observers see failure as a necessary step toward becoming a better person, arguing that it introduces new knowledge and motivates us to strive for improvement. Others claim that failure is something that simply happens in life and cannot be controlled, yet they keep trying and never give up. While these perspectives highlight the learning potential of setbacks, it is also clear that failure is not always a reliable route to major achievement. Success requires careful attention, persistent effort, and a genuine desire to grow. When people truly understand their mistakes, they are less likely to be discouraged and can maintain the enthusiasm needed to move forward. By reflecting on what went wrong, they can adjust their actions and become more effective in what they do. Therefore, failure should be regarded as an inherent part of life; if we study it wisely, we can turn it into a source of motivation rather than a reason to lose hope.

Remember that genuine love does not require you to hide your personality or to pretend to be someone you are not. If a person loves you, they will not attempt to reshape you; they will support you and treat you well. You should not allow anyone to force you to become someone else, because genuine affection means accepting your imperfections. It is better to leave anyone who tries to alter you, since their pressure can cause hurt. You may decide to change yourself, but only if it is your own choice, not because others demand it. A real transformation should come from your own desire, not from someone else’s pressure. When someone loves you, they will respect your autonomy and will not try to make you change.

Inmy experience I agree that being “mastered” stops a person from growing. First, when someone becomes convinced they have mastered a skill, they often cease to improve. For instance, imagine a manager whose sales are falling; instead of seeking new strategies, he feels defeated, believes he is no longer valuable, and avoids trying alternative products, which deepens his discouragement and makes him doubt his competence. This loss of confidence often leads the person to quit the task altogether, believing that no improvement is possible.  

Second, social feedback can reinforce this stagnation. A friend may criticize your approach, telling you that you are “stuck” or “round,” and you may internalize that judgment. Over time, you may start to doubt your abilities and avoid taking risks, much like a teenager who receives a poor grade on a test and decides never to retake it, thereby limiting his chance to improve. Such self‑doubt can become a long‑term barrier, preventing you from exploring new methods or seeking help.  

Third, fear of repeating the same mistakes keeps many from revisiting activities they love. The worry that the outcome will be identical discourages further effort, yet each subsequent try actually builds experience and helps you avoid past errors. Recognizing that you can learn from each attempt turns fear into motivation. Over time, the accumulation of small lessons turns each failure into a stepping stone for future success.  

In conclusion, perseverance is essential. You must stay optimistic, trust in your own ability to succeed, and remember that even after many setbacks you always have another chance to begin again. Believing in yourself and remaining positive are the keys to breaking free from the limits of “mastery” and continuing to grow. Therefore, embracing challenges rather than avoiding them is the true path to personal development.

I agree with Churchill thattrue success means moving from one failure to the next while keeping your enthusiasm alive. If you keep trying, even when you stumble, that determination is what matters most. First, no one can know everything, but the only way to grow is to act. When you make an effort, you learn; without effort you remain stuck. It is natural to feel discouraged after a loss, but losing interest entirely shows a lack of purpose. In those moments it is still worthwhile to push forward, because each attempt brings you closer to improvement and eventually to victory.  

Secondly, many people aspire to become better, yet some prefer to stay where they are. They enjoy the comfort of the familiar and avoid the work needed for growth. If you truly want to rise, you must be willing to step out of that comfort zone, set goals for a brighter future, and support your family with better opportunities. Staying idle makes you appear weak, as others can see that you lack ambition and settle for what you have. Ambition drives you to seek more than the present state.  

Third, if you refuse to accept failure you must seize the chance to win. The world rewards those who think carefully and avoid reckless errors, but we are all human and make mistakes. What matters is correcting them and keeping a inner drive that fuels continual self‑improvement. A strong motivation in your heart can keep you moving forward even after setbacks.  

In short, staying in the same place is acceptable if you are content, but you will never grasp the deeper meaning of life without trying at least once. Take the first step, keep your enthusiasm, and let each failure become a lesson that pushes you toward a better future.

Emerson’s remark that “to be yourself in a world that constantly tries to shape you otherwise is the greatest achievement” resonates with me. I think this captures three essential ideas: achieving success, staying true to oneself, and taking responsibility for one’s own life.

First, success matters for society because it brings people who improve the common good. Philanthropists who ease poverty, inventors who create tools such as cars, the internet and computers, and advances that make life safer and healthier all illustrate how individual achievement benefits everyone. When people strive for excellence, they help raise the overall standard of living. These contributions not only solve immediate problems but also inspire future generations to pursue their own goals. This makes life richer.

Second, being authentic is a real triumph. When we act in accordance with our own values, we show others who we truly are, without pretending. This honesty builds trust and allows us to live a purposeful, meaningful life rather than merely conforming to external expectations.

Third, owning your life gives you the power to choose your direction. Making your own decisions about the future lets you shape a fulfilling and healthier existence. Some may argue that it is easier to follow others’ guidance, but the ability to create one’s own success, to remain genuine, and to govern one’s own path is vital for personal growth and for humanity’s progress. Each person follows a unique course, and embracing one’s individuality is therefore the most rewarding accomplishment.

Some people want to finish their schooling, but they cannot for several reasons. They do not have much time because they must work, pay bills, and handle other responsibilities. Some students leave school because they want to help their family, spend more time with them, care for their younger brothers and sisters, or work to support their household. Balancing classes, work, and free time gives students the ability to do other tasks. Distance classes are a better option for many people because they can work, take care of their children, have free time for themselves and their families. Taking classes at home is the best way for people who want to finish their education at universities or high schools.

I think that offering distancelearning is a great solution for many learners. First, a lot of people would like to finish their studies, but they cannot because they have little free time. Most of them work full‑time, earn money for bills and other expenses, so they cannot attend regular classes. Others leave school early to support their families – they look after young siblings, help at home or take extra jobs. In these situations studying from home gives them the chance to keep learning while dealing with their responsibilities. Second, distance courses let students continue their education after high school and head toward university. They can work, earn the money needed for tuition and still keep up with their lessons. Because the programmes are often cheaper than traditional ones, families that cannot afford high fees can still afford them. A student can also study at his own pace, which makes concentration easier and reduces stress. He can sit at his desk, eat an apple, and focus without the usual worries of commuting or preparing for class. Finally, distance learning provides the flexibility to combine study with other duties. A learner can take care of children, do household chores, have personal free time, and spend time with family, all while attending classes. For these reasons, distance education is the best option for anyone who wants to complete a programme at high school or university.

This observation is used to illustrate the difficult climb from ordinary origins to a ministerial position, a climb that the writer suggests is shaped by the country’s military dominance rather than civilian oversight.  

Further, the essay points out that many settlements across Britain are poor, and the social hierarchy remains entrenched: those with financial means enjoy greater status, while the less affluent struggle for recognition. The writer also notes that the armed forces are tasked with safeguarding the nation’s borders, a duty that limits public spending on other services.  

Overall, the piece argues that Minister Winton’s tenure is marked by ambiguity and inaction, and that broader socioeconomic challenges in Britain amplify the difficulty of effective governance. Consequently, the author calls for a reassessment of his role and a more proactive approach to serve the public.

Choosing a professional career is a personal decision that can bring many advantages throughout life. A stable job allows you to support your family, improve your living conditions, and gain a sense of purpose. When you work in a field you enjoy, the satisfaction you receive can also make your relatives happier, because they see your success and feel proud.

For students, thinking about a future career early is important. They need to take responsibility for their choices, because the path they select will shape their lives. Education should help them explore different occupations, develop the necessary skills, and understand the demands of the job market. By doing so, they can pick a profession that matches their interests and provides long‑term security.

Even though some challenges exist, such as the need for continuous learning and the possibility of market changes, the overall benefits of having a career outweigh the drawbacks. A well‑chosen profession not only helps you meet your family’s needs but also gives you personal fulfillment and stability.

In conclusion, pursuing a professional career is a sensible choice. It enables you to contribute to your family’s well‑being, achieve personal happiness, and build a secure future, provided you approach it with responsibility and dedication.

People should choose achievementfor self‑esteem because it may help them work harder, develop more skills, and persist in achieving things. However, some people believe that praising builds self‑confidence, which they think is necessary for learning. Self‑confidence cannot help them, because they might become lazy when learning certain material. Here are three reasons why achievement should be preferred. Achievement makes students work harder than praise does. For example, imagine a student who tries very hard; if the teacher praises the student, the student may give up or become upset. The student needs achievement to stay motivated and complete the work. Praise is not a bad thing, but it is not sufficient. Therefore, people should choose achievement. Suppose you want students to complete a project on how to draw art. If one student succeeds and another receives only praise, the praise does not make sense for the successful student. But if you motivate them, it becomes part of their school history. Finally, achieving success makes students happier than merely praising them, because they can earn high points or good grades (A or B) rather than relying on praise. I would say self‑esteem comes from achievement. These are the three reasons why self‑esteem comes from achievement.

Choosing achievement as the basis for self‑esteem is beneficial because it encourages students to work harder, develop more skills, and persist in reaching their goals. Some argue that praise builds confidence, yet confidence alone can make learners complacent and less motivated to study. Therefore, the advantages of achievement outweigh those of praise.  

First, students who focus on achievement tend to be more industrious than those who rely on compliments. For instance, if a teacher constantly praises a pupil, the pupil may become discouraged or give up when the work becomes difficult. In contrast, a student driven by the desire to achieve will keep putting effort into the task until it is completed.  

Second, the drive for achievement promotes deeper learning. Imagine a class project on creating artwork; a student who succeeds in producing a quality piece gains a sense of accomplishment, whereas merely receiving praise offers little lasting motivation. The effort required to succeed becomes part of the student’s school memory.  

Finally, achieving goals makes learners happier than being praised. High marks, good grades, or mastering a skill bring genuine satisfaction, while praise alone does not. Consequently, self‑esteem grows from real achievement rather than from superficial praise.

Many students fail to pay attentionin class because they do not value their education. When teachers encourage learning, some pupils remain indifferent, showing little interest in the subject matter. In addition, the presence of mobile phones in the classroom creates further distraction. While a few schools permit students to use their phones, others prohibit them, recognizing that phones can interrupt lessons and reduce comprehension. Some learners claim they need the device because the lesson is boring, yet the phone often leads to chatting, social media, or other non‑educational activities, which hampers their own progress and that of classmates. Consequently, the overall learning environment suffers, and the effectiveness of instruction declines. Not every student benefits from technology in the classroom; those who rely on phones may miss essential content, limiting the educational opportunities available to the whole class. Therefore, it is important for schools to enforce rules that limit mobile phone use during lessons, allowing teachers to teach effectively and students to engage fully with the material.

It is often claimed that a positive mindset is essential for achieving success in life, and I largely concur, though I also see limits to this view. Firstly, a hopeful outlook can propel individuals toward achievement; consider Michael Jordan, who was cut from his high‑school varsity basketball team and inspired many young athletes. Rather than becoming discouraged, he used the setback as motivation, trained harder, and stayed optimistic, eventually becoming one of the greatest players in history. Secondly, another illustration is the rapper DaBaby. Despite being repeatedly told he would never make it, he kept a humble, positive attitude, worked tirelessly, and released hit songs that earned gold and platinum certifications, attracting millions of listeners worldwide for generations. However, I argue that a positive attitude is not the sole determinant of success. In situations such as armed conflict, people must adopt a realistic, vigilant mindset rather than an overly optimistic one, because readiness and caution are crucial for survival. In sum, while a positive outlook can certainly contribute to success, it is not an absolute requirement, and there are contexts where a more cautious approach is wiser.

In China we do not share the same view that Ralph Waldo Emerson expressed. Emerson argued that a person only becomes mature when he or she attempts something that lies beyond what he or she already masters. I disagree with this idea because people develop in many different ways, and growth does not depend solely on pushing past existing abilities.

First, acquiring new knowledge can enlarge a person’s capabilities. Students who study fresh material expand their understanding and therefore mature. For example, my mother arrived in the United States without knowing any English. After three years of study she can now speak a little English, and no one would say she is not grown up. Learning a language she had never known before clearly shows that new experiences can bring about personal development.

Second, small errors or setbacks can also contribute to maturity. In a scientific experiment a tiny mistake may ruin the whole project, and the person who makes that mistake learns how to handle uncertainty and improve his or her technique. This kind of lesson forces the learner to become more responsible and thoughtful, which is a form of growth.

Third, many everyday situations push individuals out of their comfort zones and teach them responsibility. When a person enters the workforce, he or she discovers that effort alone does not guarantee success; there are other strategies to achieve higher performance. Getting married and later having a child introduces new duties and perspectives that reshape one’s sense of self. These experiences, common in Chinese society, illustrate that growth can arise from work, family, and social interactions rather than from merely attempting the impossible.

Additionally, the rapid development of China’s economy and the constant demand for new skills mean that young people regularly face novel challenges, which further accelerates their maturation.

Emerson’s quotation, “Unless you try to do something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow,” may apply to some individuals, but it does not hold true for everyone. People differ in temperament, opportunities, and the ways they learn. Some grow through formal education, others through trial and error, and still others through relationships and cultural expectations. In China, the many factors that influence personal development show that growth can be achieved by learning new subjects, reflecting on minor mistakes, and confronting the varied responsibilities of work, marriage, and parenthood. Therefore, I reject Emerson’s claim that growth is only possible when one steps beyond what is already mastered; instead, I believe that many paths lead to maturity, and new experiences—no matter how small—can make a person grow.

The question ofwhether we should decide for ourselves or simply follow the advice of experts and authorities is a recurring dilemma in many areas of life. Some people argue that seeking guidance from those who have more experience reduces risk, while others claim that personal decision‑making leads to greater independence. In my view, when a person is isolated and lacks any prior experience, it is far more advantageous to rely on one’s own judgment rather than depend on external counsel. When you have no one to turn to for advice, which sharpens your analytical abilities and prepares you for future challenges. This self‑directed approach also fosters a sense of ownership, because you see the direct results of your decisions and can take pride in your achievements. Consequently, the habit of making independent choices builds confidence that carries over into other areas of life, such as work, relationships, and personal goals. Overall, this mindset promotes lifelong learning and personal empowerment.  

First, when you are alone you are forced to create your own experiences, especially through the mistakes you inevitably make. Each error becomes a concrete lesson that teaches you how to take responsibility for your actions and how to recover from setbacks. Over time, this accumulation of personal lessons builds a strong sense of resilience, because you learn to anticipate problems, adjust your behavior, and develop confidence in your ability to handle future challenges. The more you learn from your own failures, the more robust and self‑reliant you become, and the better equipped you are to face new situations without needing constant direction. Moreover, the process of learning from mistakes gives you a deeper understanding of the subject matter, because you are not just receiving information but actively testing hypotheses and observing outcomes. These experiences not only strengthen your problem‑solving skills but also nurture patience, because you discover that progress often requires time and repeated effort. As a result, you become more adaptable, better able to cope with unexpected changes and to seize new opportunities that arise. This habit of self‑directed learning becomes a lifelong asset that supports personal and professional growth.  

Second, deciding your own rules gives you a clear sense of direction and predictability. When you set the guidelines yourself, you can see exactly how they will affect your goals and plan accordingly, which reduces uncertainty and prevents the confusion that often arises from following someone else’s regulations. Those external rules may seem arbitrary or contradictory, leaving you unsure about their impact. By creating personal rules you know what to expect, you can evaluate the consequences of each choice, and you avoid the anxiety that comes from not knowing how outside directives will shape your path. In addition, personal rules can be adapted to your unique circumstances, allowing you to balance flexibility with structure, whereas imposed rules often ignore individual needs and can hinder rather than help your progress. Having self‑crafted rules also means you are the ultimate decision‑maker, so you can align your daily actions with your core values and long‑term objectives without being swayed by external expectations. When you follow your own guidelines, you experience less internal conflict, because your actions are consistent with the principles you have chosen for yourself. This clarity enables you to make quicker decisions, because you no longer need to weigh conflicting advice from multiple sources.  

Third, solitude prevents others from constantly interfering with your plans. When no one is watching or offering unsolicited advice, you are free to pursue the path you have chosen without feeling pressured to conform. This independence allows you to develop deep expertise in your chosen field, because you can experiment, make adjustments, and refine your skills without external constraints. As your competence grows, you naturally assume a leadership role, and people who observe your progress are more likely to respect and trust your decisions. Moreover, the absence of interference gives you the mental space to focus, which enhances creativity and problem‑solving ability, qualities that are essential for long‑term success. Constant activity is essentialfor achieving the things we want in life. When we stay busy, we are more likely to reach the objectives we set for ourselves and keep moving forward. Thomas Jefferson is a good illustration; he produced many achievements, including the Declaration of Independence, without wasting time relaxing or being idle. By setting clear goals each year and working toward them, we develop a habit of continual effort. Each new task we undertake brings us closer to our targets, and the process never truly ends because we are, at our core, people who keep moving.

Many individuals squander their time and fail to complete their aspirations. Every person carries an inner drive that pushes them onward, a motivation that fuels persistent effort. Over time we see new products—smartphones, shoes, televisions—each the result of someone’s hard work and dedication. The world advances because people are constantly doing something, generation after generation, improving and innovating.

We act with purpose because the drive to contribute is rewarding; it would be wasteful to remain idle, both for ourselves and for those who observe us. Our lives are structured around purposeful activity: attending school, pursuing higher education, and eventually establishing a career, all of which help us accomplish our goals and grow. Parents often encourage their children to stay active; for example, during summer vacation a child who stays home playing video games and neglects chores may disappoint his parents, who expect him to help with dishes or find a job. This illustrates that taking action leads to achievement, and that continuous effort is the key to success.

Ralph Waldo Emerson onceobserved that certain difficulties affect adults, but they are far more demanding for teenagers. A child already anticipates the course of his life, so when a young person grows up in a household that values and supports his activities, he feels fortunate because not everyone enjoys such a nurturing environment. In contrast, a teenager whose family shows little concern is likely to encounter greater obstacles than one who has a supportive home. Consequently, this youth must choose between becoming a responsible, respectable individual who makes his family proud without their assistance, or succumbing to a life of crime and ending up in prison. When a young person lacks familial backing, he often works tirelessly to earn money and provide food for his relatives. He often has to balance school, work, and family responsibilities, which adds to the pressure he faces. This struggle embodies the idea of being true to oneself: caring for one's family and offering younger siblings the chances he never had. Most individuals make this crucial choice during their teenage years, which is arguably the hardest period of life. This period forces them to mature quickly and to develop a clear sense of purpose. They are leaving behind their past, striving to build a new future, and refusing to return to former hardships. Those who decide early understand the weight of their decision; they learn to be authentic and to act like a true man. The world, in their view, belongs to those with strong feelings, while the weak perish. Therefore, to be oneself one must cultivate a strong mind.

Success meansmoving from one setback to another while keeping your enthusiasm alive. I agree with the statement that you should never quit, even when you stumble. Whenever you pursue something, you will inevitably encounter difficulties, and sometimes you will fall short. That is simply part of the process; giving up only stops you from reaching your goal. Throughout my own experience I have started many projects that seemed unfinished, yet I keep telling myself I will finish them eventually. Many people begin with strong motivation, achieve early wins, then lose momentum and quit when they face a failure. If you truly love what you do, you must keep chasing it, because abandoning it means you will never obtain it. Failure is a powerful word that makes most people uncomfortable. Students often become upset after a bad test or class, and the fear of being late or missing a deadline can be stressful. Just as work demands punctuality for a higher salary, consistent effort and regular practice are required to improve daily. For example, soccer players must train constantly, learning new techniques and practicing repeatedly in order to win consistently and perform correctly every time. We all dislike failing, but I have learned to view each failure as a step toward improvement rather than a waste of time. I have failed many times, but I never stop trying because I know I must complete what I start. Enthusiasm is the driving force behind achieving dreams. If you let that passion fade, you may become skilled at a task but you will not reach excellence. Think positively, stay confident that you will succeed, and keep your excitement alive. Imagine planning to attend college: you work hard, earn money, and then consider returning to studies. If you lose the excitement you originally felt, the effort becomes meaningless and you may stop moving forward. That is why I share Winston Churchill’s view that progress requires fighting through obstacles and never surrendering. In short, perseverance and sustained enthusiasm are the keys to success. Even when you encounter repeated failures, rise again, keep learning, and maintain a positive outlook. By doing so, you will become better each day and deserve the success that awaits everyone. This attitude not only helps you achieve personal goals but also builds confidence that you can handle future challenges.

I believe that collaborating in ateam is the most effective approach for students. One might wonder why working together is preferable. When learners listen to their classmates, they receive fresh perspectives on how a project or assignment should be approached. Hearing different viewpoints helps each student form a clearer idea of the task at hand. Moreover, the chance to speak up builds confidence; students feel less hesitant to share their thoughts when they know they are being heard.  

Some students favor working alone because they can set their own pace and avoid interruptions. They usually already have a topic and a plan, which makes solitary work seem comfortable. In contrast, a group allows the workload to be split into distinct sections. For instance, one member could handle the introduction, another could design the visual layout, while a third conducts the research. By assigning tasks according to strengths, each student can choose the part that feels easiest or most familiar, which often leads to higher quality work.  

Working in a group also introduces students to new peers. Teachers sometimes assign groups without letting students pick their partners, exposing them to people they have not met before. This interaction can spark innovative strategies; for example, a teammate might create a T‑chart that lists the advantages and disadvantages of a topic, helping the group decide which angle to emphasize. Such collaborative tools often reveal approaches that an individual would not consider.  

Because responsibilities are divided, the overall project tends to be completed more quickly. Each person can concentrate on a specific segment, and once a section is finished, they can offer assistance to a teammate who is struggling, thereby keeping the whole team on schedule. If you finish your part of the project or assignment, you can volunteer to help other team members. For example, someone who works alone may need more time because they are self‑reliant, yet you have the opportunity to assist them with difficult tasks.  

In my conclusion, working together teaches students to listen to each other’s ideas and makes collaboration the most effective way for them to succeed. While those skills are valuable, they do not replace the benefits of teamwork. Collaborative learning forces students to listen, negotiate, and respect differing opinions, all of which are essential competencies in academic and professional settings. Therefore, I maintain that group work is the superior method for student achievement.

Working in a group offersseveral clear advantages compared with working alone. First, collaboration makes tasks easier and quicker because members can exchange ideas and split the work among themselves. Collaboration also allows members to check each other's work, which improves the quality of the final product. Second, each person can count on the others for help, which prevents anyone from getting stuck on a problem. Third, the atmosphere tends to be less stressful; when a member is unsure, the group can provide support, so frustration is kept to a minimum.

When students work together, they learn to listen to different perspectives, which improves their communication skills. This mutual learning helps students develop critical thinking skills that are useful beyond the classroom. These advantages are especially important for academic tasks that require creativity and problem solving. These benefits make group work especially valuable for students who need to meet tight deadlines.

In contrast, working alone means a person must rely solely on themselves. If a difficulty arises, there is no one to turn to for assistance, which often leads to confusion and wasted time. Moreover, the individual has to generate all ideas and evaluate them without any feedback, and this can result in disappointment when the final result is unsatisfactory. Working alone can also limit the development of teamwork abilities that are essential in the workplace. Working alone may also cause boredom, because there is no interaction to keep the mind active.

For these reasons I prefer group work. The ability to share information means that tasks can be finished more efficiently, and the experience of teamwork is valuable for learning how to cooperate. Mutual support also builds confidence, because teammates can correct each other’s mistakes and encourage one another. Finally, the reduced pressure creates a calmer mindset, making it easier to complete assignments without unnecessary stress. Such support can reduce anxiety and help students stay motivated throughout the project. Therefore, I believe that working in a group is the best way to achieve academic success and personal development.

Consequently, many educators encourage collaborative projects to prepare students for real‑world challenges. In the long run, these experiences contribute to personal growth and better career prospects. Overall, the benefits of working together outweigh the drawbacks of working alone. Group settings provide easier problem‑solving, stronger support, and a more relaxed environment, while solitary work often leads to isolation, difficulty, and heightened frustration.

First impressions are hard to change because they create the initial picture that others keep in mind. When you meet someone for the first time, the way you present yourself becomes the reference point that shapes all later opinions. As a result, people tend to treat you according to that opening behavior, and they are reluctant to reconsider their view without compelling evidence.

The difficulty stems from the way our minds work. The first encounter forms a mental shortcut, a quick judgment that is stored and later recalled. If you appear unfriendly or distracted, observers may quickly label you as such, and that label stays active even when you act differently later. They may also doubt a sudden shift in attitude, assuming it is not genuine, which reinforces the original impression. Even if you later smile and speak politely, those who saw you upset may still remember the earlier moment and treat you with caution.

Consequently, altering how others see you takes considerable effort.

Nevertheless, a first impression is not permanently fixed. With consistent effort and genuine intentions, you can gradually modify how others see them. By behaving in a positive, reliable manner over time, the new conduct can outweigh the initial impression. In some cases, a single striking action can even overturn a previously favorable view, turning it negative, or vice versa. However, such shifts usually require sustained behavior rather than a one‑off change.

In professional settings such as job interviews, a poor first impression can linger and affect future opportunities, making it even more crucial to present yourself positively from the start. Therefore, paying attention to your first encounter is essential.

Overall, the initial picture we present to others heavily influences how we are treated and remembered. While it is challenging to change that picture, it is not impossible; deliberate, repeated actions can eventually reshape the perception, though the process is naturally slow and demanding.

Once my friend tried many substances, including cocaine, marijuana, cigarettes and alcohol. One afternoon he asked me which school I attend and whether I could go with him. I answered that I go to a regular school and said yes. After that he told me he was exhausted by his habits and wanted to become someone different. From that point on he completely changed his life and now dreams of becoming a doctor so he can help others transform as well. I agree with Emerson’s view on individuality because I can prove that the critics are mistaken, illustrate the gap between merely speaking and actually doing, and stay focused. Being true to myself does not depend on what others say about me. If I decide to pursue a new path, I must follow my own mind. For instance, I might want to become a teacher even though some people claim the salary is low, around a thousand dollars a month, and argue that the job is unimportant. Their doubts only confuse me, yet I remain determined. Perhaps they have tried and failed, which makes them think I cannot succeed, but circumstances change daily, so I need to demonstrate that their assumptions are wrong. It is essential not to heed those who try to mislead me. Moreover, there is a clear distinction between merely talking and actually making things happen, because believing in myself is valuable, but words alone do not produce results. By acting, I can benefit the world even if I sometimes doubt myself. When I show others that I have altered my life through my attitude, they approach me and ask what caused the change. I will tell them that I aim to become something different in this world, and that will be my greatest achievement. Still, I must remain concentrated, because I am human and imperfect; lack of focus can lead to mistakes, and negative people may take pleasure in my setbacks. Many avoid studying because they find school boring, and they try to persuade me to engage in harmful behavior. I must prove to them that my desire to become something else outweighs the temptation of easy entertainment. In short, embracing individuality is challenging. I need to convince others that we sometimes do not require assistance from anyone else. Trusting my own judgment, ignoring disparaging remarks, showing the difference between merely speaking and taking action, and maintaining concentration are all vital. Ultimately, achieving something beyond the ordinary is the most rewarding accomplishment, and the world indeed needs me. I believe that personal growth comes from perseverance and self‑reliance.

When a pupil studies drama, possible careers include acting, directing a production, or assisting with creative ideas for theatre or film. A student who majors in music might become a composer, manager, or continue to practice and refine his or her abilities. In both cases the knowledge acquired in the classroom provides more options for later life. Moreover, students who finish a specialised course often have better prospects than those who do not, because they can demonstrate concrete skills and a diploma that confirms their training. Parents generally believe that giving their children the chance to learn a subject they enjoy will improve their overall development and increase the likelihood of success. Overall, offering drama, music, art or other similar classes helps students grow, creates opportunities for future work, and supports the community by preparing young people to contribute positively.

Students who live far from theirschools often decide to attend classes from home instead of going to campus. In my view, this arrangement is detrimental to their learning and may harm their future prospects, because not every pupil who enrolls in online courses finishes the required assignments.  

One of the main problems is distraction. When a learner studies at home, nothing prevents them from switching attention to television, social media, or other activities. I remember a classmate named Alex who was enrolled in an online mathematics course that she needed to pass. One evening, around six o’clock after school, I visited her house and found her watching a series while the lesson was still open on her screen. She admitted that the program’s attractive visuals pulled her focus away from the work, and only after turning off the TV was she able to concentrate and make progress.  

My friend Alex was supposed to complete her assignments, but she kept getting distracted by her TV show; if she had turned it off, she would not have been distracted and could succeed in her online class.  

Students studying from home often lack someone to remind them to finish their tasks, and many forget to complete them, resulting in incomplete work.  

This semester I am enrolled in an online course and occasionally overlook an assignment, which led to a low grade last week after I failed to finish my vocabulary task. If I set a daily alarm to remind myself to study and complete my assignments, I could achieve a higher grade.  

Some people claim that studying from home offers flexibility, allowing them to work at any hour, yet others argue that it leads to poor grades.  

Poor grades may prevent you from passing the school year, but with effort you can succeed.  

For some learners, taking online courses may eventually hinder their education.  

If schools offered after‑school help, all students could succeed more comfortably, and teachers could monitor their progress.

We should also support those who feel exhausted by life, encouraging them to remain active and purposeful rather than giving up. By confronting adverse situations instead of avoiding them, we can overcome challenges and find solutions. 

Although some argue that success is hard without enthusiasm, I believe that maintaining vigor helps us prevent future problems and leads to a happier, more stable existence. In short, perseverance through failure with sustained enthusiasm is the key to achieving lasting success. Therefore, by embracing each setback with optimism and by helping others stay motivated, we can build a resilient path toward the success we seek.

Implementing adedicated after‑school homework club at our school would be an effective way to raise student achievement. Many learners struggle with assignments and need extra guidance to grasp the material before a test, and a regularly scheduled club would give them the focused support they require without disrupting regular class time.

Teachers often find it difficult to remain after school to help individual students, especially when only a few pupils show up. When a teacher spends valuable time with a single learner who does not attend, the effort feels wasted and can affect the teacher’s personal life. A structured club would allow educators to concentrate on the students who are present, making the most of the available hours and avoiding the frustration that arises from low attendance.

A homework club would create a quiet environment where students can work on assignments with assistance when needed. By staying after school, learners can clarify doubts immediately, which reduces confusion during class and improves the likelihood of achieving higher scores on exams. Moreover, completing work in a supportive setting lessens the pressure of doing homework at home, where distractions are common.

Peer interaction within the club can also boost understanding. Students who finish their work early could help classmates, explaining concepts in their own words and reinforcing their knowledge. However, the success of this approach depends on clear expectations and a disciplined atmosphere; otherwise, the session may devolve into idle chatter rather than productive study.

To encourage participation, the school could offer recognition for students who attend regularly and complete their assignments on time, such as certificates or modest rewards. Involving parents by informing them of the club’s benefits can further motivate children to take the work seriously. When students see that consistent effort leads to better grades and a lighter homework load at home, they are more likely to engage fully, ultimately raising overall academic performance.

Many peoplesay that a positive attitude is essential for success in life, and I agree. Having a hopeful outlook gives us direction and energy, and I can illustrate this with both research findings and personal experiences. First, when we wake up each morning we should consider what we need to accomplish that day. If we set clear goals and avoid laziness, the tasks no longer feel boring; instead they become sources of motivation and strength. For instance, a student who knows a test is coming the next day can plan to study the evening before, review notes, and practice more. This preparation usually leads to better performance on the exam. Second, a positive mindset encourages us to engage in activities beyond regular schoolwork, such as volunteering, preparing for the SAT, or excelling in AP courses. These extra efforts not only improve grades and test scores but also build valuable experience that helps with college applications. A weekend spent volunteering at a hospital or the library, combined with SAT study, can make a student more competitive for admission. A personal example supports this view. She also kept a record of the books her customers preferred, which helped her decide what to stock. In conclusion, a positive attitude is a crucial factor for success. If you imagine students stayinghome to take online classes, it would be great for those who cannot attend school, and online classes are a big help for them, especially when they are in the hospital. These are people who have problems such as cancer or other illnesses, and it is not harmful to any student in school. But some students say there is no problem with not coming to school, whether they are sick or not; they still attend. But many of them do not dislike school; their bodies are not strong, they get sick easily, and the school allows them to take online classes, though they have to pay. But this way is not free because students who are sick pay for all the classes and cannot play any sport; your student can stay at home with your parent. Very, when I was 5 years old and choking with cold, I took my parent and did not want to go to school, started crying. My gram father told me a story about when he was younger; school had no online classes, and some people could attend because he was becoming stronger, though it was still hard for him to bake a dough. Then, eventually, I went to school and thought about what my gram father told me. It was a long time ago, and now I am 18, grateful to my gram father. He taught me that education is harder when you stay home, and it doesn't matter whether you take online classes or not; you still attend normal classes. Sometimes you think about fun or friends, and you don't consider the amount of work, doing it later without thinking about the final result. There are two paths — light or dark — that you live; someone thinks about family and love, and they won't create something that makes their family proud, instead going to college to live a happy life with family.

Imagine a student staying at home and attending classes online. For many young people, this arrangement is a great advantage because they cannot physically go to school due to illness or hospitalization. In such cases, online learning provides a valuable opportunity to continue their education without interruption.

Some people argue that there is no problem staying away from school, but this view overlooks the difficulties faced by students whose health is fragile or who lack the strength to attend regularly. When a student is seriously ill, staying home may be necessary, and online classes allow them to keep up with lessons and avoid falling behind.

However, online learning also has drawbacks. Students miss out on face‑to‑face interaction, sports, and other activities that take place in a traditional school environment. They must also manage the financial cost of the technology and internet connection, which is not always free.

My own experience illustrates the importance of education. As a child I was often sick and reluctant to go to school, but my grandfather encouraged me to keep studying. He told me that learning is a lifelong asset that cannot be taken away. Thanks to his support, I was able to attend classes even when I was unable to go to school in person.

In conclusion, online classes are a useful tool for students who cannot attend school for health reasons. While they cannot replace all aspects of school life, they ensure that learning continues and help students build a better future.

In my view, a half‑day timetable is beneficial because it gives teachers the chance to organise enjoyable activities for the class. The main idea is that the school day can be shortened, allowing students to leave early and use the extra time at home for homework or to complete unfinished lessons. When teachers finish their lessons sooner, they can relax, study, or prepare materials for the next session. Moreover, the additional afternoon period provides the school with more time to plan future lessons, which ultimately supports better learning outcomes. Some people argue that sending children home early may lead to unproductive behaviour at home, but I believe the schedule does not have to be identical every day; flexibility lets the school adjust activities according to the needs of the students. By varying the routine, teachers can keep lessons fresh while still offering the advantage of an early finish. In addition, the early dismissal gives families a chance to engage in educational activities together, reinforcing what was learned in school. Students who use the extra time wisely often show greater responsibility and are better prepared for the challenges of later grades, which contributes to overall school performance. Therefore, the early finish allows both teachers and pupils to recharge, leading to improved focus. Teachers benefit from the reduced workload, which allows them to engage in professional development or collaborate with colleagues, enhancing the quality of instruction. Students appreciate the extra time to pursue hobbies or rest, which can improve their overall wellbeing and readiness to learn. In conclusion, the half‑day plan offers clear benefits for both learners and staff, promoting a more balanced and effective educational environment.

Many people think that once they have mastered something they cannot develop further, but this view is mistaken. I share Emerson’s opinion that what we already know gives us a solid base, yet it also creates a comfort zone that can hold us back. To grow, we must seek new experiences and challenge ourselves, because without trying we never discover what we are capable of.  

In my own life, I have found that staying in the same routine limits progress. For example, I work as a busboy in a restaurant, a job that feels safe and familiar. Although teamwork is easy there, I aspire to become a server so I can earn more and advance my career. However, my supervisors have not given me the chance to take on that role, which shows how fear of change can keep us from moving forward.  

The world offers countless possibilities for those who are willing to step outside their comfort zone. If we keep doing the same things, we miss opportunities for growth and for achieving the dreams we hold. Therefore, we should not be afraid to try new tasks, even if they seem difficult at first. By embracing change, we can improve ourselves, increase our skills, and open new doors.  

In short, the comfort of the known is useful, but it should not stop us from pursuing new goals. With determination and a positive attitude, we can break free from stagnation, explore fresh opportunities, and shape a better future. By taking the first step today, we can turn our aspirations into reality and enjoy the rewards of personal development.

Is technology harming or helping people’s lives? In my opinion it is doing more damage than good because many people cannot control how much they use it. Modern life often makes us forget how pleasant it is to live without constant digital distraction. We can still enjoy many activities that do not involve a screen: playing outside with friends, going to a library, or simply being in nature. Some say that children should be allowed free access to computers and phones, arguing that this prepares them for the future. I think that young people need limits on their online behavior, and parents should monitor what they do on the internet.

Conversely, there are those who claim that teenagers benefit from unrestricted online use because they can learn new things. While learning is important, too much time on devices can prevent youngsters from completing tasks that require face‑to‑face interaction. Real conversation helps build empathy and strengthens relationships; meeting strangers on the web can be dangerous because not everyone is trustworthy. Therefore, setting reasonable limits and having adults check online activity is essential.

Another problem is the ease of buying items from the internet without knowing the seller. Many websites look legitimate but are actually scams that aim to steal money. To stay safe, shoppers should verify that a site is reputable before entering payment details. Large platforms such as Amazon or eBay have made online shopping convenient, yet they have also created opportunities for fraudsters to set up fake stores. Consequently, users must be cautious and avoid purchasing from suspicious sources.

In addition, an overreliance on technology reduces opportunities for real‑world social interaction. Children who spend most of their time gaming or scrolling through social media miss out on building friendships in person, which can lead to a loss of childhood experiences and weaker social skills. A practical solution is to encourage kids to go outside, meet friends, and engage in activities that do not involve a screen. Only after a child has formed a solid understanding of a person should they be allowed to interact digitally.

Parents should impose clear rules about device usage and keep an eye on online behavior. By setting reasonable limits, they protect their children from harmful content, online predators, and deceptive shopping sites. When a child has shown trustworthiness, limited access can be granted, but it must always be balanced with personal contact.

Overall, technology presents more drawbacks than benefits for many people, especially young users. Its uncontrolled use can erode social connections, expose individuals to fraud, and diminish the quality of everyday life. Therefore, it is crucial to apply restrictions and promote a healthier balance between the digital world and real‑life experiences.

Many schools have suggested thatstudents should be allowed to attend lessons from home using online platforms or video‑conferencing tools. While this idea sounds convenient, it is generally ineffective because learners often become distracted by television, video games, and mobile phones, which hampers their ability to concentrate on the lesson. Moreover, a large majority of students still prefer attending school in person, since they need direct interaction with classmates and teachers, access to school facilities such as libraries and laboratories, and the structured environment that a physical classroom provides.

Students who study at home may also find it difficult to keep up with assignments, because they can easily copy test answers or rely on the internet for projects without truly understanding the material. In addition, the cost of online courses can be a burden for families that already have to pay school fees and possibly support a job.

In a traditional setting, teachers can explain concepts immediately when a student asks a question or needs assistance, which improves comprehension. The school environment also offers a library, printed textbooks, notebooks, and scheduled breaks that help organise the day. Some students also benefit from the social aspect of school, where they can develop friendships and learn to work in groups, something that is harder to achieve through a screen.

Some people argue that online learning reduces expenses and eliminates certain types of bullying based on appearance, but these benefits are outweighed by the loss of focus, reduced social contact, and limited access to learning resources. In addition, not all families have reliable internet connections, which can further restrict participation. Consequently, most students believe that attending classes in person is the better choice, as it offers clearer instruction, greater support, and a more conducive atmosphere for learning.

Beyond academics, school provides a setting where students develop essential social skills, learn to cooperate with peers, and gain confidence through group activities. These experiences are difficult to replicate online, where interaction is often limited to brief video calls. Moreover, being in a classroom helps students stay motivated, as they are surrounded by peers who can encourage each other to stay on task.

Allowing students to select a music, art, or drama class would let them discover hidden talents and try something new. While some may argue that such classes are less essential than core requirements, I think the pleasure and enrichment they bring make them valuable as optional subjects rather than compulsory ones.

Whenever you attempt something that you have already tried and it fails, there is no reason to become discouraged. The more you persist, the stronger you become and the more control you gain over yourself. It is essential to stay determined, keep a calm attitude, and trust that you will eventually become a remarkable person, and opportunities will arise.  

Attempting new challenges shows you that you are capable of achieving more than you imagined. Success depends on your own desire; if you truly wish to pursue something you enjoy, you should simply go for it and ignore the judgments of others, because only you have the power to shape your life.  

The claim made by Ralph Waldo Emerson that once you have tried something and failed, your life is finished is inaccurate. Failure does not mean the end of growth; rather, it is a step toward eventual success.  

My father, a singer, illustrates this point. He was invited to take part in a major musical project and was known for his talent. On the day of the performance he lost his voice completely, yet he gave his utmost effort. Afterward many producers expressed interest in working with him, and he eventually became a well‑known star, expanding his career dramatically. This shows that if you try something you can grow a lot because you must believe in what you want and stay sure of it.  

Never give up, just as I did when I came to the United States. At first I did not speak English, and the language barrier made schoolwork and projects difficult. However, I refused to quit, and over time my English improved and I continued to develop my skills, showing steady growth.  

Many people think that being an expert quickly guarantees a bright future, but others say that spending too much time trying to master something wastes valuable time. In reality, the amount of effort you invest matters less than the persistence you demonstrate. Those who give up after a few setbacks miss opportunities, whereas those who keep trying build resilience and eventually achieve their goals.  

Always do your best and never surrender, even when family or friends tell you that you will never progress. I do not agree with Emerson; the only constant is that everything depends on you, and perseverance should never be abandoned.

Technology has become a central part of everyday life, shaping how we communicate, work, and entertain ourselves. In my view, it is largely beneficial, but its advantages depend on how people manage it.  

One of the main positive effects is easier contact with others. Through smartphones and computers we can speak with friends and family far away, join online games, or simply chat in real time. This connectivity also makes daily tasks more convenient: we can order goods without leaving home, pay bills online, and find information instantly. For many jobs, knowing how to use digital tools is essential; applications are submitted through the internet, and remote work is now common. Even basic skills such as using a map app to locate a destination would have been impossible a few decades ago.  

However, the same ease of access can lead to problems, especially for young people. When children become accustomed to having technology at their fingertips, they may lose the habit of thinking before acting. They might expect everything instantly, which can reduce patience and perseverance. Moreover, excessive screen time can distract from schoolwork, physical activity, and face‑to‑face interaction, potentially harming health and social development.  

To get the most out of technology, we need to learn how to use it responsibly. Practising with computers, smartphones, or tablets builds confidence and equips us for work that increasingly relies on digital skills. At the same time, we should set personal limits: schedule specific times for gaming or social media, and keep devices out of bedrooms at night to protect sleep. Adults should also guide younger users, explaining why certain tools are useful and warning against misuse.  

In conclusion, technology offers many benefits, from staying connected to simplifying everyday chores, but it also brings risks when used without restraint. By acquiring basic digital literacy and establishing clear boundaries, individuals can enjoy the positives while minimizing the negatives, ensuring that technology serves as a helpful tool rather than a source of harm.

Many people experience a positive mood when something pleasant occurs, and they often try to avoid dwelling on negative feelings. Some individuals simply ignore a bad mood, hoping that engaging in enjoyable activities will lift their spirits. In my view, everyone ought to strive for constant happiness and steer clear of sadness, anger, or any unpleasant emotional state.  

Bad moods frequently arise from early‑morning fatigue or from a parent’s reprimand over something the person did not do. Consequently, a large number of people remain unhappy or maintain a pessimistic outlook. This makes it essential for us to help one another when someone is feeling low or requires support. Bullying and insincere relationships are common problems; therefore, we should encourage genuine connections and avoid those who are fake. Trusting reliable friends and reporting troubling situations to a teacher can provide needed assistance.  

Kindness is a key component of a happy life. By being considerate toward others, we create an environment where people feel valued and can maintain a positive attitude. It is also important to resist external pressure that tries to dictate our behavior, to believe in our own abilities, and to persevere despite setbacks. If others claim we are incapable, we should distance ourselves from such negativity, especially when the critics are not true friends.  

At school, a bad mood may be blamed on a teacher or on the boredom of the curriculum. Instead of attributing the cause externally, we should focus on doing our best and cultivating a constructive mindset. By staying optimistic, helping peers, and surrounding ourselves with sincere individuals, we can keep our mood uplifted and contribute to a more joyful community.

Many people claim that astudent’s self‑esteem should be built on praise and good grades, especially before exams or when trying to pass a course. In reality, self‑esteem ought to arise from the effort a student puts into their work. When pupils strive to do their best, they develop confidence that comes from personal achievement rather than external approval.  

Students often show this dedication by attending extra lessons after missing class, staying late with teachers to finish missed assignments, and studying at home after school. Some of them bring a snack or eat breakfast to keep their energy up, because they know that a healthy body supports a focused mind. They understand that confidence is essential for learning, and they work hard to organize their tasks, such as arranging papers handed out by the teacher.  

Even though they may receive encouragement when they need a high grade, they first concentrate on their studies and then seek praise as a reward, not as the source of their self‑worth. They might skip leisure time to complete homework, practice exercises during short breaks, or visit the library to read additional material that will help them succeed.  

Thus, self‑esteem should be rooted in the hard work, perseverance, and personal responsibility that students demonstrate, rather than in the applause they receive for achieving good results.

People ought to decide for themselves.Everyone should be free to choose what to do, because making personal choices helps us understand what is best for us, gives us greater freedom, and often makes life smoother. When we decide on our own, we become more aware of our preferences and goals, which guides our actions more effectively. Knowing what we want also reduces uncertainty and the chance of making mistakes that could harm us. Another reason is that we enjoy more liberty when we set our own direction. Freedom means being able to follow the path we value, rather than simply obeying someone else’s plan. If we let others decide for us, we may lose the chance to pursue our own interests, and we may feel trapped. By contrast, self‑determination lets us act according to what we consider right, and it supports personal growth. It is also true that understanding another person’s choice can be difficult. Different people have different values, priorities, and experiences, so it is natural that we sometimes struggle to see why someone else would act a certain way. This gap in comprehension can cause confusion or conflict, especially when we try to follow another’s plan without fully grasping its meaning. Therefore, relying on our own judgment avoids the frustration that comes from misreading others’ intentions. Moreover, when we make our own decisions we are more likely to find life easier. Choosing what fits our needs and abilities means we are less likely to encounter obstacles that arise from mismatched expectations. For example, selecting a career that matches our skills reduces the risk of failure and increases satisfaction. Likewise, deciding how to spend our time allows us to balance work, leisure, and relationships in a way that feels comfortable. Taking responsibility for our choices also teaches us valuable lessons. When we make a mistake, we can analyze what went wrong and adjust our future actions, which strengthens our ability to handle challenges. This learning process is difficult to experience when decisions are made for us by others. In conclusion, each individual should have the right to decide for themselves. Personal choice leads to better self‑knowledge, greater freedom, and a more harmonious life. While it may be challenging to interpret others’ decisions, the benefits of self‑determination outweigh those difficulties. Therefore, encouraging everyone to make their own choices is the best way to promote personal happiness and fulfillment.

I agree with the statement because itaccurately reflects how many people experience anxiety and self‑doubt in their daily lives. First, anxiety is widespread; most individuals constantly think about how to handle work, responsibilities and personal problems, which creates a great deal of pressure. These mental pressures often leave lasting emotional impressions that people keep hidden, fearing judgment, so they cannot easily change their circumstances. Second, many people struggle to express their true feelings. They may feel confused, scared to share their inner state, and believe that any mistake will make things permanently wrong. This reluctance to reveal their inner experience prevents personal growth. Third, a lack of confidence in oneself is common. Some individuals rely on others to act for them, feeling ashamed to act independently, which limits their ability to accomplish tasks. Overall, the essay shows that anxiety, concealed emotions, and low self‑belief are pervasive obstacles that hinder people from improving their lives. While everything can change over time and we can strive to do our best, perfection is unattainable if we are constantly worried about mistakes or the opinions of others. By accepting our imperfections and moving forward with courage, we can lead more fulfilling lives.

In my view, collaborating in a team is generally more advantageous than working by yourself. When you have the right colleagues, you can accomplish a lot more, finish projects faster and often earn higher earnings together. Working alone can feel overwhelming because you must handle all the tasks yourself, and it is uncertain whether you will complete a large assignment without spending an entire day or even two. I remember a time when my group was assigned six pallets, with only two remaining; we completed them so quickly that we even considered leaving early, but we kept working together and finished the job. In contrast, when I tried to work solo on a single pallet, the workload was too heavy for me, especially since I was new to that area, and I needed assistance from others. These experiences show that teamwork provides several clear benefits, such as shared effort, quicker results and mutual support. However, for very small, straightforward tasks where you are confident you can finish them quickly, working alone may be sufficient. Overall, unless the task is simple and self‑contained, I believe that group work is the better option.

I agree with the statement thatbeing true to yourself is essential for becoming a good person. First, if you do not stay authentic, you cannot develop the character needed for a fulfilling life. Without sincerity, it is difficult to show genuine respect toward others, and a person lacking that quality tends to have a weak personality. Moreover, a lack of self‑honesty often leads to selfish behavior, which hinders the development of kindness.  

Second, people often fail to act kindly or show consideration because they are not confident in themselves. When you are self‑assured, you are more likely to treat others with generosity and to act as a positive example in your community. By being honest with yourself, you ensure that your actions are guided by kindness rather than selfishness. In addition, confident individuals inspire trust and cooperation among those around them.  

Third, the fear of being judged can stop individuals from acting morally. If you constantly compare yourself to others, you may feel inadequate and lose the motivation to behave well. Staying true to yourself removes the pressure to measure up to external standards, allowing you to focus on personal integrity instead of comparison. This inner confidence also helps you maintain consistent ethical behavior.  

In summary, authenticity is the foundation for respect, kindness, and generosity. When you remain true to who you are, you are better able to build a good character and contribute positively to the people around you.  

Therefore, cultivating authenticity not only improves personal well‑being but also strengthens relationships and community cohesion. By staying true to yourself, you create a ripple effect that encourages others to act with respect and generosity.
