Several school districts are exploring the possibility of letting students finish their studies in three years instead of the usual four. The main reason given is that families feel they cannot afford an extra year; they want their children to start working or paying taxes sooner, and many students themselves want to enter college as quickly as possible. To make this happen, many districts offer summer courses, which they consider an effective way to compress the curriculum. Parents often worry that an additional year would increase costs and delay their children's entry into the workforce, so they encourage early graduation. Students who plan to attend university see the three‑year path as a shortcut to higher education and future career opportunities.

In contrast, other districts prefer the traditional four‑year schedule. They argue that a longer period allows students to enroll in a wider range of subjects, retake classes that are difficult, and have more flexibility to balance academics with extracurricular activities such as sports, hobbies, and exam preparation. Some students choose to stay longer because they value the friendships they have built, enjoy collaborating with peers, or have teachers they particularly like, which makes the high‑school experience more appealing. Conversely, some families value the social development that occurs during the extra year, believing that staying longer helps young people mature and build lasting relationships.

Overall, the debate centers on whether a shorter, more intensive program better serves families’ financial goals and students’ academic ambitions, or whether the extended four‑year model provides greater academic variety and social benefits. Thus, while some districts push for accelerated graduation, others maintain the conventional timeline to accommodate diverse student needs.

I believe thattechnology has brought clear benefits to people's lives. It lets us discover new things and provides entertainment such as listening to music, watching films or playing video games. Moreover, technology is used in many practical ways: searching for employment, conducting business, doing online shopping, and supporting education. Many creators, including musicians and filmmakers, rely on digital tools to produce their work, and the reach of technology is so extensive that it is present everywhere for everyone. People often say that technology makes us sedentary, but this view is misleading. While some devices may reduce physical activity, modern equipment also supports sports and helps us locate information quickly. In addition, technology enables remote work and study, allowing us to stay at home while still earning a living or completing assignments. Students benefit from digital resources that assist in writing essays, taking online quizzes and preparing for exams. Schools themselves are increasingly equipped with computers and internet access, reflecting how deeply technology is integrated into learning environments. The main purpose of technology is to simplify tasks. For example, instead of using paper for official tests, we can complete them online, which saves time and resources. Although some gadgets, like smartphones, can be costly, their ability to connect us instantly—through calls or text messages—makes them indispensable. The expense is outweighed by the convenience of communicating without traveling, and by the many other advantages technology provides to both young and older individuals. From clothing and jewelry to homes and vehicles, almost everything we use involves technology. Its widespread presence shows how it has become a fundamental part of daily life, offering numerous benefits to society as a whole.

Suppose the school day were lengthened by two hours each day. I believe this would be undesirable. Adding two hours would leave students with no time for activities after school, forcing them to skip sports, clubs, and other interests. They would become exhausted, develop a dislike for school, and possibly stop attending regularly. With such a long day, they would have little opportunity to do homework, relax, or spend time with family, which would affect their overall‑well‑being. The extra hours would also make it harder to balance study and leisure, leading to higher stress and lower motivation. Consequently, many pupils might feel sleepy and unenthusiastic during class, reducing learning effectiveness. Their personal lives would become unbalanced; they would miss out on family interaction and personal hobbies, and they would be unable to pursue the sports or clubs they enjoy. In short, extending the school day by two hours would prevent students from living a normal, balanced life. Students would have less time for homework daily, which could lower their grades and cause significant additional pressure. Family members would also find it harder to spend quality time together, weakening their support and emotional connection. The overall stress of a longer day could lead to health problems and reduced motivation for learning. Consequently, many pupils might skip classes or feel disengaged, harming their education. Therefore, the school day should remain unchanged.

Thomas Jefferson’s words urge us not to remain idle, for a life of inaction is far less rewarding than striving toward meaningful goals. He suggests that the colonies must decide whether to stay under British rule or to unite and fight for true freedom. In his view, the British monarch cares little for the colonists; he extracts taxes while showing no concern for their welfare, prioritising profit and power above all else.  

If the colonists do not resist, they risk living as slaves, dependent on a ruler who exploits them. Their families—wives, children, and homes—would suffer from a lack of food, security, and dignity. The alternative, Jefferson argues, is to take up arms, even at the cost of bloodshed, because dying for liberty makes a person a free man rather than a subjugated slave.  

He also points out that the king’s claims to new lands are limited; nobles and friends can claim these territories, leaving the ordinary people without access. Consequently, the only viable path is to reject the king’s authority, refuse to pay taxes to a ruler who does not care for his subjects, and organize themselves under their own leadership. By voting for representatives who share their interests, the colonists can create a government that truly reflects their will.  

Finally, Jefferson emphasizes that no single individual can dominate the entire world; only through collective effort can the people achieve greatness. The vision he presents calls for unity, courage, and a determination to secure freedom for themselves and future generations.

I agree that we should stay trueto ourselves rather than letting others dictate how we behave. In today’s society people often judge our actions and ignore our mistakes, but personal authenticity is more important than external approval. We must remember that we have the power to transform the world, not the other way around. This mindset gives us the strength to pursue our goals and to set an example for the next generation.

Although I sometimes feel overwhelmed and doubt my ability to finish my studies this year, I have a son who looks up to me. I want to change the world for him so that he can become a better person and help those in need. By following our own dreams we inspire our children to chase theirs, and by supporting the poor and vulnerable we create a more compassionate society. Changing our character is essential if we hope to give our children a brighter future.

At school I learned that judging people based on skin colour, ethnicity or nationality is wrong; everyone is equal. I do not alter my way of thinking to become a so‑called ‘big’ person; I remain authentic because being myself is the only way to grow.

Life is brief, so we should not worry about what others think. Instead we should be happy, follow our dreams, and work hard to succeed. I aim to study at a university, pass my exams and become a role model my son can admire. If we believe in ourselves and act with purpose, we can indeed make the world a better place.

Winston Churchill, the former British prime minister, once claimed that true success means moving from one failure to the next without ever deciding to quit. He believed that a single failure cannot bring about a successful life, and many people share this view. In my opinion, his statement is accurate because progress often follows repeated attempts. I experienced this myself when I failed a test, yet I kept studying and eventually passed the exam. This shows that those who do not succeed at first can still achieve their goals if they keep trying and are given another chance, such as a retake. Churchill’s own experience supports this idea; he faced setbacks early in his career but persisted and later achieved great things. The drive to succeed also depends on personal determination. When we truly want to pass a class or accomplish any aim, we must keep working toward it and not give up. Moreover, many individuals struggle in school and need assistance, not only for themselves but also to support their families. Helping a mother or father often motivates people to overcome difficulties and reach their objectives. Overall, the message is clear: success is built on continual effort, learning from mistakes, and refusing to stop, a principle that Churchill highlighted and that remains relevant today.

Today I’ll talk about the differences between working in a group and working by yourself, and why I prefer the former. First, consider which option you enjoy more: collaborating with others or tackling tasks alone. I chose to work in a group, and here are the reasons why.

Working together with others brings several clear benefits. A team can share ideas and suggest different ways to approach a task, which often makes the work more interesting and enjoyable. When people combine their strengths, the overall quality of the result tends to improve. Moreover, collaboration creates a social atmosphere; you get to meet new people, build friendships, and develop confidence in speaking and interacting with others. These social skills are valuable not only in school but also in future careers.

There are also drawbacks to group work. Occasionally, one member may prefer to socialize rather than contribute, which can slow progress and create imbalance. Still, the advantages usually outweigh these occasional problems.

On the other hand, working alone offers its own set of strengths. When you are by yourself, you have complete freedom to decide how to do the work, without having to consider anyone else’s opinions. This independence can make the process faster, because you are not waiting for others to finish their parts. You also avoid potential conflicts or personality clashes that sometimes arise in groups.

However, solitude has significant downsides. Without a partner to exchange ideas, you may find it harder to generate creative solutions, and the work can become monotonous. Moreover, spending too much time alone can affect your mood and self‑image; you might feel isolated, and others may perceive you as unwilling to cooperate, which can lead to negative judgments or even depression. In contrast, teamwork teaches respect for diverse viewpoints and encourages you to adapt to different ways of doing things.

Another important point is that many tasks simply cannot be completed by a single person. For example, imagine you are driving and suddenly run out of fuel in the middle of the road. If you are used to working alone, you might try to push the car by yourself, risking injury or an accident. If you have learned to work in a group, you can ask others to help push, while some stop traffic and others call for assistance, making the situation safer and more manageable.

In addition, being part of a group helps you develop essential life skills. You learn how to cooperate, share responsibilities, and support one another. These experiences foster a sense of belonging and confidence that is difficult to achieve when you work in isolation. Friendships formed through teamwork often provide emotional support that enhances overall well‑being.

Finally, I believe that social interaction is a key factor in a successful life. When you collaborate with people you trust, you build relationships that can help you in many future situations, whether in school, work, or personal matters. By helping each other and respecting one another, we create a more positive environment for everyone.

In summary, while working alone can give you independence and speed, the benefits of teamwork—greater creativity, social connection, skill development, and emotional support—make it a more valuable approach. Therefore, I strongly advocate for working in groups, as it not only improves the quality of the work but also enriches our lives and prepares us for the collaborative world we will face.

In everyday life we often let otherpeople’s opinions determine how we behave and what kind of character we develop. This tendency is especially strong when the people involved are important to us—friends, family, or a partner—because we fear losing them or making them unhappy.  

A quote by John Lubbock reminds us that “your character is what you choose to make of it.” I agree with this view; it points out a truth that many ignore. We should not allow others’ judgments to shape us, nor should we let painful events define our personality. Each of us controls our own thoughts and reactions.  

My own life shows how powerful this idea is. Three of my closest friends let negative experiences shape their characters, and the outcomes were disastrous.  

The first friend grew up being physically punished by his parents, which made him angry and led him to use violence at school. The pattern continued, and many years later, after he married, he repeatedly hit his wife whenever she displeased him. In a final act of rage he killed her and then himself.  

The second friend was a young man who became involved with many women who only used his feelings. After growing tired of being treated superficially, he began to treat women the same way, losing his ability to love sincerely. Even when he finally found a woman who truly loved him, past hurts made him withdraw, and he remained alone.  

The third friend constantly tried to appear as the person he thought others would approve of, lying to himself to gain affection. This self‑deception left him unhappy and damaged his relationships.  

These stories illustrate that we are the sole architects of our character. If we allow external opinions or adverse events to dictate who we become, we risk ending up like my friends—broken, miserable, or destructive. Therefore, we must focus on our own choices and build a character that stems from our decisions rather than from what others think.

On the other hand, a bad reason is that external pressures such as family duties or financial needs can force a young student to stop pursuing his chosen path, which is a clear drawback. Such pressure often forces young people to work long hours, which can reduce their study time and increase stress, making it harder to stay focused on their academic goals. For instance, a 17‑year‑old in the tenth grade who works to support a single mother may have to pause his studies, yet he can later return to finish his education. Young students also tend to imagine more, to think that everything is possible, and thus they acquire greater prospects for later success, since their confidence in limitless potential encourages them to explore diverse fields. In short, while circumstances can interrupt a student’s journey, age itself is not a barrier; a young person can achieve his goals if he permits himself to do so, making youth the foundation for tomorrow. Therefore, while early career decisions may be challenged by external demands, the advantages of youthful optimism and flexibility make it a worthwhile path for many students to pursue. In the end, the freedom to explore and the confidence to adapt give young learners the best chance to succeed in whatever career they eventually select.

Ralph Waldo Emersononce claimed that being yourself in a world that constantly pushes you to become something else is the greatest achievement. I agree with this statement. In today’s society many people strive to express their individuality, whether they are musicians, painters, or teachers. For example, a teacher might devise a fresh method of instruction that no one has tried before, thereby creating a distinctive style. A teenager choosing a college major, for instance, is deciding how to add value to the world. Others may criticize that choice, but ultimately the decision belongs to the individual. In short, embracing who we truly are, despite pressure and criticism, is the greatest accomplishment.

Mobile phones can serveas useful tools in the classroom when they are employed for learning purposes. Many schools now permit limited use of devices, recognizing that they can increase student engagement and provide quick access to information. Teachers often encourage students to use their phones for research, accessing educational apps, or performing calculations, which can make lessons more interactive and help learners retrieve information instantly. This flexibility allows teachers to design activities that incorporate quick fact‑finding or group sharing, which can enhance teamwork and keep students actively involved.  

Nevertheless, the same freedom can lead to distraction if students turn to games, social media, or messaging during class time. I have observed classmates who, instead of searching for a historical biography, spent the period scrolling through Instagram or playing mobile games, which not only wastes their own study time but also disrupts peers and reduces overall classroom focus. Such behavior often results in lower participation and can negatively affect the teacher’s ability to manage the lesson. When such distractions occur, teachers may have to pause the lesson to refocus the class, which reduces instructional time.  

In my own experience, a mobile phone has been a real help. While reading an English text, I encountered an unfamiliar word; a quick search on my phone gave me the definition instantly, allowing me to continue understanding the passage. The same device also assists me in mathematics, where I sometimes need to decode symbols that are not clear on the board, and the calculator function saves time. Moreover, because I have limited time to adapt to this country, I often need to look up new vocabulary or clarify instructions quickly, which the phone makes possible without delaying the class.  

Therefore, the impact of cell phones in school depends largely on how students choose to use them. When the devices are used responsibly, they become valuable resources that support learning and make schoolwork more engaging. It is the responsibility of each learner to respect the teacher’s guidelines and to avoid activities that distract from the lesson, ensuring that grades do not suffer. By feeling grateful for the opportunity to use technology, students can turn a potential distraction into a powerful aid for their education.

In my science lesson theteacher showed a fire that changed colour, demonstrating a chemical reaction. The colour shift proved that the substances were transforming into new materials, which is the essence of a chemical change. Watching the experiment made clear how careful observation and proper equipment can reveal hidden processes in the world around us.

Science, for me, is more than a subject; it is a passion that drives people to work hard for many years. Those who pursue it usually attend school and later university, where they learn systematic methods, conduct experiments, and pass assessments. The dedication required to become a scientist shows that the field is built on continual study and disciplined effort.

Understanding scientific notation also proved useful when I considered a future career as a nurse. To qualify, I would need four years of college followed by four years of specialised nursing training. The same principle of progressive study applies to many scientific professions, and mastering tools such as scientific notation helps handle large or tiny numbers that appear in research and everyday calculations.

The excitement of experimenting is what keeps many scientists motivated. I enjoy the idea of being a teacher, because sharing knowledge and watching others discover can be as rewarding as the experiments themselves. Small actsof kindness can change someone's day for the better. Even a brief compliment or a friendly smile can lift a person's spirits, showing that tiny gestures have a big impact. A simple encouraging word or a friendly smile can lift a person's spirits, while saying something reassuring like “everything will be fine” can give them hope and motivation. In contrast, harsh or negative remarks may make a person feel worthless and could push them toward despair, even thoughts of ending their life, because they begin to believe they have no purpose. Feeling insignificant can lead to deep sadness and a loss of confidence, which sometimes pushes individuals to consider suicide.  

People differ: some are compassionate, others are hostile. We decide which kind of person we want to become, and no one can force us to act against our own values. If we choose cruelty, we only cause pain to ourselves as well as to others; we may become indifferent, avoid contact, or reject help that is offered. Unkind behavior often creates a cycle where the hurt we inflict on others eventually turns back on us, leading to isolation and a reluctance to accept support.  

Treating everyone with respect and kindness, no matter who they are, makes the world less hostile and more supportive. Good people still exist, and they show that kindness and respect are essential for building strong relationships. Helping a friend in both happy and difficult moments, offering advice, and providing comfort are all expressions of genuine care. Respect fosters trust and encourages people to open up and share their feelings.  

Simple phrases such as “everything will be okay” can reassure someone and remind them of the positive side of life. By being kind to one another, we create an environment where people feel valued, are more likely to smile, and can support each other. Consistent kindness builds a community where hope replaces fear, and where everyone has the chance to thrive.

The first impression is remarkably resistant to change. I believe that once an initial impression is formed, it is very difficult to alter. This view is supported by the way we react instantly to new people or situations. For example, when a friend unexpectedly surprises me with a kind gesture, my immediate response is a broad smile because I feel genuinely happy in that moment. My mind does not have time to consider other possibilities; the reaction is immediate and powerful. The same happens when someone does something unexpectedly positive for a family member – I am surprised and delighted, and the feeling stays with me.

Because the initial reaction is so strong, it creates a lasting impression that is hard to modify. Even if later events contradict the first impression, the original impression remains dominant. For instance, a day that starts badly can later turn into a good one if a loved one or a partner does something thoughtful. Even though the circumstances improve, the original impression – the immediate feeling of surprise or disappointment – stays with me. I rarely pause to rethink the situation; the first impression dominates my perception.

The reason for this persistence lies in the way our minds record information. The first impression is formed quickly, often before we have time to analyse the situation fully. Consequently, it becomes a reference point that shapes subsequent judgments. Even when later evidence suggests a different reality, the original impression remains dominant because it was formed at a time when we were most emotionally engaged.

In conclusion, the first impression is a powerful and enduring impression that is difficult to change. It is formed instantly and remains influential even when circumstances change. This persistence is a natural part of how we perceive the world, and it explains why the first impression remains a significant factor in our lives.

The authorities should also look after homeless adolescents, many of whom leave school early. Those who abandon their studies often struggle to find employment and may end up living on the streets, where they receive no support. A curfew could give these youths a chance to obtain a modest job and become productive members of society. Their setbacks usually stem from neglecting education, being lazy, skipping classes, poor attitudes, disrespect, and excessive reliance on mobile devices. If they refuse to change, they risk falling into harmful paths, but I remain hopeful that they will improve and succeed in the future.

I agree thathelping others is essential. Being honest and sincere is important, especially when someone is struggling with mental health issues such as depression. In such cases, it is crucial to reach out, talk to the person, and show that you care. For example, my friend who suffers from depression does not need advice that tells him nothing will change; instead, spending time together, playing soccer, or doing other activities can lift his spirits. I try to give my friends courage and support, because nobody knows how much mental pain they may be experiencing. Helping others also feels good for the helper; after assisting someone, I often feel a sense of satisfaction that improves my own mood. Some people claim they do not need help, but they may actually need more support, since mental health challenges can be complex and difficult to manage. Psychologists face a demanding job, dealing with many different problems, which can be emotionally draining, yet they persist in trying to help each person they encounter.

I disagree with the proposal to bar students from sports or any extracurricular activities unless they maintain at least a B average in every class. It would be very difficult for most pupils to achieve a B in all subjects, and many of them are passionate about playing sports or joining clubs. If the rule were applied, a student who currently earns a C would find it easier to raise that grade to a C+ than to push all of his or her marks up to a B, especially when the requirement concerns every single course. Consequently, the policy would force students to aim for a B in each subject just to stay on the team, which is unrealistic.  

I also think that students who receive a C are still doing a decent job in class; they are trying hard and can pass the year with a C. In my view, we should allow those with C, B and A to participate in sports, while only restricting those who are failing, i.e., students with D or F. Those low‑performing learners are unlikely to succeed academically, and preventing them from playing might actually harm their motivation and attendance, causing them to fall further behind.  

The suggestion that a C‑grade student should be cut from activities because a B is required ignores the effort many of them put in. They are already working hard to keep their grades up, and adding the extra pressure of a universal B requirement would not make them perform better; it would only increase stress. Moreover, the rule would unfairly penalize students who are on the borderline of passing, while it does nothing to address the real problem of students who are already failing.  

In conclusion, I do not support the idea of linking sports participation to a minimum B average. Instead, schools should focus on supporting struggling learners with targeted help, and keep extracurricular opportunities open for students who are passing, regardless of whether they have a C, B or A.

For instance, in my own class the teacher asked us to work in groups. I had to attend the session and take part. During the group work we exchanged ideas, helped each other, and added contributions to the project. The teacher emphasized that simply showing up was already a step toward improvement; if we missed a meeting we could still catch up later. Mistakes were not seen as failures; they provided opportunities to do better in the next attempt, and the minister’s role was to guide us through this process. Her encouragement motivated us to stay focused, and her willingness to listen made us feel valued, which increased our confidence in contributing ideas.

Beyond the classroom, I have observed many newcomers to this country who arrive seeking better prospects that are unavailable at home. They must learn a new language, which is challenging, yet they try their best, attend classes, and practice regularly in order to improve their future prospects. Some students face long histories of hardship: they work after school to pay rent, have limited time to rest, and therefore struggle to keep up with studies. Nevertheless, many of them demonstrate how far they can progress, showing determination and effort.

Although understanding everything is sometimes difficult, I devote time each evening to study, reading books and practicing English. Reading for just twenty minutes a day helps me expand my vocabulary and improves my pronunciation, allowing me to read more quickly.

Overall, I consider myself someone who enjoys helping others, sharing new ideas, and discussing future plans. I am grateful for the program that supports us and for the teacher who continually offers new knowledge. Their guidance has been essential to my learning journey. The support I received helped me develop not only language skills but also a sense of responsibility toward my peers. I hope my experience can inspire others to keep striving today.

It is disturbing thatmany individuals are subjected to bullying by others, a situation I find hard to comprehend. The reasons often seem to be based on physical appearance, such as skin colour, or on perceived differences, a sense of superiority, or even financial advantage. Those who are bullied may become so distressed that they contemplate ending their lives, which is a tragic outcome. Meanwhile, the aggressors continue their behavior without stopping until a serious incident occurs, prompting the question of why this persists. I recognize that the experience of being bullied is painful, and it is equally distressing to witness someone inflict such harm on others. The victims deserve support, and the perpetrators should understand that their actions are unacceptable. Bullying is not only hurtful; it can lead to severe consequences, including legal action. In many places, repeated harassment can result in imprisonment, especially when it contributes to self‑harm or other dangerous behavior. To address this problem, we must work together to stop bullying. Education, empathy, and clear policies can help create safer environments, whether at school, work, or online. Everyone has a responsibility to intervene, support the vulnerable, and hold the bullies accountable. Schools, families, and community groups should promote respect and teach conflict‑resolution skills to prevent the cycle of aggression. By standing up for those who are targeted, we can build a culture where kindness replaces intimidation for everyone today.

Technology is a positivedevelopment because it lets us shop, read, and play from the comfort of our own homes. With just a few clicks we can browse online stores, download books, and join multiplayer games where we meet new people. For many who cannot drive or leave their houses, the internet provides a way to stay in contact with friends and relatives far away, using phones or video calls. Online platforms also let us find companions to chat with and participate in games together, turning solitary time into social interaction.

Many individuals find that technology supports learning. Students can use digital tools at school, complete assignments, and access educational resources that would otherwise be difficult to obtain. Older adults can read e‑books on a wide range of topics such as history, automobiles, or sports, and they can learn how to operate devices so they can call family members or friends online. The ability to order food for delivery means we can have meals without going out, and the web also offers assistance with tasks like filing taxes, either by ourselves or through professional services.

Some critics argue that technology reduces face‑to‑face interaction and keeps people from going out. While it is true that some may prefer to stay indoors, others benefit from the flexibility of working or studying from home, which avoids the need for constant social conversation. For people who feel anxious about meeting others, online communication can be a less intimidating way to connect, allowing them to build confidence before meeting in person.

The advantages of technology extend to entertainment and income. There are countless online games that can be played solo or with others, and many can be downloaded for offline use. Young people often spend hours gaming, improving their skills and, in some cases, earning money through streaming or competition. Freelancers can also earn a living by using digital platforms, and creators can monetize their content, showing that technology can be a source of income as well as leisure.

Overall, technology makes daily tasks quicker and easier, from managing household chores to accessing information. Online shopping saves time and money because we can compare prices, read reviews, and have items delivered directly to our doorstep. E‑books and digital libraries give us instant access to countless titles, so we no longer need to carry heavy physical books. In the world of gaming, communities form around shared interests, allowing players to cooperate, compete, and build lasting friendships without leaving home. Remote work has become common, letting people manage their careers while balancing personal responsibilities, which is especially helpful for those who prefer a quieter environment. For seniors, video calls make it easy to see loved ones, reducing feelings of isolation and keeping them mentally active. The internet also simplifies financial tasks; many people use online tools to file taxes, track expenses, or receive advice from professionals without visiting a office. People who feel shy in face‑to‑face situations can practice conversation skills through chat rooms or video chats before meeting in person, which builds confidence. Moreover, the ability to earn income through freelance platforms, content creation, or online gaming provides new employment opportunities for young adults and retirees alike. All these advantages show that technology enhances daily life, supports learning at any age, and creates social and economic possibilities that improve overall well‑being.

High‑school pupils ought to avoid accelerated three‑year graduation schemes. Learners enrolled in such tracks usually attend extra classes after regular hours or during summer breaks, which prevents them from enrolling in a variety of elective subjects such as foreign languages, nutrition, music, computer skills or health education. As a result they have fewer hours for homework, family interaction and leisure activities, including the enjoyment of summer vacation. Moreover, they may be forced to repeat the same course—like taking English 9 and English 10 simultaneously—leaving little room for diverse learning experiences. While some argue that early graduation lets students reach college credits sooner or enter the workforce earlier, those who pursue this path are more likely to feel overwhelmed, lose motivation, or even drop out because the accelerated schedule creates constant pressure. In contrast, the conventional four‑year program provides a balanced pace that supports academic success and personal well‑being. Therefore, students should refrain from opting for early graduation programs.

Here are three reasons why students should not attend classes online from home. First, learning at home is difficult because there is no teacher present to answer questions or give immediate help; in a classroom you can raise your hand and receive clarification right away, while at home you are left to figure everything out on your own. Second, students who are high‑achieving might consider taking courses online at home so they can finish school early and start working, but this does not mean that all learners should be forced to study remotely. Third, online learning may be convenient for some children, yet many parents prefer their children to attend school in person, and teachers often find a physical classroom easier to manage. Finally, offering all high‑school courses online would allow students to copy from one another, which undermines the quality of learning. Moreover, the lack of face‑to‑face interaction can reduce motivation and make it harder for teachers to monitor progress. In addition, students who struggle with self‑discipline may fall behind, and the absence of a structured schedule can lead to procrastination. Finally, the possibility of copying among students creates a false sense of achievement and damages the credibility of the education system. Teachers cannot provide personalized feedback when they are not physically present, which makes it difficult for students to improve their weak areas. Parents also worry that online learning reduces social interaction and may affect the development of communication skills. In a classroom, students can discuss ideas, ask questions, and learn from their peers, which enriches the learning experience and helps them develop critical thinking skills. Therefore, while online options can be useful in limited situations, the overall benefit of keeping traditional in‑person instruction is greater. Students benefit from direct interaction with teachers and classmates, which supports deeper understanding and stronger retention of material. A balanced approach that combines in‑person teaching with occasional online resources can meet diverse needs without sacrificing educational quality.

Albert Einstein once saidthat imagination is more important than knowledge. I disagree with this claim. In my view, knowledge is more essential because it underpins the way we think and act. Imagination may spark ideas, but without a solid base of knowledge it cannot be turned into something useful.

First, clear thinking requires prior understanding. If we try to imagine a situation without knowing the relevant facts, we cannot predict what will happen or decide how to proceed. When we plan a story, we need to know the setting, characters, and plot before we can shape them. Only after gathering the necessary information can we use imagination to craft a coherent narrative.

Second, many practical activities depend on knowledge. At a job, a person must know the tasks for the day; in school, a scientist must understand a plant before examining it. Even in everyday life, such as a police investigation, knowledge of the scene, evidence, and suspects is essential for solving the case. Imagination alone cannot replace this factual grounding.

Third, people perceive the world in different ways, but accurate interpretation comes from knowledge. When we look at a picture, prior knowledge helps us notice details and understand context more precisely. This makes tasks easier and more reliable.

Moreover, knowledge allows us to communicate ideas clearly. The words we use have specific meanings that depend on our understanding of the subject. Without this, even the most vivid imagination can be misunderstood.

In addition, knowledge helps us learn from experience. By remembering what has happened before, we can make better decisions in new situations. Imagination may picture possibilities, but knowledge tells us which possibilities are realistic.

Finally, imagination is valuable for creativity, but it works best when supported by knowledge. The two are complementary, yet knowledge supplies the framework that allows imagination to be applied effectively. Therefore, I maintain that knowledge is more important than imagination.

ThomasJefferson argued that we should do more because engaging in varied activities can spark students' interest and help them acquire the information they need. He suggests that without such activities, students may think differently about school and miss out on valuable experiences. Another approach is to create new sports or activities that are enjoyable, allowing students to relieve stress. When young people are constantly occupied, they may lose the chance to enjoy their youth, focusing solely on tasks that are beneficial but not always enjoyable. Inactivity, however, can also be problematic, as it often leads to spending all one's time alone and neglecting family time. Moreover, without regular activity, students may become bored and lose motivation, which can hinder their academic and personal growth. Jefferson believed that a diverse range of pursuits keeps the mind active and prevents the stagnation that comes from doing nothing. By balancing work and leisure, young people can develop discipline, confidence, and a sense of purpose. If you have many aspirations and want to achieve them, pursuing activities you enjoy enables you to accomplish more, producing wonderful results. Responsibility also plays a key role; for example, committing to a sport requires daily effort if you aim to become an excellent player or take on a challenge. Taking responsibility for one's performance, whether in sport or study, builds character and prepares individuals for future challenges. Therefore, focusing and working hard are essential; once you find a goal that brings you happiness, you can see the positive outcomes. Jefferson wrote these words to inspire creativity, enthusiasm, and a love for life, urging us to be adaptable and try many things. He encourages us to give our best, never surrender, and remain strong despite difficulties, keeping our heads high. According to Jefferson, doing what you enjoy leads to satisfying results and greater responsibility. My view aligns with his: explore the options available, pursue what you love, and remember never to give up, as Jefferson exemplifies perseverance and dedication.

I personally admire trees; they look charming, and I enjoy walking under their cool canopy on hot days. The green foliage also makes river trips more pleasant, allowing families and friends to spend relaxing time together.  

Therefore, I agree with the board’s initiative, as it encourages environmental stewardship, teaches responsibility, and creates a more pleasant setting for the whole community.

Life is a series of experiences that shape the way we think and act. The path we follow — whether it moves from easy circumstances to harder ones — determines many of the choices we make. When we face situations that repeat themselves, the way we handle them influences our decisions, and observing others who have walked a similar road can provide inspiration and help us create positive outcomes. After going through numerous challenges, looking to someone else’s life for motivation can be especially useful.

People differ in how they respond to examples. Sometimes the actions or stories of others do not spark inspiration, yet they can still give us confidence when we feel uncertain about what to do. Influence is not automatic; it depends on the individual’s mindset. There are moments when we do not need external encouragement and can rely on our own judgment to improve our situation.

As humans, we inevitably make mistakes, and learning from them is essential. While many sources can inspire us, there are times when we do not think of anyone to look up to. Recognizing that someone else has faced a similar circumstance does not mean their approach will work for us; we should treat their experience as a model to adapt, extracting the useful parts and discarding the rest.

Occasionally, shared experiences are merely coincidental, and we may feel identified with another person’s story without being inspired. Still, seeing how different people tackle the same problem can show us that multiple strategies exist. When we notice that someone else has navigated a comparable situation, we may feel a connection that motivates us, especially if we realize we are not alone.

The actions of others can also shape our own feelings. Knowing that another person has endured a similar hardship can reassure us that we, too, can overcome it. At times we need an example to boost our confidence or to feel better about ourselves; having someone who has succeeded despite comparable obstacles can provide that reassurance.

Good and bad moments are part of life, and difficult experiences can turn a person into a source of inspiration for others. While behavior can affect those around us, the impact varies according to each person’s attitudes, character, and interpretation. Therefore, being an inspiration is valuable because it allows others to see our journey, feel encouraged, and recognize that they, too, can achieve positive change.

Haveyou ever made someone feel upset? Some individuals prefer to be truthful with their friends or relatives, while others avoid honesty because they fear it may cause pain. Many people keep quiet with their friends, fearing that the truth could end the relationship permanently. I disagree with the idea that honesty must always be practiced. It is not necessary to tell the whole truth at every moment; sometimes withholding information protects the other person. When someone must convey the truth, the situation can be difficult. They worry that their words may hurt the other’s feelings or damage the friendship, and they may even fear that the other will not forgive them. Still, there are occasions when speaking honestly is essential, for example when you need to express how you truly feel toward a person or point out a behavior you dislike. In those cases, being truthful allows both parties to understand each other better. Not everyone welcomes the truth. Some friends dislike hearing criticism, whereas others appreciate it because it helps them improve and strengthens the bond. Trust grows when people feel they can rely on one another’s honesty, leading to deeper, more enjoyable friendships. If you cannot be honest, it is better to stay silent rather than say something meaningless. However, there will be moments when honesty is required, though not constantly. Think carefully before you speak, aiming for a constructive outcome rather than a perfect plan. The result may be positive, negative, or somewhere in between, but the decision to be truthful should be guided by the situation, not by a rigid rule. Therefore, choose honesty wisely, considering both your feelings and those of your friends.

In myview, self‑esteem grows when a person receives praise, and teachers are the most effective source of such encouragement. A student who hears positive remarks from a teacher feels valued and is more likely to develop confidence in his or her abilities.  

Many learners are sensitive to what others say, so they do not want their parents to point out their shortcomings. When a teacher offers criticism, the reaction can be deep sadness, because no one possesses an invincible mindset; we are all human and vulnerable. When children feel judged, they may withdraw, which reduces their willingness to participate and learn.  

Consequently, the best approach is to motivate rather than rebuke. Instead of saying “you are wrong,” one might respond, “I believe you can do better.” This kind of supportive language respects the student’s fragility and acknowledges that they may think differently or place blame elsewhere.  

Progress in learning is a slow, steady process. Education should be cultivated gradually, allowing each small achievement to reinforce the next. Harsh criticism only hinders growth, while consistent encouragement helps the child become stronger. Such a supportive atmosphere also encourages perseverance and curiosity.  

Therefore, I think it is useful to praise both oneself and peers, to say “you are good” and “you can improve.” Such affirmation builds self‑confidence, enabling a person to remain resilient regardless of external opinions. In short, fostering a positive environment is essential for the healthy development of young minds.

Connecting with both positive and negative contacts is useful: the bad ones may reveal important warnings, while the good ones can share beneficial habits. Having only a few reliable contacts is preferable to being isolated and doing everything alone.  

A private life can be satisfying, yet it should not become completely closed off. We ought to converse with others occasionally, but we must also recognize that not everyone provides accurate information. Some people may give false data, which could lead to trouble, even involving the police. Consequently, we should not trust everyone blindly. Not all individuals seek perfection, and we must ask questions, gather information, and decide whether to keep or discard a contact based on its value. In short, sharing knowledge, using technology wisely, staying informed, and exercising caution are the keys to a balanced life.

I believe it is beneficial for every student to receive guidance about future careers early, even before finishing high school. First, gaining insight into a profession at a younger age helps learners feel prepared when they finally graduate, because they will already know what path they wish to follow. This reduces the anxiety that often follows graduation, since they will not have to scramble to choose a field of study or a job. Moreover, early exposure can foster a sense of responsibility, as students become more aware of the consequences of their choices. On the other hand, some pupils resist this approach; they prefer to complete their secondary education first and use the four years after school to explore options before committing to a specific career. In short, initiating career awareness at an earlier stage is not detrimental; it can boost confidence and readiness, although a portion of students still prefers to delay such decisions until after graduation.

Technology createsan uninterrupted thread that ties individuals together across the globe, forming a virtual community where people can exchange information instantly through digital channels. This form of interaction not only reduces the time needed for contact but also offers the most convenient way to stay connected, especially for those living far apart, since a message can be sent in just a few seconds. The novelty of modern technology is also enjoyable, much like playing a popular video game that showcases its innovative capabilities. It does not impose restrictions on how people can relate to one another; instead, it enables the formation of new relationships via reputable online platforms. The speed of connection between distant users is rapid, and the financial cost of maintaining contact is low. Consequently, technology serves as a remedy for the scarcity of communication that some observers mistakenly attribute to a small minority who have never adopted these tools. Researchers who have examined the issue conclude that technology represents the most effective means of encouraging people to interact. The primary aim of technological development is to simplify human life and provide a robust channel for worldwide interaction. Designers intended to achieve the quickest possible exchange between individuals, eliminating the need for lengthy travel to meet family members for conversation. The emergence of mobile phones exemplifies this transformation, allowing people to communicate without the necessity of physical presence. Another notable advancement is the global news system, which keeps people informed about recent events anywhere on the planet. In addition to saving time, technology reduces the expense of staying in touch, making it accessible to anyone willing to use the fastest available connection. Its appeal is comparable to that of a video game, and it is offered in versions tailored to different age groups and proficiency levels. Nowadays, technology permeates nearly every aspect of daily existence. Nevertheless, a minority of individuals argue that advanced technological systems provide little benefit. Their skepticism often arises from a lack of firsthand experience with the tools or from insufficient understanding of how to employ them effectively. In many cases, people lack the basic knowledge—such as literacy, numeracy, and listening skills—that is required to exploit technology fully. Therefore, education plays a crucial role: by teaching people how to use digital devices and online services, they can reap the advantages of connectivity. In turn, technology facilitates a more convenient lifestyle and easier communication, completing a reciprocal relationship between learning and digital use.

Dowe achieve more when we are constantly occupied, or can periods of inactivity also be valuable? I believe that remaining active throughout the school year is advantageous, because it helps us develop skills and, through repeated practice, become proficient.  

First, regular activity enhances our capabilities. Students who play sports regularly gain greater stamina and maintain better health, which translates into improved concentration and performance in class. When we stay engaged in school tasks—whether participating in lessons, joining a project, or taking part in a team—we reinforce what we have learned and become quicker and more confident the next time a similar task arises. This continuous involvement also makes us more attractive to future employers, who value diligent and adaptable workers, and it provides references from teachers or community supervisors who can attest to our achievements.  

Some people argue that staying inactive prevents exhaustion and delays the signs of aging, suggesting that constant activity might be counter‑productive. While it is true that rest is necessary, complete inactivity does not promote progress. Pupils who avoid sports or extracurricular programs may have extra time for studying, yet they miss out on the physical and social benefits that activity provides. Moreover, being active does not mean working nonstop; it simply means balancing work with adequate rest, such as proper sleep and nutrition, which enable us to be energetic during school hours.  

In addition, active participation brings other rewards. Schools often grant credits for sports or competition results, and winning can bring recognition and prizes. Engaging in clubs, drama, announcements, or community service creates new experiences, expands our social circle, and fosters friendships with peers who share similar interests. These connections can be valuable both during school and later in life.  

Finally, staying active supports our long‑term goals. When we consistently apply effort, we are more likely to meet the objectives we set for the school year and beyond. This habit not only improves our academic results but also prepares us for higher education and the workforce, where the same drive can lead to better job prospects and higher earnings. In short, active involvement benefits us directly and also inspires those around us, showing that we are committed to growth rather than remaining complacent. Therefore, students should strive to be actively involved in school life, recognizing that participation is a personal choice rather than an obligation.

Winston Churchill once claimed that truesuccess means moving from one failure to the next while keeping enthusiasm alive. I disagree with this view because the statement implies that one should simply keep trying without ever losing motivation, which does not reflect the reality of many people’s experiences.  

First, when a person has suffered many setbacks, it is natural to wonder whether continuing is worthwhile. If there is no clear end in sight, the effort can feel endless and demotivating. The quote suggests that enthusiasm should never fade, yet in practice many individuals find that repeated failure without visible progress erodes their confidence and makes it harder to stay optimistic.  

Second, failure is an inevitable part of the human condition. Every person, regardless of background, encounters obstacles that test their resolve. When someone refuses to make another attempt, it is clear that the outcome will remain negative, and the chance to achieve a positive result disappears. The decision to persist or to stop rests entirely on the individual’s own will.  

My own position is that a strong sense of purpose can overcome the fear of repeated failure. If a person truly wants to reach a goal, they must keep their enthusiasm alive and be willing to try again, even after setbacks. For example, I have set a goal to finish my degree and obtain a diploma, and I plan to continue my studies after graduation. My enthusiasm for learning keeps me moving forward, and when I encounter difficulties I remind myself that each attempt brings me closer to the final achievement. This mindset shows that perseverance, combined with genuine interest, can turn failure into a stepping stone rather than a dead end.  

It is also important to recognize that negative thinking can become a self‑fulfilling prophecy. If a person convinces themselves that they will never succeed, they are less likely to take the necessary actions. Conversely, believing that one can improve and that each failure provides useful feedback helps maintain motivation. The responsibility for this attitude lies within each person; no external force can force someone to keep trying unless they themselves choose to do so.  

Finally, the idea that every failure has a solution is overly simplistic. Some problems truly have no answer, and insisting that a solution must exist can lead to frustration. Nevertheless, the right to try again remains valid. Even when a path seems blocked, a different approach or a new perspective may reveal a way forward. Companies that face bankruptcy, for instance, often look for innovative ways to restructure and survive; they do not claim that failure is impossible to overcome.  

In conclusion, while Churchill’s quotation highlights the value of persistence, it underestimates the emotional toll of continual setbacks. Maintaining enthusiasm does not mean blindly repeating the same actions; it means staying motivated, believing in one’s ability to improve, and being willing to adapt. By preserving hope and actively seeking solutions, individuals can turn failure into a meaningful part of their journey toward success.

I hope thismessage finds you well. The following statement, taken from the given prompt, claims that the first impressions are almost impossible to change, and I fully agree with it. Throughout our lives, the very first impression we receive about a person, object, or situation tends to remain vivid and lasting, influencing how we think and feel for a long time.

It is often difficult to erase that initial feeling because it is formed at a moment when we are especially receptive. For example, when a child of about six years old sees a new toy such as a Spider‑Man figure and his parents purchase it, his excitement is intense. That day becomes a memorable event that stays in his mind, and the positive impression of the toy is hardly forgotten. Such experiences show how a first impression can become a permanent mark on a person’s life.

The central idea of the statement is that the way we initially feel about something shapes our overall perception. When the first impression is pleasant, we tend to view the subject positively; when it is negative, the opposite occurs. This occurs especially when the event happens at an appropriate moment and with genuine intention, because the emotions attached to it are strong.

First impressions are hard to change because they become part of our personal narrative. The first time we encounter a situation, we quickly assign importance to it, and that importance is stored in our memory. Consequently, it is nearly impossible to alter that initial impact later on.

I can illustrate this with my own experience. When I was very young, my family bought me a small bicycle. The joy I felt that day was overwhelming, and the happiness associated with that first ride is still vivid in my mind. That early positive impression has stayed with me and influences how I view new experiences involving bikes or childhood memories.

The purpose of this writing is to show how crucial the first impression is for everyone. People who disagree with the statement may not realize how deeply the initial feeling can affect their decisions, relationships, and overall outlook. By recognizing the power of that first impression, we can become more aware of the lasting impact it has.

Consider a few common situations: receiving a brand‑new toy from parents, stepping onto a beach for the first time and seeing the endless water, or attending the first day of school. In each case, the initial reaction creates a strong impression that remains with us. Even if later events are mixed, the original feeling often dominates our recollection.

Understanding this helps us communicate better with others and make more thoughtful choices. We can explain to friends or family why a particular first impression matters, and we can reflect on how our early experiences shape our present attitudes. In doing so, we acknowledge the significance of those early moments and the role they play in our lives.

In conclusion, the statement that first impressions are almost impossible to change is well supported by everyday examples and personal experience. The initial feeling we form about something tends to stay with us, influencing our thoughts and actions for the rest of our lives. Therefore, I firmly agree that first impressions hold great importance for all people.

Sincerely,

Parentsfrequently share guidance that shows us how to act responsibly. For instance, when a child works alongside his father, the father’s suggestions help the youngster understand what is right and what is wrong. This kind of counsel teaches us to make choices that improve our lives.

Learning from several sources is valuable because each person can point out different pitfalls. If we listen to more than one person, we are less likely to fall into trouble and can become better students or children. Advice received at school is especially useful; when teachers give us direction, we tend to study harder and achieve higher grades. A gym teacher, for example, may warn us against laziness or cheating, explaining that poor performance leads to low marks and disciplinary action. Paying attention to such guidance helps us perform well on tests, because the teacher’s instructions prepare us for the exam.

Friends also offer advice both inside and outside the classroom. When they speak to us about school matters, it is usually because they care about our future and want us to succeed. Their suggestions about lifestyle choices aim to make us happier and healthier, and they may also give us tips on sports, encouraging us to play fairly and strive for victory. The coach’s instructions, for example, teach us how to win games and work together, which benefits the whole team.

Beyond education, advice plays a role in everyday decisions, such as shopping. When we consider buying something, seeking someone’s opinion helps us decide whether the product is worthwhile or not. Likewise, guidance about food choices can protect our health; without it, we might eat something harmful and face health problems. People who ignore useful advice may find themselves in trouble, especially if their actions affect their bodies negatively.

In academic subjects like mathematics, both teachers and classmates can provide helpful tips. Students often share strategies for solving problems, and teachers demonstrate methods for completing assignments and preparing for upcoming tests. This collective advice makes learning more effective.

Even everyday situations, such as riding a bus, benefit from guidance. A bus driver’s instructions on proper behavior help maintain order; without them, passengers might act recklessly, increasing the risk of accidents. Therefore, offering advice in all areas of life promotes safety and encourages good conduct.

In summary, advice from parents, teachers, friends, coaches, and other trusted individuals is essential. It equips us with the knowledge to make sound decisions, improves our academic performance, enhances our well‑being, and keeps us safe. Listening to and acting on this guidance allows us to grow into responsible, successful individuals.

Most schools enroll more than ahundred pupils, and in many high schools the curriculum is light, with a large proportion of art and music classes rather than demanding subjects. Consequently, school programs already require summer sessions for students who have not mastered essential material. Imposing a rule that forces learners to complete high school more quickly—by adding summer or evening courses and thereby sacrificing elective options—would be unwise. 

Life itself demands time for hobbies, further study, travel and other pursuits, and school work must fit into that schedule. Students who need additional support, such as recent immigrants who must spend extra hours on homework, would find a shortened four‑year program detrimental. They may lack the time needed to study effectively, and the programme would not suit their circumstances. 

Teachers would also suffer. They would have less opportunity to design engaging lessons, to explain concepts clearly, and to provide follow‑up help when students do not understand material. Preparing new topics and grading assignments already consume considerable time, so reducing the overall schedule would leave them with little spare time. 

While a few institutions might experiment with a three‑year model, this approach is not widespread and does not address the core issue. An effective educational system should retain sufficient time for both academic and extracurricular activities and remain appealing to all learners.

The city council is considering a rule that would set a 10 p.m. curfew on weekdays and a midnight curfew on weekends for teenagers. If this rule is enacted, any teen found on the streets after those times would be violating the law. The question is whether such curfews actually protect young people from trouble, or whether they unjustly limit the freedom of youth.

Curfews are useful because they keep teenagers away from hazardous situations. After dark, it is harder to see what is happening around you, and the risk of accidents, assaults or kidnapping rises. A teen who is out late may wander into a dangerous area without realizing the danger, and the illusion that “it looks cool” can quickly turn into a real threat. Moreover, nighttime brings more drunk drivers onto the roads, increasing the chance of a serious collision. When police stop a teenager after curfew, they ask whether the teen’s parents are aware of the outing and where the teen is; if the teen cannot answer, the police will contact the parents, causing worry and possible trouble for the family.

The curfew also serves as a signal that parents should be trusted. When a young person respects the designated hours, it shows that the parents’ guidance is being followed, which can strengthen the parent‑child relationship. Parents naturally want their children to behave responsibly and avoid getting into serious trouble. By enforcing a clear limit, the law gives parents a concrete tool to monitor their children’s activities and to ensure that they are not sneaking out when they are supposed to be at home.

Teenagers often believe that meeting friends at night is exciting and “cool,” but the reality is that the potential consequences outweigh the temporary thrill. The risk of being caught breaking the law, the possibility of encountering unsafe individuals, and the chance of getting into a traffic accident make nighttime outings risky. While friends may seem supportive now, they may not be there later when the teen needs help. Choosing to stay within the curfew encourages teens to plan social activities during the day or to have sleepovers, which are safer and still allow them to enjoy time with peers.

In addition, the curfew promotes respect for authority and for the values that parents instill. When teens obey the set hours, they learn to consider the feelings of their parents and the broader community. This respect can translate into better behavior overall, reducing the likelihood of more serious misconduct such as vandalism, drug use, or theft.

Overall, the curfew is a practical measure that helps keep teenagers safe, maintains parental trust, and encourages responsible behavior. By staying home after the designated times, young people avoid the dangers of the night, reduce the chance of legal trouble, and show that they value the guidance of their parents. Rather than viewing the curfew as an unnecessary restriction, it should be seen as a protective measure that supports both youth and families.

The city councilhas introduced a curfew for teenagers, setting the cutoff time at 10 p.m. This rule is necessary because youths should not be wandering the streets after dark, especially on weekends when they are expected to be home and rested. Research shows that teens who follow a curfew tend to perform better in school, while those without such limits are more likely to break the law and struggle academically.  

When teenagers are allowed to stay out late, they are more prone to engage in risky behaviour, such as loitering on the streets, attending parties where trouble can arise, or even joining gang activities. A curfew keeps them inside after 10 p.m., reducing the chances that they will get into trouble or cause trouble for others.  

The police are tasked with enforcing the rule. If an officer sees a teenager on the street after the curfew, the youth can be taken into custody and the matter reported to the parents. This may seem harsh, but it serves a protective purpose: it prevents young people from being exposed to dangerous situations and gives parents peace of mind.  

Critics may argue that a curfew infringes on personal freedom, but the primary aim is safety, not control. By keeping teenagers at home during the night, the community helps them focus on their studies, stay out of trouble, and develop in a secure environment.  

In conclusion, the curfew adopted by the city council is a sensible measure. It limits the time teenagers can spend outside after dark, supports their academic performance, and reduces the likelihood of criminal behaviour. Therefore, the curfew should remain in place to protect the well‑being of our youth.
